Suing the Parent Instead

A distributor's contract with Sub Co has an exclusive Singapore clause. The distributor, wanting to avoid Singapore, sues only Sub Co's parent in Brazil, alleging the parent induced Sub Co's breaches, although Sub Co is the obvious defendant.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

The clause may not bind the parent as a non-party, but the Brazilian suit is a transparent bypass of the clause. Per Clearlake (in Asiana), it may be restrained as vexatious or oppressive on the non-contractual ASI ground (J6.5.2).

7J1.6 Existence, validity and governing law of the clause

Rule (Threshold and burden): Per Vinmar, the party relying on the clause must show a good arguable case that it exists and applies to the dispute, i.e. "the better of the argument": more than prima facie, less than a balance of probabilities, and not a "much better argument". The court may decide questions of law but will not resolve contested facts. Incorporation and service out: per C&Y, whether a clause was incorporated (e.g., by a course of dealing) is for its proper law. Where the clause founds service out, the claimant keeps that burden inter partes (J3.2).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Back-of-Invoice Clause

For three years, Sakura Chemicals KK sent Orchid Paints Pte Ltd invoices whose reverse side said "exclusive jurisdiction: Osaka District Court". Orchid never signed them. Orchid sues Sakura in Singapore, and Sakura seeks a stay. The parties' affidavits conflict on whether Orchid ever received the reverse sides.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Sakura must show the better of the argument that the clause was incorporated by course of dealing, under the clause's proper law (Japanese law, if proved; otherwise Singapore law by the presumption of similarity). The court will not resolve the conflicting affidavits on whether the reverse sides were received. It asks whether, on the material, Sakura has the better of the argument. Sakura need not show a "much better" argument.

  • Variation: If Orchid relied on a Singapore clause to serve Sakura out, Orchid would bear the good arguable case burden at the inter partes set-aside stage (J3.2).

Rule (Governing law of the clause): Per Shanghai Turbo (CA), a clause may in principle have its own law, but absent contrary provision it follows the main contract's proper law: an express choice for the contract implies the same choice for the clause. Only one party can have the better of the argument on the governing law, and the court applies that view throughout. Separability: per C&Y, separability is a matter of substantive contract law, so ask whether the clause's governing law recognises it. If the contract is voidable but unrescinded, the clause operates.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The PRC-Law JV

A JV agreement is expressly governed by PRC law and contains a Singapore NEJC. The claimant argues the clause should be construed under Singapore law (where the waiver applies); the defendant argues PRC law governs and implies no waiver.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Absent a separate choice for the clause, the express PRC-law choice for the contract carries over to the clause (Shanghai Turbo (CA)). Only one side can have the better of the argument, and the court applies that view consistently to construction and validity. If PRC law is then proved to imply no waiver, the defendant's objection is no breach and Spiliada applies (J1.1.2). On separability, ask whether PRC law recognises it. If the JV agreement is merely voidable and not yet rescinded, the clause operates in any event.

Rule (Attacking the contract, relying on the clause, ±): Per CIMB, where the parties dispute existence or validity (as opposed to agreeing there was no contract), the dispute is decided under the contract's clauses as if valid. Why: otherwise a mere allegation of fraud would neutralise the clause (CIMB, adopting The Parouth and Ash v Lloyd's). Infection test: per PT Selecta and CIMB, ask whether the vitiating factor also infects the clause. It does only where there was clearly no concluded contract at all, or non est factum. Fraud or duress in procuring the contract, or a common mistake as to subject matter (CIMB), does not touch consent to the clause. Application example: similar to PT Selecta, where the parties expressly brought disputes about the contract's "validity" within the clause (C&Y).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Phantom Bond Sale

Batik Bank Bhd (Malaysia) sells bonds to Raffles Treasury Pte Ltd under a contract with an exclusive Kuala Lumpur clause covering "any dispute as to the existence, validity or performance of this Agreement." Raffles sues in Singapore, claiming the contract was induced by fraudulent misrepresentation about the bonds' rating, and that both parties were mistaken about which bond series was being sold. Batik seeks a stay.

  • Variation: Raffles says its treasurer signed a document presented as a non-binding term sheet, not a contract.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Raffles disputes validity, but the parties do not agree that there was no contract, so per CIMB the dispute is decided under the clause as if the contract were valid. Otherwise a bare plea of fraud would neutralise every clause (The Parouth, Ash v Lloyd's). On the infection test, fraudulent misrepresentation about the rating goes to the bargain, not consent to the clause, and common mistake as to the subject matter likewise does not touch the clause (CIMB). As in PT Selecta, the clause expressly covers "validity" disputes. So Raffles is in breach and bears strong cause.

  • In the variation, Raffles pleads, in effect, non est factum or no concluded contract at all. If that is clearly made out, the vitiating factor reaches the clause itself, and the clause falls with the contract.

Rule (Forum mandatory rules, ±): A claimant may argue that a clause sending claims to a remote forum is overridden by a Singapore statute (C1.7). Per the Week 9 handout (outline only, so the application is argument): UCTA s 13(1) may catch an onerous forum clause as restricting a right or remedy, with no s 13(2) safe harbour of the kind that exists for arbitration. CPFTA s 35(1) voids terms ousting consumer protection for a consumer. COGSA s 3(1) gives the Hague-Visby Rules the force of law for the carriage contract.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Remote Forum
  1. A Singapore SME buys accounting software from a US vendor on standard terms requiring all claims to be brought exclusively in a small court in rural Montana. (The US is not a Contracting State.)
  2. A Singapore consumer buys a sofa online from a local retailer whose T&Cs send disputes exclusively to the courts of Vanuatu.
  3. A bill of lading for goods shipped from Singapore has an exclusive clause for a forum that would apply a lower liability limit than Hague-Visby.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  1. (±) The SME argues UCTA s 13(1): a remote, onerous forum clause effectively restricts its right or remedy, and unlike arbitration there is no s 13(2) safe harbour, so the clause is subject to the reasonableness test. The vendor replies that a forum clause regulates where a claim is heard, not the right itself.
  2. Under CPFTA s 35(1), a term that ousts the consumer's statutory protections is void, so the consumer argues the Vanuatu clause cannot oust the CPFTA claim.
  3. Under COGSA s 3(1), the Hague-Visby Rules have the force of law. A forum clause that would lead to a lower liability limit may be struck down to that extent as a way around the Rules.

8J1.7 Other effects of the agreement

Rule (Damages: England): Because an EJC contains a promise not to sue elsewhere, the innocent party may claim costs thrown away abroad or its liability under the foreign judgment. Per Starlight Shipping, breach is a question of law, so summary judgment for damages to be assessed is possible. Breach lies in suing: whether the claims would succeed abroad or fail in the chosen forum is irrelevant. Damages: Singapore (−): per Tradewaves (applying Sunrock Aircraft), damages "can", not "must", be awarded. Foreign costs should normally be sought in the foreign action, and the claimant must prove the "unusual features" in Union Discount v Zoller, e.g., foreign rules that allow costs only exceptionally and no foreign costs order.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Costs Thrown Away in Texas

Under a Singapore EJC, Vanda Software Pte Ltd's customer sues Vanda in Texas anyway. Vanda spends S$400,000 defending and wins on jurisdiction. The Texas court, following the American rule, makes no costs order. Vanda sues the customer in Singapore for damages for breach of the EJC.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

In England, Starlight Shipping would make breach a pure question of law (the breach lies in suing, regardless of the merits), so summary judgment for damages to be assessed would be possible. In Singapore, per Tradewaves (applying Sunrock), damages are available but not automatic. Vanda should normally seek costs in the foreign forum, but it can point to the Union Discount v Zoller "unusual features": Texas allows costs only exceptionally (the American rule) and made no costs order. So Vanda has a reasonable case for damages.

  • Variation: If the Texas court had made a costs order in Vanda's favour (even a partial one), Vanda's Singapore damages claim would be much weaker.

Rule (ASI): Breach of a Singapore EJC (arguably also of a Singapore NEJC, per Shanghai Turbo) is a contractual basis for an ASI. No vexation is needed, and the respondent must show strong reasons why it should not issue (Cooperative Muratori; J6.3.1). Foreign EJC (−): where the clause chooses a foreign court, Singapore generally declines to restrain suit in a third country and leaves it to the chosen court, not being an "international busybody" (Akai; J6.2.6).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Two ASI Requests
  • Request 1: Under a Singapore NEJC (the Shanghai Turbo pattern), the defendant, having been sued in Singapore, starts parallel proceedings in Vietnam. The Singapore claimant seeks an ASI.
  • Request 2: Under an exclusive English clause, a party sues in India. The other party asks Singapore (where it is based) for an ASI.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Request 1: Take one ASI per foreign proceeding (J6.0.1). Under a Singapore NEJC, suing in Vietnam is not ordinarily a breach, as the parties accepted parallel proceedings; only a challenge to Singapore's jurisdiction needs strong cause (Shanghai Turbo; J6.3.1.2). So the claimant must show the Vietnamese suit is vexatious or oppressive (J6.3.2), and parallel proceedings alone are not enough (UBS v Telesto). Had the defendant sought a Vietnamese ASI against the Singapore suit, that objection would arguably breach the clause, giving a contractual basis on which the defendant must show strong reasons why the ASI should not issue (Cooperative Muratori).
  • Request 2: Singapore will generally decline. The English court, as the chosen court, is the natural forum to restrain the Indian suit, and Singapore is not an "international busybody" (Akai).

Rule (Choice of law clause not promissory, −): Per Ace Insurance v Moose, a choice of law clause is usually declaratory, so an ASI against suit in a forum that would apply another law was refused. Only very clear words make such a clause promissory, which would bring damages, an ASI and a recognition defence (C2).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
"Singapore Law, Not Ruritanian Law"

A contract says: "This Agreement shall be governed by Singapore law." It contains no jurisdiction clause. One party sues in Ruritania, whose courts will apply Ruritanian law. The other seeks an ASI in Singapore, arguing that the choice of law clause was a promise not to have Ruritanian law applied.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Per Ace Insurance v Moose, a choice of law clause is ordinarily declaratory, not a promise about where to sue or which law a foreign court applies. The ASI is refused. Only very clear words (e.g., "neither party shall bring proceedings in any forum that will not apply Singapore law") would make the clause promissory.

Rule (Recognition defence, ±): Where a debtor resists enforcement of a foreign judgment obtained in breach of the clause, there is no common law authority, but per C&Y a defence is arguable: damages for breach could cancel out the judgment sum, REFJA s 5(4)(b) deems the foreign court to lack jurisdiction absent submission, and convergence with the statutes is desirable (Merck; J7.2.6). Limits: the debtor's submission in the foreign court removes the defence, and what matters is the breach, not whether Singapore or a foreign court was chosen. The CCAA does not prohibit recognising a non-chosen court's judgment under the common law or REFJA (C&Y; J7.5).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Default Judgment from Lagos

Under an exclusive Singapore clause, a Nigerian buyer sued a Singapore seller in Lagos. The seller ignored the Lagos proceedings entirely, and the buyer obtained a default judgment, which it now seeks to enforce in Singapore at common law.

  • Variation: the seller had appeared in Lagos and defended on the merits.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

(±) The seller argues for a breach-of-clause defence. There is no common law authority, but C&Y say it is arguable: the seller's counterclaim for damages for breach would equal the judgment sum, REFJA s 5(4)(b) deems a court that sat in breach of a jurisdiction agreement to lack jurisdiction absent submission, and the common law should converge with the statutes (Merck). The CCAA does not prevent recognition of non-chosen courts' judgments under the common law or REFJA, so the argument has to come from these sources, not the CCAA.

  • In the variation, the seller submitted by defending on the merits, so the defence is gone (J7.2).

Rule (Other agreements, not examinable): A stay for breach of an international arbitration agreement is mandatory (s 6 IAA). For domestic arbitration or mediation it is discretionary (s 6 Arbitration Act; s 8 Mediation Act, "may").

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Arbitrate or Mediate First

Contract 1 has an SIAC clause in an international sale. Contract 2 has a domestic arbitration clause between two Singapore firms. Contract 3 has a "mediate before suing" clause. In each case one party sues in court.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

In Contract 1 the stay is mandatory (s 6 IAA). In Contracts 2 and 3 the court has a discretion (s 6 Arbitration Act; s 8 Mediation Act: "may"). (Not examinable, but useful for contrast.)

Rule (Non-suit or settlement agreement): "Settled; no further action in any court" is not a jurisdiction clause but a substantive accord and satisfaction defence. Proceedings in breach may be stayed or struck out as an abuse, and an ASI or damages are also possible.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Settled Dispute Revived

Two companies settle a dispute: "Full and final settlement; neither party shall bring any further action in any court in respect of the Shipment." Six months later one sues in Singapore, and the other sues in Korea.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

The settlement clause is not a choice of court agreement, so it does not go to jurisdiction or strong cause. It is a substantive defence of accord and satisfaction. The Singapore action may be stayed or struck out as an abuse, and the Korean action may be restrained by an ASI (breach of a promise not to sue), with damages for breach also available.

LAW302 · HYPO LESSON J2 · 38 HYPOTHETICALS · 5 FLOWCHARTS · 8 QUESTIONS

J2 hypotheticals: Existence when the defendant is in Singapore: service in and submission

The rules behind these hypotheticals are taught in Lesson J2, where the word-for-word pre-write is too. Do that lesson first if the rules below look unfamiliar.

Applications:
ℹ HOW TO USE THESE HYPOTHETICALS

Each concept is set out as Rule, then Hypothetical, then Application. "Variation" lines flip one fact. Exercise (Spiliada) is in J4; jurisdiction clauses are triaged in J1.

The flowcharts redraw the hypotheticals in this site's chart style: the chip on each arrow names the hypothetical (or version) that takes that path. The hypo test at the end checks you can run the facts yourself.

1J2.0 Preliminary concepts and statutory framework

J2.0(a) Existence Before Exercise

Rule: Ask (1) whether the court has jurisdiction over the defendant (s 16(1) SCJA), then (2) whether it should exercise it (J4). Per C&Y, existence comes first: presence on a fleeting visit founds jurisdiction, and the weak connection goes only to a stay. Presence and submission found jurisdiction as of right, but O 7 r 4 service on an agent and O 8 r 1(1) service out need permission. Jurisdiction may arise in the General Division, the SICC (J5) or under the CCAA (J1.2–J1.4), so run the router first (J1.0.2).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Layover

Klaus, a German engineer, is changing planes at Changi on a 9-hour layover and takes a taxi to Marina Bay for dinner. Process servers for Austral Mining Pte Ltd personally serve him with an originating claim at the restaurant. The claim concerns a mine collapse in Western Australia. There is no jurisdiction agreement.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

No jurisdiction agreement is in issue, so the CCAA and SICC routes are irrelevant and the General Division's common law rules apply. Existence: Klaus was personally served while physically present, so jurisdiction exists as of right under s 16(1)(a)(i) with O 7 r 2(1)(a), and no permission was needed. Exercise: the 9-hour connection and the Australian events do not undermine existence. They go to whether Singapore should exercise jurisdiction, so Klaus applies for a Spiliada stay (J4.1), where they weigh heavily in his favour.

J2.0(b) Statutory Source: s 16 SCJA and Allenger

Rule: Per Art 93 Constitution and Allenger, the General Division is a creature of statute. The defendant must be served in Singapore (s 16(1)(a)(i)), served outside Singapore as the Rules authorise (s 16(1)(a)(ii)), or submit (s 16(1)(b)), or fall within other written law (ss 16(2), 17(1)(c), e.g., ss 387, 376 CA).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
"The Court's Inherent Jurisdiction"

A claimant cannot serve a Thai defendant in Singapore and has not applied to serve out. It argues the High Court has "inherent jurisdiction" to hear the case because the claim is important to Singapore's financial sector.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Per Allenger, the General Division's in personam jurisdiction comes only from statute (Art 93; s 16 SCJA). With no service in, no authorised service out, no submission and no other written law, there is no jurisdiction, whatever the case's importance. The claimant must apply under O 8 r 1 to serve out (J3).

J2.0(c) Service Founds Jurisdiction; Pair the Provision With the Mode

Rule: Service both gives notice and founds jurisdiction, so even a submitting defendant must be served (O 6 r 4), whether personally or in an agreed manner (O 7 r 2(1)(d)). Must write: state the founding provision (s 16(1)(a)(i) / ss 16(2), 17(1)(c) / s 16(1)(a)(ii) / s 16(1)(b)) together with the mode of service (O 7 r 2(1)(a) / r 2(1)(b) / r 4 / s 387 CA / s 376 CA / O 8 r 1). Only s 16(1)(a)(i) needs Adams v Cape presence for a foreign company (J2.1.5).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Willing Defendant

Bao, who lives in Vietnam, emails the claimant: "I'm happy for the Singapore court to decide this. No need to serve me." The claimant files a claim and does nothing else, and Bao later ignores the proceedings.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Bao's willingness may be relevant to submission, but service is still required (O 6 r 4): service founds jurisdiction and gives notice. The claimant should agree a mode of service with Bao (O 7 r 2(1)(d)) or serve out under O 8. Then pair provision and mode in the answer, e.g., "s 16(1)(a)(i) via O 7 r 2(1)(d) agreed service on Bao's Singapore solicitors", or "s 16(1)(a)(ii) via O 8 r 1".

J2.0(d) Why Serve In

Rule: Per Zoom, after service in, the defendant bears the burden on a stay. On service out, the claimant bears it if the defendant challenges existence on forum grounds (J4.0.2).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Shareholder's Short Visit

Shareholder A wants to sue director B, who lives in Hong Kong, for breach of duty to a Hong Kong company. B is flying into Singapore next week for a conference.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Tactically, A should serve B personally while he is in Singapore (s 16(1)(a)(i)). B must then show that Hong Kong is clearly more appropriate (Spiliada stage 1 on a stay). If A waits and serves B in Hong Kong, A must show Singapore is forum conveniens when B applies to set aside service (J3.2; J4.2), which is a harder burden for A.

J2.0(e) Subject-Matter Jurisdiction (not examinable, one line)

Rule: Per Chong (seminar), subject-matter jurisdiction is off-syllabus except for the SICC (J5.1). If the defendant says the claim is non-justiciable, one line suffices: per Allenger, s 16(1) limits only in personam jurisdiction, and the court may hear any claim "unless or until prohibited either by legislation or case law", e.g., title to foreign land, or foreign penal, revenue or public law.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Bali Villa Title

A claimant serves the defendant in Singapore and asks the court to declare that the claimant owns a villa in Bali.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

One line only: in personam jurisdiction exists through service in, but per Allenger the court hears any claim unless prohibited by legislation or case law, and a claim to title to foreign land is such a case-law prohibition. Do not develop it further; it is off-syllabus.

J2.0(f) Jurisdiction vs Power

Rule: Jurisdiction (ss 16–17) is the authority to hear the claim. Per Li Shengwu, s 18 and Sch 1 concern powers and reliefs, not subject-matter jurisdiction, e.g., the power to stay under para 9 (J4.1).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
"Sch 1 Gives You Jurisdiction"

A claimant argues that because Sch 1 SCJA gives the court power to grant injunctions, the court has jurisdiction over a foreign defendant who has not been served.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Per Li Shengwu, s 18 and Sch 1 confer powers (what relief the court may grant once it has jurisdiction). They are not a source of jurisdiction. Jurisdiction must be found under ss 16–17 first. Para 9 is the power to stay, which is exercised after jurisdiction exists.

J2.0(g) Inherent Power to Prevent Abuse

Rule: Per Emilia Shipping, it is arguable that the court's inherent power to prevent abuse (now O 3 r 2(2)), e.g., where the defendant was fraudulently lured to Singapore or property was deceptively brought here, is unaffected by s 16.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Yacht Brought In by a Trick

The claimant's agent tells the owner of a superyacht that a buyer wants to inspect it in Singapore. The owner sails it in, and the claimant immediately arrests it in a claim with no other Singapore connection.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Even if the statutory requirements for jurisdiction are met, the owner can argue that the court's inherent power to prevent abuse of process (O 3 r 2(2)) survives s 16 (Emilia Shipping). The court may set aside or stay proceedings founded on property deceptively brought into the jurisdiction.

2J2.1 Service in Singapore (s 16(1)(a)(i) SCJA)

J2.1.1 Natural Person Physically Present

Rule (Basis and mode): Per s 16(1)(a)(i) SCJA, a defendant present in Singapore (at a hotel, at a trade fair) may be personally served as of right under O 7 r 2(1)(a). Presence is judged at the time of service, so it does not matter that he arrived that morning or left the next day. Temporary presence (+): per Maharanee of Baroda v Wildenstein and Colt Industries v Sarlie, presence on a short visit or in transit suffices without any substantive connection, even if the contract or accident arose wholly abroad.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Racecourse Service

Priya, an Indian art dealer, sold a painting to a French collector in Paris. The painting was later said to be a forgery. Priya flies to Singapore for one afternoon to attend the Singapore Gold Cup. The collector's process server hands her the claim in the members' enclosure, and she flies home that night.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Like Wildenstein, served at Ascot (Maharanee of Baroda v Wildenstein; Colt Industries v Sarlie), Priya was physically present when served, so jurisdiction exists as of right under s 16(1)(a)(i) and O 7 r 2(1)(a). It does not matter that the sale took place wholly in Paris, or that she arrived and left the same day; presence is judged at the moment of service.

Rule (Fraudulently induced presence, −): Per Watkins v North American Land, service may be set aside for abuse of process where the claimant lured the defendant to Singapore with, for example, a sham meeting. It will not be set aside where the defendant came for business or a holiday.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Fake Investor Meeting
  • Version 1: The collector (above) arranges, through a front company, a "meeting with an investor" in Singapore to get Priya to fly in, then serves her at the hotel lobby. There is no investor.
  • Version 2: Priya comes to Singapore on holiday, and the collector, learning of it on Instagram, serves her at Sentosa.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Version 1: The presence was fraudulently induced, so service may be set aside as an abuse of process (Watkins; see also the inherent power in J2.0(g)).
  • Version 2: The claimant merely took advantage of a voluntary holiday visit. There was no inducement, so service stands. Any unfairness goes to a stay.

Rule (Fortuity goes to exercise, ±): Per C&Y, the defendant's weak connection is irrelevant to existence but relevant to the natural forum, so a fleeting visit and foreign events support a stay (J4.1). Evaluation (±): a defendant may call jurisdiction based on a short visit arbitrary, preferring residence, domicile or nationality. But per Sirdar Gurdyal Singh, jurisdiction is territorial. Presence is also certain where residence is harder to prove, and per Chong (seminar), FNC corrects the fortuity at the exercise stage.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
"Unfair and Arbitrary"

In Version 2 above, Priya argues in an essay-style question that jurisdiction based on a holiday is arbitrary and should be replaced by a domicile test.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

(−) Priya's critique: tag jurisdiction depends on chance, not on any connection with the dispute, and invites opportunistic service. (+) Response: per Sirdar Gurdyal Singh, jurisdiction is territorial, so a person within the territory is subject to its courts. Presence is easy to prove (it is a bright line), whereas domicile or residence is harder to establish. Any arbitrariness is corrected at the exercise stage: Priya will likely obtain a Spiliada stay because Paris is clearly more appropriate (J4.1). As Chong put it, FNC corrects the fortuity.

J2.1.2 Agent of an Absent Natural Person (O 7 r 4)

Rule (Requirements): With permission on a without-notice summons, an agent may be served on behalf of the defendant if:

  • (a) the defendant does not reside in, or is absent from, Singapore;
  • (b) at the time of service the agent personally controls or manages here the defendant's affairs specifically relating to the action; and
  • (c) the agent's authority subsists or there is an ongoing business relationship.

Founding provision and formalities: per Beranek, O 7 r 4 rests on s 16(1)(a)(i), the defendant being constructively present through the agent (J3.0.2). Per C&Y, the claimant must also post the order and the claim to the defendant's address abroad within 14 days. Control or management: the agent must actually control the affairs sued on, not merely relay messages. Rosenberg's power-to-contract test is framed for companies (J2.1.5), but per C&Y "affairs" reaches any affairs of an individual.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Property Manager

Mr Tanaka lives in Osaka and owns three Singapore condominium units. His Singapore property manager, Wendy, signs leases, collects rent, instructs contractors and decides on repairs without consulting him. A tenant is injured when a balcony railing that Wendy had refused to fix gives way, and the tenant sues Mr Tanaka.

  • Variation: Wendy is only Mr Tanaka's cousin, who forwards his emails to tenants and passes their complaints on to him in Japan.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

The claimant applies without notice for permission. (a) Mr Tanaka resides abroad. (b) Wendy personally manages, here, the very affairs that the action concerns (maintenance of the units). (c) Her authority subsists. Per Beranek, jurisdiction rests on s 16(1)(a)(i), Mr Tanaka being constructively present through Wendy. The claimant must post the order and the claim to Mr Tanaka's Osaka address within 14 days.

  • In the variation, the cousin only relays messages and does not control or manage the affairs, so O 7 r 4 fails and the claimant must serve out (J3).

Rule (Exceptional, −): Per C&Y, under the old O 10 r 2 its use against an overseas individual was a "rare case", and the English Practice Direction required "great caution", refusing it where the claimant could easily serve out. Liberalised (+): per C&Y, "affairs" replaced "business or work", O 8 has liberalised service out, and permission is needed anyway, so O 7 r 4 now applies more readily. Service out available? (±): the defendant may argue permission should be refused because the claimant could serve out under O 8. Per C&Y, O 7 r 4 is not meant to make O 8 otiose, but it is unclear that permission should be withheld as a matter of course.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
"Just Serve Me in Japan"

In the main Tanaka scenario, Mr Tanaka argues that permission should be refused: the claimant could easily serve him in Osaka under O 8, and English practice treated agent service as a "rare case" requiring "great caution".

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

(−) Mr Tanaka relies on the old O 10 r 2 approach and the English Practice Direction. (+) The claimant replies (C&Y) that the rule has been liberalised: "affairs" now replaces "business or work", O 8 itself has been liberalised, and the court's permission is a safeguard in any case. O 7 r 4 is not meant to make O 8 otiose, but there is no rule that permission is withheld as a matter of course just because service out is available. On these facts, with Wendy managing the very affairs in issue, permission is likely.

J2.1.3 Company Incorporated in Singapore

Rule: Per ss 16(2), 17(1)(c) SCJA, service of the originating claim under s 387 CA (leaving it at, or sending it by registered post to, the registered office) founds jurisdiction, so Adams v Cape need not be discussed. Per Chong (seminar), in the exam simply state this pathway; the academic argument that presence or submission is still needed is not covered.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Dormant Shell

Orchid Holdings Pte Ltd is a Singapore company with no employees or operations here; it is run from Jakarta. The claimant sends the claim by registered post to its registered office at a corporate secretarial firm's address.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Jurisdiction is founded on ss 16(2), 17(1)(c) SCJA with service under s 387 CA. There is no need to show that Orchid "carries on business" in Singapore under Adams v Cape. That Orchid is run from Jakarta may support a stay (J4.1), but it does not affect existence.

J2.1.4 Registered Foreign Company (s 376 CA)

Rule (Registrability, ss 365, 368): Per s 365, a foreign company that establishes a place of business, or carries on business, in Singapore, or intends to, must register under s 368 first, lodging its Singapore registered office and its authorised representative. Carrying on business (s 366): per s 366(1), business includes administering property as agent or trustee. Per s 366(2), it excludes merely litigating, holding internal meetings, maintaining a bank account, making sales through independent contractors, accepting orders abroad, an isolated transaction completed within 31 days, or holding property.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
What Counts as Business?

Consider five foreign companies:

  1. Kiwi Dairy Ltd has a Singapore bank account and holds board meetings at a Singapore hotel twice a year.
  2. Alpine Watches AG sells into Singapore only through an independent distributor and accepts all orders in Geneva.
  3. Nordic Trust AS administers Singapore properties as trustee for Norwegian pension funds.
  4. Rio Coffee Ltda completed one coffee sale here over 20 days.
  5. Thames Advisory Ltd leases an office on Robinson Road with six staff advising clients.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

(1), (2) and (4) are excluded from "carrying on business" by s 366(2) (bank account and internal meetings; independent-contractor sales and orders accepted abroad; an isolated transaction within 31 days). (3) is business by s 366(1) (administering property as trustee). (5) is plainly carrying on business, so Thames must register under s 368. Only (3) and (5) are registrable.

Rule (Scenario A, registered and trading, +): Per ss 16(2), 17(1)(c), the company is served under s 376(a) (its Singapore registered office) or s 376(b) (its authorised representative's residential or contact address), without Adams v Cape. Scenario B (ceased business, not deregistered, +): per s 376(c), a company that "has ceased to maintain a place of business in Singapore" is served at its registered office abroad, or under (a)–(b) if the Singapore office or representative remains. Scenario C (ceased and deregistered, −): per Tao Commodity, s 376 is unavailable after deregistration, registration having supplied the nexus, so the claimant must serve out (J3.1). Scenario C reply (+): per C&Y, the plain words of s 376(c) cover the deregistered company, ceasing business being the precursor to deregistration, and the purpose is that companies that traded here cannot escape local creditors. Tao is a Registry decision not reviewed by the CA.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Thames Advisory's Three Lives

Thames Advisory Ltd (England) registers under s 368 in 2019. A Singapore client sues it for negligent advice.

  • Scenario A (2022): Thames is still trading from Robinson Road.
  • Scenario B (2024): Thames closed the Robinson Road office in 2023 but is still on the ACRA register. Its authorised representative still lives in Singapore.
  • Scenario C (2026): Thames closed the office in 2023 and was deregistered in 2025. The client sues for advice given in 2022.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • A: Serve at the registered office (s 376(a)) or on the authorised representative (s 376(b)). Jurisdiction follows via ss 16(2), 17(1)(c), and there is no need for Adams v Cape.
  • B: Thames "has ceased to maintain a place of business in Singapore", so s 376(c) allows service at its registered office in England. Because the representative remains, s 376(b) is also available.
  • C (±): (−) Thames relies on Tao Commodity: once deregistered, the nexus supplied by registration is gone, so s 376 is unavailable and the client must serve out under O 8 (J3.1). (+) The client replies (C&Y) that s 376(c) on its plain words covers a company that has ceased business, which is the normal precursor to deregistration; its purpose is to stop companies that traded here escaping local creditors; and Tao is only a Registry decision. A prudent client also applies to serve out in the alternative.

Rule (Does s 376 confer jurisdiction? ±): Route 1 (C&Y, run this): s 376 itself confers jurisdiction via ss 16(2), 17(1)(c), to spare local creditors from having to serve out. Route 2 (Tao): registration is "a statutory parallel to or substitute for" corporate presence, and s 376 is only the mode of service. Both routes cover Scenarios A–B, but only Route 1 survives deregistration.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Same Facts, Different Theory

In Scenario C above, the judge asks counsel: "Is s 376 a source of jurisdiction, or merely a mode of service?"

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Counsel for the client runs Route 1: s 376 is "other written law" under ss 16(2), 17(1)(c) and itself confers jurisdiction, so it applies whenever its words apply, including after deregistration. Counsel for Thames runs Route 2 (Tao): registration substitutes for presence, so once Thames is deregistered there is nothing for s 376 to serve into. The answer decides Scenario C, though it makes no difference in A and B.

J2.1.5 Never-Registered Foreign Company

Rule (s 376 unavailable, must write): Although Division 2 applies to a registrable but unregistered company (s 365), per C&Y s 376(a)–(b) fail because there is no Singapore office or representative, and (c), read holistically, is not meant for a company still trading here. So the claimant relies on s 16(1)(a)(i) and must prove presence.

Rule (Adams v Cape limbs):

  • Limb 1 (fixed place): the company carries on business at or from a reasonably permanent fixed place, e.g., its office, whether it owns, leases or licenses it. Per Littauer Glove, a representative taking orders from a hotel for a few days is not enough.
  • Limb 2 (more than a minimal period): per Dunlop v Cudell, a nine-day trade-fair stand sufficed, unlike a one-day visit.
  • Limb 3 (whose business?): where the company acts through a representative, it is present only if the representative carries on the company's business, not his own (Okura). This is shown by premises acquired for him, fixed pay versus commission, and the degree of control.
  • Power to contract (±): per Adams v Cape, the key question is whether the representative can bind the company without prior approval. Per C&Y, that power is neither exclusive nor conclusive, and the agent may also run his own business from the same place.
  • Non-trading company: per Adams v Cape, for a charity or holding company, substitute its corporate activities for "business".
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Unregistered Tech Start-Up

Kangaroo AI Pty Ltd (Australia) never registered in Singapore, but:

  • Facts 1: It rents a desk in a WeWork in Tanjong Pagar on a 12-month licence, with two salaried employees who sign customer contracts up to A$500,000 without head-office approval.
  • Facts 2: Its sales director flew in for three days and took orders from his Marina Bay Sands hotel room.
  • Facts 3: It had a booth at the 10-day Singapore FinTech Festival.
  • Facts 4: It uses an independent Singapore consultant, Raj, on commission. Raj works from his own office, also represents three other companies, and must send every deal to Sydney for approval.
  • Facts 5: Kangaroo AI's parent is a holding company that holds its board meetings in Singapore at a permanently leased boardroom.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

s 376 is unavailable (there is no registered office or representative, and Kangaroo AI is not a company that has ceased business), so the claimant must prove presence under Adams v Cape for s 16(1)(a)(i).

  • Facts 1: Present. There is a reasonably permanent fixed place (a licence suffices; ownership is not needed), for more than a minimal period, and the employees carry on Kangaroo's business (salaried, under its control) and can bind it without prior approval.
  • Facts 2: Not present. Like Littauer Glove, taking orders from a hotel for a few days is not a fixed place for more than a minimal period.
  • Facts 3: Arguably present. Like Dunlop v Cudell's nine-day trade-fair stand, a 10-day booth is a fixed place for more than a minimal period.
  • Facts 4: Not present. Per Okura, Raj carries on his own business (commission, own office, multiple principals), and he cannot contract without approval. Per C&Y, power to contract is neither exclusive nor conclusive, but every indicator here points the same way.
  • Facts 5: Not present. The parent is a separate company, so its boardroom is not Kangaroo AI's place of business. Only if the claimant sued the holding company itself would Adams v Cape's substitution of "corporate activities" for business apply, and then regular board meetings at a permanent boardroom may suffice (Adams v Cape).

Rule (Mode 1, officer, O 7 r 2(1)(b), as of right): If the company is present, the claimant leaves the claim with its chairperson, president, secretary, treasurer or other officer. Per Yeo and Beranek (J3.0.2), it is the company's own presence that counts, so serving an officer on holiday when the company itself is absent is doubtful (contra COSCO; B Atmaram).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The CEO on Holiday
  • Version 1: Kangaroo AI is present (Facts 1). The claimant serves its CFO at the WeWork desk.
  • Version 2: Kangaroo AI has no Singapore presence at all, but its CEO is on holiday at Sentosa and is handed the claim.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Version 1: The company is present, so service on an officer under O 7 r 2(1)(b) is good, as of right.
  • Version 2 (±): (−) Per Yeo and Beranek, the company's own presence is what founds jurisdiction under s 16(1)(a)(i), and an officer's personal presence does not make the company present. (+) The claimant relies on COSCO and B Atmaram, which accepted service on an officer. Flag that this is doubtful; the safer course is to serve out.

Rule (Mode 2, agent, O 7 r 4, with permission): Per Rosenberg, the agent must be obliged to bring the claim to the company's notice, the company must carry on business at a fixed place here, and the agent must have power to contract; otherwise the company trades "through", not "by", him. Per C&Y, the agent need not be a full-time employee. Link to the action (−): per Rosenberg, the action must relate to the business the agent manages. Where the cheques were drawn by the head office abroad and the agent could do only liaison work, service is set aside and the claimant must serve out. Narrower than Adams v Cape: per C&Y, r 4 needs power to contract, control of affairs specifically relating to the action, and permission, none of which Adams v Cape requires. So a claimant prefers r 2(1)(b) and pleads presence alongside.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Liaison Office and the Bounced Cheques

Paris Bijoux SA has a Singapore liaison office with a part-time manager, Mei, who meets customers and forwards their orders to Paris but cannot sign contracts. A Singapore retailer sues Paris Bijoux over cheques drawn by the Paris head office that bounced. The retailer obtains permission to serve Mei under O 7 r 4.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Per Rosenberg, O 7 r 4 fails on two grounds. (i) Mei has no power to contract, so Paris Bijoux trades "through" her rather than "by" her. That she is part-time is not itself fatal (C&Y). (ii) The action (cheques drawn in Paris) does not relate to the business Mei manages, which is liaison only. Service is set aside, and the retailer must serve out (J3). Lesson: O 7 r 4 is narrower than Adams v Cape, so a claimant should plead presence and serve an officer under r 2(1)(b) where it can.

Rule (Unregistrable, no place of business, −): Where the company merely holds a bank account or accepts orders abroad (s 366(2)), or sells online from abroad (there is no virtual presence: Lucasfilm, by analogy), neither s 376 nor Adams v Cape applies. The claimant serves out (J3.1), unless an agent here satisfies O 7 r 4 or Singapore solicitors accept service (J2.2.2).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Online Sneaker Store

SoleKicks LLC (Delaware) sells limited-edition sneakers to Singapore buyers through its website and ships them from Oregon. A buyer receives fakes and sues.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

SoleKicks has no place of business in Singapore. A website is not a "virtual presence" (Lucasfilm, by analogy), and accepting orders abroad is excluded from business by s 366(2). So s 376 does not apply and Adams v Cape is not satisfied. The buyer must serve out under O 8 (J3.1), unless SoleKicks has a Singapore agent who meets O 7 r 4, or it instructs Singapore solicitors to accept service.

J2.1.6 Partnerships and LLPs

Rule:

  • Firm name (O 56 r 1): the claimant may sue a partnership or limited partnership in its firm name if the partners carry on business in Singapore. Per C&Y, this gives no in personam jurisdiction, so each partner to be made liable must be served or submit.
  • Mode of service (O 56 r 3(1)): serve any partner, or the person controlling the business at the principal place of business. If the firm is dissolved, serve every partner in Singapore.
  • Sole trader (O 56 r 9, −): per C&Y, r 9 does not reach a non-resident foreign individual trading here through an agent; otherwise he would be worse off than a foreign partnership, with all his Singapore assets exposed.
  • LLP: per C&Y, an LLP is a body corporate served at its registered office under LLP Act s 93 (by analogy with s 387 CA), which should found jurisdiction since s 17 SCJA is not exhaustive.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Architects, the Sole Trader and the LLP
  1. Lim & Partners, an architecture partnership with offices in Singapore, designed a leaky roof. Partner A lives in Singapore; Partner B has emigrated to Canada. The client sues "Lim & Partners" and serves the office manager at the principal place of business.
  2. The firm has since been dissolved.
  3. Ahmad, a Malaysian resident, trades in Singapore as "Ahmad Interiors" through a local agent. The client sues "Ahmad Interiors" under O 56 r 9 and serves the agent.
  4. Design Collective LLP is a Singapore LLP.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  1. Suing in the firm name is permitted because the partners carry on business here (O 56 r 1), and service on the person controlling the business at the principal place of business is good (O 56 r 3(1)). But per C&Y, that gives no in personam jurisdiction over Partner B personally. To make B liable, the client must serve B (out of jurisdiction, J3) or show that B submitted.
  2. If the firm is dissolved, every partner in Singapore must be served (O 56 r 3(1)).
  3. Per C&Y, O 56 r 9 does not reach a non-resident foreign individual trading here through an agent. The client must use O 7 r 4 (agent) with permission, or serve out.
  4. Serve the LLP at its registered office under LLP Act s 93. By analogy with s 387 CA, this should found jurisdiction, since s 17 SCJA is not exhaustive.

J2.1.7 Router Drill: Pair Status, Founding Provision and Mode

Rule summary:

  • Individual present here → s 16(1)(a)(i) + O 7 r 2(1)(a). Individual abroad with an agent here → O 7 r 4 (permission). Otherwise → serve out.
  • Singapore company → ss 16(2), 17(1)(c) + s 387.
  • Registered and trading → ss 16(2), 17(1)(c) + s 376(a)/(b).
  • Registered, ceased, not deregistered → s 376(c) at the registered office abroad, or (a)–(b).
  • Registered, ceased, deregistered → s 376(c), arguing against Tao; otherwise serve out.
  • Registrable, never registered (s 365(a)), with a place of business here → s 16(1)(a)(i) + Adams v Cape, then O 7 r 2(1)(b) on an officer, or r 4.
  • Intends only (s 365(b)), or not registrable → serve out, unless an agent satisfies O 7 r 4.
  • Partnership → firm name under O 56 r 1 if the partners carry on business here, plus jurisdiction over each partner sued.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Seven Defendants

A fraud victim, Victoria, wants to sue seven defendants:

  1. Dmitri, a Russian individual who is attending a conference in Singapore this week.
  2. Dmitri's sister Olga, in Moscow, whose Singapore lawyer-turned-manager runs her Singapore investments, including the one in issue.
  3. Volga Pte Ltd, a Singapore company.
  4. Volga Trading AG (Swiss), registered under s 368 and trading from Raffles Place.
  5. Volga Shipping SA (Panama), registered, ceased business in Singapore in 2024 but not deregistered.
  6. Volga Logistics BV (Netherlands), which has an unregistered warehouse office in Jurong with staff.
  7. Volga Media Ltd (Cyprus), which only plans to open a Singapore office next year.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  1. s 16(1)(a)(i) + O 7 r 2(1)(a), personal service as of right this week.
  2. O 7 r 4 with permission: Olga is absent, and the manager personally manages her affairs relating to the action (rests on s 16(1)(a)(i), Beranek). Post the order and the claim to Moscow within 14 days.
  3. ss 16(2), 17(1)(c) + s 387 (registered office).
  4. ss 16(2), 17(1)(c) + s 376(a) or (b).
  5. s 376(c) at its registered office in Panama, or (a)–(b) if a Singapore office or representative remains.
  6. s 16(1)(a)(i): prove Adams v Cape presence (a fixed place, more than a minimal period, its own business), then O 7 r 2(1)(b) on an officer, or O 7 r 4.
  7. Intending to set up only (s 365(b)), so there is no presence. Serve out under O 8 (J3).

3J2.2 Submission (s 16(1)(b) SCJA)

J2.2.1 Starter and Framework

Rule (Starter): The claimant argues that the defendant submitted by some act under s 16(1)(b) SCJA, usually to cure irregular service or a jurisdictional objection, though the originating claim must still be served (O 6 r 4). Per Allenger, submission was added to s 16 in 1993.

Rule (Two levels of jurisdiction): Per Williams & Glyn's, a defendant contesting jurisdiction submits only to the court's jurisdiction to decide jurisdiction, not to its jurisdiction over the merits. Contesting service, or seeking a stay pending foreign proceedings, while "vigorously protesting" is not submission.

Rule (The test): Per Zoom (adopting Williams), submission requires a step that is "only necessary or only useful" if the objection had been waived or never entertained. Per C&Y (Spamhaus), it is a clear and unequivocal step incompatible with the position that there is no jurisdiction. It is a question of fact based on the defendant's conduct as a whole.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Defendant Who Turned Up

Sunrise Resorts Ltd (Maldives) is served in the Maldives without permission, so service is irregular. Through Singapore counsel it: (1) files an application to set aside service, "vigorously protesting" jurisdiction; (2) files an affidavit explaining why the Maldives is the right forum; and (3) attends the hearing of the set-aside application.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

By applying to set aside service, Sunrise invokes only the court's jurisdiction to decide jurisdiction (Williams & Glyn's), so it has not submitted to the merits jurisdiction. None of steps (1)–(3) is "only necessary or only useful" if the objection had been waived (Zoom). Each is consistent with contesting jurisdiction, and none is a clear and unequivocal step incompatible with the objection (Spamhaus). There is no submission, and the irregular service is not cured.

Rule (Scope and effect): Per C&Y, submission cures irregular service but cannot confer subject-matter jurisdiction (J2.0.2). Per Williams and Glencore, a foreign defendant may limit its submission claim by claim, unlike a claimant. Submission vs agreement to submit: per C&Y, a Singapore jurisdiction clause is a promise to submit, enforced by service out under O 8 r 1(3) or para 63(3)(d)(iv), (r) (J3), or by strong cause (J4.3). It is not submission by conduct.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Partial Defence and the Clause

A Korean defendant is sued in Singapore on two claims: (A) breach of a supply contract, and (B) infringement of a Singapore trade mark. It files a merits defence to claim A only, expressly stating that it contests jurisdiction over claim B. The supply contract also contains a Singapore NEJC.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

The defendant has submitted on claim A. A defendant may limit submission claim by claim (Williams; Glencore), so the reservation on claim B is effective. Submission on claim A also cures any irregularity in service for claim A. As for the clause: it is an agreement to submit, not submission by conduct. It matters because it gives a gateway for service out (O 8 r 1(3); para 63(3)(d)(iv), (r)) and puts strong cause on the defendant if it objects (J1.1.1; J4.3). It does not by itself make the defendant someone who "has submitted" under s 16(1)(b).

J2.2.2 Acts Amounting to Submission (+)

Rule (Defence on the merits / striking out): Per C&Y (Spamhaus), filing a merits defence or a striking-out application without protest is submission, and raising an EJC in a summary judgment affidavit is no protest.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Strike-Out First

A Hong Kong defendant served in Singapore files an application to strike out the claim as disclosing no reasonable cause of action, without any reservation. Two months later it applies to set aside service. Separately, in its affidavit resisting summary judgment, it mentions that "the contract contains a Hong Kong exclusive jurisdiction clause."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

A striking-out application asks the court to decide the merits (or at least the claim's viability), which is useful only if jurisdiction is accepted. Made without protest, it is submission (Spamhaus, C&Y). Mentioning the EJC in a summary judgment affidavit is not a protest against jurisdiction, so it does not save the defendant. Its later set-aside application fails.

Rule (Stay sought alone, ±): Per Zoom (The Jian He; Chan Chin Cheung), an FNC stay sought without contesting existence ordinarily is submission at common law, as the defendant accepts that jurisdiction exists. But per O 6 rr 7(6), 12(5), a defence or affidavit stating an exercise challenge is not submission (J2.2.4).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Stay-Only Application

A Malaysian defendant validly served in Singapore files an affidavit stating that "the court should not exercise jurisdiction because Malaysia is the natural forum", then applies only for a Spiliada stay, without challenging existence.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

(+) The claimant argues that at common law, per Zoom (following The Jian He and Chan Chin Cheung), a stay application alone accepts that jurisdiction exists and is submission. (−) The defendant relies on O 6 r 12(5) (and r 7(6)): an affidavit stating that the court should not exercise jurisdiction is not submission. Whether that protection extends beyond the filing to arguing the stay in court is the ROC 2021 uncertainty in J2.2.4.

Rule (Substantive relief in a jurisdictional application): Per Zoom (explaining Republic of the Philippines v Maler Foundation), praying for, e.g., the release of funds within an immunity stay application, pursued whatever the outcome of the stay, invokes rather than contests jurisdiction.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
"Stay It, But Unfreeze My Money"

A foreign state-owned company served in Singapore applies for a stay on immunity grounds, and in the same application asks the court to release US$5m frozen by an earlier injunction, whether or not the stay is granted.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Asking for substantive relief (release of funds) that would be pursued whatever the stay outcome invokes the court's jurisdiction over the dispute (Zoom, explaining Maler Foundation). That is a step useful only if jurisdiction is accepted, so it is submission despite the immunity plea.

  • Variation: If release were sought only as a consequence of a successful stay, it would be consistent with the objection and so not submission.

Rule (Participation despite reservations): Per Shanghai Turbo (SGCA), deep, active participation in a non-party's injunction application went beyond a neutral, pre-emptive procedural step and contradicted repeated express reservations. A reservation is "not a silver bullet".

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Over-Eager Reserver

A PRC defendant repeatedly writes "without prejudice to our objection to jurisdiction" on every filing, but files lengthy affidavits opposing (on the merits) an injunction sought by a third-party shareholder, cross-examines that shareholder's witness, and seeks costs against her.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Like Shanghai Turbo, the defendant's deep and active participation in the injunction proceedings went well beyond a neutral, pre-emptive procedural step. Its conduct as a whole contradicts its reservations, and a reservation is "not a silver bullet". It has likely submitted.

Rule (Claimant and counterclaim): Per Glencore, a foreign claimant suing here submits to "all the incidents of litigation", including counterclaims and an ASI. Per Lakshmi Anil Salgaocar (HC), filing a counterclaim here is likewise premised on jurisdiction. Multi-party litigation: per Glencore, shipowners who brought claims and counterclaims in multi-party proceedings submitted for litigation not wholly distinct from the litigation the ASI protected, despite later settlement or discontinuance.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Shipowner's Counterclaim

After a collision in the Singapore Strait, the owner of MV Aurora (Greek) sues the owner of MV Borneo in Singapore, and Borneo counterclaims. The cargo interests join with their own claims, and Aurora counterclaims against them too. Aurora then settles with Borneo, discontinues its Singapore action, and sues the cargo interests in Greece over the same collision. The cargo interests seek an ASI in Singapore, and Aurora says it is no longer before the Singapore court.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

By suing in Singapore, Aurora submitted to "all the incidents of litigation", including counterclaims and an ASI (Glencore). In multi-party litigation, its claims and counterclaims are submission for litigation not wholly distinct from that which the ASI protects, and later settlement or discontinuance does not undo it (Glencore). Its counterclaim against the cargo interests is independently premised on jurisdiction (Lakshmi). Singapore has jurisdiction to grant the ASI.

Rule (Instructing local solicitors to accept service): Per Rothschild, instructing Singapore solicitors to accept service is submission. Per Shanghai Turbo (SGCA) and COSCO (HC), it is service in Singapore under O 7 r 2(1)(d), founding jurisdiction under s 16(1)(a)(i). Argue both; Yeo prefers submission (YPH lecture: COSCO "should be confined to the submission reasoning") (J3.0.2).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
"Our Lawyers Will Accept Service"

A Japanese defendant's in-house counsel writes: "We have instructed Drew & Co, Singapore, to accept service on our behalf." The claimant serves Drew & Co. The defendant then applies to set aside on the ground that it is abroad and no permission to serve out was obtained.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Two routes defeat the set-aside. (1) Submission: per Rothschild, instructing local solicitors to accept service is submission under s 16(1)(b). Yeo prefers this analysis. (2) Service in: per Shanghai Turbo (SGCA) and COSCO (HC), service on solicitors authorised to accept it is service in Singapore by agreed mode (O 7 r 2(1)(d)), founding s 16(1)(a)(i). Yeo says COSCO "should be confined to the submission reasoning". Either way, no permission to serve out was needed. (The defendant may still seek a stay, J4.)

Rule (Incorporation or registration, ±): A company arguably submits by incorporation or registration here. But per C&Y this is unnecessary since s 387 or s 376 founds jurisdiction via ss 16(2), 17(1)(c), so run it only as a fallback. Registration (±): (−) per Tao Commodity (HC Registry), registration compelled on pain of a fine is not voluntary, so it is not submission. (+) Per Chong (seminar), the company chose to do business here, so it arguably submitted.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Registration as Submission

In the Thames Advisory Scenario C (J2.1.4: deregistered, so s 376 is disputed), the client adds a fallback argument that Thames submitted to Singapore jurisdiction by registering under s 368 in 2019.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

(−) Thames relies on Tao Commodity: registration is compelled by statute on pain of a fine, so it is not a voluntary act and not submission. (+) The client relies on Chong: Thames chose to carry on business here, and registration is the price of that choice, so it is voluntary in the relevant sense. Run this only as a fallback to s 376(c).

J2.2.3 Acts Not Amounting to Submission (−)

Rule (Notice of intention to contest): Per O 6 r 6(4), filing a notice of intention to contest or not contest within 14 days (if served in Singapore) or 21 days (if served out) is not submission or a waiver of improper service. Defence or affidavit stating the challenge: per O 6 rr 7(4)–(6), 12(3)–(5), a defence or affidavit stating that the court has no jurisdiction or should not exercise it is not submission, if filed within 21 days (served here) or 5 weeks (served out).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Careful Timeline

A Thai defendant is served out of jurisdiction on 1 March. On 15 March it files a notice of intention to contest. On 1 April it files a defence stating: "The Defendant contends that the Court has no jurisdiction, alternatively should not exercise it."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

The notice of intention to contest was filed within 21 days of service out, so per O 6 r 6(4) it is neither submission nor a waiver of improper service. The defence was filed within 5 weeks of service out and states both an existence and an exercise challenge, so per O 6 r 7(4)–(6) it is not submission.

  • Variation: If the defendant had been served in Singapore, the deadlines would be 14 days (notice) and 21 days (defence or affidavit).

Rule (Notice of appointment of solicitor): Per Malayan Banking v Zhang Zhencheng, a notice of appointment of solicitor filed in order to challenge jurisdiction is not submission (by parity with O 6 r 12(5)). The claimant cannot then serve those solicitors, unlike in COSCO, where the defendant agreed.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Serving the Solicitors on Record

A Chinese defendant files a notice of appointment of Singapore solicitors in order to challenge service out. The claimant, worried that service out was defective, re-serves the claim on those solicitors and argues that this is valid service in Singapore.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Per Malayan Banking v Zhang Zhencheng, appointing solicitors to challenge jurisdiction is not submission. Since the defendant never agreed that the solicitors could accept service (contrast COSCO), service on them is not valid service under O 7 r 2(1)(d).

Rule (Case conference): Per C&Y, attending the case conference after signalling a challenge in the defence is not submission, the court dealing with jurisdiction first (O 9 r 7). Observer; defensive acts: per C&Y, attending a hearing as an observer, with a caveat that attendance is not submission (Grains and Industrial Products), or purely defensive participation, e.g., resisting an injunction to save one's job (International SOS v Overton), is not submission.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Showing Up Without Giving In
  1. A defendant that challenged jurisdiction in its defence attends the case conference.
  2. Another defendant's counsel attends a hearing "as an observer only, and without submitting to jurisdiction."
  3. An employee abroad, sued by his former employer for breach of a non-compete, resists an interim injunction that would stop him working at his new job, while maintaining his jurisdictional objection.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

None of these is submission. (1) Attending a case conference after signalling a challenge is not submission (O 9 r 7: jurisdiction is dealt with first). (2) Attendance as an observer with an express caveat is not submission (Grains and Industrial Products). (3) Purely defensive participation to protect one's livelihood is not submission (International SOS v Overton). Contrast the deep participation in Shanghai Turbo (J2.2.2).

Rule (Fall-back stay: set aside, then stay): Per Zoom and Williams, a stay prayed for as a fall-back to setting aside service is not submission, even in the same summons, because the prayers are considered in sequence. Risk: arguing the stay first was "unnecessarily risky" in Zoom, so make clear that existence is still contested. Arguing forum within the challenge: on service out, per Zoom, the defendant should run forum arguments within the set-aside application. Per C&Y, running a separate stay on the same FNC arguments is "wholly unnecessary and likely counter-productive" and may not be tolerated under ROC 2021 case management.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Ordering Mistake

An Indonesian defendant served out files one summons praying: "(1) service be set aside; (2) alternatively, the action be stayed on FNC grounds." At the hearing, counsel argues prayer (2) first and at length, then briefly mentions prayer (1). Counsel also files a separate stay application repeating the same FNC arguments.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

A fall-back stay in the same summons is not submission, because the prayers are considered in sequence (Zoom; Williams). But arguing the stay first was "unnecessarily risky" in Zoom; counsel should make clear that existence is still contested. The separate stay application is a further mistake. On service out, forum arguments belong inside the set-aside application (the claimant must show Singapore is forum conveniens there). A duplicate stay is "wholly unnecessary and likely counter-productive" (C&Y) and may be disallowed under ROC 2021 case management.

Rule (Stay pending foreign proceedings): Per Williams (as limited in Zoom), a stay pending the foreign court's ruling on, e.g., a guarantee's validity, needed to decide jurisdiction, is not submission. But this holds only if the court can stay without first assuming jurisdiction, which is unclear under Sch 1 para 9 or inherent powers, as Singapore lacks an equivalent of the English statutory power.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Waiting for the Swiss Court

A Swiss defendant says the guarantee containing the Singapore jurisdiction clause was forged, and the issue is already before the Zurich court. It asks Singapore to stay the action pending the Zurich ruling on validity (which decides whether the clause, and so jurisdiction, exists).

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Per Williams, a stay sought in order to determine jurisdiction is not submission. But Zoom limits this: it works only if the Singapore court has power to stay without first assuming jurisdiction. Under Sch 1 para 9 SCJA or the inherent powers, that is unclear, since Singapore has no equivalent of the English statutory power. The defendant should frame the application carefully as part of its jurisdiction challenge.

Rule (Unconnected steps): Per 6DM v AE Brands Korea, a statutory demand issued by the defendant outside the suit, with a reservation, is not submission. Earlier suit; recognition application: per Lakshmi Anil Salgaocar (HC), submission in an earlier suit does not carry over to a fresh suit, and seeking recognition of foreign receivers is not premised on jurisdiction over the dispute. Governing law clause: choosing Singapore law is not submission. By analogy, per Vizcaya Partners (a recognition case), a choice of law plus doing business here is not even implied consent to jurisdiction.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Four Things That Don't Count

A Korean company, Hanbit, is sued in Singapore by Pine Ltd and contests jurisdiction. Pine argues Hanbit submitted because:

  1. Hanbit had served a statutory demand on Pine in Singapore (outside this suit), expressly reserving its position on jurisdiction.
  2. Hanbit had defended an earlier, now-concluded Singapore suit by Pine on the merits.
  3. Hanbit's Korean receivers had applied in Singapore for recognition of their appointment.
  4. The contract is governed by Singapore law, and Hanbit does business with Singapore customers.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

No submission in any case. (1) A statutory demand outside the suit, with a reservation, is an unconnected step (6DM v AE Brands Korea). (2) Submission in an earlier suit does not carry over to a fresh suit (Lakshmi). (3) Seeking recognition of foreign receivers is not premised on jurisdiction over the dispute (Lakshmi). (4) A Singapore governing law clause is not submission, and per Vizcaya Partners (by analogy), a choice of law plus doing business here is not even implied consent to jurisdiction.

J2.2.4 Unclear: Failed Challenges and Stays Under ROC 2021

Rule:

  • Deemed submission dropped: per C&Y, ROC 2014 deemed a defendant to submit if its challenge failed or no order was made, regardless of voluntariness. ROC 2021 dropped this, leaving the effect of a failed challenge unclear.
  • Broad reading (defendant, argue this): O 6 rr 7(6), 12(5) treat an existence or exercise challenge as not submission, removing the Zoom trap for a stay sought alone. Support / counter: one textbook (para 2.058) confines the rules to filing and serving, so arguing FNC in court would still be submission under Zoom. Per Chong (seminar), that split is not obvious, since the rules are "quite encompassing".
  • Narrow reading, failed existence challenge (−): per C&Y, if the defendant fails on existence and takes no further step, it has not submitted, and O 9 r 8 directions should not deem submission against the Ideals.
  • Narrow reading, failed exercise challenge (+): per C&Y, r 7(6) protects only the filing, so if the FNC stay fails, the defendant submits at that point, because a stay accepts that jurisdiction exists.
  • Why it matters abroad (±): if the claimant enforces in another country, that country's own rules decide whether the Singapore stay application was submission. Per Henry v Geoprosco, an FNC challenge was submission, but per IGCF v Al Jomaih (PC 2025) it is a protest, not acceptance, as REFJA s 5(3)(a)(i) also provides (J7.1.2.4).
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Two Failed Challenges
  • Defendant A (UAE) is served out of jurisdiction. It challenges existence (no good arguable case on any gateway) and loses. It then takes no further step and does not file a defence.
  • Defendant B (UAE), served in Singapore during a visit, files an affidavit under O 6 r 12(3) saying the court should not exercise jurisdiction, applies for a Spiliada stay only, and loses.

The claimant obtains Singapore judgments against both and seeks to enforce them in the UAE, and later in a Commonwealth country that follows the Privy Council.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Defendant A: Under ROC 2014 it would have been deemed to submit on losing. ROC 2021 dropped that. On the narrow reading (C&Y), a defendant that fails on existence and takes no further step has not submitted, and O 9 r 8 directions should not be used to deem submission against the Ideals. Here this hardly matters in Singapore, because the court has found it has jurisdiction (the existence challenge failed). Submission matters for recognition abroad.
  • Defendant B: (+) On the broad reading, O 6 r 12(5) protects B: its exercise challenge is not submission, which removes the Zoom trap. Chong says the rules are "quite encompassing". (−) On the narrow reading (C&Y; textbook para 2.058), r 12(5) protects only the filing. Once B argued the stay in court and lost, it submitted at that point, because a stay application accepts that jurisdiction exists.
  • Abroad: In the enforcing country, its rules decide submission. Under Henry v Geoprosco, B's FNC challenge would count as submission. Under IGCF v Al Jomaih (PC 2025), and consistently with REFJA s 5(3)(a)(i) in Singapore's own statute, it is a protest, not acceptance. So the claimant's enforcement abroad may turn on which view that court follows (J7.1.2.4).

LAW302 · HYPO LESSON J3 · 46 HYPOTHETICALS · 6 FLOWCHARTS · 8 QUESTIONS

J3 hypotheticals: Existence when the defendant is abroad: service out

The rules behind these hypotheticals are taught in Lesson J3, where the word-for-word pre-write is too. Do that lesson first if the rules below look unfamiliar.

Applications:
ℹ HOW TO USE THESE HYPOTHETICALS

Each concept is set out as Rule, then Hypothetical, then Application. "Variation" lines flip one fact. Forum factors are in J4; jurisdiction clauses in J1.

The flowcharts redraw the hypotheticals in this site's chart style: the chip on each arrow names the hypothetical (or version) that takes that path. The hypo test at the end checks you can run the facts yourself.

1J3.0 Roadmap in one hypothetical

Rule (order of work): (1) Can the defendant be served in Singapore instead? (2) Is approval needed at all (O 8 r 1(3))? (3) Does Singapore "have the jurisdiction" (CCAA)? (4) Is Singapore "the appropriate court": nexus, forum conveniens, serious question (PD para 63(2))? (5) Mode of service. (6) The defendant's response: set aside (existence) or stay (exercise). (7) Is a jurisdiction agreement in play? (8) Will the judgment be recognised abroad?

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Pearl Fisheries v Andaman Seafood

Pearl Fisheries Pte Ltd (Singapore) contracted to buy frozen tuna from Andaman Seafood Co Ltd (Thailand). Andaman is not registered in Singapore, has no Singapore office and has not instructed Singapore lawyers. The contract was negotiated by WhatsApp between Pearl's Singapore-based director and Andaman's Bangkok sales manager, is expressly governed by Singapore law, and requires delivery CIF Singapore. The tuna arrived thawed and rotten. The contract has no jurisdiction or service clause.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  1. Threshold: Andaman is in Thailand, is not registered, and has not authorised solicitors to accept service, so it cannot be served here (state this first, per Chong). Jurisdiction depends on s 16(1)(a)(ii) SCJA + O 8.
  2. Approval needed? The contract is silent on service, so O 8 r 1(3) is unavailable.
  3. "Has the jurisdiction"? There is no CCAA choice of Singapore, so no.
  4. "Appropriate court": Pearl applies by summons without notice with a supporting affidavit (O 8 r 1(2); PD para 63(1)). (a) Nexus: para 63(3)(d)(iii) (governed by Singapore law); (d)(i) (made in Singapore, if acceptance was received here); and (e) (breach in Singapore, since delivery was due here), pleading (p) in the alternative. (b) Forum: Pearl must show Singapore is clearly more appropriate (Spiliada), or "on balance" (Oro Negro). (c) Serious question: subsumed under (e) because it engages the merits; it must be shown separately if Pearl relies only on (d).
  5. Mode: Pearl serves personally in Thailand before considering any substituted service (Consistel).
  6. Response: Andaman may apply to set aside (Pearl keeps the burden on all three limbs, Zoom) or seek a stay (Andaman bears the burden). Neither is submission (O 6 r 7(6), r 12(5)).
  7. Clause: there is none, so Spiliada applies.
  8. Recognition: a Singapore judgment founded on O 8 may be unenforceable in Thailand if Thai law requires presence or submission, so weigh this before suing here (J7).

2J3.0.2 Threshold: service in or service out?

Rule (the text): s 16(1)(a)(i) founds jurisdiction on service "in Singapore in the manner prescribed". (ii) founds it on service "outside Singapore in the circumstances authorised by and in the manner prescribed". So the limbs divide either by where service occurs or by where the defendant is. O 7 is headed "Service in Singapore" and O 8 "Service Out". A claimant cites the headings for the first reading; a defendant calls them mere procedural labels. Why it matters (must write): the answer decides (i) whether the claimant must prove Adams v Cape presence of a foreign company to use O 7 r 2(1)(b) (officer) or O 7 r 4 (agent), and (ii) whether the claimant can reach a defendant abroad without the O 8 controls.

Rule (COSCO: where service occurs): Per COSCO, a foreign company that agreed to be served through its Singapore solicitors was served in Singapore under O 7 r 2(1)(d) ("in any manner agreed"), founding jurisdiction under s 16(1)(a)(i). Reasons: what counts is where service is effected, not whether the defendant is Singapore-based; nothing in O 7 confines it to local defendants; requiring O 8 approval only to then serve solicitors here wastes court time (the Ideals); and Shanghai Turbo and Rothschild confirm it. Note: the judge accepted that the foreign company could equally be served under O 7 r 2(1)(b) on its chairman while he was here. That is the step the critics attack.

Rule (Yeo: where the defendant is): Per Yeo, limb (i) asks only for the manner of service because the defendant's presence is the nexus, whereas (ii) adds "circumstances authorised", delegating the nexus to the Rules. So the limbs divide by where the defendant is.

  • If COSCO were right, a foreign company could be caught by serving its officer on holiday or in transit (criticising B Atmaram v Essa Industries, where a Pakistani company's chairman was served on a visit).
  • Further, substituted service in Singapore could reach an absent defendant without O 8, contrary to Consistel, and the claimant could even apply to dispense with service altogether.
  • Solicitors: per Yeo, service on solicitors instructed to accept it is submission (s 16(1)(b)), and COSCO should be confined to that reasoning. This matters because submission has a scope: a defendant that reserved its objections can still put the O 8 requirements in issue.
  • O 7 r 4: per Yeo, it addresses absent principals, supplies its own nexus (the agent's control of the affairs to which the action relates) and needs permission, so it fits limb (ii). The Rules' in/out division need not match the SCJA's.
  • No nexus, no (ii): substituted service and service on officers of foreign companies set out no nexus, so they cannot rest on (ii) and cannot reach an absent defendant at all.
  • Policy: the 1993 amendments confirmed the pre-1963 structure (territorial service as of right, extraterritorial service on connecting factors, submission). Reading (i) to cover absent defendants "sends the wrong signal" about Singapore's reach.

Rule (Beranek: constructive presence): Per Beranek, the limbs divide by whether the defendant is present, actually or constructively, when served. COSCO reached the right result for the wrong reason: the foreign company was constructively present through solicitors authorised to accept service. O 7 r 4 rests on limb (i): the principal is deemed present through the agent, and the rule asks about the agent's authority, not whether Singapore is appropriate; if it were service out, it would sit in O 8. O 7 r 2(1)(b) requires the company itself to be present, not merely its officer.

Rule (Lecturer's position, submit this): The limbs divide by where the defendant is. Authorising Singapore solicitors to accept service is submission (s 16(1)(b)), a waiver of the O 8 hoops, not "deemed presence": the solicitors do not carry on the defendant's business here (Adams v Cape). Per Chong (mid-term feedback), in line with Beranek, O 7 r 2(1)(b) and r 4 both arguably rest on limb (i), not (ii) (cf COSCO), so the company must be present and the officer or agent is merely the mode.
