Rosenberg: the agent must have power to contract, so the company trades "by" and not merely "through" him, which is a strong sign that the company is present. Per the slides, r 4 also reaches a natural-person principal. Anomaly: per Chong (citing Toh Kian Sing), if the agent's control means the company is present, how is it "absent" under O 7 r 4(a)? This is unresolved; flag it in one line.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Solicitors and the Reservation

Golden Harvest SA (Brazil) is sued in Singapore by a Singapore trader for breach of a soybean contract with no Singapore connection except that the trader is Singaporean. Golden Harvest's general counsel emails: "We have instructed Rajah & Co to accept service, without prejudice to our position that the Singapore court lacks jurisdiction and is not the appropriate forum." The trader serves Rajah & Co without seeking O 8 approval.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • COSCO reading: service on solicitors authorised to accept it is service in Singapore under O 7 r 2(1)(d), so s 16(1)(a)(i) founds jurisdiction and O 8 is irrelevant. Golden Harvest can only seek a stay, bearing the stage 1 burden.
  • Yeo / lecturer's reading: what founds jurisdiction is submission (s 16(1)(b)), and submission has a scope. Golden Harvest expressly reserved its objections, so it submitted only to being served, not to the O 8 requirements. It can still put nexus, forum and a serious question in issue, with the burden on the trader. That reserved scope is the practical difference between the two readings.
  • Beranek reading: Golden Harvest was constructively present through solicitors authorised to accept service, so the result is the same as COSCO but for a different reason.
  • Answer: submit the lecturer's view. The solicitors do not carry on Golden Harvest's business here (Adams v Cape), so "presence" is a fiction; submission, limited by the reservation, is the honest analysis.

Rule (The chairperson-on-holiday problem): Where the dispute is wholly foreign and the chairperson is merely on holiday here, per Chong (mid-term feedback) the defendant is the company, not the chairperson. Serving him under O 7 r 2(1)(b) founds jurisdiction only if the company is itself present (Adams v Cape). Maharanee of Baroda (transient presence) is for a natural-person defendant. His presence is only the practical precondition for handing him the papers. Without the company being present, this is service on an absent company, which belongs in O 8 (Week 6 slides). Alternative: if he is here doing the company's business, use O 7 r 4, meeting all of r 4(1), including control of the affairs the action relates to. Bottom line: otherwise a claimant could skip both Adams v Cape and O 8 by serving the CEO on holiday.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Chairman at the F1

A contract for cement between Karachi Cement Ltd (Pakistan) and a Dubai buyer was made in Dubai, and the cement was delivered in Karachi. Karachi Cement has no Singapore office. Its chairman flies to Singapore for the Grand Prix, and the buyer (which has a Singapore subsidiary) serves him at the paddock, claiming service on the company under O 7 r 2(1)(b).

  • Variation: the chairman is in Singapore for a week negotiating, with full authority, the very contract later sued on.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

The defendant is Karachi Cement, not the chairman. O 7 r 2(1)(b) is a mode of serving a company that is present. It does not make an absent company present. Karachi Cement carries on no business at a fixed place here (Adams v Cape), so service is on an absent company and belongs in O 8. Maharanee does not help, as it concerns a natural-person defendant. B Atmaram points the other way, but it is the very case Yeo criticises. If this worked, any claimant could bypass both Adams v Cape and O 8 by catching a CEO on holiday.

  • In the variation, consider O 7 r 4. The chairman personally controls, here, the company's affairs relating to the action (the contract being negotiated), so with permission he could be served as agent. All of r 4(1) must be met, and if his control here makes the company present, the r 4(a) "absent" anomaly arises (Chong/Toh Kian Sing).

Rule (Which route is most onerous, practice): Per the slides, O 7 r 2(1)(b) is as of right; O 7 r 4 needs permission; O 8 r 1(1) "appropriate court" needs approval on three requirements, with the burden on the claimant. So advise the claimant to serve in wherever it can (J2.1.7).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Choosing the Route

A claimant can (i) serve an officer of a foreign company that has a permanent Singapore branch, (ii) serve its Singapore agent under O 7 r 4, or (iii) serve out in Germany.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Choose (i) first. It is as of right and the defendant then bears the stay burden. (ii) needs permission and meets the narrower Rosenberg requirements. (iii) needs approval on all three limbs, with the burden on the claimant throughout.

3J3.1 Service out (s 16(1)(a)(ii) SCJA; O 8 ROC 2021)

J3.1.1 Starter and Framework

Rule (Approval and application): Per O 8 r 1(1), the originating process may be served out with approval where the court "has the jurisdiction" or "is the appropriate court". Per O 8 r 1(2) and PD para 63(1), (4), the claimant applies by summons without notice, with an affidavit stating why, where the defendant is or may be found, and whether the process's validity needs extending. No approval needed: per O 8 r 1(3), none is needed where the contract allows service out (J3.1.5). Per O 8 r 1(4), approval for the originating process carries later court documents with it.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Follow-Up Documents

Pearl Fisheries (J3.0) obtains approval and serves its originating claim in Bangkok. Two months later it wants to serve an application for summary judgment and an amended statement of claim on Andaman in Bangkok.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Per O 8 r 1(4), approval for the originating process carries with it later court documents in the action, so no fresh approval is needed. Pearl's original affidavit must have stated why approval was sought, where Andaman is or may be found, and whether the claim's validity needed extending (PD para 63(4)).

Rule (Route 1, "has the jurisdiction"): Per C&Y, this presumably covers an exclusive choice of court agreement designating Singapore under the CCAA, where the chosen court must hear the case and cannot decline for FNC (CCAA s 11; J1.3). Per Chong (answer scheme), the CCAA contract goes on this ground.

  • Why (Yeo): read with s 16(1)(a)(ii), the limb is circular, so "has the jurisdiction" must mean jurisdiction under other written law (s 16(2) SCJA), i.e. the General Division as exclusively chosen court in a Hague case.
  • Puzzle (C&Y): if the court already "has" jurisdiction, it is unclear why approval is needed or on what criteria the AR decides.
  • Other chosen-court cases (Yeo): where the General Division is chosen outside the CCAA, use "appropriate court", which is easily met because the defendant must show strong cause (J3.2).
  • Agreement ≠ jurisdiction (Yeo, citing British Wagon v Gray): consent alone confers no jurisdiction. An agreement to submit is not submission under s 16(1)(b) but a nexus for service out.
  • Exercise challenge (C&Y): outside the CCAA the defendant may still challenge exercise (FNC, or strong cause for a non-CCAA EJC), with the burden on the defendant, as in a service-in case (J4).
  • SICC: per SICC Rules O 5 r 6(2), no permission is needed to serve a party to a written jurisdiction agreement, or where the agreement allows service out. Otherwise, per O 5 r 6(1), the SICC must "have the jurisdiction" and be "appropriate" (J5).
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Hague Clause and the Non-Hague Clause
  • Contract 1 (2021): Bavaria Brewing GmbH and a Singapore distributor agree "the Singapore High Court shall have exclusive jurisdiction". The contract says nothing about service.
  • Contract 2 (2021): the same clause in a contract between the distributor and Shanghai Hops Co (the PRC is not a party to the HCCCA, but the chosen court, Singapore, is in a Contracting State).
  • Contract 3: an asymmetric clause: Bavaria submits to the exclusive jurisdiction of the Singapore courts, while the distributor may sue in any competent court.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Contracts 1 and 2: Both are exclusive choices of a Contracting State's court in an international commercial case, so the CCAA applies and Singapore must hear them (s 11). Approval is sought on the "has the jurisdiction" ground (Chong; C&Y). Yeo explains why: read literally, the limb is circular, so it must mean jurisdiction conferred by other written law (the CCAA via s 16(2)). The C&Y puzzle remains: what is left for the AR to decide? Perhaps only whether the clause is a CCAA clause. (The open point in J1.3: the defendant may argue inter partes that the claim is outside the CCAA.)
  • Contract 3: Asymmetric, so not a CCAA clause (CHLOE V). Use "appropriate court": the nexus is para 63(3)(r) / (d)(iv), and the forum limb is easily met because the restricted party objecting would bear strong cause (Yeo). Remember British Wagon v Gray: the clause does not itself confer jurisdiction. It is a nexus that justifies service out.
  • Exercise: in Contract 3 (outside the CCAA), the defendant may still challenge exercise, bearing the burden of strong cause. In Contracts 1 and 2 it cannot (s 11(2)).
  • SICC variation: if the clause named the SICC, no permission would be needed to serve a party to the written jurisdiction agreement (SICC Rules O 5 r 6(2)).

Rule (Route 2, "appropriate court"): Per PD para 63(2), restating Zoom's common law requirements, the claimant shows (a) a good arguable case of sufficient nexus; (b) Singapore is forum conveniens; (c) a serious question to be tried. Together: per Recovery Vehicle 1, the three are assessed for consistency, not in isolation, so a finding on the gateway must square with the merits. Thresholds: a good arguable case on nexus means "the better of the argument" (Vinmar), more than a prima facie case (Bradley Lomas), but not "a much better argument" or a balance of probabilities. Only a serious question is needed on the merits (Bradley Lomas).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Inconsistent Findings

A claimant relies on gateway (f)(i) (a tortious act in Singapore) against an Indian defendant, saying the defendant made a fraudulent misrepresentation by phone to Singapore. For the merits, it says the representation was made in Mumbai, at a meeting, and was then relayed to Singapore by a third party.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Per Recovery Vehicle 1, the three requirements are assessed together for consistency. The claimant cannot locate the act in Singapore for the gateway while pleading facts on the merits that place it in Mumbai. On nexus, it must show the better of the argument (Vinmar), more than a prima facie case (Bradley Lomas). On the merits, it need only show a serious question. Its inconsistent case fails the nexus limb. (Chong would also say that a misrepresentation made abroad belongs under (f)(ii), with (n) in the alternative: J3.1.2.)

Rule (Why extraterritorial jurisdiction, handout Q): Disputes with absent defendants that are strongly connected with Singapore (a Singapore contract, a tort here, Singapore assets) should be triable here; otherwise the claimant is forced abroad even where Singapore is the natural forum. From exorbitant to appropriate: traditionally service out was "exorbitant": jurisdiction is territorial, and serving a defendant abroad intrudes on the foreign State's sovereignty, hence circumspection and the burden on the claimant (Consistel). Now: per Abela v Baadarani and Four Seasons v Brownlie (adopted by C&Y), there are no "muscular presumptions" against serving abroad; the decision is "a pragmatic one in the interests of efficient conduct of litigation in an appropriate forum", which makes it "extraordinary", not "exorbitant". Why (Yeo): what reaches the foreign State is notice of the proceedings, not a sovereign command. Singapore courts still say "exorbitant" but mean comity-based caution, and should keep the caution of Société Générale v Dreyfus before hauling a foreigner here.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Essay Question

"Service out of the jurisdiction is an exorbitant exercise of power that should be used sparingly." Discuss with reference to a Singapore claimant whose Indonesian distributor stole its trade secrets and is selling copies across Southeast Asia.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Why extraterritorial: the dispute is strongly connected with Singapore (the claimant, the secrets, and the loss), so without service out the claimant would be forced to Indonesia even if Singapore is the natural forum. Exorbitant: the traditional view (Consistel) is that service abroad intrudes on Indonesia's sovereignty, so the court must be circumspect and the burden lies on the claimant. Modern view: Abela and Four Seasons reject "muscular presumptions"; the question is pragmatic efficiency, so the power is "extraordinary", not "exorbitant" (adopted by C&Y). Yeo's synthesis: only notice reaches Indonesia, not a command, so "exorbitant" now means comity-based caution, as in Société Générale v Dreyfus. The quotation overstates the position: the power is used whenever a real nexus and appropriateness are shown, with caution rather than reluctance.

Rule (Why the reform, CJC Report): r 1(1) prescribes criteria rather than a list, so the claimant need not scrutinise "the long list ... in the hope of fitting into one or more descriptions", and no category that should be heard here is accidentally omitted. Cautious: per C&Y, Singapore did not adopt FNC as the sole test, but it is bolder than England, whose PD gateways remain closed. Why keep the gateways: per Foxton J (adopted by C&Y), they supply "an objective, justifiable and ... internationally recognised nexus", which matters for comity, for recognition of the Singapore judgment abroad, and in the competitive dispute resolution market; the natural forum test alone "is rather more judgmental". Distinct roles: per Four Seasons v Brownlie, gateways set the legal maximum of jurisdiction; forum conveniens only limits it and never enlarges the court's reach. One gateway (Yeo, evaluative): Singapore now has one gateway, "sufficient nexus", within the court's bounded discretion, so a claim outside every listed factor may still qualify. Technically a claim within a factor could still lack sufficient nexus, but since the reform liberalises, that is probably not intended. Critique (Yeo): it risks being "an open territory with no fence", since almost any claim fits (n). Singapore may answer by weighing substantive connections at the forum stage, or by a "real and substantial connection" test within sufficient nexus. Territoriality survives in residual form: the factors supply a recognised nexus, comity counsels caution, Singapore judgments need presence or submission abroad, and the Moçambique rule remains. Is the reform significant? (evaluative): partly. Per C&Y, the heads survive almost word for word, and Li Shengwu had already made (n) near open-ended. The real change is conceptual: a non-exhaustive list, no pro-defendant construction, appropriateness rather than fitting a statutory box, and room to expand.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Claim That Fits No Box

A Singapore crypto fund sues an anonymous Cayman-incorporated market maker for manipulating the price of a token. The trading took place on a Bahamian exchange. The only Singapore connections are that the fund's servers, staff and investors are in Singapore, and that the market maker's trading bot was coded by a Singapore contractor. No listed para 63(3) factor clearly fits.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Under the old O 11 list the fund would have had to fit a statutory box, and doubts were resolved in the defendant's favour. Now the list is non-exhaustive (CJC Report), so the fund argues "sufficient nexus" directly (Yeo's "one gateway"), pointing to the Singapore coding and the loss suffered here. (−) The market maker argues that this is Yeo's "open territory with no fence": the gateways exist to supply an internationally recognised nexus (Foxton J), and a Singapore judgment on such thin links may not be recognised in Cayman. (+) The fund replies that the court can police weak links at the forum stage, and that a forum conveniens finding cannot enlarge reach (Four Seasons) but the non-exhaustive gateway can. Evaluation: this is where the reform is genuinely significant, because the conceptual shift lets the claim in; whether it succeeds then depends on forum.

Rule (Round 1, without notice): Only the claimant is before the AR. It bears the burden and owes full and frank disclosure of matters against it (the defendant's links with the foreign State, the foreign proceedings, gateway weaknesses). Per Zoom and C&Y, material non-disclosure can found a set-aside unless the defendant waived it. Round 2, inter partes: the defendant applies to set aside under O 6 r 7(5)(a) / r 12(4)(a) (within 5 weeks if served out), and jurisdiction falls with the service. Per Zoom and Li Shengwu, the legal burden stays on the claimant on all three requirements, though it is practically higher now that the defendant contests. Flexibility: per C&Y (citing NML Capital and IM Skaugen), absent abuse the claimant may rely on a new cause of action or gateway not in the without-notice application, and the court weighs developments after approval. Evidential burden: the defendant must evidence its own counter-arguments (e.g., that the contract is governed by foreign law). Practice (Chong): attack on all fronts, even where one requirement looks conclusive.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Undisclosed Lawsuit in Seoul

A Singapore shipyard obtains approval to serve a Korean shipowner. Its affidavit does not mention that the shipowner had already sued the shipyard in Seoul on the same contract a month earlier. Inter partes, the shipowner applies to set aside. The shipyard then argues, for the first time, a new gateway, (p), and a new cause of action in restitution.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Non-disclosure: the Seoul action is plainly material to forum, so its omission breaches the duty of full and frank disclosure, and approval may be set aside on that ground alone (Zoom), unless the shipowner waived it (e.g., by arguing the merits without raising the point). Burden: inter partes, the shipyard still bears the legal burden on all three requirements (Zoom; Li Shengwu), and practically more so now that there is opposing evidence. New gateway and claim: absent abuse, the shipyard may rely on (p) and the restitution claim (NML Capital; IM Skaugen), and the court may weigh developments since approval (e.g., progress in Seoul). Defendant's tactics: the shipowner must itself evidence any counter-argument (e.g., Korean governing law) and should attack all three limbs and the non-disclosure (Chong).

Rule (Nexus per claim): Per C&Y and IM Skaugen (CA), a factor must be shown for each claim against each defendant, so contract and tort claims need one each. One factor per claim suffices, the factors being disjunctive (Li Shengwu, citing Tassell v Hallen). No aggregation: per IM Skaugen (CA), distinct claims cannot be pooled, and an assignment does not merge the assigned claims into one aggregate claim. Exception (C&Y): (a) turns on the defendant, not the claim. Approval may be granted on terms or for part of the claim.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Engine Failures

Nordsee Shipping AS assigns to its Singapore subsidiary all its claims against an engine maker, Motoren AG (Germany), over defective engines on four vessels. The subsidiary sues Motoren in contract and in tort. Only one vessel's engine failed in Singapore waters; the others failed in the North Sea.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

A gateway is needed for each claim (contract and tort) and for each vessel's claim (IM Skaugen (CA)). The subsidiary cannot pool them into one aggregate claim, and the assignment does not merge them. The Singapore failure may support (f)(ii) for the tort claim on that one vessel. The North Sea claims need their own factors. If none is found, approval may be granted only for part of the claim. Exception: if Motoren had property in Singapore (e.g., shares in a Singapore subsidiary), (a) would cover all claims, because it turns on the defendant, not the claim (C&Y).

Rule (Interpreting the factors): Per C&Y, read the factors more liberally now that they sit in a PD. There is no need to resolve doubts in the defendant's favour. Old O 11 case law still helps, and English (PD 6B) and NSW cases help with care. Choice of law: Singapore choice of law rules decide whether a "contract" exists or a claim is "founded on a tort" (C2; C3).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Is It a Tort?

A Singapore company sues a Japanese company for "breach of confidence" over information leaked in Tokyo, relying on gateway (f).

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Whether this is "founded on a tort" is a characterisation question for Singapore choice of law rules (C3), not Japanese law and not domestic labels. Under the modern liberal reading, doubts are not resolved in the defendant's favour. If (f) is doubtful, breach of confidence may also fit (o) (fiduciary or restitution) or the non-exhaustive fallback.

Rule (Defendant's options when served out, handout):

  • Ignore: risks a default judgment, though it may be unenforceable in the defendant's home State, where its assets are, if that State requires presence or submission.
  • Set aside (existence): no nexus, no serious question, Singapore not forum conveniens, or non-disclosure. The burden is on the claimant, so this is usually the defendant's best first move (J4.2).
  • Stay (exercise): FNC, or a foreign EJC or arbitration clause. The burden is on the defendant (J4.1).
  • Defend on the merits (submission), or go on the offensive: sue at home or seek an ASI against the claimant (J6).
  • What decides it: where the burden lies, the strength of the nexus, where the defendant's assets are, costs, and the risk of submitting.

Recognition implication (evaluative): O 8 jurisdiction is not internationally recognised at common law, which looks only to presence in, or submission to, the adjudicating forum (J7). So the Singapore judgment may be unenforceable where the defendant's assets lie; weigh this before preferring Singapore.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Advising Andaman Seafood

Andaman (J3.0) has been served in Bangkok and asks for advice. All its assets are in Thailand. Assume Thailand enforces foreign judgments only where the defendant was present or submitted.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Ignore: Pearl would get a default judgment, but it would be hard to enforce in Thailand, since Andaman was neither present in nor submitted to Singapore. This is risky if Andaman ever acquires assets in Singapore or in a country that recognises O 8 jurisdiction.
  • Set aside (recommended first move): Pearl bears the burden on all three limbs. Andaman should attack nexus (e.g., argue that delivery was CIF, so performance arguably took place at the port of loading), forum (witnesses in Thailand) and non-disclosure, if any.
  • Stay: Andaman would bear the burden, so this is only a fall-back.
  • Merits defence: that would be submission, and any judgment would then be enforceable in Thailand.
  • Offensive: Andaman could sue in Bangkok for a declaration of non-liability.
  • Pearl's side: Pearl should weigh the recognition problem before suing. A Bangkok judgment might be more useful even if Singapore is more convenient.

J3.1.2 Requirement (a): Good Arguable Case of Nexus (the para 63(3) factors)

Factor (a): Domicile, Residence, Business or Property

Rule: The claimant seeks relief against a defendant who is domiciled, ordinarily resident, carrying on business, or has property in Singapore. Per Elan Impex, the claimant must show a good arguable case basis for seeking relief from the defendant. Catch-all: the connection is with the defendant, not the claim, so contract, tort and restitution claims can all be lumped under (a). Neutral: (a) says nothing about the merits, so requirement (c) must be proved separately (J3.1.4).

  • Domicile: per C&Y, Singapore law decides it. Per Peters Roger, the domicile of origin (the father's if the child is legitimate and born in his lifetime; otherwise the mother's) persists until a domicile of choice is acquired by voluntary residence plus an intention to remain and make a home there. Citizens: the Women's Charter s 3(5) presumption that Singapore citizens are domiciled here may guide the court, though arguably it is confined to family matters (C&Y). Company: per Gasque v IRC, a company is domiciled in its place of incorporation.
  • Ordinary residence: per Levene v IRC, residence "with some degree of continuity and apart from accidental or temporary absences", voluntarily adopted with a settled purpose (Tjong Very Sumito). Companies: per C&Y, there is no uniform meaning. The tax test (central management and control) is inapt for amenability, and it is strongly arguable that Adams v Cape presence establishes ordinary residence.
  • Carrying on business: per C&Y, this applies to individuals as well as companies, with no fixed-place or minimal-period requirement on the wording, so it appears enough that the defendant is carrying on business here when permission is sought.
  • Property: per Lehman Brothers, the property (e.g., shares, a bank account) need not relate to the claim. Per Bunge, it need not be substantial (a share in a Singapore subsidiary sufficed). But per C&Y, insubstantial property weakens the forum analysis under (b).
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Four Absent Defendants
  1. Mr Lee, born in Singapore to a Singaporean father, emigrated to Australia in 2015 with no fixed plan to stay, and now lives in Perth on a renewable work visa. He is sued in tort over a car accident in Malaysia.
  2. Ms Kaur, an Indian national, has lived and worked in Singapore for eight years on an Employment Pass and is currently on a six-month secondment to London when sued.
  3. Rhine Consulting GmbH has no Singapore office, but its consultants fly in monthly to advise Singapore clients, including in the month the claimant applies.
  4. Fjord Holdings AS owns 1 share in a dormant Singapore subsidiary.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  1. Domicile: Mr Lee's domicile of origin is Singapore (his father's, as he was legitimate and born in his father's lifetime). It persists until he acquires a domicile of choice in Australia by residence plus an intention to remain and make a home there (Peters Roger). With no fixed plan to stay, that intention is doubtful, so he is arguably still domiciled in Singapore. As a citizen, the Women's Charter s 3(5) presumption may also guide the court, though arguably it is confined to family matters. Factor (a) is satisfied, but the claimant must show a serious question separately.
  2. Ordinary residence: eight years of voluntary residence with a settled purpose (Levene; Tjong Very Sumito), and the London secondment is a temporary absence. She is ordinarily resident here.
  3. Carrying on business: per C&Y, the wording has no fixed-place or minimal-period requirement, so Rhine's regular advisory trips, including in the month of the application, arguably suffice, even though they would fail Adams v Cape for service in.
  4. Property: 1 share is "property in Singapore". It need not relate to the claim (Lehman), nor be substantial (Bunge). But per C&Y, so trivial an asset weakens the case at the forum stage.

Factor (b): Injunction

Rule: The claimant seeks an injunction ordering the defendant to do, or refrain from doing, something in Singapore. Per Lakshmi Anil Salgaocar v Chilton, the injunction must be part of the substantive relief and have a reasonable prospect of being granted. Not enough: an interlocutory Mareva (Karaha Bodas), or a mandatory injunction compelling the defendant to perform the agreement abroad (C&Y). ASI: on its wording (b) covers only conduct "in Singapore", and per C&Y interlocutory injunctions are excluded, so it does not obviously carry an ASI against foreign proceedings. Per Chong (answer scheme), seek the ASI as ancillary relief in the substantive action served out, so that amenability comes from that service (J6).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Three Injunctions
  1. A Singapore franchisor sues a former Malaysian franchisee to stop it using the franchisor's trade name at its Singapore outlet.
  2. A creditor seeks only a freezing order over a Hong Kong debtor's Singapore bank account, pending a Hong Kong judgment.
  3. A Singapore claimant seeks an ASI to restrain the defendant's Indian proceedings.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  1. Satisfied: a final injunction about conduct in Singapore that forms part of the substantive relief and has a reasonable prospect of grant (Lakshmi).
  2. Not satisfied: a Mareva is interlocutory (Karaha Bodas).
  3. Doubtful: an ASI restrains conduct in India, not in Singapore, and an interim ASI is interlocutory. Per Chong, frame the ASI as ancillary relief within a substantive claim served out on another factor (e.g., (d) or (r)), so that amenability comes from that service (J6).

Factor (c): Necessary or Proper Party

Rule: A foreign defendant (D2) is a necessary or proper party to the claim against an anchor defendant (D1) who has been duly served. Per AK Investment, this head is anomalous: it rests on no territorial connection between the claim and Singapore (The Brabo). Caution: D2 must not be brought in "as a matter of course" (The Golden Mariner) merely because the alternative is two suits.

  • The anchor claim: per AK Investment, that D1 is sued only to bring in D2 is not fatal (The Brabo; Derby v Larsson), but the claim against D1 must not be "bound to fail" (otherwise D1's presence is a device). A point of law going to jurisdiction is normally decided at this stage. Duly served: per C&Y, if D1 has not been duly served when the application is made, it is dismissed, and approval wrongly given is set aside unless the claimant obtains retroactive leave; irregular service of D1 may be curable. Collapse: per Elan Impex, if the action against D1 is struck out, D2 ceases to be a necessary or proper party.
  • Is D2 a proper party? Per AK Investment (adopting Massey v Heynes), ask whether, had D1 and D2 both been here, both would have been proper parties: the claims must involve "one investigation", be "closely bound up", or share a "common thread" (the same transaction or conspiracy). Merits: per AK Investment, a serious issue against D2 is the summary judgment test (Seaconsar). Per J H Rayner, a D2 with a good defence (limitation, no privity) cannot be a proper party.
  • Limits: per C&Y, an additional trustee who is not a joint trustee of the same trust is not necessary. England bars chaining (serving D3 off D2 when D2 was served under the same head). (c) is neutral, so run J3.1.4.
  • Application (Chong, AY23-24): D2's pre-contractual misrepresentation and D1's post-contractual breach of a supply contract share no common question of law or fact, so D2 is not a proper party (unless D1 is sued vicariously).
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Conspiracy and the Sham Anchor

Cobalt Pte Ltd claims that its former CFO (D1, resident in Singapore) conspired with a Dubai trading house (D2) and a Cyprus shell (D3) to siphon funds through fake invoices.

  • Version 1: D1 is duly served in Singapore. Cobalt seeks approval to serve D2 under (c).
  • Version 2: The claim against D1 is obviously time-barred.
  • Version 3: Cobalt has not yet served D1 when it applies to serve D2.
  • Version 4: Cobalt seeks to serve D3 under (c) as a necessary or proper party to the claim against D2.
  • Version 5: Cobalt's claim against D2 is only that D2's director made pre-contractual misrepresentations inducing Cobalt to sign a supply contract, while the claim against D1 is for D1's later breach of that supply contract.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Version 1: If D1 and D2 had both been in Singapore, they would both be proper parties: the claims involve "one investigation" and a "common thread" (the same conspiracy) (Massey v Heynes, adopted in AK Investment). Cobalt must show a serious issue against D2 on the summary judgment test (Seaconsar), and D2 must not have a knock-out defence (J H Rayner). Even though the head is anomalous (The Brabo), it applies; the court must not admit D2 "as a matter of course" just to avoid two suits (The Golden Mariner), but here the claims really are bound up. As (c) is neutral, prove a serious question separately.
  • Version 2: A claim against D1 that is "bound to fail" (time-barred) makes D1's presence a device, so (c) fails (AK Investment). Contrast: suing D1 mainly to bring in D2 is not fatal if the claim against D1 is genuine (Derby v Larsson). If the claim against D1 is later struck out, D2 ceases to be a proper party (Elan Impex).
  • Version 3: D1 has not been duly served, so the application is dismissed, and any approval wrongly given is set aside unless retroactive leave is obtained (C&Y). Irregular service of D1 may be curable.
  • Version 4: Chaining is barred in England. Serving D3 off D2, who was itself served under (c), is impermissible, so Cobalt needs an independent factor for D3.
  • Version 5: As in Chong's feedback, pre-contractual misrepresentation and post-contractual breach share no common question of law or fact, so D2 is not a proper party (unless D1 is sued vicariously for D2's director's acts).

Factor (d): Contract

Rule (two requirements): Per C&Y, the claim must enforce, rescind, annul or recover damages in respect of a contract, and the contract must be (i) made in Singapore or through an essential step here; (ii) made through an agent here for a principal abroad; (iii) governed by Singapore law; or (iv) contain a Singapore jurisdiction term.

  • Existence and denial: per Tecnomar, the claimant needs only a good arguable case that the contract exists, so the defendant's denial of formation or authority is not fatal. Which law: per C&Y, formation is tested by the contract's proper law under Singapore PIL, not Singapore domestic law, so a contract valid under foreign law counts even if it lacks consideration. Claim denying the contract: per C&Y, once unclear, but now largely academic: the list is non-exhaustive and may be read generously, so a claim that the contract is void qualifies if one of limbs (i)–(iv) is shown.
  • Parties: per C&Y, it is unsettled whether the contract must be between the claimant and the defendant. Against: Chen v BHNV held (d) "plainly inapplicable" against a non-party defendant. For: per C&Y, an assignee, subrogated insurer, or third party entitled to enforce under the proper law steps into the original party's shoes and may rely on (d).
  • (d)(i) made in Singapore: per C&Y, it is open whether domestic law or choice of law rules locate formation. Assuming domestic law, per Transniko, a contract made by telephone or other instantaneous communication is made where the offeror receives acceptance, and one accepted by conduct where the conduct occurred. Counterparts: per C&Y, a contract signed in counterpart may be made in two places. Essential step: includes negotiations culminating in the contract. Per DJS Solutions, a contract negotiated over WhatsApp by the claimant's director, who was based here and ran the claimant's business from Singapore, was made here even though he travelled.
  • (d)(ii) through an agent here: per National Mortgage, the agent needs only authority to negotiate, not to contract. Per DJS Solutions, the relief must relate to the contract made by or through the defendant's agent, not merely one the agent introduced.
  • (d)(iii) governed by Singapore law: per Shanghai Turbo and Recovery Vehicle 1, apply Singapore choice of law rules (express, implied or objective proper law: C2). Not decisive: per Amin Rasheed, the policy was impliedly governed by English law, yet leave to serve out was refused because Kuwait was the appropriate forum (J4.2).
  • (d)(iv) jurisdiction term: per Vizcaya Partners (adopted by C&Y), an agreement to submit to Singapore is not inferred from a Singapore governing law clause; the clause itself must give the Singapore court jurisdiction. Where it exists, see (r) and J3.2.
  • Neutral: each limb is a connecting factor that says nothing about breach, so requirement (c) must be proved separately. Hence a claimant who says no contract was formed may still use (d), needing only a good arguable case of the Singapore connection.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Yacht Charter Deal

Nautilus Charters Pte Ltd (Singapore) agreed to charter a yacht from Aegean Yachts SA (Greece). Facts:

  • Negotiations were by WhatsApp between Nautilus's director, Ben (who runs Nautilus from Singapore but sent several messages from a trip to Bali), and Aegean's Athens office.
  • Aegean's Singapore broker, Chloe, introduced the parties and negotiated terms but had no authority to sign.
  • The final offer came from Aegean; Ben accepted by WhatsApp from Singapore. (Alternatively: Ben accepted by paying the deposit from Bali.)
  • The contract says "governed by Singapore law" but has no jurisdiction clause.
  • Aegean denies a contract was ever concluded, saying its manager lacked authority to make the final offer.
  • Under Greek law, which Aegean says governs, a charter without a written signed document is void.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Existence: Nautilus needs only a good arguable case that a contract exists (Tecnomar), so Aegean's denial of authority is not fatal. Formation is for the putative proper law under Singapore PIL (C2). If that is Singapore law (the express choice), Greek formalities are irrelevant.
  • (d)(i): Assuming domestic law locates formation (an open point, C&Y), an instantaneous acceptance is made where the offeror (Aegean, in Athens) receives it (Transniko), so the contract was made in Athens, not Singapore. But (d)(i) also covers an essential step here: as in DJS Solutions, negotiations conducted by Ben, who runs Nautilus from Singapore, are an essential step taken here even though he sometimes travelled. If acceptance was by conduct (paying the deposit from Bali), the contract was made in Bali.
  • (d)(ii): Chloe needed only authority to negotiate, not to sign (National Mortgage), and the relief relates to the very contract she negotiated (DJS Solutions), so (d)(ii) is satisfied.
  • (d)(iii): The express Singapore law choice satisfies this limb under Singapore choice of law rules (Shanghai Turbo; Recovery Vehicle 1). But per Amin Rasheed, governing law is not decisive of forum.
  • (d)(iv): Not available. The Singapore governing law clause does not imply a jurisdiction agreement (Vizcaya).
  • Serious question: (d) is neutral, so Nautilus must separately show a serious question of breach (J3.1.4).
  • Variation (parties): if Nautilus's insurer, having paid out, sues Aegean by subrogation, C&Y say it may rely on (d) because it steps into Nautilus's shoes. Contrast Chen v BHNV: (d) is "plainly inapplicable" against a non-party defendant, e.g., Aegean's parent company.

Factor (e): Breach in Singapore

Rule: The defendant failed to deliver or pay in Singapore, or broke the contract abroad in a way that made performance in Singapore impossible. Per C&Y, this turns on place of breach and place of performance, the latter fixed by an express term or the proper law. Alternative places (−): per C&Y (citing Recovery Vehicle 1), where the obligation could be performed in Singapore or abroad, non-performance is not a breach "in Singapore". Repudiation: per Mutzenbecher, the place of breach is arguably where the defendant's repudiatory act (e.g., a wrongful sale) occurred. Multiple or continuing breaches: where goods were due here but the defendant wrongfully sold them abroad, there is both a failure to perform here and a repudiatory act abroad. Per C&Y (citing Briggs), the claimant may rely on the Singapore breach, but relief is limited to the losses flowing from it. Continuing breach: per C&Y, the forum finding may colour where the breach is located, so a Singapore natural forum tends to locate it here. Merits-engaging: whether there is a breach at all is decided by the contract's proper law (C2), so a good arguable case of breach under that law subsumes requirement (c).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Diverted Rubber

A Vietnamese seller agreed to deliver rubber to Singapore. Instead, it sold the cargo to a higher bidder in Shanghai (a repudiatory act there) and never delivered to Singapore.

  • Variation: the contract said payment "may be made in Singapore or Hanoi at the Buyer's option", and the claim is by the seller for non-payment.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

There are two breaches: the failure to deliver in Singapore (where performance was due under the express term) and the repudiatory sale in Shanghai. Per Mutzenbecher, the place of breach for repudiation is arguably Shanghai. Per C&Y (citing Briggs), the buyer may rely on the Singapore breach (non-delivery here) for (e), but relief is confined to the losses flowing from that breach. If Singapore is the natural forum, that tends to locate a continuing breach here. Because (e) engages the merits, a good arguable case of breach under the proper law also satisfies requirement (c).

  • In the variation, payment could be made in either Singapore or Hanoi, so non-payment is not a breach "in Singapore" (C&Y, citing Recovery Vehicle 1). The seller needs another factor.

Factor (f): Tort

Rule (characterisation): Per C&Y (citing IM Skaugen (HC), unchallenged on appeal), "tort" is tested by Singapore's choice of law rules: double actionability with the flexible exception (Rickshaw), for local and foreign torts alike. So a claimant may use (f) even though the claim fails under Singapore law, if the exception applies the foreign law (C3). Equitable claims: per Recovery Vehicle 1 (HC), dishonest assistance, knowing receipt and breach of directors' duties were described as torts. Such claims may need (f) because (o) covers only restitution and claims against trustees or fiduciaries (C&Y).

Rule (double actionability at the gateway, unresolved): Per IM Skaugen (HC), there is no good arguable case in tort unless the claim is actionable under both laws, for both limbs of (f). Per Nippon Catalyst, the rule is irrelevant to service out, being directed at fairness, not at locating the forum. Shen Sophie: IM Skaugen's broad approach should be followed, but that view was expressed mainly for the natural forum stage, and the court "say[s] no more" about the gateway stage, so the split stands. For (submit): per Shen Sophie, it weeds out claims bound to fail at trial, and the court must locate the tort anyway, the place of the tort being prima facie the natural forum (JIO). Against: per Shen Sophie, nothing in (f) requires locating the lex loci delicti, and the requirement forces expert evidence of foreign law early. Per Yeo, weeding out weak claims is the serious-question filter's job, so keep choice of law for the trial. Safe course: plead actionability under Singapore law and the foreign law (C3), and flag the controversy.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Defamatory Blog and the Unknown Foreign Tort

A Singapore restaurateur sues a Thai food blogger for a post written and uploaded in Bangkok that accused the restaurant of using expired ingredients. Thai law (proved) treats the post as actionable criminal and civil defamation. Singapore law might treat it as fair comment.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Characterisation: whether this is a "tort" for (f) is for Singapore choice of law (double actionability with the Rickshaw flexible exception). At the gateway (±): (+) (IM Skaugen (HC); Shen Sophie): the restaurateur must show a good arguable case of actionability under both Singapore and Thai law. This filters out claims bound to fail, and the court has to locate the tort anyway, since the place of the tort is prima facie the natural forum (JIO). (−) (Nippon Catalyst; Yeo): double actionability concerns fairness at trial, not locating the forum; (f) does not require identifying the lex loci delicti; and front-loading Thai expert evidence is wasteful, because the serious-question filter already weeds out weak claims. Safe course: plead actionability under both laws and flag the split. If fair comment defeats the claim under Singapore law, the restaurateur argues the flexible exception applies Thai law alone (C3).

Rule ((f)(i) act or omission here): The tort, wherever committed, is constituted at least in part by an act or omission in Singapore. Internet: per Chen v BHNV, posting or sending occurs where the defendant was based at the time. Omission: per IM Skaugen (HC), it occurs where the person who failed to act was, not where the effect of the failure was felt. Misrepresentation abroad: per Chong (AY23-24 feedback), where the misrepresentation was made abroad, use (f)(ii), not (f)(i), with (n) in the alternative.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Where Did It Happen?
  1. The Thai blogger above uploads the post while visiting Singapore.
  2. A Norwegian engineer, working from Oslo, fails to send a safety warning about a crane to a Singapore shipyard; the crane collapses in Singapore.
  3. A Dubai seller makes misrepresentations at a meeting in Dubai to a Singapore buyer, who then pays from Singapore.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  1. Posting occurs where the defendant was based when she posted (Chen v BHNV). If she uploaded while in Singapore, (f)(i) is available.
  2. The omission occurs where the engineer was (Oslo), not where the effect was felt (IM Skaugen (HC)). (f)(i) fails, so use (f)(ii) for the damage suffered here.
  3. The misrepresentation was made in Dubai, so per Chong, plead (f)(ii) (damage here), not (f)(i), with (n) in the alternative.

Rule ((f)(ii) damage here, threshold): The claim is founded on, or seeks damages for, damage suffered in Singapore. Per IM Skaugen (CA), not all the damage need be here, but it must not be "merely trivial". Contrast Nippon Catalyst (followed in Vibrant Group), which requires it to be "significant". Damage, not its effects: per IM Skaugen (CA), distinguish the financial act of incurring the loss from its end result felt here by the claimant, which does not suffice. Not enough: per Nippon Catalyst, that the claimant is a Singapore entity with a Singapore account into which the defendant failed to pay; per Lakshmi Anil Salgaocar v Chilton, legal fees incurred here on the service-out application itself.

Rule ((f)(ii) scope of recovery): Per C&Y, a claim founded on damage (damage as a constituent element) lets the claimant recover all its losses, including those abroad; a claim for damages recovers only the Singapore damage. Effects felt here: per C&Y, whether effects merely felt in Singapore can found a nexus under the non-exhaustive list "remains to be seen"; if so, the claimant recovers only Singapore damage. Merits-engaging: a good arguable case of a tortious act or damage here subsumes requirement (c).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Fraudulent Fund Manager

A Singapore company invested US$10m in a Cayman fund on the strength of a fraudulent pitch delivered in London. It wired the money from its Singapore account to the Cayman fund's Swiss bank. The fund collapsed. The company's Singapore shareholders lost the value of their shares, and the company paid S$50,000 in Singapore legal fees for the service-out application.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Where was the damage suffered? Per IM Skaugen (CA), distinguish the incurring of loss (parting with the money, arguably when the Singapore account was debited) from the end-result effects felt here (a poorer Singapore company and unhappy shareholders). The effects do not suffice. That the company is a Singapore entity with a Singapore account is not enough on its own (Nippon Catalyst), and the legal fees for the application obviously do not count (Lakshmi). The company argues that the debit of its Singapore account is the damage, and that it is more than "merely trivial" (IM Skaugen (CA), the lower threshold) and indeed "significant" (Nippon Catalyst; Vibrant Group, the higher one). Scope: deceit is founded on damage (damage is an element), so if (f)(ii) is satisfied, the company recovers all its losses, wherever suffered (C&Y). If it relied only on effects felt here (an open question under the non-exhaustive list), recovery would be limited to Singapore damage. Merits: a good arguable case of damage here also satisfies requirement (c).

Rule (statutory localisation): Per Online Safety (Relief and Accountability) Act 2025 s 101, a Part 10–12 tort is treated as committed in Singapore if any element was initiated in or from Singapore, was perceived here, or caused harm here, which carries an online claim into (f). Defamation: per Week 4 materials, each publication is a separate tort, and few foreign-publication claims clear the nexus and forum hurdles (C3).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Deepfake Video

A US-based anonymous account posts a deepfake intimate video of a Singapore influencer. It is viewed by her followers in Singapore and Malaysia. Separately, a defamatory article about her is published in a Malaysian newspaper with a small Singapore readership.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

If the deepfake claim is a Part 10–12 statutory tort under the Online Safety (Relief and Accountability) Act 2025, s 101 treats it as committed in Singapore because it was perceived here and caused harm here, so it falls within (f). For the defamation claim, each publication is a separate tort. The Singapore publication (downloads and readership here) can found (f)(i), but recovery is confined to that publication, and with a small readership the claim may struggle on nexus and forum (C3).

Factors (g)–(i): Property

Rule: (g) possession of or title to immovable property in Singapore, but not unpaid rent (Agnew v Usher). (h) e.g., enforcing a trustee's duty to account for the sale proceeds of local land held on trust, even though the land has already been sold (Stype Investments), or an assignee's repairing covenant (Tassell v Hallen). (i) a debt secured on immovables, or rights in movables in Singapore, including beneficial ownership of shares in a Singapore company (Goodwill Enterprise). Cryptoassets: per Cheong Jun Yoong v Three Arrows, there being no settled rule, there is a good arguable case that cryptoassets are located where the person controlling the private key resides (residence, not domicile, best showing control). Status: the Appellate Division did not decide the point, since factor (p) was independently made out and the claimant needed only one factor.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Absent Landlord, Trustee and Crypto Holder
  1. A Singapore tenant sues an Australian landlord for possession of a Holland Village shophouse; another claim is only for unpaid rent.
  2. A Singapore beneficiary sues a trustee who now lives in Canada to account for the proceeds of a Bukit Timah bungalow sold in 2023.
  3. A claimant asserts beneficial ownership of shares in a Singapore company registered in the name of a Hong Kong nominee.
  4. A claimant sues a Dubai resident for the return of stolen USDT held in a wallet whose private key the defendant controls from Dubai. Separately, the claimant says the theft occurred through a Singapore-based platform.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  1. Possession falls within (g). Unpaid rent alone does not (Agnew v Usher), so it needs another factor.
  2. (h) covers the trustee's duty to account for the proceeds of Singapore land, even though the land has been sold (Stype Investments).
  3. (i) covers beneficial ownership of shares in a Singapore company (Goodwill Enterprise).
  4. Under Three Arrows there is a good arguable case that the USDT is located where the private-key controller resides (Dubai), so (i) fails. But (p) (the cause of action arising in Singapore through the Singapore platform) may be made out independently, as it was in Three Arrows, which is why the Appellate Division did not decide the crypto location point.

Factor (j): Trusts; (k)–(l) Estates and Administration

Rule: (j) the claimant seeks to execute the trusts of a written instrument that ought to be executed according to Singapore law, against the defendant as trustee. Per C&Y, the trust property need not be in Singapore, so an absconding trustee cannot escape by removing assets. Governing law: absent an express choice, the law with the closest and most real connection governs the trust (Trisuryo Garuda); a modern deed may let it change where a successor trustee operates elsewhere (Ivanishvili v Credit Suisse). (k) administration of the estate of a person who died domiciled in Singapore. (l) an administration action within O 32 ROC concerning the estate or trust.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Runaway Trustee

A family trust deed, with no express governing law, was drafted in Singapore for Singapore beneficiaries, with a Singapore trustee. The trustee moved all trust assets to Jersey and then emigrated to New Zealand. A successor trustee was later appointed in Jersey under a clause allowing the "proper law to change to the law of the place of administration".

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

(j) applies if the trust "ought to be executed according to Singapore law". With no express choice, the closest and most real connection (Trisuryo Garuda) is with Singapore (the drafting, the beneficiaries, the original trustee). The trustee cannot escape by moving the assets to Jersey: the property need not be in Singapore (C&Y). (−) But the deed allows the proper law to change. Per Ivanishvili v Credit Suisse, the appointment of a Jersey successor trustee may have moved the governing law to Jersey, which would take the trust outside (j). If the settlor died domiciled in Singapore, (k) would also cover administration of the estate, and (l) any O 32 administration action.

Factor (m): Enforcement of Judgment or Award

Rule: The claimant sues on a foreign judgment or award against a judgment debtor abroad. Per C&Y, "judgment" means a foreign judgment enforceable by common law action, in executable form (Karaha Bodas). Outside (m): per C&Y, local judgments and judgments registrable under REFJA or RECJA, where notice of registration can be served on the debtor abroad without permission (J7). No pre-judgment Mareva: per Karaha Bodas (following Mercedes-Benz v Leiduck), (m) cannot found a Mareva over the defendant's local assets in anticipation of a judgment not yet obtained. Forum: per Licea v Curacao Drydock, forum conveniens is irrelevant to an enforcement action, which is not a fresh suit against the debtor. Assets: per Demirel, assets in Singapore are not required, but the claimant must show a real prospect of a legitimate benefit. Per C&Y, filter by forum conveniens or by legitimate benefit, not both (J7).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Three Judgments and a Freeze
  1. A Brazilian money judgment (Brazil is not a REFJA country) against a Brazilian debtor who has no Singapore assets but is expected to receive a large payment from a Singapore buyer next year.
  2. A Hong Kong judgment registrable under REFJA.
  3. A creditor expects to win a New York judgment next month and wants a Mareva now over the debtor's Singapore account, relying on (m).
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  1. Within (m): a final foreign money judgment enforceable by common law action. Forum conveniens is irrelevant (Licea). Singapore assets are not required (Demirel), but the creditor must show a real prospect of a legitimate benefit, which the expected payment from the Singapore buyer arguably provides. Use forum conveniens or legitimate benefit as the filter, not both (C&Y).
  2. Outside (m): register it under REFJA instead, and the notice of registration can be served abroad without permission (J7).
  3. Fails. There is no judgment yet, and (m) cannot found a free-standing pre-judgment Mareva (Karaha Bodas, following Mercedes-Benz v Leiduck).

Factor (n): Claims Under Written Law

Rule: The claim is made under a section of a Singapore Act. Per Li Shengwu, "any other written law" bears its plain meaning: no genus unites the CDSA and TSOFA beyond serious crimes, so ejusdem generis is rejected, and "any" means any Singapore statute. Applied: the AG's committal claim fell within (n) as a claim under s 7(1) SCJA, not a tangential statutory reference. The over-expansion objection: per Li Shengwu (obiter, as read by C&Y), a claimant could in principle rely on s 18(1) with para 14 of the First Schedule (power to grant "all reliefs and remedies at law and in equity") for almost any civil claim. Answer: the risk is "more illusory than real": the claimant still needs a good arguable case that the facts justify those powers, and Singapore must still be forum conveniens, so a claim lacking a Singapore connection will in all likelihood be set aside. But: per Li Shengwu, s 18 and the First Schedule confer powers and reliefs, not subject-matter jurisdiction, which is "the critical difference" from s 7, relied on by the AG.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Statutory Claims
  1. A Singapore consumer sues a Hong Kong online retailer under the CPFTA for unfair practices.
  2. The AG seeks committal of a US-resident academic for a Facebook post scandalising the Singapore judiciary, under s 7(1) SCJA (pre-AJPA facts).
  3. A claimant with a pure Thai contract claim argues it can use (n) because s 18(1) and para 14 of the First Schedule SCJA give the court power to grant "all reliefs and remedies".
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  1. "Any other written law" means any Singapore statute (Li Shengwu), so a CPFTA claim falls within (n).
  2. As in Li Shengwu, the committal claim is made under s 7(1) SCJA, a statute conferring the contempt power, so it falls within (n). Today, cite (t) first (J3.1.2 below).
  3. In principle (obiter in Li Shengwu, as C&Y read it), s 18(1) with para 14 might make (n) cover almost any claim. But the risk is "more illusory than real": the claimant must show a good arguable case that the facts engage those powers, and that Singapore is forum conveniens. A pure Thai contract claim will almost certainly fail at the forum stage. Also note the "critical difference": s 18 and Sch 1 confer powers, not jurisdiction (unlike s 7).

Factor (o): Restitution or Fiduciary

Rule: Per Chen v BHNV, two conjunctive requirements: the claim is restitutionary, or against the defendant as trustee or fiduciary; and the defendant's liability arises out of an act (e.g., receipt of the funds) done in Singapore. Scope: per C&Y, a quantum meruit qualifies only if it rests on unjust enrichment, not contract (Rabiah Bee). Equitable compensation, an account of profits and a constructive trust are covered.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Mistaken Payment

A Singapore company mistakenly pays S$2m into the Singapore account of a Malaysian supplier. The supplier's director in Johor transfers it out. Separately, a Singapore-based director of the claimant, now living in Indonesia, took a secret profit from a deal concluded in Singapore.

  • Variation: a quantum meruit claim for work done under an existing contract with a Thai company.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

The mistaken-payment claim is restitutionary, and the defendant's liability arises from receipt in Singapore (the Singapore account), so both limbs of (o) are met (Chen v BHNV). The secret profit claim is against a fiduciary for an act (the deal) done in Singapore, so it is covered, as are an account of profits and a constructive trust.

  • In the variation, a quantum meruit resting on the contract is contractual, not restitutionary, so it falls outside (o) (Rabiah Bee); use (d) instead.

Factor (p): Cause of Action Arose in Singapore

Rule: Per Kishinchand (applied in Vibrant Group), ask where in substance the cause of action arose. Per IM Skaugen (CA), this is a fact-centric review of all material facts. Per Li Shengwu, it is where "the essential factual material" arose. Per C&Y, the difference between these formulations is negligible, and not all the facts need arise here. Application (Kishinchand): the beneficiary's location on acquiring the interest and the trustee's location at vesting were insignificant; where the claimant gave instructions, and the trust's purpose (operating an overseas account for a Singapore business), located the cause of action here. Not a cause of action: per Li Shengwu, a committal application is quasi-criminal, not founded on a civil "cause of action", so the AG could not use (p).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Swiss Account for the Singapore Business

A Singapore businessman, Raj, asked his cousin in Geneva to open and hold a Swiss bank account on trust for Raj's Singapore trading business. Raj gave all instructions from Singapore. The cousin (now in Geneva) refuses to account. The cousin argues the trust arose when he signed the account documents in Geneva.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

As in Kishinchand, where in substance the cause of action arose is not fixed by where the trustee signed or where the beneficial interest vested. Those are insignificant. The essential factual material (Li Shengwu) is that Raj gave instructions from Singapore and the trust's purpose was to operate an account for a Singapore business. On a fact-centric review (IM Skaugen (CA)), the cause of action arose in Singapore, even though not every fact did. (p) is merits-engaging, so the serious question is subsumed.

Factor (q): Contribution or Indemnity; (r) Submission or Agreement to Submit; (s) Written Law

Rule (q): Per Ang Ming Chuang, a claim for contribution or indemnity in respect of a liability enforceable by proceedings in Singapore against the defendant. Per C&Y, if the claim derives from a Singapore statute, (s) is also available.

Rule (r): The claim concerns "matters in which the defendant has submitted or agreed to submit". Per C&Y, submission by a step in the Singapore proceedings founds jurisdiction anyway, so (r) is mainly used for agreement, where the contract neither provides a local method of service nor allows service out (otherwise O 8 r 1(3)). Agreement ≠ submission: per Shanghai Turbo (CA), a Singapore EJC or NEJC is an agreement to submit, satisfying (r) and (d)(iv); submission itself is the defendant's conduct in the proceedings under s 16(1)(b) (J2.2). (r) or (d)(iv)? Per C&Y, (r) does not limit the kinds of claim; the agreement does, its scope construed under its proper law. So (r) carries a tort or restitution claim within the clause (J1.5), whereas (d) needs a claim in respect of the contract. Neutral: prove (c) separately; the forum limb falls away in practice, since the defendant's objection to Singapore is itself a breach (J3.2).

Rule (s): Per Li Shengwu and C&Y, this is confined to Singapore written law. A claim enforces a statute only where (i) the statute gives a right to bring the claim, or (ii) it is brought for contravention of a statutory rule with prescribed consequences. Power-conferring provisions: per Li Shengwu, it is "incongruous" to speak of enforcing them, so a claim under an Act that grants a right qualifies, but a committal application does not, its purpose being to protect the administration of justice.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Construction Chain and the Clause
  1. A Singapore main contractor is sued in Singapore by the owner for defective piling. It wants to bring in the Korean piling subcontractor (abroad) for contribution.
  2. The Korean subcontractor's subcontract contains: "The Subcontractor submits to the non-exclusive jurisdiction of the Singapore courts" for "all disputes in connection with this Subcontract". The main contractor's claim is in tort (negligent misstatement about soil tests).
  3. The owner also has a statutory claim under the Building Control Act for contravention of a rule with prescribed consequences.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  1. (q): a contribution claim in respect of a liability (to the owner) enforceable by proceedings in Singapore against the main contractor (Ang Ming Chuang). If the contribution right derives from the Civil Law Act, (s) is also arguable.
  2. (r) over (d)(iv): the clause is an agreement to submit (Shanghai Turbo (CA)). Because (r) is not limited to contract claims, and the clause's own scope ("in connection with") covers the tort claim (J1.5), (r) carries the tort claim. (d)(iv) would need a claim "in respect of" the subcontract. (r) is neutral, so show a serious question separately. On forum, if the subcontractor objects, that is itself a breach of the NEJC's waiver, so it bears strong cause (J3.2).
  3. (s): a claim for contravention of a statutory rule with prescribed consequences enforces Singapore written law, so (s) is available. Contrast a committal application, which seeks to vindicate a power, so it is not "enforcement" (Li Shengwu).

Factors (t)–(u): Committal and Pre-Action Disclosure

Rule: Per PD para 63(3)(t), a committal order under O 23. Per (u), production of documents or information to identify possible parties, trace property before proceedings, or in the interests of justice. Effect: the Li Shengwu problem (no "cause of action" under (p), and no "enforcement" under (s)) now has its own factor, so the claimant cites (t) first and (n) in the alternative for a committal.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Anonymous Scammer

A Singapore victim of a phishing scam wants (i) a US-based exchange to disclose who controls the wallet receiving the stolen funds, and (ii) later, committal of a London-based defendant for breaching a Singapore injunction.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

(i) falls within (u): production of information to identify possible parties and trace property before proceedings. (ii) falls within (t), a committal order under O 23, with (n) in the alternative (as in Li Shengwu). (p) and (s) are not needed and would fail for the reasons in Li Shengwu.

Fallback: The Non-Exhaustive List (must write)

Rule: Per the CJC Report and C&Y, para 63(3) is non-exhaustive, so approval may be given even though the claim falls outside a restrictive reading, provided sufficient nexus is shown (e.g., the defendant has substantial assets here, or the transaction was structured through Singapore). Query (evaluative): per AK Investment, not every listed factor shows a nexus at all (gateway (c); also (a) property unrelated to the claim); weak links are filtered through forum. Conversely, per Yeo, a claim within a listed factor probably has sufficient nexus. Restraint: per C&Y, how far courts will go remains to be seen; keeping the old heads may signal self-restraint, so argue the closest listed factor first.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Deal Structured Through Singapore

A Vietnamese buyer and an Indonesian seller of coal both used a Singapore escrow agent and a Singapore bank to close their deal, and the seller holds S$20m in a Singapore account. The buyer sues the seller for misrepresentation (made in Jakarta, with loss in Vietnam).

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Argue the closest listed factor first: (a) (property here, which need not relate to the claim) and possibly (f)(ii) (weak, as the loss was in Vietnam). Then, in any event, the non-exhaustive fallback: the transaction was structured through Singapore (escrow, bank) and the seller has substantial assets here, which together give sufficient nexus. Weak links are then filtered at the forum stage (AK Investment). C&Y caution that the courts' appetite for the fallback "remains to be seen".

Pattern: Negative Declaration That No Contract Exists

Rule: Where the claimant seeks a declaration that no contract was concluded with the defendant, which is suing on it abroad:

  • Usable (1): (d)(i), if the negotiations were conducted and concluded here, needing only a good arguable case of the connection; (d)(iii), if the putative proper law of the alleged contract is Singapore law (Lew v Nargolwala; C2).
  • Usable (2): (p), arguably, reading "cause of action" generously, if the formation events occurred here; (n), through para 14 of the First Schedule (Li Shengwu) for the declaration.
  • Not usable: (e) (the claimant alleges no breach; the breach claim is the defendant's, abroad); (c) (no anchor defendant); (b) (an ASI against the foreign proceedings is separate: J6); (s) (no Singapore statute).
  • Then: none of these engages the merits of the declaration, so state the serious question separately, and the case is won or lost on forum (J4.2).
  • Clause in a related contract: where a concluded contract between the parties has a Singapore EJC wide enough to catch the dealings, the defendant's forum objection is a breach requiring strong cause (Bunge; J3.2).
  • Infection: but a claimant who says no contract was concluded must meet the infection point before relying on that contract's clause (J1.6).
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
"We Never Agreed"

Merlion Metals Pte Ltd negotiated, at meetings in Singapore, a draft nickel supply contract with Kazakh Mining JSC, with a draft Singapore governing law clause. Merlion says it never accepted the final draft. Kazakh Mining sues Merlion in Almaty for US$30m for breach. Merlion seeks a Singapore declaration that no contract exists and wants to serve Kazakh Mining. Separately, the parties have an older, concluded 2020 framework agreement with a Singapore EJC covering "all dealings between the parties in nickel".

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Usable factors: (d)(i): the negotiations were conducted (and, on Kazakh Mining's case, concluded) here, and Merlion needs only a good arguable case of that connection, not of the contract's existence. (d)(iii): the putative proper law of the alleged contract is Singapore law (the draft clause; Lew v Nargolwala). (p), arguably, because the formation events occurred here. (n), via para 14 of the First Schedule (Li Shengwu).
  • Not usable: (e), because Merlion alleges no breach (the breach claim is Kazakh Mining's, in Almaty); (c), because there is no anchor defendant; (b), because an ASI against the Almaty suit is a separate matter (J6); (s), because no statute is involved.
  • Serious question: none of the factors engages the merits of the declaration, so Merlion shows it separately. The case is likely won or lost on forum (J4.2), where the Almaty proceedings weigh heavily.
  • The 2020 EJC: if the framework agreement's clause is wide enough to catch these dealings, Kazakh Mining's forum objection is a breach, so it bears strong cause (Bunge; J3.2). There is no infection problem for that clause, because Merlion does not deny the 2020 agreement. If Merlion were relying on a clause in the disputed contract, it would have to meet the infection point (J1.6).

J3.1.3 Requirement (b): Singapore Is Forum Conveniens

Rule: The claimant must show Singapore is clearly the more appropriate forum (Spiliada; AK Investment). Being merely as appropriate as the foreign forum is not enough (Sudarga). Flag: per Oro Negro, Singapore need only be "on balance" the more appropriate forum, "whether by a hair or by a mile" (Siemens); cite both and argue the facts in the alternative. Burden: per Zoom, the Spiliada test is the same as on a stay; only the burden differs. It stays on the claimant both without notice and on the defendant's set-aside application; only a stay after valid service puts stage 1 on the defendant. Run J4.2 with the stage 1 factors (J4.1.2), the SICC factor (J4.4) and stage 2 (J4.1.3).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Evenly Balanced Case

A Singapore claimant sues a Philippine defendant over a contract governed by Singapore law and performed in Manila. The witnesses are split evenly between Singapore and Manila.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

On Sudarga/AK Investment, the claimant must show Singapore is clearly more appropriate; if the factors are evenly balanced, Singapore is merely as appropriate, and approval fails. On Oro Negro, Singapore need only be more appropriate "on balance", "whether by a hair or by a mile" (Siemens), so the Singapore governing law may tip the balance. Cite both standards and argue in the alternative. The burden stays on the claimant at the without-notice and set-aside stages (Zoom).

Rule (If stage 1 fails, second bite?): Unsettled. Per Konamaneni and Allenger, failure is "the end of the matter", since otherwise the court would confer jurisdiction where none was established. Per Spiliada itself, Yeo and Shen Sophie, the claimant may still show substantial injustice abroad. Open: Oro Negro and IM Skaugen (CA) left it open (Chong). Per C&Y, stage 2 should apply to the claimant, O 8 having expanded jurisdiction (J4.2). Service in v out: whether Spiliada arises after service in or out changes the burden, the stage 2 debate, and the weight given to jurisdiction founded as of right. Jurisdiction agreement: where a party is in breach, strong cause on that party replaces this inquiry (J3.2; J4.3).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Dissident's Claim

A Singapore company owned by a dissident from Ruritania sues a Ruritanian state-linked company. Ruritania is clearly the more appropriate forum on connecting factors (stage 1 fails for the claimant). But the claimant has cogent evidence that it would not receive a fair trial in Ruritania.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

(−) The defendant relies on Konamaneni and Allenger: stage 1 failure on service out is the end of the matter, because otherwise the court would create jurisdiction that was never established. (+) The claimant relies on Spiliada itself, Yeo, Shen Sophie and C&Y: stage 2 (substantial injustice abroad) should still be available, especially now that O 8 has expanded jurisdiction. Oro Negro and IM Skaugen (CA) left the point open. Argue both; on these facts, the case for a second bite is at its strongest.

J3.1.4 Requirement (c): Serious Question to Be Tried

Rule: Subsumed (+): per Bradley Lomas (adopted in Li Shengwu and C&Y; also IM Skaugen (CA)), where the gateway itself engages the merits, a good arguable case on it clears the lower merits bar, so (c) need not be shown separately. Examples: (e) a breach committed here; (f) a tortious act, omission or damage here; (p) the cause of action arising here. Proved separately (−): where the gateway is a neutral connecting factor, (c) is a distinct hurdle: (a) and (r) expressly, and on the same logic (d) and (c); for a negative declaration, (n) and (p) too. Standard: per Seaconsar (cited in AK Investment), a substantial question of fact or law that the claimant bona fide wishes to try, i.e. not frivolous or vexatious (e.g., prima facie evidence of breach, or documented loss). Time bar: per Recovery Vehicle 1, a time-barred claim cannot meet the merits requirement, so check the applicable limitation period (FLPA; C1). Fact and law: per Bradley Lomas, on fact the court looks primarily at the claimant's case and does not try disputes on affidavit, though the defendant may show the evidence is incomplete or plainly wrong. On law, the court may go fully into the issue and refuse approval if the claimant's case is bound to fail. But: per AK Investment, it will not decide a controversial question of law in a developing area on hypothetical facts, unless the point goes to the existence of jurisdiction. Purpose: per American Cyanamid and Seaconsar, it screens out frivolous or vexatious claims against foreign defendants; it is a merits filter, and the court does not decide difficult questions of law at this stage.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Two Gateways, Two Merits Burdens

Pearl Fisheries (J3.0) relies on (e) (breach in Singapore) and, alternatively, (d)(iii) (Singapore law). Andaman says: (1) the tuna was perfectly frozen when loaded, supported by a Thai inspection certificate; (2) Pearl's claim is time-barred under Thai law, which Andaman says applies to limitation as a substantive matter under the FLPA; (3) whether a CIF buyer can sue for deterioration in transit is a developing area of law.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Under (e): a good arguable case of breach in Singapore engages the merits, so (c) is subsumed (Bradley Lomas). Under (d)(iii): the factor is neutral, so Pearl must separately show a serious question (a substantial, bona fide question that is not frivolous: Seaconsar), e.g., the survey report showing rotten tuna on arrival.
  • (1) Factual dispute: the court looks primarily at Pearl's evidence and does not try the conflict on affidavit, but Andaman may show that Pearl's evidence is plainly wrong or incomplete (Bradley Lomas).
  • (2) Time bar: this is a question of law that the court may decide now. If the claim is time-barred under the applicable law (FLPA characterises foreign limitation as substantive: C1), it cannot meet the merits threshold (Recovery Vehicle 1).
  • (3) Developing law: the court will not decide a controversial point in a developing area on hypothetical facts (AK Investment), unless it goes to the existence of jurisdiction. So Pearl passes the serious-question filter, whose purpose is only to screen out frivolous claims (American Cyanamid; Seaconsar).

J3.1.5 Service Out Without the Court's Approval (O 8 r 1(3))

Rule: Per O 8 r 1(3), approval "is not required if service out of Singapore is allowed under a contract between the parties". Basis: per C&Y, party autonomy; an incremental step from the old O 10 r 3 (a contractual local method of service, even on an overseas defendant, for claims under that contract). Scope: per C&Y, it presumably applies where the parties submitted to Singapore by contract and the contract permits service out; a bare Singapore clause with no service provision must go through r 1(1) (J3.2). SICC contrast: it mirrors SICC Rules O 5 r 6(2) (J5.2.4), but not exactly: r 1(3) asks for a contract allowing service, not a choice of court agreement.

Rule (NW Corp, read widely): Per NW Corp, a clause choosing English law, referring disputes to the Singapore courts and providing for "service of process by registered mail" fell within r 1(3), so posting the originating process to the defendant in Hong Kong needed no approval. Reasons: the rule says "out of", not "outside", Singapore, so no place of service need be named; a contract "allows" service out if it agrees to service of Singapore process on a foreign defendant not ordinarily here. Purpose: r 1(3) spares the claimant a redundant approval where the defendant has consented to jurisdiction being founded by service, consistent with the Ideals of expedition and efficiency. Context: the clause named the Singapore courts in the same breath, and the contract recorded the defendant's Hong Kong place of business, so "service of process" could only mean service of Singapore process abroad.
