Rule (What "allowed" means, Yeo, evaluative): Three readings: the contract allows (i) an agreed method that can work in or out of Singapore; (ii) a method expressly or impliedly usable for service out; or (iii) service out without prior approval. Choice: (i) clashes with O 8 r 2(1)(a), which contemplates service out "in the manner agreed" after approval, so a bare agreed method is not enough. (ii) is most persuasive, since the defendant cannot claim surprise. (iii) fits party autonomy and differs little from (ii). Rationale: an agreement allowing service out is an implied agreement to submit, so the defendant's submission may be qualified (e.g., by a reservation of objections). GD v SICC (Yeo): agreeing to SICC jurisdiction alone allows service out without approval (SICC Rules O 5 r 6(2)(a)), but agreeing only to General Division jurisdiction does not, even in a Hague case; Yeo argues the latter should also suffice.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Three Service Clauses
  1. "This Agreement is governed by English law. Disputes shall be referred to the courts of Singapore. Service of process may be effected by registered mail to the addresses in Schedule 1." (Schedule 1 lists the defendant's Hong Kong office.)
  2. "Notices under this Agreement may be given by email to the addresses in Schedule 1." (There is no jurisdiction clause.)
  3. "The courts of Singapore shall have exclusive jurisdiction." (There is no service clause; the case is within the CCAA.)
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  1. As in NW Corp, r 1(3) applies. "Out of" Singapore requires no named place; the clause names the Singapore courts in the same breath and the contract records a Hong Kong address, so "service of process" can only mean service of Singapore process abroad. The claimant posts the claim to Hong Kong with no approval.
  2. A notices clause is not an agreement allowing service of process out. Yeo rejects reading (i), that a bare agreed method is enough, because it clashes with O 8 r 2(1)(a) (service "in the manner agreed" after approval). On his preferred reading (ii), the method must be usable for service out, and a notices clause is not. Approval under r 1(1) is needed, though the email method may then be used as the mode.
  3. A bare Singapore clause with no service provision does not "allow service out". Go through r 1(1) on the "has the jurisdiction" ground (CCAA). Yeo argues this is anomalous: an SICC clause alone would permit service without permission (SICC O 5 r 6(2)(a)), and a General Division choice in a Hague case should too.

Rule (Consequence for the defendant): Per NW Corp, service under r 1(3) founds jurisdiction without approval, so the defendant cannot dispute its existence, only its exercise on natural forum grounds, where the burden is its own (J4.1). Clause naming Singapore: where the contract also names the Singapore courts, the defendant's forum challenge is itself a breach, so it must show strong cause (J3.2; J4.3). Related routes: where the agreed mode is service in Singapore, it is service in under O 7 r 2(1)(d) (COSCO). Per C&Y, r 2(1)(d) is looser than old O 10 r 3: the action need not relate to the contract containing the agreed method, and the agreement need not be a contract (no consideration is needed). Solicitors: where the defendant instructs Singapore solicitors to accept service, it is treated as service in (C&Y), better analysed as submission (Yeo; J2.2.2). Per C&Y, the practical difference between service in by agreement and r 1(3) is now small.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Hong Kong Defendant Fights Back

In Clause 1 above, the Hong Kong defendant applies to set aside service, arguing there is no gateway and Hong Kong is the natural forum.

  • Variation: the contract instead says "Process may be served on the Defendant's Singapore agent, Kwan & Co", and the claim is in tort, unrelated to the contract.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Because service was validly effected under r 1(3), jurisdiction exists, so there is no gateway question to argue (NW Corp). The defendant can only seek a stay (exercise), bearing the burden. And because the clause also refers disputes to the Singapore courts, its forum challenge breaches the clause, so it must show strong cause (J4.3).

  • In the variation, service on Kwan & Co in Singapore is service in by agreed mode (O 7 r 2(1)(d); COSCO). Unlike old O 10 r 3, r 2(1)(d) does not require that the action relate to the contract containing the agreed method, so the tort claim is fine (C&Y). Yeo would analyse this as submission.

J3.1.6 Mode of Service: The Hierarchy of Service

Rule (two sequential steps, must write): Per Beranek, ask first about the right to serve the defendant, then about the mode of serving the originating process. Right: if the defendant is present here, service is as of right (s 16(1)(a)(i)); if absent, only through O 8, by approval (r 1(1)) or agreement (r 1(3)). Mode: personal service (O 6 r 4, per C&Y), or, if that is impracticable, substituted service (O 7 r 7, per Yeo) or dispensation with personal service (O 7 r 1(2), per Xu Xiangrong).

Rule (Consistel: the hierarchy): Per Consistel, where the defendant left Singapore before the originating process was issued, the claimant must first seek permission to serve out; substituted service arises only if personal service is impracticable: "a hierarchy of service which must be adhered to". Reasons: personal service is not impracticable merely because the defendant is abroad; comity requires circumspection over an absent defendant; otherwise the claimant would bypass the court's scrutiny of forum conveniens, making the service-out rules otiose. Not retrospective: that substituted service in fact brought the claim to the defendant's notice does not validate it after the event. Exceptions (±): substituted service without first serving out is allowed where the defendant (i) left Singapore to evade service (Re Urquhart), or (ii) moves constantly between countries, so personal service is futile (Ng Swee Hong). Applied: neither applied in Consistel: the defendants had long lived in the UAE, made enquiries when told of the attempted service, and were not peripatetic. Status: Beranek doubted the exceptions, but it is an AR decision and Consistel is High Court, so per Chong, both sides should follow Consistel.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Email Shortcut

A Singapore lender sues two former directors of a borrower: (A) Mr Haddad, who moved to Dubai in 2019 and has lived there openly since, and (B) Ms Volkov, who flew out of Singapore the day after receiving a letter of demand and has since been seen in Bali, Phuket, Tbilisi and Istanbul. The lender obtains an order for substituted service by email in Singapore on both, without seeking approval to serve out. Both emails are read.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Step 1 is the right to serve. Both directors are absent, so the right exists only through O 8 (Beranek). Step 2 is mode. Per Consistel, the lender had to seek permission to serve out first; substituted service is a mode for when personal service is impracticable, and being abroad does not make it impracticable. That the emails were read does not cure the defect retrospectively.

  • Haddad: like the Consistel defendants, a long-term, settled UAE resident, so neither exception applies. Service is set aside.
  • Volkov (±): she arguably left to evade service (Re Urquhart) and moves constantly between countries (Ng Swee Hong). Both Consistel exceptions are arguable, so substituted service without first serving out may stand. Beranek doubted the exceptions, but it is only an AR decision, so follow Consistel.

Rule (Substituted service out): Per Janesh s/o Rajkumar ("CHEFPIERRE"), the court may order substituted service out of jurisdiction on an unknown defendant (by email, NFT airdrop or social media), using its inherent power even though no rule expressly provides for it (Yeo). So Janesh goes to the mode, not the right: the claimant still needs approval under O 8 r 1(1), and Consistel is untouched.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Anonymous NFT Thief

A Singapore collector's Bored-style NFT is stolen by a hacker known only by a wallet address. The collector obtains approval to serve out under O 8 r 1(1) and then seeks an order to serve by airdropping an NFT containing the claim into the thief's wallet.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

As in Janesh ("CHEFPIERRE"), the court may order substituted service out by NFT airdrop under its inherent power. That concerns the mode. The collector rightly obtained O 8 approval first (the right), so Consistel's hierarchy is respected.

Rule (The shortcut cases, −): Three cases let a claimant reach an absent defendant by service in Singapore:

  • COSCO: service on the defendant's Singapore solicitors, who confirmed their authority to accept service, is service in under O 7 r 2(1)(d) and s 16(1)(a)(i). This is better explained as submission (Yeo) or constructive presence (Beranek).
  • Xu Xiangrong v Fu Xianwei: no approval to serve out is needed before personal service on a foreign defendant is dispensed with, where ordinary service is then effected here (by email to his Singapore solicitors), following Madison Pacific (approval is needed only if the document is served out). Caveat: where the defendant is abroad and has not submitted, the court should still consider forum "for good order", with circumspection given comity towards the foreign State.
  • Malayan Banking v Zhang Zhencheng: a notice of appointment of solicitor filed to challenge jurisdiction is not submission (by parity with O 6 r 12(5)), so the claimant cannot then serve that solicitor. Caveat: the alternative prayer to dispense with personal service, raised only on appeal, was rejected, but a fresh application is not barred.

Evaluation (Chong): Consistel's hierarchy (followed in Beranek) is the correct framework, and COSCO and Malayan Banking are wrong. They and Xu Xiangrong each let the claimant reach an absent defendant while skipping step 1, the scrutiny of nexus and forum. Full and frank disclosure: because the application is without notice, the claimant must disclose matters against approval; material non-disclosure can found a set-aside (Zoom).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Dispensation Route

A Singapore company sues a Chinese individual, Mr Fu, who lives in Shanghai and has never been to Singapore, but who has retained Singapore solicitors for an unrelated matter. The company (a) applies to dispense with personal service and (b) emails the claim to Mr Fu's Singapore solicitors. It never seeks O 8 approval.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

(+) The company relies on Xu Xiangrong (following Madison Pacific): approval is only needed if the document is served out, and here it is served in (by email to Singapore solicitors) after dispensation, so no O 8 approval is needed. Even so, per the Xu caveat, since Mr Fu is abroad and has not submitted, the court should consider forum "for good order", with comity-based circumspection. (−) Mr Fu relies on Consistel and Chong: this is a shortcut that skips step 1 (the right to serve an absent defendant) and so bypasses the nexus and forum scrutiny O 8 requires. Note also that solicitors retained for an unrelated matter, without authority to accept service, are not like the COSCO solicitors; and if they had only filed a notice of appointment to challenge jurisdiction, Malayan Banking says that is not submission. Answer: submit that service should be set aside under the Consistel hierarchy, while acknowledging Xu.

4J3.2 Founding jurisdiction under a jurisdiction agreement where the defendant is abroad

(Where the defendant is served in Singapore as of right, a foreign clause goes only to exercise: J4.0.2.)

Rule (Route): Per Week 9 slides and C&Y, if the contract allows service out, serve without approval (O 8 r 1(3)). Strictly this needs only an agreement to service out, not a choice of court agreement, though the two usually come together. Which ground: otherwise seek approval under O 8 r 1(1). "Has the jurisdiction" is arguably reserved for CCAA cases (J1.3); at common law use "appropriate court" and the three PD para 63(2) requirements. SICC: for an SICC clause, including a post-2016 "Singapore High Court" clause, no permission is needed (SICC Rules O 5 r 6(2)(a)), and exercise is tested under O 2 r 3 (Chong, answer scheme; J5).

Rule (Singapore EJC or NEJC: in principle v in practice, must write): In principle, the claimant must still make out all three requirements, even inter partes. Nexus: the clause itself, under para 63(3)(r) ("agreed to submit") or (d)(iv) (Shanghai Turbo (CA)). In practice, the claimant need only show a good arguable case that the clause is valid, binds the defendant and covers the dispute (J1.5–J1.6), plus a serious question, shown separately because (d)(iv) and (r) are neutral. Forum: need not be proved. If the defendant contests it, that breaches its promise, so per Shanghai Turbo (CA) the defendant bears strong cause (J4.3), whether it challenges existence or exercise. If the defendant never raises forum, the claimant need prove nothing on it.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Shanghai Turbo Pattern Abroad

A Singapore-law share purchase agreement between Singapore buyer Kite Capital and Chinese seller Mr Liu says: "The parties submit to the non-exclusive jurisdiction of the Singapore courts." It has no service clause. Kite sues Mr Liu (in Shanghai) for breach of warranty, and Mr Liu applies to set aside service, arguing (a) the clause does not cover warranty claims, (b) the claim has no merit, and (c) China is the natural forum.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Kite needs approval under O 8 r 1(1) ("appropriate court"), since there is no service clause and the CCAA does not apply to a NEJC. Nexus: the clause itself, under (r) and (d)(iv) (Shanghai Turbo (CA)). Inter partes, Kite bears the burden of showing a good arguable case that the clause is valid, binds Mr Liu and covers warranty claims (attack (a)). Serious question: (r) and (d)(iv) are neutral, so Kite shows a serious question of breach separately (attack (b)). Forum: Kite need not prove Singapore is forum conveniens. Mr Liu's objection (c) is itself a breach of the NEJC's narrow waiver, so Mr Liu must show strong cause (Shanghai Turbo (CA)), whether his challenge is framed as a set-aside or a stay. Had he never raised forum, Kite would have needed to prove nothing on it.

Rule (Singapore clause with no promise under its proper law): First construe the clause under its proper law (J1.1). Per Chong (answer scheme), where the clause, read under Ruritanian law, contains no promise, the defendant breaches nothing by objecting, so the test is plain forum conveniens, with the burden on the claimant. Then: the Singapore clause is only a factor; weigh the governing law against the possibility of transfer to the SICC (J4.4), and raise the Konamaneni stage 2 issue if stage 1 points abroad.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Ruritanian-Law NEJC

Same as above, but the SPA is governed by Ruritanian law, and Mr Liu proves that under Ruritanian law "submit to non-exclusive jurisdiction" carries no waiver of forum objections.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Construed under its proper law, the clause contains no promise not to object, so Mr Liu's objection is no breach. Kite must prove Singapore is clearly the more appropriate forum (J4.2), with the clause as one factor in its favour. Kite can also point to the possibility of transfer to the SICC, where foreign law can be argued by submission, against the Ruritanian governing law factor (J4.4). If stage 1 points to Ruritania, raise the Konamaneni second-bite question (J3.1.3).

Rule (Non-party defendant): Per Chong (AY23-24 feedback), the clause cannot be used to saddle a non-party (e.g., a director) with a burden, and facts far less exceptional than Global Partners v Babcock & Brown do not bring him within its party scope (J1.5). So the claimant must show Singapore is forum conveniens against him, and the SICC has no primary jurisdiction over him, only transfer under SICC Rules O 2 r 4(1)(c) (J5).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Adding the Director

Kite also wants to sue the target company's Shanghai-based director personally for fraudulent misrepresentation. He is not a party to the SPA or its clause.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

The clause cannot put strong cause on the director, because he is a non-party and nothing like the Global Partners facts (named Indemnified Persons who took part in the impugned decisions) brings him within its party scope. Kite must find a gateway for him (e.g., (c) necessary or proper party, if the claims share a common thread, or (f)) and prove Singapore is forum conveniens against him. If the main action is in the SICC, the SICC has no primary jurisdiction over him; he could only come in by transfer under SICC Rules O 2 r 4(1)(c) (J5).

Rule (Inter partes attacks, burden by limb): Nexus ("there is no agreement" / "it is void" / "it does not cover this dispute"): the burden stays on the claimant, because the agreement is the basis of the extraordinary jurisdiction. Serious question: on the claimant, as for any claim. Forum ("Singapore is not forum conveniens") or a stay instead: the defendant is in breach of the EJC or NEJC, so strong cause, with the burden on the defendant. The burden is always on the party seeking release from its promise (Week 9 slides; Shanghai Turbo (CA)).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Attacking Every Limb

In the Kite v Liu scenario, Mr Liu argues: (1) his signature on the SPA was forged, so there is no agreement; (2) the warranty claim is hopeless; (3) China is more convenient.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

(1) goes to nexus, so Kite bears the burden of a good arguable case that the clause exists and binds Mr Liu (J1.6). (2) goes to the serious question, also Kite's burden. (3) goes to forum: if the clause exists, Mr Liu is seeking release from his promise, so he bears strong cause. Each limb carries its own burden.

Rule (Foreign EJC: strong cause on the claimant throughout): A claimant suing in Singapore despite a foreign EJC is in breach. Without notice: it needs a nexus through another factor (the defendant's residence or property here, or a breach or tort here), a serious question, and strong cause in place of forum conveniens. Inter partes: per C&Y and Week 9 slides, the burden on every limb stays on the claimant, and the same holds if the defendant seeks a stay instead of a set-aside. Note the reversal when served in: the defendant applies for the stay, yet the claimant must show strong cause (J4.3). Foreign NEJC: plain Spiliada: the claimant is not in breach (Shanghai Turbo; J1.1), so the forum limb is ordinary Spiliada, with the clause carrying little weight. Burden: on a set-aside (existence), the claimant must show Singapore is clearly forum conveniens (J4.2); on a stay (exercise), the defendant bears stage 1 (J4.1).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Tokyo Clause

A Singapore buyer sues a Japanese seller despite "exclusive jurisdiction of the Tokyo District Court" (Japan is not an HCCCA party, so the CCAA does not apply).

  • Version 1: The seller is in Tokyo, and the buyer seeks approval to serve out.
  • Version 2: The seller's CEO is served in Singapore while the seller has a permanent Singapore branch (service in), and the seller applies for a stay.
  • Version 3: The clause is instead "non-exclusive jurisdiction of the Tokyo District Court".
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Version 1: The clause cannot be the nexus, because it points to Tokyo. The buyer needs another factor (e.g., (e) non-delivery in Singapore), a serious question, and strong cause instead of forum conveniens. Inter partes, the burden stays on the buyer on every limb, whether the seller seeks a set-aside or a stay.
  • Version 2: Jurisdiction exists as of right. The seller applies for the stay, but the buyer must show strong cause, because it is the party in breach. That is the reversal (J4.3).
  • Version 3: Foreign NEJC, so no breach. On a set-aside, the buyer must show Singapore is clearly forum conveniens. If the seller had been served in Singapore and sought a stay, the seller would bear stage 1. The clause carries little weight either way.

Rule (Strategy, must write): Advising the claimant: serve in wherever possible. Served in, the defendant is usually confined to a stay and bears stage 1; served out, the claimant must clear all three limbs (Zoom; C&Y). Advising a defendant served out: challenge existence (set aside), not exercise; unless the defendant is itself in breach, the burden then stays on the claimant throughout. Fall-back stay: per Zoom, it is not submission, but running it on the same material is "wholly unnecessary and likely counter-productive", and it takes on a burden the defendant could have left with the claimant (J4.2).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Advising Both Sides

Kite Capital (claimant) and a Malaysian defendant with no Singapore presence, Bunga Bhd, are in a dispute with no jurisdiction clause. Bunga's CFO visits Singapore regularly. Kite asks whether to wait for the CFO's next visit or to serve out now. Bunga's lawyers, served out, ask whether to apply to set aside or for a stay.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

For Kite: serving the CFO personally would not found jurisdiction over Bunga unless Bunga itself is present (J3.0.2, the chairperson-on-holiday problem). So Kite must serve out, and it should prepare to carry all three limbs and give full disclosure. If Bunga ever opens a fixed place of business here, serve in then, because Bunga would bear the stay burden. For Bunga: apply to set aside (existence), keeping the burden on Kite throughout, and run all forum arguments within that application. Do not file a separate stay on the same material: it is not submission (Zoom), but it is "wholly unnecessary and likely counter-productive", and it volunteers for a burden Bunga could have left with Kite.
