LAW302 · HYPO LESSON J6 · 28 HYPOTHETICALS · 7 FLOWCHARTS · 8 QUESTIONS

J6 hypotheticals: Anti-suit injunctions: stopping a party suing abroad

The rules behind these hypotheticals are taught in Lesson J6, where the word-for-word pre-write is too. Do that lesson first if the rules below look unfamiliar.

Applications:
ℹ HOW TO USE THESE HYPOTHETICALS

Each concept is set out as Rule, then Hypothetical, then Application. (+) helps the applicant; (−) helps the respondent. An ASI is an equitable in personam order against the respondent, not the foreign court; breach is contempt; it indirectly interferes with the foreign court, so comity runs through every step (SNIA; C&Y).

The flowcharts redraw the hypotheticals in this site's chart style: the chip on each arrow names the hypothetical (or version) that takes that path. The hypo test at the end checks you can run the facts yourself.

1J6.0 Roadmap in one hypothetical

Rule (structure): (1) Preliminary points (is it an ASI; source of power; interim or permanent; General Division or SICC; foreign refusal to stay; promptness). (2) Name the basis, because the elements differ (Cooperative Muratori; slide 20):

  • Contractual: amenability + breach of the clause + no strong reasons; natural forum and injustice drop out.
  • Vexation: amenability + sufficient interest (usually natural forum) + vexation + no undue injustice to the respondent (Kirkham).
  • Abuse of process: amenability + self-evident interest; the respondent's foreign advantage is no answer (BCS v Baker).

Then: (3) amenability; (4) sufficient interest; (5) legitimate interest (any one suffices); (6) no undue injustice (vexation only); (7) special situations. One ASI per foreign proceeding (Chong): analyse each foreign claim and each foreign ASI application separately.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Merlion Ports v Gulf Dredging

Merlion Ports Pte Ltd and Gulf Dredging LLC (UAE) sign a dredging contract with "the non-exclusive jurisdiction of the Singapore courts" (Singapore law). Merlion sues Gulf in Singapore (Suit X), and Gulf defends without contesting jurisdiction. Gulf then (i) sues Merlion in Dubai for the same sums, and (ii) applies in Dubai for an injunction restraining Merlion from continuing Suit X.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Analyse the two Dubai steps separately (Chong):

  • (i) The Dubai claim: under a Singapore NEJC, suing elsewhere is not a breach (J6.3.1.2), so Merlion must rely on vexation (J6.3.2). That requires amenability (Gulf defended Suit X, so it submitted), sufficient interest (Singapore as the natural forum, J6.2.3), vexation (e.g., a late duplicate suit that should have been a counterclaim), and no undue injustice to Gulf (J6.4).
  • (ii) The Dubai anti-suit application: seeking to stop Suit X is in substance an objection to Singapore's jurisdiction, which the Shanghai Turbo narrow waiver forbids. That is arguably a breach, supporting a contractual anti-anti-suit injunction (J6.3.1.2; J6.5.1): amenability + breach + no strong reasons, with natural forum dropping out.
  • Merlion bears the burden throughout and must name each basis (Kirkham; Cooperative Muratori).

2J6.0.2 Preliminary points

Rule (Is it an ASI?): Per Oro Negro, an ASI restrains the respondent from commencing or continuing proceedings in a foreign court. An order that merely stops the respondent purporting to act for the applicant is not an ASI, even though it practically ends the foreign proceedings, so the ASI framework does not apply (C&Y). Statutory moratorium: per C&Y, ss 64–65 IRDA let the court restrain local or foreign proceedings against a company proposing a scheme or compromise: in effect a statutory ASI, outside the general framework.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Rogue Director and the Scheme
  1. A former director of Singapore company Petro Nusantara Pte Ltd, removed by the shareholders, keeps instructing Mexican lawyers to litigate in Petro's name in Mexico. Petro seeks an order restraining him from purporting to act for Petro.
  2. Petro proposes a scheme of arrangement and seeks to restrain a Mexican creditor from suing it in Mexico.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

(1) As in Oro Negro, the order stops the ex-director from acting for Petro; it does not restrain a party from suing on its own account. It is not an ASI, so the Kirkham/Cooperative Muratori framework does not apply, even though the effect is to end the Mexican suit. (2) A moratorium under ss 64–65 IRDA can restrain foreign proceedings against a scheme company. This is effectively a statutory ASI, outside the general framework (C&Y).

Rule (Source of power): Per C&Y, the General Division may grant injunctions where "just or convenient" under s 4(10) CLA, and has the s 18(2) SCJA First Schedule powers (para 14; the handout also lists para 5). For a permanent ASI the source is unsettled: (−) per Swift-Fortune (CA, arguably obiter as a Mareva case) and Hilton (HC, Ang J, bound by it), s 4(10) is interlocutory only, and permanent power lies in s 18(2) with para 14. (+) Per R1 International (HC), and Chan, Tan and Poon on a plain reading (C&Y), s 4(10) also gives permanent power. The CA in Sun Travels merely noted Ang J's view, so it turns on whether "by an interlocutory order" governs injunctions or only receivers. Arbitration: per R1 International and C&Y, an interim ASI in aid of Singapore- or foreign-seated arbitration issues under s 12A(2) with s 12 IAA, whatever the seat (s 12A(1)); a permanent ASI for a foreign seat is not found in s 12A. Limits: the court may refuse where the foreign seat makes it inappropriate (s 12A(3)) and acts only if the tribunal cannot act effectively (s 12A(6)); non-urgent orders need the tribunal's permission or the parties' written agreement (s 12A(5)); urgent ones preserve evidence or assets (s 12A(4)). Proceedings abroad: per C&Y, s 4(10A) CLA (in force 2022) gives power to grant interim relief, if just or convenient, in aid of civil or commercial proceedings commenced or to be commenced in a foreign court, subject to ss 4(10B)–(10D). Power is not discretion. Governing law: per C&Y, ASIs are governed solely by the lex fori.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Which Section?
  1. After a full trial finding that Gulf's Dubai claim breached an exclusive Singapore clause, Merlion seeks a permanent ASI.
  2. Merlion wants an interim ASI to stop Gulf suing in Dubai in breach of an LCIA arbitration clause seated in London. The LCIA tribunal has not yet been constituted, and the Dubai hearing is next week.
  3. Merlion wants an interim ASI in aid of proceedings it has started in the Hong Kong court.
  4. Gulf argues that UAE law, which governs the contract, does not recognise ASIs.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  1. (±) On Swift-Fortune/Hilton, s 4(10) CLA is interlocutory only, so the permanent power must be s 18(2) SCJA with para 14 of the First Schedule. On R1 International (and the plain reading), s 4(10) also covers permanent injunctions; Sun Travels left this open. Plead both sources.
  2. Interim relief in aid of a foreign-seated arbitration is available under s 12A(2) with s 12 IAA (s 12A(1): "whatever the seat"). The court may refuse if the London seat makes it inappropriate (s 12A(3)), and acts only because the tribunal cannot act effectively yet (s 12A(6)). (±) Urgency helps only so far as s 12A(4) allows: urgent orders are those needed to preserve evidence or assets, and an ASI is not obviously one. If it is not, s 12A(5) requires the tribunal's permission or the other party's written agreement, and no tribunal yet exists to give it. A permanent ASI for a London seat would not come from s 12A (J6.2.7).
  3. s 4(10A) CLA gives power to grant interim relief in aid of Hong Kong proceedings, but Singapore must still justify interfering with the Dubai court (J6.2.5).
  4. Irrelevant. Whether to restrain foreign proceedings is governed solely by the lex fori, Singapore law (C&Y; C1.3).

Rule (Interim v permanent): The same Kirkham framework applies, but per Grover v SetClear, an interim ASI issues "sparingly and with great caution", and the respondent gets the benefit of the doubt where the facts are unclear (−). A permanent ASI after a merits judgment declaring breach needs less caution (+) (C&Y). Practicality: an interim ASI is often a practical necessity against anticipated foreign proceedings; its effect is often "virtually that of a permanent" one, and it may be sought before the respondent sues abroad. SICC: per BCS v Baker and C&Y, the same framework governs the SICC; if seised by transfer, it applies unmodified; if seised under a written SICC agreement, sufficient interest and strong reasons are modified. If the respondent ignores the ASI: breach is contempt, so the ASI bites only if the respondent has assets or a presence in Singapore (SNIA; C&Y). A foreign judgment obtained in breach is refused recognition as contrary to public policy (Nimbus; C&Y; J7.2.4), and damages for breach of the clause may be claimed (J1.7).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Disputed Settlement

Two parties signed what one says is a settlement agreement ("no further proceedings in any court"); the other says it was only a draft. The first seeks an interim ASI against the other's new Thai suit.

  • Variation: after trial, the Singapore court has found the settlement binding, and the applicant seeks a permanent ASI. The respondent has no Singapore assets.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

At the interim stage the court acts "sparingly and with great caution" (Grover v SetClear), and where it is unclear whether the settlement was concluded, the respondent gets the benefit of the doubt. The applicant may still argue that, without an interim ASI, the Thai case will proceed so far that a later permanent order is pointless (the "practical necessity" point).

  • In the variation, after a merits finding of breach, a permanent ASI needs less caution (in Grover v SetClear itself, a permanent ASI enforcing a settlement was upheld). But with no Singapore assets, the contempt threat bites little (SNIA). The applicant's real protection is that any Thai judgment obtained in breach will be refused recognition in Singapore on public policy grounds (Nimbus), plus damages for breach of the settlement (J1.7).

Rule (Foreign court refused a stay, +): Per Lakshmi, comity does not generally bar an ASI if Singapore is clearly the more appropriate forum and the respondent sued vexatiously. Similar to SNIA, an ASI was granted though Texas had refused a stay. No estoppel (+): per Lakshmi, the foreign court's natural forum ruling raises no issue estoppel, because the ASI test also needs vexation and the outcome should not turn on scheduling. Comity (−): the foreign court is best placed to decide its own natural forum (Amchem; Barclays v Homan; Deutsche Bank v Highland, per Lakshmi). Most cases sit between Airbus's "stricter" approach (ASIs only to protect jurisdiction or public policy) and the "laxer" one (any vexation suffices). Middle ground (+): per Lakshmi, a sufficient connection plus unconscionable conduct breaches no comity, absent exceptional circumstances; deference is weaker where the respondent carved an issue out of pending Suit X to sue abroad, and a refusal given while a Singapore appeal was pending should not decide the outcome by scheduling. Timing (must write if the applicant waited): per C&Y, the applicant should object abroad and seek the ASI here simultaneously; delay is not excused by pending objections abroad (Sun Travels), and comity weighs more the later the application (Lakshmi).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The BVI Court Said No

A Singapore estate is litigating in Singapore (Suit X) over ownership of Singapore condominiums held through a BVI company. The respondent sues in the BVI over the BVI share. The estate applies to the BVI court for a stay, and the BVI court refuses, holding the BVI to be the natural forum, while the estate's Singapore appeal on a related point is pending. The estate then seeks an ASI in Singapore, three months after the BVI claim was filed.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

(+) The BVI refusal does not bar an ASI: comity is not breached where Singapore is clearly more appropriate and the respondent sued vexatiously (Lakshmi; SNIA, granted despite Texas refusing a stay). There is no issue estoppel, because the ASI test also requires vexation, and the result should not depend on which court happened to rule first, especially as the BVI ruling came while the Singapore appeal was pending (Lakshmi). (−) The respondent invokes comity: the BVI court is best placed to decide its own forum (Amchem; Barclays v Homan; Deutsche Bank v Highland), and on Airbus's stricter view ASIs are only to protect jurisdiction or public policy. Middle ground: Lakshmi's sufficient connection plus unconscionable conduct (carving the share issue out of Suit X to sue in the BVI) justifies the ASI. Timing: the estate should have sought the ASI at the same time as its BVI stay application. Three months is not fatal at an early stage, but comity weighs more the later the application (Sun Travels; Lakshmi).

3J6.1 Amenability

Rule: Amenability is always required, whatever the basis (Cooperative Muratori; Koh Kay Yew; C&Y). Submission or valid service (+): the respondent submitted (appearing, defending or counterclaiming in Suit X) or was validly served in or out of Singapore (Koh Kay Yew; Westbridge v Mittal). Claimant here (+): per Glencore, a respondent that sued the applicant in Singapore submitted to all the incidents of litigation, including related relief such as an ASI. No challenge (+): similar to BCS v Baker, a respondent that took part in Suit X without contesting jurisdiction is amenable. Service out alone may not suffice (−): similar to Akai, where the respondent, though served out on ostensible evidence, was not amenable because it had no presence or assets here and only opposed the ASI. Reply (+): the slides contrast Kirkham, and the settled view (C&Y; Cooperative Muratori) is that valid service or submission suffices; lack of assets goes only to effectiveness. Not amenable (−): if the respondent is abroad and has not submitted, the applicant must first obtain permission to serve the ASI claim out under O 8 r 1 (J3.1).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Four Respondents
  1. Gulf Dredging defended Suit X without contesting jurisdiction.
  2. Texan Oil Inc sued Merlion in Singapore last year, and is now suing Merlion in Texas on related claims.
  3. Jeddah Trading has no Singapore presence or assets. Merlion obtained approval to serve it out under O 8 and served it in Jeddah. Jeddah appears only to oppose the ASI.
  4. Cairo Marine is in Egypt, has not been served and has not appeared.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  1. Amenable: it submitted by defending Suit X without objection (like BCS v Baker).
  2. Amenable: by suing in Singapore it submitted to all the incidents of litigation, including an ASI (Glencore).
  3. (−) Jeddah relies on Akai: served out, with no presence or assets, and only opposing the ASI, so not amenable. (+) Merlion replies that the settled view (C&Y; Cooperative Muratori; contrast Kirkham) is that valid service founds amenability. Lack of assets affects only how effective the ASI will be.
  4. Not amenable. Merlion must first get approval to serve out under O 8 r 1 (J3.1). Without it, no ASI can issue however vexatious Cairo's suit is.

4J6.2 Sufficient interest

(Classify first. Natural forum is only a proxy: it proves interest, but Singapore may have interest without it, and there must be a good reason for Singapore rather than the foreign court to stop the foreign proceedings (BCS v Baker, citing Barclays v Homan). For a contractual ASI, natural forum does not arise (Cooperative Muratori); a Singapore clause supplies the connection, but if Singapore is not chosen, the point stays live (J6.2.6–J6.2.7).)

J6.2.1 Jurisdiction Agreement for Singapore

Rule: Singapore EJC (+): per Westbridge v Mittal and C&Y, the clause itself supplies the connection, even if the parties and events have no other link with Singapore; no natural forum inquiry is needed. Why (+): per Cooperative Muratori (citing Turner v Grovit and UniCredit), the applicant need not show Singapore is more appropriate, because the agreement does that; it should take more to sanction a breach than to deny a natural forum (Yeo, endorsed in Vinmar). Singapore NEJC (+): arguably, per Shanghai Turbo and C&Y, the clause works like an EJC to supply the connection. Contrast: it supplies interest only; suing abroad is not itself a breach (J6.3.1.2). SICC clause, exclusive or not (+): per C&Y, Spiliada is irrelevant; O 2 r 3 SICC Rules 2021 supplies the connection test (the SICC may decline only if exercising jurisdiction is contrary to its international and commercial character, or an abuse of process, and not solely because the action is connected to a foreign State). Exception (−): not so if the claim is not international and commercial, or suing in the SICC is abusive (e.g., tactical delay).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Clause Is the Connection
  1. An Indian buyer and a Brazilian seller, with no Singapore links, agree "exclusive jurisdiction of the Singapore courts". The buyer sues in Mumbai. The seller seeks an ASI in Singapore.
  2. The same, but the clause is a Singapore NEJC.
  3. The same, but the clause is a written SICC agreement, and the seller first sat back for 18 months to see how the Mumbai case went.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  1. The EJC itself supplies sufficient interest, even with no other Singapore connection (Westbridge v Mittal). The seller need not show Singapore is the natural forum (Cooperative Muratori, citing Turner v Grovit and UniCredit).
  2. The NEJC arguably supplies interest (Shanghai Turbo), but suing in Mumbai is not itself a breach, so the seller must show vexation or abuse for a legitimate interest (J6.3.2–J6.3.3).
  3. The O 2 r 3 test supplies the connection, and Spiliada is irrelevant. But the seller's 18-month "wait and see" approach may make its SICC use abusive, which would defeat sufficient interest (C&Y; J6.3.1.3).

J6.2.2 Protecting Singapore's Own Process

Rule: Self-evident interest (+): per BCS v Baker, where the foreign claim abuses Singapore's process (e.g., relitigating Suit X), natural forum is irrelevant: Singapore's interest in protecting its processes, jurisdiction and judgments is "generally self-evident", and only Singapore can judge the need for protection. Concurrent proceedings (−): in non-contract cases, where the Singapore and foreign actions are both pending, per Baker v BCS (SICC) and C&Y, the applicant must show Singapore is the natural forum. Consecutive proceedings (+): once Singapore has given judgment, it has interest in protecting the judgment from collateral attack by relitigation of res judicata issues abroad (Baker v BCS; C&Y). Per BCS v Baker, the need extends to anticipated judgments but is underscored once judgment exists. Which is it? Per BCS v Baker, ask when the specific claim to be enjoined was raised abroad, not when the actions began (C&Y's footnote states this the other way; follow the judgment). Resisting enforcement (−): per Baker v BCS and C&Y, it is a "fine line": if the respondent merely resists the applicant's enforcement of the Singapore judgment abroad, Singapore generally leaves it to the foreign court. Foreign judgment already given (−): per BCS v Baker (citing ED & F Man v Haryanto), an ASI stopping the respondent relying abroad on the foreign court's own judgment is ordinarily inappropriate; exceptional circumstances are needed (Sun Travels; J7.6). Interest without natural forum (+): similar to Shell v Coral Oil (per BCS v Baker), where England had a "very strong interest" in shielding a party already protected by its ASI from further vexatious Lebanese claims.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Trust Judgment Attacked in California

In Suit X, the SICC held that shares were held on trust for BCS-Co. While BCS-Co's enforcement proceedings were pending in California, the losing party, Baker, did three things there:

  • (a) In 2021 (before the Singapore judgment), Baker sued in California on a different claim (wrongful settlement).
  • (b) In 2023 (after the Singapore judgment and the dismissal of the appeal), Baker added a new "judicial estoppel" claim in California that repackages the trust issue.
  • (c) Baker opposes BCS-Co's application to enforce the Singapore judgment in California, arguing it was obtained without due process.
  • (d) Baker also obtained a California judgment on (a) and now seeks to enforce it in Texas.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • (b) Consecutive: the question is when the specific claim was raised (2023, after judgment), not when the California action began (2021) (BCS v Baker). Singapore's interest in protecting its judgment from collateral attack is self-evident; natural forum is irrelevant.
  • (a) Concurrent: at the time, both actions were pending and it was not a contract case, so BCS-Co would have had to show that Singapore was the natural forum (Baker v BCS).
  • (c) Resisting enforcement: a "fine line". Merely resisting enforcement in California is for the California court to decide; Singapore generally will not intervene.
  • (d) Foreign judgment given: restraining Baker from relying on the California court's own judgment is ordinarily inappropriate (ED & F Man v Haryanto). BCS-Co would need exceptional circumstances (Sun Travels), and the relief would really be an AEI (J7.6).
  • Shell v Coral Oil angle: if Singapore had already granted BCS-Co an ASI and Baker kept launching new vexatious Californian claims, Singapore would have a "very strong interest" in protecting that earlier order, even if California is also a natural forum.

J6.2.3 Alternative Fora: Singapore Is One Forum

Rule: Natural forum (+): per BCS v Baker and Airbus, an ASI is normally granted where Singapore is the natural forum and the other requirements are met. Per Lakshmi, the applicant must show Singapore is "clearly the more appropriate forum", weighing the quality, not quantity, of the JIO factors. Lakshmi, real substance (+): a BVI share mattered only because its subsidiaries held 22 Singapore condominium units, so the BVI's link was only the place of incorporation. Lakshmi, witnesses (+): video links reduce the weight of witness location, but third-party witnesses (e.g., bank officers) compellable here and not shown to be compellable abroad matter where the dispute is factual. Lakshmi, overlap (+): different reliefs abroad do not show different issues; where the foreign claim and Suit X are binary, proof of one disproves the other. Lakshmi, little weight (−): governing law matters little where both systems are common law and the issues factual; little weight goes to a place of performance that assumes the respondent's claim succeeds, a place of enforcement offset by the applicant's undertaking, or the place of an oral telephone contract; residence in third States is neutral. Natural forum alone is not enough (−): per SNIA and C&Y, otherwise Singapore could arrogate to itself a mere difference of view about the natural forum; in SNIA the ASI turned on the lost contribution claim. Advantages are not connecting factors (+): similar to SNIA, Texas lawyers' evidence-gathering, contingency fees and an early trial were advantages to the plaintiffs, not connecting factors.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Helicopter Crash Litigation

A helicopter owned by a Brunei company crashes in Brunei, killing passengers, including Texans. The families sue the French manufacturer in Texas. The manufacturer seeks an ASI in Singapore (assume amenability and that Singapore is a candidate forum because the maintenance company is Singaporean). The manufacturer argues: (a) Singapore is the natural forum; (b) in Texas it cannot bring a contribution claim against the Singapore maintenance company, which will submit to Singapore but not Texas. The families argue: (c) Texas offers contingency fees, early trial dates and specialist aviation lawyers, so Texas is the natural forum.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

(a) Natural forum is necessary, not sufficient (SNIA): Singapore will not grant an ASI merely because it disagrees with Texas about the natural forum. (b) This is the real ground: losing the contribution claim available only here makes the Texas suit oppressive (as in SNIA), subject to undertakings that preserve the families' legitimate advantages (J6.4). (c) Contingency fees, early trial and expert lawyers are advantages to the families, not connecting factors; they do not make Texas the natural forum (SNIA). Applying Lakshmi: if the only Texas link is the families' residence, the real substance of the dispute is elsewhere (Brunei and Singapore), and compellable third-party witnesses (e.g., the Singapore maintenance engineers) matter more than convenient ones.

J6.2.4 Single Forum: Only the Foreign Court Can Hear the Claim

Rule: Framing (must write): where the respondent's claim (e.g., a foreign antitrust claim) lies only abroad, Singapore can never be the natural forum. Per Airbus and BCS v Baker, ask whether Singapore still has sufficient interest and whether pursuing the claim is unconscionable. Per C&Y, the ASI is especially harsh, denying the respondent its only redress. Not Spiliada availability: "single forum" means Singapore law gives no cause of action, so the question is unconscionability, not appropriateness. Insolvency (+): per BCS v Baker (citing Stichting Shell), Singapore has interest in protecting its administration of an insolvency against a creditor suing abroad. Predominantly Singaporean dealings (+): similar to Midland Bank v Laker, where an English bank's dealings with Laker were "overwhelmingly English" (Airbus). Contrast (−): if the dealings were in a third State under its law, an ASI merely because the respondent is amenable here would be "surprising" (Airbus, on a hypothetical Indian bank). Singapore public policy (+): per BCS v Baker and Airbus (citing Laker v Sabena); in very exceptional cases this may override even a foreign EJC (C&Y). Not unconscionable (−): similar to British Airways v Laker, where BA and BCal, by taking licences to fly UK–US routes, voluntarily submitted to US antitrust law.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The US Antitrust Claim

A collapsed Singapore budget airline's liquidators sue in the US under the Sherman Act (treble damages), alleging that a Singapore bank conspired with rival airlines to drive it out of business. There is no equivalent claim under Singapore law. The bank seeks a Singapore ASI.

  • Version 1: all the bank's dealings with the airline were Singapore banking business, under Singapore law, from Singapore.
  • Version 2: the bank's dealings were through its Mumbai branch, under Indian law.
  • Version 3: the defendants are rival airlines that had taken licences to fly US routes.
  • Version 4: the claimant is a single creditor suing abroad to jump the queue in the Singapore liquidation.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

This is a single-forum case: only the US can hear a Sherman Act claim, so Singapore can never be the natural forum. The questions are sufficient interest plus unconscionability (Airbus; BCS v Baker), and an ASI here is especially harsh because it removes the only redress (C&Y).

  • Version 1 (+): like Midland Bank v Laker, the dealings were "overwhelmingly" Singaporean, so an ASI is consistent with comity.
  • Version 2 (−): an ASI just because the bank is amenable here would be "surprising" (Airbus's hypothetical Indian bank).
  • Version 3 (−): like British Airways v Laker, the rivals voluntarily submitted to US antitrust law by flying US routes, so the US suit against them is not unconscionable.
  • Version 4 (+): protecting Singapore's administration of the insolvency gives sufficient interest (BCS v Baker, citing Stichting Shell), and the suit is an abuse (J6.3.3).
  • Public policy: if a Singapore public policy on the point were engaged, that too could ground interest, very exceptionally even against a foreign EJC (Laker v Sabena; C&Y).

J6.2.5 Dual Fora: Singapore Is Neither

Rule: General rule (−): where the respondent sued in Court A and the natural forum is Court B, per Airbus comity generally requires Singapore to have sufficient interest before interfering. Per Akai, Courts A and B may legitimately differ, and Singapore should not be an "international busybody" (C&Y; heeded in R1 International). Natural forum powerless (−): similar to Airbus, where India, the natural forum, could not reach the claimants, Court B's inability to restrain the respondent does not justify Singapore acting: "only the courts of an interested jurisdiction can act". That Court A does not apply FNC is also not enough. Extreme cases (+): per Airbus and C&Y, an ASI may issue without sufficient connection in "extreme cases", e.g., where the foreign State's conduct forfeits the respect comity normally requires. Strong reasons by analogy (+): per R1 International (HC, obiter; C&Y), a permanent ASI supporting a foreign arbitration may issue on strong reasons (e.g., the seat lacks effective interim measures); arguably by analogy where Court B cannot grant ASIs. s 4(10A) CLA (±): arguably gives power to grant interim relief in aid of Court B's proceedings, but it confers power only; Singapore must still justify interfering with Court A.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Indian Crash and the Texas Suit

An Airbus-type aircraft crashes in India. The families of Indian victims sue the manufacturer in Texas. India, where the inquiry and the evidence are, is the natural forum but cannot grant ASIs against the families. The manufacturer has a Singapore subsidiary and asks Singapore for an ASI because "the Indian court cannot help, and Texas doesn't apply FNC properly".

  • Variation: the Texas proceedings are a sham orchestrated by a foreign government to extort the manufacturer, with forged evidence.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Singapore is neither the natural forum (India) nor the chosen forum. Per Airbus, comity requires sufficient interest, and Singapore has none. India's inability to restrain the families does not justify Singapore acting ("only the courts of an interested jurisdiction can act"), nor does Texas's approach to FNC. Singapore should not be an "international busybody" (Akai). Even if s 4(10A) CLA gave power to aid Indian proceedings, it gives no reason to interfere with Texas.

  • In the variation, an extreme case where the foreign State's conduct forfeits comity's respect might justify an ASI without sufficient connection (Airbus; C&Y).
  • Analogy (+): by analogy with R1 International (strong reasons for supporting a foreign arbitration where the seat lacks interim measures), the manufacturer argues that India's inability to grant ASIs is a strong reason. This is weak against Airbus.

J6.2.6 EJC for a Foreign Court

Rule: Go to the chosen court (−): where the respondent sued in Court A in breach of an EJC for Court B, per C&Y the applicant should ordinarily seek the ASI from Court B. Similar to Akai, where the insurer had not applied to the English court though Akai, having sued there, was amenable to it. Reply (+): per Chong, Akai is old and its "busybody" point may carry less force today, especially where Court B is in an HCCCA Contracting State. Reasons to come here (+): Court B does not grant ASIs or lacks the remedy, or the applicant must shield its Singapore assets from Court A's judgment. Rebuttal (−): per C&Y, Singapore has generally declined even then; as in Akai, any later enforcement against Singapore assets is "an entirely different matter", met by resisting recognition (J7).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The London Clause and the Mumbai Suit

A reinsurance contract has an exclusive English courts clause. The reinsured (Indian) sues the reinsurer in Mumbai. The reinsurer, which has substantial Singapore assets, applies for an ASI in Singapore, not London, arguing that it needs to protect its Singapore assets from any Mumbai judgment.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

(−) The chosen court is London, so the reinsurer should apply there (C&Y; Akai, where the insurer had not gone to the English court although Akai was amenable there). Protecting Singapore assets is "an entirely different matter", properly handled by resisting recognition of a Mumbai judgment in Singapore later (J7; Akai). (+) Chong: Akai is dated, and the "busybody" concern is weaker where London is in an HCCCA Contracting State (J6.5.3). The reinsurer may also argue that London would decline to act for some reason. But per C&Y, Singapore has generally declined even then.

J6.2.7 Arbitration Seated Abroad

Rule: Busybody risk (−): per C&Y, Singapore generally refrains from ASIs supporting foreign arbitration; per R1 International (obiter), a permanent ASI needs strong reasons (e.g., the seat lacks effective interim measures); interim ASIs come from s 12A IAA. Contract supplies the connection (+): per UniCredit (UKSC, persuasive), Spiliada is not the test; parties should be held to their bargain by any court before which they "can properly be brought" (Enka), and Airbus's sufficient-interest rule was tied to non-contractual cases. An ASI enforcing an arbitration agreement always comes from a court that is neither the natural nor the agreed forum. Comity and connection (+): per UniCredit, comity has little role where the foreign court's State and the seat's State are both New York Convention States. A Singapore-law arbitration agreement is a substantial connection, like the English-law rights in UniCredit; whether personal jurisdiction alone suffices was left open (IPOC). Applying here is not a breach (+): per UniCredit (cf Model Law art 9), the arbitration agreement does not impliedly bar applying to a court for relief holding the other party to it, though choosing a foreign seat implies no agreement to sue in Singapore.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Paris-Seated Arbitration and the Russian Suit

A Russian buyer and a Singapore-incorporated seller agreed to ICC arbitration seated in Paris, with the arbitration agreement governed by Singapore law. The buyer sues in Moscow, claiming that sanctions make arbitration impossible. Paris courts do not grant ASIs. The buyer has a Singapore subsidiary and was validly served. The seller seeks a permanent ASI in Singapore.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

(−) Singapore usually refrains from supporting foreign-seated arbitrations by ASI (C&Y), and the seat (Paris) is the natural supervisor. A permanent ASI is not available under s 12A IAA, and R1 International requires strong reasons. (+) UniCredit (persuasive): this is a contractual ASI, so Spiliada and Airbus's sufficient-interest rule are beside the point; the parties should be held to their bargain by any court before which they "can properly be brought" (Enka). Comity has little weight because Russia and France are both New York Convention States, and Russia is obliged to refer the parties to arbitration. The arbitration agreement is governed by Singapore law, a substantial connection, as English law was in UniCredit. The seat (Paris) cannot grant ASIs, which is a strong reason under R1 International. Applying to Singapore does not breach the arbitration agreement (UniCredit; Model Law art 9). Whether personal jurisdiction alone would have sufficed was left open (IPOC).

5J6.3 Legitimate interest (any one suffices)

Rule (Choosing the basis): breach of agreement (J6.3.1), vexation (J6.3.2), abuse of process (J6.3.3), or public policy (J6.3.4); the categories are not closed (C&Y). Per BCS v Baker, abuse invokes the inherent power (disruption to Singapore's processes); vexation invokes equity (the personal equities); the overriding test is the interests of justice. Keep them apart (must write if run together): per Cooperative Muratori, a contractual ASI is a distinct species (citing VKC); the strands are conceptually distinct, so do not argue that breaching the clause is itself vexatious. Breach needs no vexation (Sun Travels; C&Y).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Muddled Submission

Counsel for an applicant argues: "The respondent breached the Singapore EJC by suing in Seoul, which is vexatious and oppressive, and Singapore is the natural forum, so the ASI should issue."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

This conflates two distinct bases (Cooperative Muratori). On the contractual basis, the applicant needs only amenability, breach of the EJC, and no strong reasons shown by the respondent; natural forum and vexation are unnecessary (Sun Travels). Vexation is a separate equitable basis with its own elements (natural forum, vexation, no undue injustice). Counsel should plead breach as the primary ground and, if needed, vexation in the alternative, each analysed separately.

J6.3.1 Breach of Agreement

J6.3.1.1 Step 1: Breach

Rule: Exclusive clause breached (+): breach is a question of interpretation under the clause's proper law (C&Y). Per Sun Travels, breach is a separate basis: no unconscionability is needed, and the ASI ordinarily issues absent strong reasons. Rationale: per Finaport, equity's jurisdiction to ensure contractual bargains are honoured, on the "clear and simple ground" that the respondent promised not to sue abroad (The Angelic Grace, per Sun Travels). Comity matters less, as Singapore enforces the bargain rather than claiming the dispute. Other agreements (+): per C&Y, the same applies to arbitration agreements, agreements not to sue (e.g., the settlement in Grover v SetClear), and in principle a mediation agreement valid under its proper law whose enforcement is not contrary to Singapore public policy. Caution (−): per C&Y (BTN v BTP), suing is not always a breach of an arbitration agreement; a conditional clause may let parties sue in court until arbitration is invoked.

Rule (Multi-tiered clause, +): Similar to Finaport, where "shall first attempt" negotiation, then SMC mediation, then litigation was mandatory, "shall first" wording makes negotiation or mediation a precondition, so suing abroad first breaches it; there is no principled distinction between tiered clauses and EJCs or arbitration agreements. Scope: suing is not a per se breach, so the ASI restrains the respondent only until the preconditions are met, with liberty to apply; a non-contractual ASI was refused there. Impracticality no answer: per Finaport (citing Don King), a beneficiary suing on the trustee's rights cannot complain that the tiers are impractical; it takes the bargain as it is.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Four Agreements Not to Sue
  1. A trustee's contract with a crypto custodian says the parties "shall first attempt to negotiate for 30 days, then shall refer the dispute to mediation at the Singapore Mediation Centre, and only thereafter may commence proceedings in the Singapore courts". A beneficiary, suing on the trustee's cause of action, sues the custodian in Hong Kong immediately, saying the tiers are unworkable.
  2. A settlement agreement: "No party shall commence any further proceedings anywhere in respect of the 2022 Cargo."
  3. An arbitration clause: "Either party may refer a dispute to SIAC arbitration; until a party does so, either may sue in any competent court."
  4. "This Agreement is governed by Australian law." One party sues in California, arguing that California will apply Californian law.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  1. As in Finaport, the "shall first" wording makes negotiation and mediation mandatory preconditions, so suing in Hong Kong now is a breach, and there is no principled distinction from an EJC. The beneficiary, suing on the trustee's rights, takes the bargain as it is and cannot complain that it is impractical (Don King, cited in Finaport). But suing is not a per se breach, so the ASI restrains the Hong Kong suit only until the preconditions are met, with liberty to apply.
  2. An agreement not to sue, enforceable by a contractual ASI (as in Grover v SetClear).
  3. Suing in court is not a breach until arbitration is invoked (BTN v BTP; C&Y).
  4. A choice of law clause is ordinarily declaratory, not promissory (Ace Insurance), so it carries no implied promise not to sue where Australian law will not be applied; "very clear language" is needed. And, as in Ace, if the Californian court would in fact apply Australian law, the premise fails anyway. Briggs's view that suing to defeat the chosen law "looks like" a breach should be argued only if the clause expressly promises not to sue where that law will not apply.

J6.3.1.2 Singapore NEJC: Generally No Breach

Rule: No breach (−): per C&Y and Shanghai Turbo, suing abroad under a Singapore NEJC is not ordinarily a breach, the parties having accepted parallel proceedings; only a challenge to Singapore's jurisdiction (e.g., a stay application in Suit X) needs strong cause. So the applicant relies on vexation or abuse. Breach arguable (+): per the handout, Shanghai Turbo's narrow-waiver reading implies a promise not to object to Singapore's jurisdiction, so seeking an ASI or declaration abroad to stop Suit X is in substance such an objection, and so a breach. Construction: breach turns on construing the clause under its proper law, e.g., whether it makes the court first seised exclusive. Suing to stop enforcement of rights (±): similar to Sabah Shipyard v Pakistan, where Pakistan's local injunction against calling on a guarantee stopped Sabah suing in England under an English NEJC; (+) the English CA called this "clearly a breach of contract". But (−): per UBS v Telesto and C&Y, Sabah is a vexation case: the wrong lay in suing to stop Sabah enforcing its contractual rights, not in breaching the NEJC. So plead vexation in the alternative.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Gulf's Two Dubai Steps (from J6.0)

Recall: under a Singapore NEJC, Gulf (i) sued in Dubai and (ii) sought a Dubai injunction against Suit X.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

(i) No breach: the NEJC contemplates parallel proceedings (Shanghai Turbo). Merlion must show vexation or abuse. (ii) (+) Gulf's narrow waiver (a promise not to object to Singapore's jurisdiction) is breached by an application abroad to stop Suit X, so a contractual ASI is available. Merlion relies on Sabah Shipyard, where the English CA called a similar foreign injunction "clearly a breach". (−) Gulf relies on UBS v Telesto: Singapore reads Sabah as a vexation case. So Merlion should plead vexation in the alternative for step (ii) as well. Construction: if the clause said "the court first seised shall have exclusive jurisdiction", suing in Dubai after Suit X would itself be a breach.

J6.3.1.3 SICC Written Jurisdiction Agreement

Rule: This applies only where the SICC was seised under a written agreement; after a transfer, apply J6.3.1.4 unmodified (C&Y). Starter: the SICC may decline only under O 2 r 3(2), so upholding the clause is even stronger than in the General Division; but an ASI, unlike a stay, affects the foreign court, so comity still matters (Donohue). Exclusive SICC clause (+): arguably the strong reasons test does not apply at all, so foreign proceedings in breach should always be restrained. Modified test (−): alternatively, strong reasons are modified to fold in O 2 r 3(2); an applicant that waited without good reason, taking a tactical "wait and see" approach while the foreign proceedings advanced, should be refused by an SICC that takes its international character seriously, or such tactics go to discretion. Non-exclusive SICC clause (−): the parties implicitly accepted suits elsewhere, so the SICC should refrain where the foreign proceedings began before the SICC proceedings; the applicant will likely rely on vexation.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The SICC Applicant Who Waited

Under an exclusive SICC clause, a Korean party sued in Seoul in January. The Singapore party filed in the SICC in February, but did not seek an ASI until November, after Seoul had held two evidential hearings. It explains that it wanted to see whether the Seoul court would dismiss the claim first.

  • Variation: the SICC clause is non-exclusive, and the Seoul suit came first.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

(+) On one view (C&Y), because the SICC clause is exclusive and the SICC can decline only under O 2 r 3(2), the strong reasons test does not apply at all, so the ASI should issue. (−) On the modified view, strong reasons fold in O 2 r 3(2): a tactical "wait and see" delay while Seoul progressed is the kind of conduct an SICC that respects its international character should refuse to reward (or treat as going to discretion). Comity still matters because an ASI affects Seoul (Donohue).

  • In the variation, the parties implicitly accepted suits elsewhere, and Seoul came first, so the SICC should refrain; the applicant would have to show vexation (C&Y).

J6.3.1.4 Step 2: Strong Reasons (burden on the respondent)

Rule: Starter (must write): once the respondent has sued abroad in breach, the ASI ordinarily issues unless the respondent shows strong reasons (Sun Travels; Cooperative Muratori; Donohue). Per C&Y, this is in practice the strong cause test for stays (J4.3), and consistency between the two matters (Vinmar). The respondent's lost juridical advantage may count here (Cooperative Muratori).

  • Applicant itself in breach (−): where the clause lets the respondent sue abroad (so its suit breaches nothing) but the applicant promised to submit there, per Chong (answer scheme), seeking the ASI is the applicant's own breach, so arguably the applicant bears strong cause.
  • Third parties or claims outside the clause (−): similar to Donohue, where New York proceedings in breach of an English EJC continued because they involved non-parties and RICO claims outside the clause; an ASI would fragment the litigation. Reply (+): per Asiana, fragmentation "should not be overstated", especially for arbitration agreements; per UniCredit, for arbitration, parallel proceedings carry no weight in themselves. Where the respondent deliberately split contract and tort claims, the fragmentation is its own (Clearlake, in Hai Jiang).
  • Foreign property (−): per Impala v Wanxiang and C&Y, enforceability abroad may be a strong reason where the claim concerns property or shares abroad, especially to recover them, as the situs courts control them. Reply (+): the respondent refused a reasonable offer to arbitrate that would have avoided the prejudice (Impala); a bare "unenforceable in some places" argument fails, as that risk was foreseeable (Impala; Westbridge v Mittal).
  • Applicant's submission abroad (−): per UniCredit, the discretion, like delay, may weigh the applicant having submitted abroad (defending on the merits, counterclaiming), arguably waiving the clause. Contrast (+): per IGCF v Al Jomaih (PC), applying abroad for a stay in favour of arbitration or to recall an injunction is protest, not submission; but contesting jurisdiction does not excuse delay.
  • Foreign court bound to decline (+): per UniCredit, comity has little role where the foreign State is bound by treaty to decline jurisdiction (art II(3) NYC; arguably art 6 HCCCA).
  • No strong reasons (+): a foreseeable commercial risk or an advantage the respondent bargained away does not count, so the clause is enforced by ASI.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Shanghai Shares Dispute

Under an exclusive Singapore clause, a Chinese investor (respondent) sues a Singapore fund (applicant) in Shanghai to recover shares in a Shanghai-listed company, and also sues the fund's two Chinese directors (non-parties) for fraud under PRC law. The respondent argues: (a) a Singapore judgment ordering return of the shares would be unenforceable in China, where the shares and share registry are; (b) the claims against the directors are outside the clause, and an ASI would split the case; (c) the applicant itself filed a defence on the merits in Shanghai before seeking the ASI; (d) China is obliged by the New York Convention to refer arbitration-clause disputes to arbitration, but this is a court clause.

  • Facts relevant to replies: the fund had offered to arbitrate in Shanghai, and the investor refused. The investor deliberately sued the directors in tort in Shanghai, though the same facts underlie a contract claim covered by the clause.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

The investor is in breach, so the ASI ordinarily issues unless it shows strong reasons (Sun Travels; Cooperative Muratori), applying the same standard as strong cause (J4.3).

  • (a) Foreign property (−): a claim to recover shares situated in China, where the situs courts control the register, can be a strong reason (Impala v Wanxiang). (+) But the investor refused a reasonable offer to arbitrate that would have avoided the problem (Impala), and a general "unenforceable in some places" risk was foreseeable when it agreed to Singapore (Westbridge v Mittal).
  • (b) Third parties (−): as in Donohue, non-parties and claims outside the clause may justify letting the foreign case continue. (+) Per Asiana, fragmentation "should not be overstated", and here the investor deliberately split contract and tort claims, so the fragmentation is self-inflicted (Clearlake, in Hai Jiang).
  • (c) Applicant's submission (−): by filing a merits defence in Shanghai, the fund arguably submitted and waived the clause, which goes to discretion (UniCredit). Contrast: had the fund only applied in Shanghai for a stay, that would be a protest, not submission (IGCF v Al Jomaih), though contesting jurisdiction would not excuse any delay.
  • (d) The New York Convention argument does not apply to a court clause. Arguably, if both States were HCCCA Contracting States, art 6 would play the same role (J6.5.3), so comity would weigh little.
  • Applicant in breach twist (Chong): if the clause had let the investor sue anywhere, but bound the fund to submit to any court the investor chose, the fund's ASI application would itself be the breach, so the fund would arguably bear strong cause.

J6.3.1.5 Delay and Comity

Rule: Comity re-enters with delay (−): per Sun Travels (following Ecobank and Sea Powerful), comity is relevant to delay even in contractual cases, and how far the foreign proceedings have progressed matters more than the length of the delay, since an ASI then wastes more foreign court resources (C&Y). Application: similar to Hilton (HC), where the Maldivian proceedings were "too far advanced". Early stage (+): if only the claim has been filed, or a jurisdiction challenge is pending, that points to the ASI (Baker v BCS (SICC); C&Y). Per ZHD v SQO, where no merits hearing is imminent or has been held, the length of delay alone does not point against it. Contesting jurisdiction is no excuse (−): per Sun Travels (citing The Angelic Grace, Toepfer and Ecobank), there are no "two bites at the cherry"; similar to ADM v PT Budi, refused on "general discretionary considerations and the needs of comity". Foreign judgment already given (−): per Sun Travels, exceptional circumstances are then needed; the relief is really an AEI (J7.6). Where delay sits (±): per C&Y, English law treats strong reasons (justifications for suing abroad) as distinct from discretion (the applicant's delay or unconscionable conduct) (Donohue; ADM); Sun Travels cited ADM approvingly, but the point is open and makes little practical difference. Applicant's unconscionable conduct (−): an ASI is equitable, so dilatoriness or unconscionable conduct (e.g., misleading the foreign court) may lose it (Donohue; C&Y).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Three Delayed Applicants
  1. Sun Resorts: sued in the Maldives in breach of a Singapore arbitration agreement. It spent 18 months challenging the Maldivian court's jurisdiction, lost, and then sought an ASI in Singapore, by which time the Maldivian trial had concluded and judgment was pending.
  2. ZenCo: waited 10 months, but the foreign court has only received pleadings and no merits hearing is scheduled.
  3. Dragon Ltd: applied promptly, but had earlier told the foreign court (falsely) that it had no objection to that court's jurisdiction.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  1. Contesting jurisdiction abroad does not excuse delay: there are no "two bites at the cherry" (Sun Travels, citing The Angelic Grace, Toepfer and Ecobank). Sun Resorts should have objected in the Maldives and applied here at the same time. The foreign proceedings are "too far advanced" (Hilton), and comity weighs heavily (ADM v PT Budi). Refused. If the Maldivian judgment has been given, exceptional circumstances are needed and the relief is an AEI (J7.6).
  2. Early stage: per ZHD v SQO, the length of the delay alone does not count against the ASI where no merits hearing is imminent; this points to granting it (Baker v BCS).
  3. Unconscionable conduct (misleading the foreign court) may disentitle Dragon to equitable relief (Donohue; C&Y).
  • Where delay sits: whether delay is part of "strong reasons" or of the general discretion is open (Donohue; ADM; Sun Travels). One line suffices: either way, Sun Resorts' delay defeats the ASI.

J6.3.2 Vexation or Oppression

(Non-contractual ASIs: amenability + sufficient interest (usually natural forum) + vexation + no undue injustice (Kirkham). J6.3.2 and J6.4 are "two sides of the same coin".)

Rule: Starter (must write): per Kirkham and UBS v Telesto, an ASI issues only in "the clearest of circumstances"; the overarching question is whether the ends of justice require it (SNIA). Unconscionability: used interchangeably with "vexatious or oppressive" (the latter is preferred) but technically wider (C&Y); per Asiana, unconscionability is the underlying principle, and the list is not closed.

Rule (Categories):

  • Bad faith or no good reason (+): similar to Lakshmi, where the BVI suit began years after accrual and a day after Mr J learned the estate would take over the Singapore suit, and should have been a counterclaim.
  • Bound to fail (±): (+) per Kirkham, suing on a hopeless claim is vexatious; (−) per VKC, the court should be prudent, because weakness is only "a factor ... together with more weighty factors". Stress conduct, e.g., a claim "cynically created and pursued" after agreeing a new arrangement inconsistent with it (VKC).
  • Oppressive procedures or extreme inconvenience (+): e.g., ex parte seizures, or a remote venue or foreign language (Kirkham; C&Y).
  • Key witness not compellable (+): per UBS v Telesto and C&Y.
  • Rights unlawfully challenged (+): per Evergreen v Volkswagen and C&Y, e.g., to undo a right established under Singapore law.
  • Lost remedy available only here (+): SNIA (the lost contribution claim against the Malaysian operator), oppressive if the applicant's undertakings protect the respondent's legitimate advantages.
  • Relitigation (+): similar to BCS v Baker (the judicial estoppel claim repackaged the decided trust issue): both vexatious and an abuse.
  • Parallel proceedings alone not enough (−): per UBS v Telesto, especially where the parties agreed a NEJC. Something more (+): per PT Sandipala, the case is stronger where parties and claims significantly overlap and the respondent voluntarily took part in Suit X, now far advanced; per Asiana (citing VEW v VEV), duplication plus something more may be vexatious.
  • Deliberate fragmentation (+): similar to Clearlake (contract in one forum, tort in another); per Hai Jiang, undecided here but "justified in some circumstances", consistent with Tomolugen's "bold approach".
  • Claim unknown here is not vexation (−): per British Airways v Laker, respect for foreign substantive law is part of comity (e.g., treble damages), unless the claim is used oppressively or targets a transaction overwhelmingly centred here (Midland Bank v Laker).
  • Suing a non-party to bypass the clause: see J6.5.2, scenario 4 (Asiana).
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Estate Litigation Spree

A deceased Singapore businessman's estate is suing his business partner, Mr J, in Singapore (Suit X) over beneficial ownership of companies holding Singapore real estate. The parties have a Singapore NEJC in their shareholders' agreement. Mr J:

  1. sues in the BVI, years after the claim accrued and one day after learning the estate would take over Suit X, on a claim that could have been a counterclaim in Suit X;
  2. sues in Hong Kong on a claim that the estate says is hopeless (it was released in a 2019 deed);
  3. obtains an ex parte seizure order in a remote jurisdiction, with proceedings in a language neither party speaks;
  4. sues in Jakarta, where the key witness, a retired Singapore banker who refuses to travel, cannot be compelled;
  5. sues in New York, after Suit X has been running for three years with Mr J's full participation, on exactly the same issues;
  6. sues in Texas for treble damages under RICO, a claim Singapore law does not know, over transactions conducted mostly in Singapore.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

The estate must show the "clearest of circumstances" (Kirkham; UBS v Telesto).

  1. Bad faith: like Lakshmi, a long-delayed suit filed the day after a trigger in Suit X, which should have been a counterclaim, is vexatious.
  2. Bound to fail (±): hopelessness is only a factor (VKC). The estate should stress conduct: Mr J signed the 2019 release and then "cynically" pursued a claim inconsistent with it (VKC), which makes the suit vexatious.
  3. Oppressive procedures and extreme inconvenience (Kirkham).
  4. Key witness not compellable (UBS v Telesto), especially if the banker's evidence is central.
  5. (−) Parallel proceedings alone are not enough, especially under a NEJC (UBS v Telesto). (+) But "something more" exists: the parties and claims overlap completely, and Mr J voluntarily took part in Suit X, which is far advanced (PT Sandipala; Asiana, citing VEW v VEV).
  6. (−) A claim unknown to Singapore law is not itself vexatious; respect for foreign substantive law is part of comity (British Airways v Laker). (+) But where it targets a transaction overwhelmingly centred in Singapore, it may be oppressive (Midland Bank v Laker).
  • Deliberate fragmentation: if Mr J sued in contract in New York and in tort in Texas on the same facts, that deliberate split (Clearlake) may be vexatious; the point is undecided in Singapore but "justified in some circumstances" (Hai Jiang; Tomolugen).
  • Lost remedy: if the estate could only bring a contribution claim against a third party in Singapore, the foreign suits would deprive it of that remedy (SNIA).
  • Rights challenged: if Mr J's Jakarta suit sought to undo a right established under Singapore law, it would be vexatious (Evergreen v Volkswagen).

J6.3.3 Abuse of Singapore's Process

(Amenability + self-evident interest only: slide 20, Kirkham (a) and (b).)

Rule: Starter (must write): per BCS v Baker, this ASI rests on the inherent power to protect the integrity of Singapore's processes, jurisdiction and judgments, focusing on the disruption the foreign proceedings cause; interest is self-evident, and natural forum is irrelevant.

  • Relitigating decided matters (+): similar to Masri (No 3), where after an English judgment that a 1992 agreement had not been terminated, the defendants sued in Yemen for the opposite declaration without any enforcement there: a collateral attack, not resistance to enforcement.
  • Duplicate suit pending appeal (+): similar to Beckkett v Deutsche Bank, where Beckkett sued in South Jakarta for the same declarations on the same grounds while its Singapore appeal was pending.
  • Could and should have been raised (+): per BCS v Baker (citing Elektrim), a Henderson-type abuse.
  • Insolvency (+): per BCS v Baker (citing SNIA), suing abroad to gain an advantage over other creditors in Singapore insolvency proceedings.
  • A new label does not matter (+): as in BCS v Baker, the judicial estoppel claim was the decided trust issue under a new label ("different sides of the same coin"), added as an afterthought; that it could not be brought here is irrelevant.
  • Foreign policy does not outweigh the affront (+): per BCS v Baker (citing Beckkett).
  • Genuinely new facts (−): as in BCS v Baker, where the Wrongful Settlement Claims rested on later-discovered facts and were not restrained.
  • Resisting enforcement is not abuse (−): see J6.2.2.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
After Judgment in Suit X

The Singapore High Court declares (in Suit X) that a distribution agreement between Lion Pharma and Sana Drugs (Indonesia) was validly terminated. Sana:

  1. sues in Jakarta for a declaration that the agreement was not terminated, without any attempt by Lion to enforce Suit X in Indonesia;
  2. while its Singapore appeal is pending, files the identical claim in South Jakarta;
  3. sues in Jakarta for an alleged misrepresentation by Lion during the agreement, which it could have raised in Suit X but chose to hold back;
  4. sues in Jakarta under an Indonesian "unfair termination of distributors" statute, a claim unavailable in Singapore, on the same facts;
  5. sues in Jakarta for Lion's alleged bribery of a Sana employee, discovered a year after judgment;
  6. opposes Lion's application to register the Singapore judgment in Indonesia.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Singapore's interest in protecting its judgment is self-evident, and natural forum is irrelevant (BCS v Baker).

  1. Restrain. This is a collateral attack seeking the opposite declaration, not resistance to enforcement (Masri (No 3)).
  2. Restrain. A duplicate suit pending appeal (Beckkett v Deutsche Bank).
  3. Restrain. A claim that could and should have been raised in Suit X (Elektrim; Henderson).
  4. Restrain. The statutory label is new, but in substance it is the decided termination issue ("different sides of the same coin": BCS v Baker). That the claim is unavailable in Singapore is irrelevant, and Indonesian policy does not outweigh the affront to Singapore's processes (Beckkett). Sana's "advantage" abroad is no answer; it is what makes the suit abusive (J6.4).
  5. Do not restrain. Genuinely new facts not decided in Suit X (as with BCS v Baker's Wrongful Settlement Claims).
  6. Do not restrain. Merely resisting enforcement abroad is for the Indonesian court (J6.2.2).
  • Insolvency variant: if Lion were in Singapore liquidation and Sana sued abroad to jump ahead of other creditors, that would also be an abuse (SNIA, via BCS v Baker).

J6.3.4 Singapore Public Policy

Rule: Basis (+): per C&Y, an ASI may give effect to Singapore public policy, in very exceptional cases overriding even a foreign EJC; similar to Petter v EMC, where an English ASI protected an employee in employment litigation despite a foreign EJC (see also Evergreen). High threshold (−): per Stichting Shell (citing Barclays v Homan) and C&Y, an ASI is appropriate only where Singapore's and the foreign State's policies are "so at variance" that comity is overridden.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Employee and the Massachusetts Clause

A Singapore-based engineer employed by the Singapore subsidiary of a US tech company signed stock-option terms with an exclusive Massachusetts courts clause and a two-year worldwide non-compete. When he joins a Singapore competitor, the US parent sues him in Massachusetts.

  • Variation: the foreign law simply sets a different limitation period for wage claims.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

(+) Like Petter v EMC, the engineer argues that Singapore public policy protecting employees in employment disputes justifies an ASI even against a foreign EJC. That is very exceptional (C&Y). (−) The US parent argues Stichting Shell/Barclays v Homan: only where the two policies are "so at variance" that comity is overridden. A non-compete may be enforceable in some form in both systems.

  • In the variation, a mere difference in limitation periods is nowhere near "so at variance", so no ASI.

6J6.4 No undue injustice to the respondent

(Vexation ASIs only. Abuse of process: the advantage is irrelevant (BCS v Baker). Contractual ASIs: no separate limb; the respondent's points go to strong reasons (Cooperative Muratori).)

Rule: Balancing (must write): per Kirkham, vexation and injustice to the respondent are "two sides of the same coin", and the injustice "feeds into" vexation (Cooperative Muratori). Per SNIA and C&Y, weigh the respondent's loss of a legitimate juridical advantage against the injustice to the applicant if the ASI is refused. Factors (C&Y): (i) the advantage lost (e.g., higher damages, discovery, a jury trial), which counts for less where the foreign court is not the natural forum (UBS v Telesto); (ii) the remedy sought abroad; (iii) how far the foreign proceedings have advanced. Undertakings neutralise (+): as in SNIA (undertakings preserved the plaintiffs' Texas advantages in Brunei) and Lakshmi (an undertaking to consent to a mirror BVI judgment). Cynically created advantage (+): as in BCS v Baker (citing VKC), the US-only judicial estoppel claim, raised after the trust issue was fully argued, was "cynically" pursued to attack the Suit 3 judgment. Abuse, advantage no answer (+): per BCS v Baker, "it is the very existence of an advantage outside the forum which may justify injunctive relief". Genuine advantage outweighs (−): where the respondent would lose a genuine advantage (e.g., a claim against a party suable only abroad) with no undertaking from the applicant, and the foreign court is a natural forum.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Balancing the Helicopter Case (from J6.2.3)

The families suing in Texas would lose (a) contingency-fee funding, (b) American-style discovery, (c) a jury trial, and (d) a claim against a Texas-based component maker that cannot be sued in Singapore. The manufacturer offers undertakings to (i) fund the families' reasonable legal costs in Singapore, (ii) give voluntary disclosure equivalent to US discovery, and (iii) not take any limitation point.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Weigh the families' lost advantages against the manufacturer's lost contribution claim (SNIA). Advantages (a)–(c) count for less because Texas is not the natural forum (UBS v Telesto), and undertakings (i)–(iii) neutralise them, as in SNIA. But (d) is a genuine advantage, a claim against a party suable only in Texas, and the manufacturer offers nothing to neutralise it. If the component maker is central, the balance may tip against an ASI, or the ASI may be confined so the families can still pursue that party in Texas. Contrast: in an abuse case, a foreign-only advantage is no answer at all (BCS v Baker). And if the families had created the Texas advantage cynically, by timing their claim to exploit a US-only doctrine after losing elsewhere, it would count for little (BCS v Baker, citing VKC).

J6.4.1 Conclusion and Fallbacks

Rule: Granted: amenable + interest + a legitimate basis + no undue injustice (given undertakings), so an interim or permanent ASI issues, if necessary only until the preconditions in the clause are met. Refused: for lack of interest, delay or strong reasons. Fallbacks: foreign courts can take offence (the Düsseldorf CA refused to serve an English ASI), so the applicant may prefer a stay application abroad, damages for breach (J1.7), a declaration, resisting recognition of the foreign judgment (J7.2.6), or an anti-enforcement injunction (J7.6).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
When the ASI Is Refused

Sun Resorts (J6.3.1.5, refused for delay) asks what else it can do.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

It can (i) continue to seek a stay in the Maldives, (ii) claim damages in Singapore for breach of the arbitration agreement (J1.7; subject to Tradewaves), (iii) seek a declaration of breach, (iv) resist recognition of any Maldivian judgment in Singapore as obtained in breach (J7.2.6; Nimbus-type public policy), or (v) in exceptional circumstances, seek an AEI (J7.6). It should also bear in mind that some foreign courts react badly to ASIs (Düsseldorf refused to serve one).

7J6.5 Special situations

J6.5.1 Anti-Anti-Suit Injunctions

Rule: Protecting Singapore proceedings (+): per Airbus and C&Y, Singapore may restrain the respondent from seeking a foreign ASI against Suit X, on the usual requirements. Contractual anti-anti-suit (+): it may also issue where a foreign ASI has breached or would breach the contract; similar to Sabah Shipyard, where the English CA upheld an ASI against Pakistani proceedings that stopped Sabah calling on a guarantee under an English NEJC. Caution (−): after UBS v Telesto, plead vexation as well as breach.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Threatened Pakistani Injunction

A Malaysian shipyard holds a performance guarantee from a Pakistani state entity, with an English-style NEJC for Singapore. The shipyard sues on the guarantee in Singapore. The state entity tells the shipyard it will apply in Karachi for an injunction preventing the shipyard from calling on the guarantee or continuing the Singapore suit.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Singapore may grant an anti-anti-suit injunction to protect its own proceedings (Airbus; C&Y), subject to amenability, interest and the other requirements. On the contractual basis, the Karachi application would breach the NEJC's narrow waiver (an objection to Singapore's jurisdiction), and Sabah Shipyard called such conduct "clearly a breach". But since UBS v Telesto treats Sabah as a vexation case, the shipyard should also plead vexation: the Karachi application is designed to stop it enforcing its contractual rights.

J6.5.2 Third Parties: Quasi-Contractual ASIs (slide 19's four scenarios)

(Set-up: A and B agreed a Singapore EJC; C is a non-party connected to the contract or dispute.)

Rule:

  • Scenario 1: A sues B and C; B seeks the ASI (±): (+) the ASI against A's claim on B rests on breach; (−) C's presence and claims outside the clause may be strong reasons (Donohue); (+) fragmentation "should not be overstated" (Asiana).
  • Scenario 2: C sues A; A seeks the ASI (+): the ASI rests on the clause only if C is bound. Per Hai Jiang, C is bound if it derives rights from a party by subrogation, assignment, or a statutory or equitable right, taking the benefit subject to the burden. Vandepitte beneficiary: similar to Finaport, where Techteryx, suing in Hong Kong under the Vandepitte procedure, was bound by the trustee's tiered clause because the cause of action remained the trustee's (not a derived-rights case: there was no transfer). Variant (applicant denies being a party): per Hai Jiang, where the respondent sues the applicant abroad on a contract that the applicant denies being party to, the claim is "inherently subject" to the clause; the applicant must show (a) breach, (b) its right to enforce the clause, (c) validity, and (d) that the foreign claim is within scope.
  • Scenario 3: A sues C; C seeks the ASI (−): per VKC v VJZ, C cannot use CRTPA s 2(1)(b): Parliament deliberately extended the Act to arbitration agreements (s 9) but not jurisdiction clauses, and an EJC confers no substantive benefit. Critique (+, Chong): if an EJC were merely procedural, its breach could not found an ASI or damages. Routes left open (+): s 2(1)(a) if the contract expressly confers the right; s 2(3); or equity as in Hai Jiang (VKC). Comparison: Global Partners v Babcock & Brown (NSWCA): group companies that took part in the decisions complained of and were "Indemnified Persons" could rely on the clause. Fallback: otherwise C must show vexation to C in its own right (Asiana).
  • Scenario 4: A sues C; B seeks the ASI (±): per Asiana, B may restrain A's suit against non-party C only if (a) construction (−): the clause on its true construction covers claims against C, which needs a "quite clear indication" (Asiana, adopting Team Y&R); or (b) bypass (+): the real purpose of suing C is to bypass the clause, making the suit vexatious as between A and B (Asiana, citing Clearlake and Giorgio Armani). Rejected (−): B's "sufficient interest" (e.g., its liability to indemnify C) is not enough (Lord Scott in Donohue), being over-inclusive; C may still seek its own ASI if the suit is vexatious to C.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Charterparty Family

A (Shipowner) and B (Charterer) have a charterparty with an exclusive Singapore clause covering "all disputes between the parties". C is variously B's cargo insurer, B's director, or B's subsidiary.

  1. Scenario 1: A sues B and B's director (C) in Rotterdam: contract claims against B, and tort and fraud claims against C.
  2. Scenario 2: B's cargo insurer (C), subrogated to B, sues A in Shanghai.
  3. Scenario 2 variant: A sues "B Group Holdings" in Shanghai under the charterparty; B Group Holdings says it never was a party.
  4. Scenario 2 (Vandepitte): B holds the charterparty claims on trust for C, which, under the Vandepitte procedure, sues A in Hong Kong on B's cause of action, ignoring a "shall first mediate" tier in the clause.
  5. Scenario 3: A sues B's director (C) in Rotterdam for inducing B's breach. C seeks an ASI relying on the Singapore clause.
  6. Scenario 4: A sues B's wholly owned subsidiary (C) in Rotterdam, with a claim that mirrors exactly its claim against B. B seeks the ASI, pointing to its contractual obligation to indemnify C.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  1. Against A's claim on B, there is a contractual ASI (breach). But C's presence and the tort claims outside the clause may be strong reasons (Donohue). B replies that fragmentation "should not be overstated" (Asiana).
  2. The subrogated insurer derives its rights from B, so it takes the benefit subject to the burden and is bound by the clause (Hai Jiang). A can get a contractual ASI.
  3. A's claim is "inherently subject" to the clause (Hai Jiang). B Group must show breach, its right to enforce the clause, the clause's validity, and that the Shanghai claim is within scope.
  4. As in Finaport, C sues on B's cause of action, so it is bound as B would be, including by the mediation tier. The ASI restrains C until the tier is completed, and C cannot complain that the tier is impractical.
  5. C cannot rely on CRTPA s 2(1)(b) (VKC v VJZ). Chong's critique: the "procedural" label is inconsistent with ASIs and damages for breach. C might argue s 2(1)(a) or s 2(3) if the clause names directors, or the equitable route, or the Global Partners reasoning if C was an "Indemnified Person" involved in the impugned decisions. Otherwise C must show vexation in its own right (Asiana).
  6. (a) "All disputes between the parties" gives no "quite clear indication" that it covers claims against C (Asiana; Team Y&R). (b) But A's mirror claim against B's subsidiary looks like a bypass of the clause, which makes it vexatious as between A and B (Clearlake; Giorgio Armani). B's indemnity liability alone is not enough (Lord Scott in Donohue, rejected as over-inclusive in Asiana). C may also seek its own ASI if the suit is vexatious to C.

J6.5.3 HCCCA / CCAA Cases

Rule: Starter: the HCCCA reduces but does not remove parallel proceedings, since a non-chosen Contracting State court must generally decline save under art 6; Singapore may grant interim measures whatever the chosen court (s 10 CCAA). Art 7: it neither requires nor precludes interim measures; they are not "judgments" (art 4), but per Hartley–Dogauchi they support the agreement, so an interim or permanent ASI arguably falls within art 7.

  • Singapore EJC; suit in a non-Contracting State (+): an ordinary contractual ASI; the chosen court's ASI upholds the agreement.
  • Singapore EJC; suit in another Contracting State (+): Singapore, as chosen court, may be given more leeway; the foreign court should itself have declined under art 6, so the ASI supports the Convention scheme.
  • Foreign Contracting-State EJC; suit in a non-Contracting State (−): no HCCCA concern arises, but Singapore should not be an "international busybody" (Akai).
  • Foreign Contracting-State EJC; suit in another Contracting State (±): (+) a Singapore ASI arguably makes the clause more effective, especially if the chosen court cannot grant ASIs. (−) If the suing court took jurisdiction under an art 6 exception, an ASI would undermine the HCCCA's uniform rules, so Singapore should generally refrain.
  • ASI against the chosen court (−): never supports the agreement and should not issue.
  • s 4(10A) CLA (±): power is not discretion; the Akai objection remains.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Five Hague Combinations

A 2022 contract has an exclusive clause:

  1. Singapore EJC; the respondent sues in Thailand (not a Contracting State).
  2. Singapore EJC; the respondent sues in Germany (a Contracting State).
  3. English EJC; the respondent sues in India (not a Contracting State); the applicant asks Singapore for an ASI.
  4. English EJC; the respondent sues in Mexico (a Contracting State), whose court took jurisdiction under an art 6 exception (manifest injustice); the applicant asks Singapore.
  5. Mexican EJC; the respondent sues in Mexico (the chosen court), and the applicant asks Singapore (a non-chosen court) to restrain the Mexican proceedings.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  1. An ordinary contractual ASI (J6.3.1); as the chosen court, Singapore upholds the agreement.
  2. Even more leeway: Germany should have declined under art 6, so a Singapore ASI supports the Convention scheme. Interim ASIs are in any case outside the CCAA (s 10), and arguably art 7 accommodates them.
  3. No HCCCA concern, but London (the chosen court) should act; Singapore is not an "international busybody" (Akai; J6.2.6).
  4. (±) (+) An ASI would make the English clause more effective, particularly if England is unwilling to grant one. (−) But Mexico took jurisdiction under an art 6 exception, so a Singapore ASI would undermine the HCCCA's uniform scheme and fragment States' responses. Singapore should generally refrain.
  5. An ASI by a non-chosen court against proceedings in the chosen court never supports the agreement and should not issue (C&Y). s 4(10A) CLA would give power to aid other proceedings, but not a reason to do this.

J6.5.4 Anti-Enforcement Injunctions (pointer)

Rule: Where the foreign court has already given judgment, the applicant needs an AEI: run J6.1–J6.4 as the floor, then the Sun Travels "exceptional circumstances" overlay in J7.6 (e.g., fraud; no knowledge of the proceedings until judgment).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Too Late for an ASI

A Singapore company learns that a Kazakh court gave a US$40m default judgment against it last month in proceedings it was never told about, brought in breach of a Singapore arbitration agreement. The judgment creditor is about to enforce it in Dubai.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

An ASI is too late, because the foreign judgment exists. The company needs an anti-enforcement injunction: it must satisfy the ordinary ASI requirements (amenability, interest, breach) plus exceptional circumstances (Sun Travels). Having had no knowledge of the proceedings until judgment is one of the recognised exceptional circumstances, alongside fraud (J7.6).
