LAW302 · HYPO LESSON J7 · 33 HYPOTHETICALS · 8 FLOWCHARTS · 8 QUESTIONS

J7 hypotheticals: Foreign judgments: enforcement, recognition and AEIs

The rules behind these hypotheticals are taught in Lesson J7, where the word-for-word pre-write is too. Do that lesson first if the rules below look unfamiliar.

Applications:
ℹ HOW TO USE THESE HYPOTHETICALS

Each concept is set out as Rule, then Hypothetical, then Application. "Creditor" = judgment creditor; "debtor" = judgment debtor; X = country of origin; Y = a third country. (+) helps the creditor; (−) helps the debtor.

The flowcharts redraw the hypotheticals in this site's chart style: the chip on each arrow names the hypothetical (or version) that takes that path. The hypo test at the end checks you can run the facts yourself.

1J7.0 Roadmap and regime router

Rule (order): (1) Does the party want to enforce the judgment (sword: recover money) or have it recognised (shield / estoppel)? (2) Which regime: CCAA, then REFJA, then common law? (3) Are the requirements met? (4) Does a defence apply? (5) Does the debtor want an AEI instead?

Rule (Regime router):

  • CCAA first (ousts REFJA): if X is an HCCCA Contracting State and the X court is the court chosen in an exclusive COCA (or its transferee), the creditor proceeds under the CCAA (J7.5). Per REFJA s 2A, if X is also gazetted, the creditor cannot fall back on REFJA if the CCAA route fails.
  • Common law fallback (±): per s 21 CCAA the common law remains open, but per C&Y the CCAA is almost always better for the creditor (non-money relief, no limitation period, simpler procedure). After a CCAA refusal, suing at common law may be abusive if it re-ventilates the same issues.
  • REFJA (not examinable): if X is gazetted (per the handout: HK, Brunei, Australia, India, Malaysia, NZ, Pakistan, PNG, Sri Lanka, UK), note in one line that the creditor could register, then run the common law.
  • Common law residual: sue on the debt the judgment creates, usually by summary judgment. Per C&Y, the debtor gets leave to defend only by showing a fair or reasonable probability of a real defence under J7.2, never the merits.
  • Non-money judgments: an injunction or specific performance order is enforceable only under REFJA (s 4(4)) or the CCAA. At common law, the creditor sues afresh on the original cause and pleads the judgment as res judicata.
  • Recognition only: J7.1.1–J7.1.3 must be met and no J7.2 defence apply, but there is no money requirement.
  • In rem, test: per Pattni v Ali (adopted by the SGCA), a judgment is in rem if the X court, where the property was situated, adjudicated title against the world; Singapore characterises it by the X proceedings' nature and intended effect (C&Y). In rem, effect: the property must have been in X when proceedings began (also s 5(3)(b) REFJA). Such judgments are usually recognised (e.g., as proof of title in a conversion claim), free of the six-year bar, and a good-faith purchaser is protected against fraud.
  • Memorandum of Guidance (−): MoGs (e.g., with DIFC, China SPC) are non-binding statements of each side's existing law, so the judgment must still satisfy the common law or REFJA (C&Y).
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Seven Judgments Arrive at a Singapore Law Firm
  1. A Mexico City court judgment for US$3m, given as the court chosen in a 2021 exclusive clause.
  2. A Hong Kong High Court money judgment (no clause).
  3. A Tokyo District Court money judgment (no clause).
  4. A German court order for specific performance of a share transfer (no clause).
  5. A Brazilian court judgment dismissing a Brazilian company's claim against a Singapore company. The Brazilian company now sues again in Singapore on the same claim.
  6. A Panamanian admiralty court judgment selling a vessel to a buyer "free of all encumbrances". The vessel later calls at Singapore, and a former mortgagee sues the buyer in conversion.
  7. A Chinese court judgment, where the creditor relies on the Singapore–China SPC Memorandum of Guidance.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  1. CCAA (Mexico is a Contracting State; the court was chosen in an exclusive COCA). If Mexico were also gazetted, REFJA would be unavailable as a fallback (REFJA s 2A). The common law remains open (s 21 CCAA), but the CCAA is better, and re-running refused issues at common law may be abusive.
  2. Hong Kong is gazetted, so note in one line that it could be registered under REFJA, then run the common law (since REFJA is not examined).
  3. Common law action on the judgment debt, probably by summary judgment. The debtor gets leave to defend only on a real J7.2 defence, never on the merits.
  4. Not enforceable at common law (non-money). Sue afresh in Singapore on the share transfer obligation and plead the German judgment as res judicata (J7.3.1). Neither REFJA nor the CCAA applies: Germany is not a gazetted REFJA country, and there is no choice of court agreement.
  5. Recognition only (shield): the Singapore company pleads the Brazilian judgment as cause of action estoppel. J7.1.1–J7.1.3 apply, but there is no money requirement.
  6. In rem: the Panamanian court, where the vessel was located when proceedings began, adjudicated title against the world (Pattni v Ali). It is recognised as proof of the buyer's title, free of the six-year bar, and the good-faith buyer is protected.
  7. The MoG is non-binding. The Chinese judgment must still meet the common law requirements.

2J7.0.3 Common law procedure: serving the originating claim

Rule: The creditor enforces by a fresh action in the General Division, so the debtor must be served; service founds in personam jurisdiction. Service in: as of right (J2.1). Service out: s 16(1)(a)(ii) SCJA and O 8 r 1(1): Singapore must be "the appropriate court", which per para 63(2) SCPD 2021 needs (a) a good arguable case of nexus; (b) forum conveniens; (c) a serious question. Nexus (+): para 63(3)(m): the action enforces a judgment enforceable at common law in executable form (C&Y); a good arguable case is more than a prima facie case (Bradley Lomas). Merits subsumed (±): per Li Shengwu, a serious question need not be shown separately where the factor engages the merits; arguably (m) does, since the merits are whether the judgment is enforceable. Assets in Singapore? (±): per Demirel (Eng), assets are not required, but the creditor must show a real prospect of a legitimate benefit (future assets, examining the debtor, a judgment about to go stale). Forum conveniens required? (±): (+) per Licea v Curacao, FNC does not arise, as enforcement is not a fresh suit on the merits, consistent with Art 13(2) Hague Judgments Convention. (−) England (Demirel) and Canada (Chevron v Yaiguaje) keep an FC or FNC filter, so per C&Y Licea may be revisited. Why FC is ill-fitting (+): per C&Y, (i) FC picks one forum for the merits, whereas enforcement may be pursued in several places; (ii) the court facilitates an obligation already fixed rather than adjudicating; (iii) requiring both FC and a legitimate benefit is overkill. Filter against abuse (±): (−) some filter is sensible, as a creditor may sue to harass the debtor or to "launder" the foreign judgment through a Singapore judgment; (+) that concern is absent where the creditor targets the debtor's Singapore assets. Alternatively, FC satisfied (+): even if FC is required, the debtor's Singapore assets point to Singapore as the place of enforcement (Spiliada).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Chasing the Ecuadorian Oil Judgment

An Ecuadorian court awarded villagers US$500m against Petro Andes Corp (incorporated in Delaware). The villagers' Singapore lawyers want to enforce in Singapore.

  • Version 1: Petro Andes has US$50m in a Singapore bank account. It is served in Delaware.
  • Version 2: Petro Andes has no Singapore assets, but its Singapore subsidiary is due to pay it a US$20m dividend next year.
  • Version 3: Petro Andes has no Singapore assets and no prospect of any. The villagers want a Singapore judgment so they can then register it in Malaysia and Brunei under reciprocal arrangements that do not cover Ecuador.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

The villagers serve out under para 63(3)(m): the action enforces a foreign judgment enforceable by common law action in executable form. They need a good arguable case (Bradley Lomas). The merits question (is the judgment enforceable?) arguably engages (m), so a serious question is subsumed (Li Shengwu).

  • Version 1: FC (±): per Licea, FC is irrelevant, since enforcement is not a fresh merits suit (cf Art 13(2) HJC). Petro Andes cites Demirel and Chevron v Yaiguaje (itself a case about enforcing an Ecuadorian judgment) to argue for an FC filter. C&Y explain why FC is ill-fitting: the villagers may enforce in many places at once, the court only gives effect to a fixed obligation, and requiring FC on top of legitimate benefit is overkill. In any event, the US$50m in Singapore makes Singapore the natural place of enforcement, so FC would be satisfied.
  • Version 2: Assets now are not required (Demirel); a real prospect of legitimate benefit (the future dividend) suffices.
  • Version 3: This is the "laundering" concern: using a Singapore judgment to unlock other regimes, not to reach Singapore assets. A filter is sensible here (C&Y), whether framed as FC or as legitimate benefit (only one is needed, per C&Y). Permission is likely refused.

3J7.1 Common law: requirements for enforcement

Rule (Starter): Per C&Y (cf Ong Han Nam), the creditor must show the judgment is (a) on the merits; (b) given by a court with international jurisdiction over the debtor; (c) final and conclusive; and (d) a fresh money judgment for a definite sum, not a tax, fine or penalty. The same apply to recognition, save (d). The burden is on the creditor. Check presence first; if that fails, submission.

J7.1.1 Judgment on the Merits

Rule: Per The Sennar (No 2), a judgment is on the merits if the court found the facts, stated the law or applied it to liability or quantum, not merely ruled on a point of procedure. Default judgment (+): on the merits even though the debtor did not appear and the court may not have considered the evidence; non-participation goes only to fraud or natural justice (C&Y). Interlocutory judgment (±): it counts if it finally decides the issue and is not on a "procedural" issue; per The Sennar (No 2), a ruling that a claim is barred by a jurisdiction clause is substantive, but one on service or security for costs is not. Limitation ruling (+): per s 5 FLPA, dismissal as time-barred under any law is deemed on the merits. Judgment on a judgment (−): per Sang Cheol Woo (not following Morgan Stanley v Pilot Lead (HK)), a judgment merely declaring another judgment enforceable is unenforceable at common law, and per REFJA s 3(4)(c) not registrable; enforce the original directly. Why not (C&Y): it (i) never examined the issues; (ii) decides only its territorial effect in X (Merck: no estoppel); (iii) would launder the original judgment, with Singapore testing the wrong court. Contrary view (+): Desert Palace (HC) saw no difficulty, but per C&Y it did not grapple with the theory.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Five Rulings From Abroad
  1. A Malaysian default judgment against a Singapore businessman who ignored the proceedings.
  2. A Dutch ruling that a cargo claim is barred by a Sudanese exclusive jurisdiction clause.
  3. An Indonesian ruling ordering the claimant to give security for costs.
  4. A Thai ruling dismissing a claim as time-barred under Thai law.
  5. A Hong Kong judgment declaring a Las Vegas casino's Nevada judgment enforceable in Hong Kong. The casino wants to enforce the Hong Kong judgment in Singapore.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  1. On the merits. A default judgment counts even though the court may not have examined the evidence; the businessman's non-appearance can only be raised through fraud or natural justice (C&Y).
  2. On the merits. Like The Sennar (No 2), a ruling that a claim is barred by a jurisdiction clause is substantive.
  3. Not on the merits. It is purely procedural.
  4. Deemed on the merits by s 5 FLPA, so it can be pleaded as res judicata.
  5. (−) A judgment on a judgment. Per Sang Cheol Woo (declining to follow HK's Morgan Stanley v Pilot Lead), it is not enforceable at common law (and not registrable under REFJA s 3(4)(c)). It never examined the issues, only fixes the Nevada judgment's effect in Hong Kong (Merck), and enforcing it would "launder" the Nevada judgment through Hong Kong. (+) The casino cites Desert Palace, but per C&Y it did not engage with the theory. The casino must enforce the Nevada judgment directly (and then face the gambling public policy point: J7.2.4).

J7.1.2 International Jurisdiction of the X Court

Rule: Singapore's rules (−): per C&Y, the test is Singapore's conflict rules, which are narrower than Singapore's own bases of jurisdiction, with no mirror image. So the X court's service-out jurisdiction does not count, and its own finding on jurisdiction creates no estoppel. Four grounds: per Republic of India v Deutsche Telekom (SGCA), the debtor must have been present in X, or have claimed or counterclaimed, voluntarily appeared, or agreed in advance to submit; residence is not listed. Closed categories (−): per Schibsby v Westenholz, the grounds are closed. A real and substantial connection between X and the claim (the Canadian ground in Beals v Saldanha) has not been adopted.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Ontario Land Deal

A Singapore investor bought land in Florida from Canadian sellers. The deal fell through, and the sellers sued the investor in Ontario. The Ontario court took jurisdiction under its rules permitting service out because the contract had a "real and substantial connection" with Ontario (the sellers lived there and negotiated from there). The investor was never in Ontario, did not appear, and never agreed to Ontario jurisdiction. The Ontario court held, in its judgment, that it had jurisdiction.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

International jurisdiction is tested by Singapore's conflict rules, not Ontario's, and there is no "mirror image" (C&Y), so it does not matter that Ontario (or even Singapore) would take jurisdiction on service out. The only grounds are presence, claiming or counterclaiming, voluntary appearance, or prior agreement (India v Deutsche Telekom). They are closed (Schibsby), and the Canadian real-and-substantial-connection ground (Beals v Saldanha) is not part of Singapore law. The Ontario court's own finding on jurisdiction raises no estoppel (J7.3.2.3). The judgment is not enforceable.

J7.1.2.1–J7.1.2.2 Presence: Timing, Federal States, Natural Persons

Rule: Time of presence: per Adams v Cape, the debtor must be present in X at the time of suit, meaning when the X process was served, not when it was issued. Federal systems (±): per Adams v Cape (obiter, "with varying degrees of doubt"), presence anywhere in a federation may suffice for a federal court, but a state court needs presence in that state; (−) C&Y question this, since federal judgments are "foreign" in other US states. Temporary presence (+): per Adams v Cape (obiter), voluntary presence suffices even if temporary. Involuntary presence (−): presence must be voluntary; a debtor lured by the creditor's fraud or brought there under duress was not present (C&Y). Virtual presence (−): per Lucasfilm, presence must be physical; a website targeting X consumers or adverts in X magazines do not suffice. Residence without presence (±): (+) per United Malayan Banking (obiter) and C&Y, residence suffices a fortiori, being a stronger tie; (−) English law stresses presence (Rubin), and India v Deutsche Telekom omits residence. Contrast REFJA (−): per s 5(3)(a)(iv), residence is required and mere presence is not enough.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Mr Ong's Travels

Mr Ong, a Singapore resident, is sued in several places:

  1. California: the claim was issued while he was on a two-day business trip to San Francisco, but served a week later, after he had returned to Singapore.
  2. Texas state court: he was served while changing planes at Dallas airport (a two-hour transit).
  3. US federal court in New York: he was served while on holiday in Florida.
  4. Thailand: a business rival tricked him into flying to Bangkok for a fake investor meeting, and served him at the hotel.
  5. England: his online shop shipped to UK customers and advertised in UK magazines; he never went to England.
  6. Hong Kong: he has a flat there and lives there four months a year, but was in Singapore when served.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  1. Not present. Presence is judged at service, not issue (Adams v Cape).
  2. Present. Voluntary, even if temporary, presence suffices (Adams v Cape, obiter), and he was in Texas when served by a Texas state court.
  3. (±) Per Adams v Cape (obiter, doubtfully), presence anywhere in the federation may suffice for a federal court. C&Y question this: a New York federal judgment is "foreign" in the sense that it is not obviously a judgment of the whole US for this purpose.
  4. Not present. His presence was procured by fraud, so it was involuntary (C&Y).
  5. Not present. A website and adverts are virtual, not physical, presence (Lucasfilm).
  6. (±) (+) Residence is a stronger tie than fleeting presence, so it suffices a fortiori (United Malayan Banking, obiter; C&Y). (−) English law emphasises presence (Rubin), and India v Deutsche Telekom lists presence, not residence, so absent from Hong Kong at service, he was not subject to its court. Contrast: under REFJA (Hong Kong is gazetted), residence is required and is the relevant test (s 5(3)(a)(iv)); in the Texas transit case, REFJA would not be satisfied by mere presence.

J7.1.2.3 Presence: Companies

Rule: Per Adams v Cape, a company is present in X if, for more than a minimal period, its own business was carried on at or from a fixed place of business (its own, at its own expense, or a representative's), through its servants or a representative. Per Littauer Glove, a reasonably permanent place suffices. Short but fixed (+): per Dunlop v Cudell, a nine-day trade-fair stand was a fixed place of business. No fixed place (−): per Littauer Glove, a representative merely staying at a hotel for a few days taking orders did not carry on business at a fixed place. Whose business? (±): the representative must carry on the debtor's business, not its own; ask whether the debtor acquired the premises, paid a fixed salary rather than commission, and controlled the business. Most weight goes to whether the representative could bind the debtor without specific prior authority. Own business (−): as in Adams v Cape, where Cape's Illinois marketing companies (NAAC, AMC and CPC) carried on their own business, so Cape was not present in the US. Go-between (−): per Vogel, a representative who merely introduced customers or passed on orders without authority to bind carried on its own business. Non-trading debtor: substitute corporate activities for "business".

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Was Nusantara Present in Texas?

A Texas court gave judgment against Nusantara Asbestos Pte Ltd (Singapore) for asbestos injuries. At the time of service:

  • Version 1: Nusantara had a leased warehouse in Houston, staffed by its own salaried employees, who signed sales contracts without head-office approval.
  • Version 2: Nusantara's products were sold through Lone Star Marketing Inc, an independent Texas company that owned its own premises, was paid commission and had to get Nusantara's approval for every contract.
  • Version 3: Nusantara's sales director spent four days at a Houston hotel taking orders.
  • Version 4: Nusantara had a stand at a 10-day Houston industrial trade fair, during which it was served.
  • Version 5: A Texas agent introduced customers and passed orders to Singapore but could not bind Nusantara.
  • Version 6: Nusantara's charitable foundation (a non-trading body) ran a permanent Houston office for its grant programme.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  1. Present. A fixed place, its own business, salaried employees, and power to bind without prior authority (Adams v Cape).
  2. Not present. Like Cape's Illinois marketing companies (NAAC, AMC, CPC), Lone Star carried on its own business: its own premises, commission, and no power to bind without approval.
  3. Not present. A hotel for a few days is not a fixed place of business (Littauer Glove).
  4. Present. Like the nine-day stand in Dunlop v Cudell, a 10-day trade-fair stand is a fixed place for more than a minimal period.
  5. Not present. A go-between without authority to bind carries on its own business (Vogel).
  6. Not present. The foundation is a separate body, so its office is not Nusantara's place of business. Substituting "corporate activities" for business (Adams v Cape) helps only where the judgment debtor is itself non-trading: a judgment against the foundation could rest on its permanent Houston office.

J7.1.2.4 Submission by Conduct (if presence fails)

Rule: Test: per Nimbus, the debtor submitted only by a step that necessarily waived its objection to jurisdiction, judged practically, as business people would. Per IGCF (PC), adopting Rubin, a step "only necessary or only useful" if the objection was waived is submission.

  • Claimant or merits defence (+): suing in X (including related counterclaims or set-off), or filing a defence on the merits (C&Y; Malaysia Marine).
  • Merits plea with jurisdiction challenge (±): (+) pleading the merits where X procedure permits but does not require it is submission; (−) if X procedure requires both and the debtor maintained its objection throughout, there is none; (+) unless the debtor could withdraw the merits plea after losing on jurisdiction and did not.
  • Jurisdictional objection (−): as in Nimbus (objecting in Colombo under the Sri Lankan Arbitration Act, losing, then taking no part, was not submission).
  • Setting aside on FNC grounds (+): per Henry v Geoprosco, asking the X court to decline a jurisdiction it had is submission; Nimbus assumed Henry is law without deciding.
  • Henry should not be followed (−): per IGCF (PC), Henry's existence/exercise line is "unrealistic and irrational", no common law jurisdiction follows it, and REFJA s 5(3)(a)(i)(C) reverses it. Per C&Y, a failed set-aside on any ground is a protest (Re Dulles).
  • Stay application (±): (+) on Henry's logic, a stay accepts jurisdiction; (−) per IGCF, a stay for arbitration or on FNC grounds is a protest, unless the debtor sought more (e.g., consequential relief on the merits).
  • ROC analogy (±): (−) O 6 r 7(6) and O 6 r 12(5) ROC 2021 say challenging the exercise of Singapore's jurisdiction is not submission; (+) per C&Y this may not carry over: there is no mirror image, and international jurisdiction uses narrower criteria.
  • Whose law (±): per Giant Light Metal (approving Akai), Singapore law decides, with X procedure as context; per C&Y it would be strange to find submission where X law would not treat the step as such, though Rubin left this open.
  • Inchoate submission (±): per Giant Light Metal, weigh (a) the connection between the claims (a matter of degree that may span separate later proceedings between the same parties) and (b) fairness to both, disregarding technical procedural impediments. Application (+): as in Giant Light Metal (the same parties and claims refiled after settlement talks failed; separate case numbers were a technicality) and Murthy v Sivajothi (submission to a Florida foreclosure action extended to related fraud cross-claims).
  • Composition plan (−): per Humpuss, the debtor's unilateral inclusion as a creditor in an X composition plan is not by itself submission.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
What Did Sinar Do in Court?

Sinar Shipping Pte Ltd (Singapore, no presence in X) faced proceedings in X. Consider what it did in each case:

  1. It filed a defence on the merits without protest.
  2. X procedure required it to plead its merits defence at the same time as its jurisdiction challenge, and it maintained its challenge throughout and lost.
  3. As in (2), but after losing on jurisdiction, X procedure allowed it to withdraw its merits plea, and it did not.
  4. It objected under the X arbitration statute that the dispute should go to arbitration, lost, and then took no further part.
  5. It applied to set aside service on the ground that X was forum non conveniens, and lost.
  6. It applied for a stay in favour of arbitration, and also asked the X court to order the release of its seized vessel on the merits.
  7. It sued the claimant in X on an earlier invoice; the claimant then started new proceedings in X (a different case number) on the same subject matter after settlement talks failed, and Sinar did not appear.
  8. The claimant's insolvency administrator listed Sinar as a creditor in an X composition plan without Sinar's involvement.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  1. Submission: a merits defence is a step "only necessary or only useful" if the objection is waived (IGCF/Rubin; Malaysia Marine).
  2. No submission: X procedure required both, and Sinar maintained its objection throughout (C&Y).
  3. Submission: it could have withdrawn the merits plea after losing on jurisdiction, and did not (C&Y).
  4. No submission: exactly Nimbus (objecting in Colombo, losing and then taking no part).
  5. (±) Under Henry v Geoprosco, an FNC set-aside asks the court to decline a jurisdiction it has, so it is submission (and Nimbus assumed Henry is law). But IGCF (PC, 2025) calls Henry's distinction "unrealistic and irrational"; no common law jurisdiction follows it, and Singapore's own REFJA s 5(3)(a)(i)(C) reverses it. Per C&Y, a failed set-aside on any ground is a protest (Re Dulles). Submit no submission. ROC analogy: Sinar may cite O 6 r 7(6)/r 12(5), but there is no mirror image, so the ROC rules do not settle international jurisdiction (C&Y).
  6. (±) A stay in favour of arbitration alone is a protest (IGCF), but seeking substantive merits relief (release of the vessel on the merits) goes further and is likely submission.
  7. Inchoate submission (+): as in Giant Light Metal, the same parties and the same claims refiled after settlement talks failed are closely connected, and separate case numbers are a technicality. Fairness supports imputing Sinar's earlier submission. (Compare Murthy v Sivajothi: submission extended to related cross-claims.)
  8. No submission: unilateral inclusion in a composition plan is not, by itself, submission (Humpuss).
  • Whose law: Singapore law decides, with X procedure as context (Giant Light Metal, approving Akai). C&Y: it would be odd to find submission where X law itself would not.

J7.1.2.5 Submission by Agreement

Rule: Express agreement (+): per United Malayan Banking, an advance agreement in a clause to the jurisdiction of the X court suffices. Implied agreement (±): (−) per Malaysia Marine and other RECJA cases, it must be express; (+) per Vizcaya Partners (PC), it may be implied if the debtor actually consented in advance; it need not be contractual, and whether it exists is for the contract's proper law. Per C&Y, whether Singapore follows is open. Insufficient indicia (−): per Vizcaya Partners, choosing X law and doing business in X (even if these founded jurisdiction under X procedural law), holding shares in an X company, or making or performing the contract in X are not enough.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Gibraltar Brokerage

A Singapore investor had a brokerage account with a Gibraltar broker. The account terms said "governed by Gibraltar law", and the investor traded through Gibraltar daily, but there was no jurisdiction clause. The broker obtained a Gibraltar default judgment for margin calls.

  • Variation: the terms said "the Client irrevocably submits to the jurisdiction of the Gibraltar courts."
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

(−) On the RECJA line (Malaysia Marine), submission by agreement must be express, so it fails. (+) On Vizcaya Partners (PC), it can be implied if there was actual advance consent, determined under the proper law (Gibraltar law). But per Vizcaya itself, a choice of X law plus doing business in X is not enough, even if those facts founded jurisdiction under Gibraltar's own procedural rules. So no submission, even on the wider view. Whether Singapore adopts Vizcaya's implied-agreement route is open (C&Y).

  • In the variation, there is express advance agreement (United Malayan Banking), so international jurisdiction exists despite the default.

J7.1.3 Final and Conclusive

Rule: Per Sang Cheol Woo, a judgment is final and conclusive if (a) the X court cannot vary, reopen or set it aside (though an appellate court may hear an appeal) and (b) the X court regards it as res judicata. Per Humpuss and Carl Zeiss, this is tested by X law, proved by expert evidence. Default judgment (+): per Humpuss and Eleven v Boxsentry, final if given final effect until set aside, even though the debtor may still apply to set it aside. Interlocutory judgment (±): per Lakshmi, final if it finally decides the parties' rights on that issue, but not if provisional, or decided on a good arguable case and reopenable at trial (First Laser). Appeal pending (±): (+) per C&Y, a pending appeal does not as such defeat finality, though Singapore may stay enforcement; (−) as in Sang Cheol Woo (a provisionally enforceable Seoul High Court judgment was not res judicata under Korean law until the Supreme Court ruled), check X law. Limitation knock-on (+): per Sang Cheol Woo, the six-year period runs from when the judgment became final under X law (consistent with REFJA s 4(1)(b)).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Korean Appeal Ladder

A Korean claimant obtained (i) a Seoul District Court judgment in 2015, (ii) affirmed by the Seoul High Court in 2017, which declared it "provisionally enforceable", and (iii) finally affirmed by the Korean Supreme Court in 2020. Expert evidence shows that under Korean law a judgment becomes res judicata only on final appellate decision. The claimant sues in Singapore in 2025. Separately, (iv) the claimant holds an Indonesian default judgment against another party that can still be set aside on application, and (v) a Hong Kong interlocutory ruling on the governing law, made on a good arguable case in a stay application.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Finality is tested by Korean law (Humpuss; Carl Zeiss). As in Sang Cheol Woo, the High Court's "provisionally enforceable" judgment was not res judicata until the Supreme Court ruled in 2020, so the judgment became final then. Limitation: the six-year period runs from 2020 (when it became final), so the 2025 action is in time (Sang Cheol Woo; consistent with REFJA s 4(1)(b)). (iv) A default judgment is final if given final effect until set aside (Humpuss; Eleven v Boxsentry). (v) A ruling on a good arguable case in a stay application is provisional and reopenable at trial, so it is not final on that issue (First Laser; contrast Lakshmi for interlocutory rulings that do finally decide an issue). Appeal pending: had the Supreme Court appeal still been pending, a merely pending appeal would not as such defeat finality (C&Y), but Korean law treats such judgments as not yet res judicata, so it would not be final; at most, Singapore would stay enforcement.

J7.1.4 Fresh Money Judgment for a Definite Sum

Rule: Definite sum (+): fixed or arithmetically ascertainable; a final, definite costs order is enforceable even where the merits judgment has no money order (C&Y). Fresh obligation (±): per Poh Soon Kiat, whether the judgment imposes a fresh obligation depends on X law; as there ("shall remain liable" in a later Californian fraudulent-transfer judgment was surplusage), where a later order merely restates liability under an earlier judgment, sue on the earlier one. Non-money judgment (−): specific performance or an injunction is not enforceable at common law (a relic of indebitatus assumpsit); register under REFJA or the CCAA, or sue afresh and plead res judicata. Reform (±): per C&Y, following Merck's call for convergence, the common law should enforce non-money relief, as REFJA, the CCAA and Canada (Pro-Swing v Elta) do; the indirect res judicata route reaches the same result, less efficiently. Money order among other orders (+): per Giant Light Metal, a definite-sum order among other orders founds an action in debt (there, a refund due once the buyer made the generator sets available for collection). Severance of mixed orders (±): (−) per Giant Light Metal (obiter), severance is confined to penal or revenue elements; (+) per C&Y, a money order should be severable whenever it is not interdependent with the non-money order. Tax, fine or penalty (−): not enforceable (J7.2.5).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Generator Dispute and Other Orders
  1. A Chinese court ordered a Singapore buyer to return defective generator sets and ordered the Chinese seller to refund RMB 5m "upon the buyer making the generator sets available for collection". The buyer has made them available. It sues the seller in Singapore for the refund.
  2. The same Chinese judgment also ordered the seller to pay "reasonable costs to be assessed". They have not been assessed.
  3. A Californian court first gave a money judgment against a debtor (2018), then, in 2021, a separate judgment setting aside the debtor's transfer of assets to his wife, which added that the debtor "shall remain liable" for the 2018 sum. The creditor sues in Singapore on the 2021 judgment.
  4. An English court (assume no REFJA) orders a Singapore company to deliver up confidential documents.

  1. As in Giant Light Metal, a definite-sum order among other orders founds an action in debt, and the condition (making the generator sets available) has been met, so the refund is enforceable.
  2. Costs "to be assessed" are not yet a definite sum, so not enforceable until assessed. Once assessed, a final costs order is enforceable even if the merits order had no money element (C&Y).

J7.1.5 Reciprocity (left open)

Rule: Exam weight (Chong): one line suffices: Merck left reciprocity open, and later cases have not discussed it, so it is no bar. For (−): per Merck, reciprocity is "entirely consonant" with comity and with the CCAA, REFJA and MORA. Against (+): per C&Y, the common law enforces private rights, not sovereignty; reciprocity is waning globally, rarely induces reciprocation, and penalises the creditor for policy it cannot control; the statutes are negotiated schemes on top of the common law floor. Liberal if adopted (+): per Merck, any requirement would be liberal (e.g., de jure or presumed reciprocity).

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

One line: Merck left reciprocity open and no later case has adopted it, so it is no bar. If pressed: (−) the debtor says reciprocity fits comity, Merck's preferred basis, and the statutory schemes. (+) The creditor says the common law protects private rights, reciprocity punishes it for its government's policy, and in any event any requirement would be liberal (presumed reciprocity), which Ruritania likely meets.

4J7.2 Common law: defences (burden on the debtor: Eleven v Boxsentry)

J7.2.1 Mistake: No Review of the Merits

Rule: General rule (+): per Godard v Gray and Ralli v Angullia, that the X court erred in fact or law, even on Singapore law, is irrelevant; Singapore does not sit on appeal. Error of Singapore law (±): per Merck, it is open whether misapplying Singapore law breaches substantive public policy, the court being guardian of Singapore law; Merck contrasted existent errors (settled law misapplied) with retrospective ones (a considered view on an unsettled point later proved wrong). Patent errors only (±): per C&Y, if the ground is accepted, only patent errors count.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Misapplied Singapore Statute

A Malaysian court, applying Singapore law (the governing law), held that a Singapore company's exclusion clause was valid. (i) The debtor says the Malaysian court got the facts wrong about when the goods were delivered. (ii) It also says the Malaysian court ignored a clear Court of Appeal ruling that such clauses fail the UCTA reasonableness test. (iii) Alternatively, it says the Malaysian court took a reasonable view on an unsettled point, which a later Singapore case decided the other way.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

(i) Errors of fact are irrelevant (Godard v Gray; Ralli v Angullia). (ii) (±) Per Merck, it is open whether misapplying settled Singapore law (an existent error) offends Singapore's substantive public policy, given Singapore's role as guardian of its own law. If the ground exists, only a patent error would count (C&Y); ignoring a clear CA ruling may qualify. (iii) A reasonable view on unsettled law later shown to be wrong is a retrospective error and should not count.

J7.2.2 Fraud

Rule: Per Hong Pian Tee, the test depends on the type. Per Ee Hoong Liang, extrinsic fraud is fraud the debtor had no opportunity to examine and challenge, going to the court's jurisdiction; intrinsic fraud is fraud it could have challenged, going to the merits (e.g., false statements at trial) (Ong Han Nam).

  • Extrinsic (−): e.g., witnesses bribed, the debtor never served, or the creditor inducing the debtor to let judgment go by default. Per Hong Pian Tee, Abouloff applies: no new evidence is needed, and the fraud may be raised even though it was rejected abroad or is raised for the first time here.
  • Intrinsic (+): e.g., perjury or forged documents at trial. Per Hong Pian Tee, the debtor needs fresh evidence that reasonable diligence would not have uncovered and that would likely have changed the result.
  • Materiality (+): per Ong Han Nam, for either type the fraud must have produced the judgment; a catalogue of non-disclosures is not enough unless it was the effective cause of the findings.
  • Characterisation (+): as in Ee Hoong Liang (non-disclosure of settlement payouts going to quantum was intrinsic).
  • Default and summary judgments (+): per Eleven v Boxsentry, the intrinsic test applies to a default judgment even though the debtor took no part; per Ee Hoong Liang, a summary judgment the debtor knew of is not akin to a default judgment.
  • Domestic cases irrelevant (+): per Ee Hoong Liang, Takhar and Façade v Mero (no diligence requirement) concern domestic judgments; comity applies.
  • Critique (±): (−) per C&Y, Hong Pian Tee sides with the fraudster against his negligent opponent (Briggs), and the line is hard to draw (Beals); (+) but the SGCA has reaffirmed it (Ong Han Nam).
  • Exam focus (Chong): classify the fraud as extrinsic or intrinsic; the elements of deceit need not be proved.
  • Fraud by the court (±): (−) per C&Y, extrinsic fraud includes fraud by the court (e.g., a bribed judge), overlapping with natural justice, so Abouloff applies; (+) per the slides it is open whether Abouloff or Hong Pian Tee governs; arguably, if an appeal was available, the debtor could have challenged it (Ee Hoong Liang). Chong's view (−): treat it as extrinsic for policy reasons, as the debtor can hardly raise the corruption before that court.
  • Threshold and bars (+): per Owens Bank v Bracco, plausible evidence of a prima facie case is needed. Fraud cannot be raised where pleading it is abusive, or where a second X judgment has rejected it (House of Spring Gardens v Waite), which in Singapore matters mainly for extrinsic fraud.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Six Fraud Pleas Against an Indian Judgment

A Mumbai court gave judgment against a Singapore company, Kopi Trading, for breach of a coffee supply contract. Kopi alleges:

  1. The claimant bribed two of Kopi's former employees to give false evidence for the claimant.
  2. The claimant told Kopi that the case was being settled and that it need not file a defence, then took a default judgment.
  3. The claimant's managing director lied in the witness box about the delivery dates. Kopi's lawyers had the shipping records showing the lie but did not use them.
  4. The claimant forged a quality certificate. Kopi discovered the forgery only last month, through a criminal investigation in India, and could not reasonably have found it earlier. The certificate was central to the finding of breach.
  5. The claimant did not disclose that it had been paid partly by its insurer, which inflated quantum.
  6. The trial judge was bribed by the claimant. An appeal to the Bombay High Court was available but not pursued.
  • Add-on: Kopi raised the fraud in plea (2) in a second Mumbai action, which rejected it.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Classify first (Chong).

  1. Bribed witnesses = extrinsic (Kopi had no opportunity to examine the bribery). Under Abouloff (via Hong Pian Tee), no new evidence is needed, and the plea can be raised even if it was rejected in Mumbai.
  2. Inducing default = extrinsic. This goes to whether Kopi had a chance to be heard at all.
  3. Perjury = intrinsic. The shipping records were available, so reasonable diligence would have uncovered the lie, and the plea fails. Even under Briggs's critique (the rule favours the fraudster over the negligent victim), the SGCA reaffirmed Hong Pian Tee in Ong Han Nam.
  4. Forgery = intrinsic, but there is fresh evidence not discoverable with reasonable diligence that would likely have changed the result, so it succeeds. It also meets materiality, because the certificate was central (Ong Han Nam). Kopi needs plausible prima facie evidence (Owens Bank v Bracco).
  5. Intrinsic, like Ee Hoong Liang (non-disclosure going to quantum), so the diligence test applies. A list of non-disclosures is not enough unless it was the effective cause of the findings (Ong Han Nam).
  6. Judicial bribery (±): C&Y treat it as extrinsic (it overlaps with natural justice), and Chong agrees for policy reasons: Kopi could hardly raise it before the bribed judge. The counter-argument (slides; Ee Hoong Liang) is that an appeal was available, so it should be treated like intrinsic fraud.
  • Add-on: where a second Mumbai judgment has rejected the fraud, raising it again may be barred (House of Spring Gardens v Waite). That matters mainly for extrinsic fraud, which can otherwise be re-raised.
  • Default variant: if the Mumbai judgment were a default judgment and Kopi's complaint were perjury in the claimant's affidavit, the intrinsic test still applies (Eleven v Boxsentry). Takhar and Façade v Mero (no diligence requirement) are domestic cases and irrelevant (Ee Hoong Liang).

J7.2.3 Natural Justice

Rule: Per Jacobson v Frachon (C&Y), the X court must have given the debtor notice and then an opportunity to present its case. Default after proper service (+): a debtor personally served who chose not to appear has no complaint (Sang Cheol Woo; C&Y). Later participation no cure (−): as in Paulus Tannos (PKPU summons not served in time; later participation under protest irrelevant). Whose view (±): (−) per Paulus Tannos, Singapore alone decides, unbound by the X court's view that service was proper; (+) but where the debtor's appeal on notice is pending in X, ruling is premature. Substantial justice (±): (−) per Adams v Cape, natural justice extends to substantial justice (e.g., damages set at counsel's average award without assessing each claim); (+) per Paulus Tannos and Sang Cheol Woo, it is unclear Singapore adopts this, and the debtor should first seek correction in X. Mere irregularity or merits (+): per Sang Cheol Woo, breach of a reasonable expectation that an X procedural rule would apply is no defence; complaints about Korea's deemed confession rule or the damages assessment were merits challenges already reviewed by the appellate court.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Jakarta Restructuring Order

An Indonesian court approved a PKPU (debt restructuring) plan binding a Singapore guarantor, Mr Tan. The summons was delivered to him two days after the creditors' meeting. He later attended a hearing under protest. He is now sued in Singapore on the plan.

  • Variation A: Mr Tan was personally served in good time but chose not to attend.
  • Variation B: The Indonesian court held that service was proper; Mr Tan's appeal on that point is pending in Indonesia.
  • Variation C: The Indonesian court fixed each of 200 creditors' claims at an average figure proposed by counsel, without assessing them individually.
  • Variation D: Mr Tan complains that the Indonesian court applied a deemed-admission rule he did not expect, after which the appellate court reviewed the damages.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

No timely notice, so natural justice is breached (Jacobson v Frachon). Later participation under protest does not cure it (Paulus Tannos). Singapore decides for itself, unbound by the Indonesian court's view of service.

  • A: No defence. Proper service plus a choice not to appear (Sang Cheol Woo).
  • B: Singapore decides independently (Paulus Tannos), but while the appeal on notice is pending, a ruling may be premature because the appellate court may correct the error.
  • C (±): Adams v Cape treats average-award damages without individual assessment as a breach of substantial justice. Whether Singapore adopts that extension is unclear (Paulus Tannos; Sang Cheol Woo), and Mr Tan should first seek correction in Indonesia.
  • D: A merits or irregularity complaint, not natural justice (Sang Cheol Woo: Korea's deemed-confession rule and the reviewed damages were merits points).

J7.2.4 Public Policy

Rule: Per Burswood, a higher standard than domestic public policy applies. Per Poh Soon Kiat (applied in Sang Cheol Woo), enforcement must (a) offend a fundamental principle of justice or deep-rooted tradition; (b) offend the general community; (c) offend fundamental morality, decency or liberty; or (d) go against a rule protecting the public interest.

  • Hierarchy (±): per Poh Soon Kiat, statutory policy outranks common law "higher" international policy, which outranks domestic policy. Per C&Y and Chong, a statute is not automatically international policy; only one of an equally high, extraterritorial kind counts (a matter of interpretation: JIO Minerals).
  • Judgment, not cause of action (+): per Merck and C&Y, at common law the effect of enforcing the judgment must offend, not the cause of action (unlike RECJA s 3(2)(f)).
  • Egregious cause (−): a cause as egregious as a contract under extreme physical duress, or a drug-trafficking contract (ED&F Man v Haryanto), infects the judgment. Per Israel Discount Bank, a judgment on a guarantee procured by undue influence may be refused. Critique (+): per C&Y, Israel Discount Bank wrongly looks to the cause of action absent egregiousness, and undue influence is arguably only domestic policy.
  • Breach of a Singapore ASI (−): per Nimbus and C&Y, a judgment obtained in breach of a Singapore ASI is contrary to public policy; breach of a foreign ASI is arguably not, by itself.
  • Gambling, statutory policy (−): per Venetian Macau (HC 2026, REFJA), adopting Poh Soon Kiat, gambling save as regulated is contrary to Singapore policy; as s 5(2) CLA is statutory, it prevails, so enforcing a judgment on a casino debt is contrary to public policy. Common law route (−): per Poh Soon Kiat (obiter), a judgment not registrable under RECJA for its gambling cause is likewise unenforceable at common law; per Venetian Macau, s 5(2) draws no distinction between direct claims and actions on foreign judgments; convergence (Merck) points the same way. Creditor's reply (±): (+) Burswood (s 5(2) is only domestic policy), followed in Star v Yong Khong Yoong; (−) per Venetian Macau, Burswood turned on the repealed RECJA's cause-of-action test and binds only there. Recharacterisation (±): (−) per Poh Soon Kiat (left open), the action on the judgment may be recharacterised as a direct claim for the gambling debt; (+) the creditor sues on the judgment debt, and common law policy targets the judgment (Merck).
  • Statutory interest (+): as in Sang Cheol Woo (Korea's statutory 20% judgment interest, payable to the private creditor to deter delay, offended no public policy).
  • Different foreign policy (+): per Yap Chai Ling, that X's policy differs does not mean Singapore's is breached.
  • No estoppel; no new facts (±): (−) per Yukos and India v Deutsche Telekom, the X court's ruling on X's public policy creates no estoppel on Singapore's; (+) but per Wu Shun Foods, the debtor cannot raise a fact going to Singapore policy that it should have raised in X.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Macau Casino, the Cocaine Deal and the Sky-High Interest
  1. A Macau casino sues in Singapore on a Macau judgment for HK$30m in gambling markers signed by a Singapore businessman.
  2. A Colombian judgment enforces a contract for the "sale of agricultural products" that was in fact a cocaine shipment.
  3. An Israeli judgment enforces a guarantee that the debtor's elderly father signed under his son's undue influence.
  4. A Thai judgment was obtained after the creditor ignored a Singapore ASI restraining the Thai proceedings.
  5. A Korean judgment awards 20% statutory post-judgment interest to the creditor.
  6. A US judgment on a cause of action unknown to Singapore law (e.g., tortious interference with prospective economic advantage).
  7. The debtor relies on a fact (that the creditor was unlicensed under Singapore law) which it knew of but did not raise in the foreign proceedings.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  1. (−) Per Venetian Macau (HC 2026, adopting Poh Soon Kiat), gambling other than regulated gambling is contrary to Singapore policy, and because s 5(2) CLA is statutory it sits at the top of the hierarchy. s 5(2) draws no distinction between a direct claim and an action on a foreign judgment, and Poh Soon Kiat (obiter) and Merck's convergence point agree, so the judgment is unenforceable. (+) The casino relies on Burswood (s 5(2) only domestic policy) and Star v Yong Khong Yoong. Venetian Macau answers that Burswood turned on the old RECJA's cause-of-action test and is confined there. Recharacterisation: the debtor can also argue that the "judgment" action is really a claim for the gambling debt (left open in Poh Soon Kiat); the casino replies that common law policy targets the judgment (Merck).
  2. Egregious cause (ED&F Man v Haryanto: drug trafficking), which infects the judgment, so it is refused.
  3. (±) Israel Discount Bank refused a judgment on a guarantee procured by undue influence. C&Y criticise this: it looks at the cause of action without the egregiousness that justifies doing so, and undue influence is arguably only domestic policy. Following C&Y and Merck, the judgment should be enforced.
  4. Contrary to public policy (Nimbus): obtained in breach of a Singapore ASI. Breach of a foreign ASI would arguably not suffice on its own.
  5. Enforceable, as in Sang Cheol Woo: statutory interest payable to a private creditor offends no fundamental policy.
  6. At common law the effect of enforcement must offend, not the cause of action (Merck; contrast RECJA s 3(2)(f)), so it is enforced. A merely different foreign policy is not a breach of Singapore's (Yap Chai Ling).
  7. Per Wu Shun Foods, the debtor cannot raise a public-policy fact it should have raised abroad. Equally, the foreign court's view of its own public policy creates no estoppel on Singapore's (Yukos; India v Deutsche Telekom).
  • Hierarchy note: if the debtor relied on some other Singapore statute, ask whether it embodies a policy of an equally high, extraterritorial kind, which is a question of interpretation (JIO Minerals). Not every statute qualifies (C&Y; Chong).

J7.2.5 Foreign Penal, Revenue and Other Public Laws; Punitive Damages

Rule: Per Maler Foundation, a judgment is not recognised if it directly or indirectly enforces X's penal, revenue or other public law. Characterisation is for the lex fori; per Huntington v Attrill, "penal" means a suit in favour of the State for penalties. Label not conclusive (−): as in Maler Foundation (State-pursued civil forfeiture of officials' presumptively ill-gotten property, in the State's favour, was penal). Non-money and in rem (−): the exclusion applies equally to a judgment in rem or a forfeiture order. Private creditor (+): per Raulin v Fischer, a sum recoverable by a private litigant in its own interest is enforceable; as in Sang Cheol Woo (penal means payable to the State). Punitive damages to a private party (±): (+) per C&Y, refusing them would be anomalous when Singapore awards punitive damages in tort (ACB v Thomson Medical); (−) the point is uncertain, Licea leaving open US RICO treble damages, and s 4(5) REFJA and s 16 CCAA limit non-compensatory damages. Public component (−): per Schnabel v Lui (NSW), punitive damages punishing non-compliance with the court's orders are penal even though paid to the creditor; contrast Benefit Strategies (SA): punitive damages for brazen fraud have no public element. Severance (+): per Licea, enforce the unobjectionable part if clearly identifiable and separable (compare s 4(5) REFJA; ss 16, 19 CCAA).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Philippine Forfeiture and the US Treble Damages
  1. The Republic of Ruritania obtains a "civil" judgment in its own courts forfeiting to the State a former minister's assets, presumed under a statute to be ill-gotten, and seeks to enforce it against his Singapore bank account.
  2. A Ruritanian tax authority's judgment for unpaid income tax.
  3. A New York judgment awards a Singapore company's victim US$1m compensatory damages plus US$2m RICO treble damages, payable to the victim.
  4. A Californian judgment awards US$500,000 punitive damages to a private claimant for the defendant's brazen fraud.
  5. A Texas judgment awards a private claimant US$300,000 punitive damages for the defendant's repeated breach of the court's own injunction.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  1. Penal. The civil label is not conclusive (Maler Foundation). State-pursued forfeiture in the State's favour is a penalty in the Huntington v Attrill sense. The exclusion applies equally to orders in rem or forfeiture orders.
  2. Revenue law. Not enforceable.
  3. (±) The compensatory US$1m is enforceable (a private litigant suing in its own interest: Raulin v Fischer). The treble element: Licea left RICO treble damages open. C&Y argue that refusing private punitive awards is anomalous given ACB v Thomson Medical, but REFJA s 4(5) and CCAA s 16 cap non-compensatory damages, and courts may follow those statutes. At minimum, sever and enforce the compensatory part (Licea).
  4. (+) Punitive damages for fraud paid to a private party have no public element (Benefit Strategies), and are consistent with ACB v Thomson Medical, so arguably enforceable.
  5. (−) Punitive damages punishing defiance of the court's orders have a public component, so they are penal even though paid to the claimant (Schnabel v Lui).

J7.2.6 Proceedings in Breach of a Dispute-Resolution Agreement

Rule: Breach first (±): per Prof Chong (March 2026 answer scheme), the defence needs a breach, so the clause must have promissory content (an EJC, not a non-promissory clause); per C&Y, the debtor loses the objection if it submitted to the X court. For the defence (−): per C&Y, no case decides it, but (i) the debtor could recover damages for the breach here anyway (Union Discount; cf Tradewaves), possibly cancelling the judgment sum; (ii) REFJA s 5(4)(b) is an analogue, favouring convergence (Merck); (iii) it fits the HCCCA's party autonomy. Compare UK CJJA s 32. Against (+): no Singapore authority recognises it, and the HCCCA does not itself prohibit recognising a non-chosen court's judgment. Chosen court; strong cause (±): submitted that the breach matters, not whether Singapore or Y was chosen; and the X court's finding of strong cause goes to its own exercise of jurisdiction, so it should not estop Singapore on breach (cf Merck). REFJA analogue (−): per s 5(4)(b), the X court is not deemed to have jurisdiction where its proceedings breached the agreement, unless the debtor submitted.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Judgment That Ignored the Clause

A Singapore seller and a Nigerian buyer agreed an exclusive English courts clause. The buyer sued in Lagos anyway. The seller appeared only to contest jurisdiction, lost, and then took no part. The Lagos court held there was "strong cause" to keep the case despite the English clause. The buyer seeks to enforce the Lagos judgment in Singapore.

  • Variation A: the clause was "the parties submit to the non-exclusive jurisdiction of the English courts".
  • Variation B: the seller defended on the merits in Lagos.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

First, international jurisdiction: the seller was not present in Nigeria, and contesting jurisdiction is not submission (Nimbus; IGCF), so the judgment fails J7.1.2 anyway. Assume, for the defence, that jurisdiction is established. (−) The seller argues for a breach-of-clause defence: it could recover damages equal to the judgment for the breach (Union Discount), so enforcement is circular; REFJA s 5(4)(b) recognises exactly this defence, and Merck favours convergence; and party autonomy (the HCCCA's philosophy) supports it (compare CJJA s 32). That England, not Singapore, was chosen is irrelevant; the breach matters. The Lagos court's "strong cause" ruling concerned Lagos's own exercise of jurisdiction and should not estop Singapore on breach. (+) The buyer says no Singapore case recognises the defence, and the HCCCA does not forbid recognition of non-chosen courts' judgments.

  • Variation A: a non-exclusive clause contains no promise not to sue in Lagos, so there is no breach and no defence (Chong).
  • Variation B: by submitting on the merits, the seller lost the objection (C&Y; REFJA s 5(4)(b) "unless the debtor submitted").

J7.2.7 Conflicting Judgments

Rule: Inconsistent Singapore judgment (−): per Merck and C&Y, the foreign judgment is not recognised if inconsistent with a Singapore judgment between the same parties, earlier or later; a later Singapore judgment prevails because the creditor should have raised the foreign judgment there, and for internal coherence (compare s 15(1)(d) CCAA). Competing foreign judgments (±): per Merck (endorsing Prof Yeo; First Global Funds; Showlag), where two foreign judgments are both recognisable, the earlier prevails (compare s 15(1)(e) CCAA; s 5(1)(b) REFJA). Singapore proceedings pending (±): per Merck, it is open whether a judgment given while Singapore proceedings on the same subject matter were pending is recognised; (+) Prof Yeo would recognise it; (−) Art 7(2) Hague Judgments Convention allows refusal where Singapore was seised first and the dispute is closely connected with Singapore.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Three Courts, One Patent Licence

A Singapore licensor and a Japanese licensee dispute royalties.

  1. A Singapore court held in 2023 that no royalties were due. The licensor later obtained a Japanese judgment (2024) that royalties were due, and seeks to enforce it in Singapore.
  2. Instead, the licensee obtained a Japanese judgment (2022) that no royalties were due, then the Singapore court (2023), unaware of it, held royalties due. The licensee now seeks recognition of the Japanese judgment as a defence to enforcement of the Singapore judgment.
  3. A Korean judgment (2021) held royalties due; a Japanese judgment (2022) held none due. Both are recognisable.
  4. The Singapore action began in 2021 and is still pending; a Japanese judgment was given in 2022.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  1. The 2024 Japanese judgment is inconsistent with the earlier Singapore judgment, so it is not recognised (Merck).
  2. A later Singapore judgment also prevails: the licensee should have raised the Japanese judgment in the Singapore action, and internal coherence demands it (Merck; compare s 15(1)(d) CCAA).
  3. The earlier one prevails, the 2021 Korean judgment (Merck, endorsing Yeo; First Global Funds; Showlag; compare s 15(1)(e) CCAA and s 5(1)(b) REFJA).
  4. Open (Merck). (+) Yeo would recognise the Japanese judgment. (−) Art 7(2) Hague Judgments Convention would permit refusal because Singapore was seised first and the dispute is closely connected with Singapore.

J7.2.8 Satisfaction and Limitation

Rule: Satisfaction (−): only the balance can be enforced; a satisfied judgment cannot be enforced again (cf REFJA s 4(3), (9)). Six years, not twelve (−): per Poh Soon Kiat, an action on a foreign judgment is on an implied debt, so s 6(1)(a) Limitation Act's six years applies, not s 6(3)'s twelve years (which covers only Singapore judgments). When time runs (+): from the date of the judgment; per Sang Cheol Woo, when it became final and conclusive under X law. Recognition or in rem (+): per Murakami (HC), a judgment in rem declaring rights in property is not subject to the six-year bar, nor is recognition generally, as no implied debt is sued on.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Old Californian Judgment

Continuing the Poh Soon Kiat-style facts (J7.1.4, item 3): the 2018 Californian money judgment (final in 2018) is sued on in Singapore in 2025. The debtor has paid US$100,000 of US$1m. The creditor argues the 12-year period for judgments applies. Separately, the creditor wants to rely on a 2016 Californian in rem judgment declaring it the owner of a painting now in Singapore.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Per Poh Soon Kiat, the action is on an implied debt, so the six-year period (s 6(1)(a)) applies, not the 12-year period (s 6(3)), which is only for Singapore judgments. Time ran from 2018 (when it became final under Californian law: Sang Cheol Woo), so the 2025 action is out of time. Even if it were in time, only the US$900,000 balance would be enforceable. The 2016 in rem judgment, by contrast, is not subject to the six-year bar (Murakami), so it can still be recognised as proof of title.

5J7.3 Recognition: foreign judgment as res judicata

(Here (+) helps the party relying on the judgment; (−) the party resisting it. The judgment must meet J7.1.1–J7.1.3 with no J7.2 defence, but there is no money requirement.)

Rule (Representation not to rely, −): per Showlag v Mansour (C&Y), a party who represented that it would not rely on the judgment may face estoppel by representation (a cross-estoppel).

J7.3.1 Cause of Action Estoppel

Rule: Per Arnold, it arises where the cause of action is identical, between the same parties or privies, on the same subject matter; per C&Y it is an absolute bar absent fraud or collusion. No merger (+): per Ocean Tankers (SGCA, preliminary view), the original claim does not merge into a foreign judgment, unlike a Singapore judgment, so the foreign loser could re-sue here; whether registration under REFJA or the CCAA merges it is "arguable". Shield (+): the unsuccessful foreign claimant re-sues in Singapore on the same cause, so the defendant pleads the foreign judgment (e.g., a German declaration of non-liability) as res judicata. Sword for non-money judgments (+): the winner holding a non-money order outside REFJA and the CCAA sues afresh on the same cause and pleads the judgment; if recognisable, it binds without the merits being reopened.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The German Declaration and the Second Bite

A Singapore buyer sued a German manufacturer in Munich for defective machinery and lost; the Munich court declared the manufacturer not liable under the contract. The buyer now sues the manufacturer in Singapore for breach of the same contract.

  • Variation A: the buyer won in Munich (€2m) but, instead of enforcing, sues afresh in Singapore for €3m on the same cause.
  • Variation B: the buyer won in Munich an order for replacement of the machinery (non-money), and wants that effect in Singapore.
  • Variation C: during settlement talks, the manufacturer wrote: "We will not rely on the Munich judgment if you agree to mediate," and the buyer mediated.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Same parties, same cause of action, same subject matter, so cause of action estoppel is an absolute bar (Arnold). The manufacturer pleads the Munich judgment as a shield.

  • Variation A: per Ocean Tankers (preliminary view), a foreign judgment does not merge the original claim, so the buyer could technically re-sue in Singapore. But the manufacturer can plead cause of action estoppel against the buyer's attempt to relitigate quantum, and abuse of process arguments may apply (J7.3.3).
  • Variation B: a non-money order is not enforceable at common law, so the buyer sues afresh in Singapore for replacement and pleads the Munich judgment as res judicata on liability (the "sword" route). If recognisable, it binds without reopening the merits.
  • Variation C: the manufacturer's representation may found a cross-estoppel by representation barring its plea (Showlag v Mansour).

J7.3.2 Issue Estoppel

J7.3.2.1 Requirements and Limits

Rule: Per Merck (adopting The Sennar (No 2)): (a) a foreign judgment capable of recognition; (b) identical parties or privies; (c) the same issue. Necessary, not collateral (±): the finding must have been necessary to the decision (Merck, citing Carl Zeiss). Finality per issue (±): the decision on the specific issue must be final under X law; for a civil-law judgment, only the dispositif may bind, not the reasoning. Identity of issue (−): per Gonzalo Gil White (SGCA), the party relying bears the burden, with special caution for foreign rulings: (1) were the issues framed the same way? (2) if so, did they arise under different laws? If so, there is no identity. As in Gonzalo Gil White (Mexican concurso rulings under Mexican law shared no identity with a Singapore-law claim), look at identity of issues, not consequences. Outer limits (−): per Merck, no estoppel where (i) the issue is one Singapore decides for itself; (ii) the judgment is territorially limited to X; (iii) the party, a foreign defendant, had bona fide reasons (cost, triviality, unfamiliar procedure) not to contest the issue fully (Carl Zeiss); or (iv) Singapore's substantive public policy forestalls it. Why caution for defendants (−): per C&Y, the X claimant chose X, whereas the defendant was brought there, may rationally have limited its defence, and may not have expected the issue to bind it worldwide. Pure law (−): no estoppel on a pure question of law that does not directly affect the parties' rights (Merck).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Pharma Patent Fight

Merck-style facts: two pharmaceutical companies, both using the name "Lionmed", litigate worldwide.

  1. A German court, in a civil-law judgment, held in its reasoning that a 1970 co-existence agreement was governed by German law; the dispositif only dismissed the trade mark claim.
  2. An English court held, as a necessary step to its decision, that the co-existence agreement was governed by English law and had been breached by the use of "Lionmed" in the UK.
  3. A US court held, in passing, that the agreement "probably" prohibited online use; the decision turned on laches.
  4. A Mexican court held, under Mexican insolvency law, that one company's rights under the agreement had been extinguished in its concurso; the other company now raises in Singapore a Singapore-law contractual claim on the agreement.
  5. A small Brazilian claim (worth US$5,000) was not defended in detail by the defendant, which considered it trivial; the Brazilian court found the agreement valid.
  6. The English court also held, as a general proposition of English law, that co-existence agreements are construed strictly.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  1. For a civil-law judgment, only the dispositif may bind, not the reasoning, so there is no estoppel on governing law (Merck).
  2. (+) Necessary to the decision, and governing law can found an estoppel (Merck, J7.3.2.4). (−) But the finding that the agreement was breached in the UK is territorially limited, so it does not decide whether use in Singapore is a breach (Merck, limit (ii)).
  3. Collateral, not necessary, so there is no estoppel (Carl Zeiss).
  4. Different framing and different laws (Mexican insolvency versus Singapore contract), so there is no identity of issue. Look at the issues, not their consequences (Gonzalo Gil White). The party relying bears the burden, and special caution applies.
  5. A foreign defendant with bona fide reasons (triviality, cost) for not contesting fully should not be estopped (Merck, limit (iii); Carl Zeiss). C&Y explain why: the claimant chose Brazil, and the defendant was brought there and rationally limited its defence.
  6. A pure question of law that does not directly affect the parties' rights raises no estoppel (Merck).

J7.3.2.2 Procedural and Interlocutory Rulings

Rule: The debate (±): (−) per Merck, a decision on a procedural issue (e.g., a Y court's ruling that an X judgment raises an estoppel under Y law) is not on the merits and founds no estoppel; (+) per Lakshmi, estoppel may arise from interlocutory decisions, where procedural issues are usually decided. Better test (±): per C&Y, the procedural/merits label is unhelpful, since the two overlap (The Sennar (No 2)); ask whether the issue is one Singapore retains the prerogative to decide (administration of justice, sovereignty). Narrow approach (±): per Desert Sun (cited in Lakshmi), an interlocutory ruling on service or jurisdiction estops only if (a) the issue was expressly submitted, (b) the specific issue of fact was raised and decided, and (c) Carl Zeiss caution is borne in mind; as in Desert Sun (an Arizona ruling on jurisdiction did not decide the narrower issue of the attorneys' authority). Broad approach (+): in English law estoppel covers procedural and substantive issues; as in The Sennar (No 2) (the Dutch ruling that a Sudanese EJC barred the claim was substantive).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Arizona Lawyers

An Arizona court held, on an interlocutory application, that it had jurisdiction over a Singapore company because the company's US attorneys had entered a general appearance. The Singapore company says those attorneys were never authorised to appear. The creditor says the Arizona ruling estops the company from arguing lack of authority in Singapore.

  • Variation: a Hong Kong court ruled, on an interlocutory application, that an exclusive Shanghai clause barred the claim.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Narrow approach (Desert Sun): estoppel needs the specific issue (the attorneys' authority) to have been expressly submitted and decided. As in Desert Sun, a general ruling on jurisdiction does not decide the narrower issue of authority, so there is no estoppel. C&Y's better test: whether the company submitted to Arizona is an issue Singapore decides for itself (J7.3.2.3), so no estoppel in any case.

  • In the variation, a ruling that a jurisdiction clause bars the claim is substantive (The Sennar (No 2)), and interlocutory decisions can found estoppel (Lakshmi), so the Hong Kong ruling may bind, if it was final on that issue.

J7.3.2.3 Issues Singapore Decides for Itself (−)

Rule: International jurisdiction: whether the debtor submitted to the X court is for Singapore's conflict rules; per Roch LJ in Desert Sun, an estoppel from the X court's finding of voluntary submission would "sub-contract" that question. Forum non conveniens: per Lakshmi, the X court's refusal to stay because X is the natural forum raises no estoppel against a Singapore ASI application: there is no identity of subject matter (an ASI needs vexation or oppression), and estoppel would turn on scheduling. Critique (C&Y): estoppel always depends on scheduling; Lakshmi is better explained as each court deciding its own appropriateness, though the X ruling may still bear on comity. Public policy: per India v Deutsche Telekom (via Gonzalo Gil White), the X court's ruling on X's public policy does not estop the debtor on Singapore public policy. HCCCA applicability: per Prof Chong (March 2026 answer scheme), the X court's ruling that a clause falls within the HCCCA raises no estoppel, each Contracting State court deciding for itself whether the HCCCA applies.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Four Rulings Singapore Will Not Be Bound By

A BVI court, in litigation between two Singapore families:

  1. held that the Singapore defendant had "voluntarily submitted" to the BVI court;
  2. refused to stay its proceedings, holding the BVI to be the natural forum;
  3. held that enforcing the agreement offended no BVI public policy. Separately, 4. an English court held that a Singapore-designating clause fell within the HCCCA.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  1. Whether there was submission is for Singapore's conflict rules. Estoppel would "sub-contract" the question (Desert Sun, Roch LJ).
  2. No estoppel against a Singapore ASI (Lakshmi): an ASI requires vexation, so the subject matter is not identical, and estoppel should not turn on which court ruled first. C&Y's better explanation is that each court decides its own appropriateness. But the BVI ruling may still bear on comity.
  3. The BVI's view of BVI public policy does not estop the debtor on Singapore public policy (India v Deutsche Telekom).
  4. Each Contracting State court decides for itself whether the HCCCA applies (Chong), so there is no estoppel.

J7.3.2.4 Specific Issues

Rule: Governing law (+): per Merck (HC, not appealed) and Chong (governing law is not so sensitive that Singapore must decide it itself), a foreign ruling on governing law can found an estoppel, but per First Laser only if decided at the final trial, not on a stay application decided on a good arguable case. Different choice of law rules (±): (+) per First Laser, it is immaterial that X's choice of law rules differ, since estoppel never required the Singapore court to reach the same result; (−) per Gonzalo Gil White, if the issue arose under different laws in each court, there is no identity. Narrow reading (+, Chong): identity fails only where Singapore's rules would select Singapore law, the court being custodian of Singapore law (as in Gonzalo Gil White: Mexican insolvency law v the Singapore law of incorporation); otherwise X's different rules should not matter. Forum mandatory rule (−): where the X court held an exemption clause valid but it is void under UCTA applying as an overriding rule (s 27(2)), Merck's public policy limit blocks the estoppel. Judgment on a judgment (−): per Merck, a judgment declaring another judgment enforceable raises no estoppel on liability.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Exemption Clause and the Choice of Law
  1. After a full trial, a Hong Kong court held that a shipbuilding contract was governed by English law (applying Hong Kong choice of law rules, which differ slightly from Singapore's). One party seeks to estop the other on governing law in Singapore.
  2. A Hong Kong court on a stay application held, on a good arguable case, that the contract was governed by English law.
  3. A Malaysian court, applying Malaysian choice of law rules, held a contract governed by Malaysian law; Singapore's rules would have selected Singapore law for the question (the capacity of a Singapore-incorporated company).
  4. A Delaware court held valid an exemption clause in a contract with a Singapore consumer; under UCTA, applying as an overriding rule (s 27(2)), the clause is void.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  1. Estoppel likely. Governing law is not an issue Singapore must decide for itself (Merck; Chong), and it was decided at the final trial. That Hong Kong's choice of law rules differ is immaterial (First Laser); estoppel never needed Singapore to reach the same result.
  2. No estoppel. It was decided on a good arguable case at the stay stage, not at trial (First Laser).
  3. (±) (−) Per Gonzalo Gil White, the issue arose under different laws in each court, so there is no identity. (+) On Chong's narrow reading, identity fails only where Singapore's rules would select Singapore law, as here (the corporate capacity of a Singapore company, where Singapore is custodian of its own law). So, exceptionally, no estoppel.
  4. No estoppel. A forum mandatory rule (UCTA s 27(2)) reflects Singapore's substantive public policy, which blocks the estoppel (Merck's limit (iv)).

J7.3.3 The Rule in Henderson v Henderson

Rule: Per Humpuss, where a party raises an issue or claim in Singapore that could and should have been raised in the foreign proceedings, the court weighs all the circumstances, including whether the Singapore action collaterally attacks the foreign judgment, fresh evidence, and bona fide reasons for not raising it abroad. No need for the same parties (±): a claimant may be barred from suing a new defendant who should have been sued abroad (Humpuss). Not every point (+): the foreign litigation need not have covered every point for raising a point here to be abusive.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Indonesian Composition

In Jakarta, a Singapore creditor litigated its claims against an Indonesian shipping group's parent and lost on the validity of a guarantee. It now sues in Singapore (a) the group's Singapore subsidiary, which co-guaranteed the same debt and could have been joined in Jakarta, and (b) the parent, on a fresh argument (that the guarantee was varied) that it knew of during the Jakarta case but did not run.

  • Variation: the creditor discovered the variation document only after the Jakarta judgment.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

(b) The variation argument could and should have been raised in Jakarta. Weighing all the circumstances (Humpuss), it is a collateral attack on the Jakarta judgment, so it is abusive. The Jakarta litigation need not have covered every point. (a) Identical parties are not required (Humpuss): if the subsidiary should have been sued in Jakarta, suing it now may also be abusive, though the creditor can argue it had bona fide reasons (e.g., the subsidiary was not then within the Jakarta court's reach).

  • In the variation, fresh evidence is a strong reason against abuse.

J7.3.4 The Arnold Exception

Rule: Per TT International, for local judgments the estopped party must show that the earlier decision on the issue directly affects the parties' future rights; is clearly wrong; erred on a point not reasonably arguable before the earlier court; involves no claw-back of accrued rights; and that great injustice would follow. Foreign judgments (±): per Merck, it is open whether the exception applies; the CA weighed (i) not at all; (ii) issue estoppel only; (iii) a wider "working justice" test; (iv) testing the issue's conclusiveness by X law. Per C&Y, (iv) is best, consistent with finality under X law.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Clearly Wrong Rent Review

A Hong Kong court, construing a 50-year lease of a Singapore warehouse held by a Hong Kong company, held that the rent-review clause allowed only upward reviews. Later, a Singapore Court of Appeal decision on an identically worded clause held it allows downward reviews too. The tenant, estopped by the Hong Kong ruling, faces 30 more years of above-market rent.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
