Hypos: Engine (map, menus, distinctions, self-critique, ledger)

⚡ BIG IDEA

The engine is your exam technique, not legal theory. It gives you a map to find the right blocks, menus to open and frame an answer, distinctions to break a statement apart, and a ledger to finish cleanly.

The theory behind these hypos is taught in Lesson 1. Do that lesson first if the rules below look unfamiliar.

How to work through a hypo
  1. 1Read the rule (teal box). It puts the sheet's point in plain words. The exact wording to use in the exam is in the Lessons and Sheet tabs.
  2. 2Read the hypothetical (amber box). Before reading on, decide what the rule says about these facts.
  3. 3Tap Application (green box) and compare it with your answer.
  4. 4The exam cue (violet box) lists question words that should send you to this block. Each block ends with a quick check.
Applications:
ℹ NOTE
About these hypos

This page teaches section 1 of your sheet, which is about exam technique rather than theory. The "hypos" here are therefore sample exam statements, and each worked answer shows a tool being used on one.

The rules are written in plain words. Your exact sheet wording, with its quotations, is still in the Lessons and Sheet tabs.

The Core and Theorist versions of the sheet are the same in this section, except for the map in 1.1. The Theorist version lists some extra cards and tests. The Core version adds a row for the four Core cards.

11.1 The map: week → archetype → cards → tests

▤ IN PLAIN WORDS
The item

The map is a table. For each topic in the course it tells you three things: which archetype (ready-made answer plan) to lead with, which theorist cards to use, and which step-by-step tests to run.

The Core version adds one more row, for the four Core cards. They are Core A on law-making, Core B on judges and lawyers, Core C on what law is, and Core D on testing a theory on a new issue.

Why it matters: in the exam you have seconds to decide where to look. The map turns a question into a short list of blocks.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Exam Statement

The exam statement says that Devlin was right that a society may protect its shared morality through law, and that Singapore's 2007 decision to keep s 377A shows why.

✔ APPLICATION · Using the mapDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Work through the map in order.

  • Find the topic. The statement is about whether law may enforce morality. That is the slide week 6 topic, covered in lectures 7 and 9.
  • Find the archetype. Enforcement of morals is archetype 7, so archetype 7 leads your answer.
  • Find the cards.
    • In the Core version, use cards 14.12, 14.13, 14.15 and 14.16.
    • In the Theorist version, use cards 14.12 to 14.17, which add Stephen and Tan Seow Hon's article on marriage.
  • Find the tests. Use 15.6, which is Devlin's list of questions, and 15.7, which is Hart's test for when the criminal law may step in.
  • Core version only. Also open Core A (13.3), because this statement is about what a legislator should do. The two points you want are P5 on majority morality and P6 on enforcing morality.

After thirty seconds you know your plan: use 7.3 on Devlin's jury test, 7.4 on whether society falls apart, 7.6 on what happened in 2007, the Devlin card at 14.15, and the test at 15.6.

21.2 Menus

1.2.1 The six hooks

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

A hook is your opening move. There are six to choose from, and you use one per essay.

HookWhat you doSentence pattern
SourcePoint out that the statement is nearly a quotation from a known writer, then ask whether that writer's own limit has been left out.This is very close to what [George, Thunder's amoral lawyer, or Devlin] says. The question is whether his own qualification survives.
WordPick the one word that claims too much, such as "necessarily", "simply" or "always".Everything turns on [the word], and that word commits the statement to more than it can defend.
Ally turnsName the writer who seems to support the statement, then show that this writer rejects its conclusion.The statement's natural ally is [Hart, Devlin, Pepper or Rawls], yet he rejects where it ends up.
CaseUse a real example that tests the statement straight away.[Riggs, the 2007 decision to keep but not enforce, Ordinance 11, or the Jaffa Cakes case] tests the statement at once.
ConcessionAgree with the true part, then show the overreach and why.The statement is right that [the true part]. It does not follow that [the overreach], because [the principle].
Self-application (once per script)Apply the statement to itself.The statement is itself [a philosophy or a moral verdict], so it cannot be true in the way it claims.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
One statement, six openings

Take this statement: legislators must simply reflect majority moral opinion as accurately as possible.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Here is how each hook would open an answer on that statement.

  • Source. The statement sounds like Devlin. But Devlin insists that his test is not a matter of counting heads, so his own qualification undoes it.
  • Word. Everything turns on "simply". That word treats the legislator as someone who only writes down what others think.
  • Ally turns. Devlin looks like the statement's friend, yet he says that for a law-maker majority opinion is not enough.
  • Case. The 2007 decision to keep s 377A but not enforce it tests the statement. The majority's view won in the result, but that was not the whole reason given.
  • Concession. The statement is right that the majority settles who gets to make law in a democracy. It does not follow that the majority settles what the law should say, because having the right to decide is different from deciding rightly.
  • Self-application. The statement is itself a moral claim about what legislators owe. So ask whether that claim reflects majority opinion.

Choose one of these per essay. A second hook only uses up time.

1.2.2 The five theses

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

A thesis is your answer in one sentence. There are five forms.

ThesisWhen it helpsSentence pattern
Numbered (your default)Almost always. It tells the marker exactly how many points to expect.I make [two or three] claims: (1) ...; (2) ...; (3) ...
DistinctionWhen the statement is half right.The statement is right about [A] and wrong about [B]. The difference is [a distinction from 1.3].
Who and whatWhen the statement treats a vote or a role as settling everything.[The majority, the Constitution or the role] settles who decides, not what is right.
ConditionalWhen one word in the statement can mean two things.If [the word] means X, the statement holds but says nothing much. If it means Y, it is false, and Y is the meaning it needs.
Two hatsWhen a question asks what you would do as both a law-maker and a judge.As an MP I would [vote against or amend]. As a judge I would [enforce or read down]. The answers differ because the two roles ask different questions.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL

Use the same statement about legislators and majority opinion, and try each thesis form on it.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Numbered. I make two claims: (1) majority opinion is evidence that legislators must weigh; (2) it cannot be their only concern, because legislators are trustees who must use their own judgment.
  • Distinction. The statement is right about who decides and wrong about what is right. That is distinction 1.3(1).
  • Who and what. The majority settles who decides, not what is right.
  • Conditional. If "reflect" means "take into account", the statement is true but adds very little. If it means "copy down exactly", it is false, and copying down is the meaning the statement needs.
  • Two hats. This form does not fit here, because the statement is not about a bill. Save it for bill questions (12.6).

1.2.3 Steelman, closes, roadmap, lines, reformulation

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

These are the other tools for building and closing an essay.

  • Steelman (120 to 150 words). This means making the best possible case for the statement before you criticise it. Say what the best case is, give a Singapore example that supports it, then say what it really shows and where it stops.
  • Close on verdict and principle (your default). Say that the statement is therefore right, wrong or overstated, and give the governing reason.
  • Close back on the hook. Return to the word or case you opened with and show what the essay has established about it.
  • Close on the actor. Use this only if the question names someone, such as a judge, an MP or a lawyer. Give one concrete consequence for that person.
  • Roadmap. Use none, or one sentence that names the limbs and the distinction you will use.
  • Memorable lines. Use only one per script. The sheet offers three of its own: a constitutional democracy can move moral questions between institutions but cannot remove them; law is a floor, not a ceiling; and easy cases are easy because lawyers share a theory. It also offers Thunder's point that pointing to your role does not explain your role.
  • Reformulation. Once per script, where one sentence can repair the statement, write out a better version of it.
✔ APPLICATION · To the same statementDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Applied to the same statement about legislators:

  • Steelman. The best case is equal respect. Counting every citizen's view equally treats them all as equals. Indranee Rajah said in 2007 that in most cases Parliament would go with the majority unless there was a reason to protect the minority. That shows majority opinion matters. It does not show it is the only thing that matters.
  • Roadmap. I take the two limbs, the word "simply" and the demand for accuracy, in turn, using the difference between who decides and what is right.
  • Close on verdict and principle. The statement is therefore overstated, because the majority settles who decides, not what is right.
  • Close back on the hook. Read again, the word "simply" shows the error: legislators have to judge, as trustees.
  • Close on the actor. For the MP, this means voting on reasons she could defend to the people who disagree with her.
  • Memorable line. A constitutional democracy can move moral questions between institutions but cannot remove them.
  • Reformulation. A defensible version would say that legislators must weigh majority moral opinion, and decide on reasons they can defend to those who disagree.

31.3 Organising distinctions

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

These distinctions are tools for breaking a statement apart. Each line gives the statement it cracks and how.

#DistinctionStatement it cracksHow it cracks it
(1)who decides v what is right (12, 11.5)The majority voted for it, so it is right.The vote settles who gets to decide. Whether the decision is right is a separate question.
(2)presupposed v operative (9.8)Morality necessarily decides every case.Morality sits in the background of every case, because judges must care about being faithful to law. It actively decides only hard cases.
(3)floor v ceiling (11.7, 10.5)If no rule forbids it, a lawyer may do it.Law sets the minimum, not the most that can be asked.
(4)aim v mechanism (6.10)To avoid imposing a way of life, only harm may justify law.The aim survives, but the harm test is neither required nor neutral.
(5)punish v regulate v promote (7.9)The state must not enforce morality.Ask which kind you mean: jail, a licence or a school curriculum.
(6)validity v obligation (8.7)It is valid law, so citizens must obey.Knowing something is law does not settle whether you should obey it.
(7)observer v participant (8.3)Historians call the Junta's decrees law, so they were law.That is fine for someone describing history. A judge deciding a case claims to be correct, which is a different thing.
(8)principle v policy (9.2)Courts must refuse new claims to avoid a flood of cases.The flood as a matter of cost is for Parliament. The flood as unfair liability out of proportion to fault is a matter of principle for courts.
(9)acceptable to all v sound (6.4)An argument everyone accepts is a good argument.Everyone being able to accept it does not make it true.
(10)unjust system v rule v outcome (10.11)A lawyer must never help a guilty man go free.Ask where the injustice lies: in the whole system, in one rule, or only in this result.
(11)usurpation v abdication (12.2)Judges must leave everything to Parliament.Taking over others' work is one failure. Refusing to do your own work is another.
(12)accessible v accepted (5.7)Finnis's goods are self-evident, so everyone must accept them.A good can be open to everyone's reason without everyone agreeing to it.
(13)form v content (3; 13.1)A published, clear law is a just law.Being clear and public is about form. Being just is about content.
(14)urges v ends (5.6)The law should follow human nature.Ask whether "nature" means what people crave or what people are for.
(15)trustee v stenographer (12.3)MPs must vote exactly as polls say.An MP is trusted to judge, not hired to take notes.
(16)mandated v compatible (11.4)Positivism forbids judges using moral concepts.Legal positivism requires very little and allows much more.
(17)text-first v goal-first (9.7)Dworkin and the crits do the same thing.Dworkin starts from the law's text. The crits start from the goal they want.
(18)mindset v outcome (10.10)Pepper and Thunder would act completely differently.They often do the same thing for different reasons.

Your sheet adds one more point: judge rival models by how persuasive and useful they are, because neither can be proved (Liu, Week 11).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL

The statement says that Dworkin's model of judging is simply false and Kennedy's is simply true.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

You cannot prove either model, because no one can see inside a judge's mind while the judge decides. So do not try to prove one and disprove the other. Ask three more useful questions instead:

  • which model is more persuasive;
  • which model is more useful;
  • which model better fits what a human being doing this job would be likely to experience.

Blocks 9.7 and 14.22 give you the material.

41.4 Self-critique bank

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

Every strong answer gives up something small so that the rest of the argument stands. These are the concessions the sheet gives you, and when to use each one.

ConcessionUse it whenHow it looks in an answer
Tan Seow Hon's catch. Broad consensus can go badly wrong while a local legislature is trying to do right. Hart: amputation requests compared with solo climbing (7.2.3). Pepper: the payday lender (10.1.1).

Rule of thumb: one concession per essay, placed just after your strongest point, and then answered.

Two Essays in One Script

The exam asks two questions. Q1 says judges only apply the law. Q2 says a legislator's only concern is the majority's will.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Plan the two answers together so that nothing is used twice.

  • In Q1 you use Riggs, well-meaning liars (2.5), the judge who says "alas" (9.1), and broad historical consensus (11.5). Tick each one as you use it.

The ledger stops you repeating yourself across essays, and it also stops you forgetting the strongest example for each archetype.

HYPO LESSON 2 · ARCHETYPE 2 · ABOUT 53 MIN · 60 QUESTIONS

Hypos: LP v NLT, and why theory matters

⚡ BIG IDEA

Calling something "law" involves a value judgment, so the choice between legal positivism and natural law is a live one. Hard cases such as Riggs turn on a theory of what makes something law.

The theory behind these hypos is taught in Lesson 2. Do that lesson first if the rules below look unfamiliar.

How to work through a hypo
  1. 1Read the rule (teal box). It puts the sheet's point in plain words. The exact wording to use in the exam is in the Lessons and Sheet tabs.
  2. 2Read the hypothetical (amber box). Before reading on, decide what the rule says about these facts.
  3. 3Tap Application (green box) and compare it with your answer.
  4. 4The exam cue (violet box) lists question words that should send you to this block. Each block ends with a quick check.
Applications:
ℹ NOTE
About these hypos

Each block on this page has three parts: the rule in plain words, a made-up set of facts, and a worked answer. The names, countries and statutes in the facts are invented.

Your exact sheet wording, with its quotations, is still in the Lessons and Sheet tabs. This page explains the same points in easier language.

Two terms come up all the time. Legal positivism says law is identified by where it comes from, such as Parliament or the courts, and not by whether it is good. Natural law theory says that law is connected to morality, so that a rule can be so unjust that it fails as law.

12.0 The archetype in one line

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

The position. Deciding what counts as law is not neutral. It involves a value judgment. So the argument between legal positivism and natural law is a real and live one, and hard cases such as Riggs depend on your theory of what makes something law.

The opening. Legal positivism makes two claims:

  1. law is a social fact, which you identify by its source and not by whether it is good;
  2. law has no necessary link with morality.

Both claims make sense. But a positivist still has to choose whose recognition counts as making something law, and that choice is a judgment. And in Riggs, all the judges agreed that the law bound them, yet they split over what it required. So theory decides hard cases.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Vaccine Payout

Ruritania's Vaccine Injury Compensation Act says that any person who suffers serious injury after a vaccination under the national programme shall be paid $500,000. Dev is deep in debt. Straight after his vaccination he injects a contaminant into his own arm, falls seriously ill, and claims the money. He is later convicted of public mischief and fined $2,000. Every judge accepts that the Act is valid and binding, and on its words Dev qualifies.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Start by asking what the judges are really disagreeing about. It is not whether to obey the Act, because they all accept it binds them. They disagree about what the law actually is.

  • One judge thinks the law is only the words of the Act. On that view, Dev gets paid.
  • Another judge thinks the law also includes the old common-law principle that nobody may profit from their own wrong. On that view, Dev gets nothing.

Nothing in the Act tells you which judge is right. You need a theory of what counts as law. So anyone who says that finding the law is just neutral fact-finding is wrong on these facts. Block 2.8.1 takes this case through the full Riggs card.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

the statement says identifying law is neutral or just looking it up, or that theory is optional.

22.1 Is LP merely descriptive?

📘 Learn 2.1 in Lesson 2 →
🔑 Trigger words: neutral, objective, merely describes, cross-purposes

2.1.1 LP and NLT are not at cross-purposes

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

Some people say the two schools are talking past each other. On that view, legal positivism says what the law is, and natural law says what the law ought to be, so they never really clash.

Tan Seow Hon (TSH) replies that when you look closely, both schools are answering the same question: what is law? Natural law really does claim to say what the law is, at least in extreme cases. So the disagreement is genuine.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Marovian Land Decree

Marovia's Parliament follows the correct procedure to pass a Land Decree. It takes, with no compensation, every farm owned by a member of the Halani minority. Asha, a Halani farmer, asks two professors one question: is the Decree law, so that the bailiff can lawfully take her farm?

  • Professor Lim, a positivist, says yes: it was properly enacted, so it is law, though wicked.
  • Professor Okafor, a natural lawyer, says no: it is so unjust that it is not law at all.

A commentator says the professors are not really disagreeing, because one is describing the law and the other is moralising.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

The commentator is wrong, and Asha's question shows why. She asked one question: may the bailiff lawfully take her farm? The two professors gave opposite answers to it.

Okafor is not saying what the law should become. He is saying what the law is right now, and that the bailiff has no lawful power. Lim is answering the same question the other way. If two people give opposite answers to the same question, they disagree. So this is a real dispute about what law is, and not a case of two people doing different jobs.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

LP and NLT are at cross-purposes; LP says what law is, NLT what it ought to be.

2.1.2 Treating official recognition as conclusive is a choice

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

Legal positivists identify law by looking at what courts and officials uphold. But treating that recognition as the final word is itself a choice. Once the highest court upholds a plainly unjust rule, the injustice stops mattering. That outcome comes from the choice to treat official recognition as decisive.

Liu's slides make two further points.

  • The argument goes in a circle. Positivism finds law in what courts uphold, so what it assumes at the start is also what it concludes at the end.
  • It is a value judgment. To say that what people regard as law simply is law involves judging, and not merely describing.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Decree Reaches the Top Court

Asha challenges the Land Decree. Marovia's highest court holds that the Decree was passed in proper form, and upholds it. Professor Lim writes that this settles the matter. He says he is only describing things: the Decree is what Marovian officials treat as law, so it is law, and he has no view on whether it is good.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Lim thinks he is only describing. In fact his statement contains two judgments.

  1. He chose his test. He decided that the court's acceptance is what makes something law. He did not observe that. It was his choice, and it is exactly that choice which makes the Decree's injustice irrelevant.
  2. His argument is circular. He began by assuming law is whatever officials uphold. He then found that the Decree is law because officials uphold it. His starting assumption has become his conclusion.

What Lim can truly describe is what Marovian officials regard as law. The step from that to saying it is therefore law is a judgment, not a description.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

LP is neutral, objective or merely describes.

2.1.3 The steelman for LP, and why preferring it is still a value choice

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

The best case for legal positivism, from Liu, has three parts:

  • lawyers need to be able to look up what the rules are;
  • you have to know what the law is before you can try to change it;
  • positivism grew up in states with no shared moral outlook, where people needed a test of law that everyone could apply.

But preferring positivism for a society of many beliefs is still a value choice. You prefer it because you value certainty and peace.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Client Who Wants a Straight Answer

Mei runs a café in a city-state of many faiths and ethnic groups. She asks her lawyer, Ravi, whether a new by-law makes her close by 11 pm. Ravi reads the by-law and says yes. Mei's cousin says Ravi should first ask whether the by-law is just. Ravi replies that people here disagree about morality. If the test of law depended on everyone's moral views, nobody would know what the rules were. He tells clients what the law is, and reform is a separate matter.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Ravi's points are good ones, and they are the best case for positivism. He does need to know the law before he can argue for changing it. And a test based on sources lets people of different faiths share one legal system.

But look at the reasons he gives. Each one is a value:

  • certainty, so that people know the rules;
  • peace among people who disagree;
  • keeping legal advice separate from arguments about reform.

So choosing positivism because it suits a diverse state is a choice based on values. It is not a neutral description of how law is. In an answer, first accept the best case, then show that it rests on a value judgment.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

lawyers just tell clients what the law is; in a diverse society only LP works.

2.1.4 The trap: no necessary connection still allows contingent ones

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

The second claim of legal positivism says there is no necessary connection between law and morality. The important word is "necessary".

Connections that just happen to exist are fine. Morality can influence the law, be written into it, and be used to criticise it. The maxim used in Riggs was a legal rule with moral content, and that does not trouble a positivist at all (Liu). Some laws, such as parking rules, involve no moral test whatever.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Grossly Unfair Term

Ruritania's Contracts Act says that a contract term is void if it is grossly unfair. A student writes that this proves positivism is false, because here the law contains morality.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

The student has walked into the trap. Three points show why.

  • A positivist would say the unfairness test is law because a recognised source, the Act, put it there. The moral content got in by a choice that Parliament happened to make. If Parliament repealed the clause, the test would disappear.
  • Positivism only denies that law must contain morality, everywhere and by definition. One law that contains morality does not touch that claim.
  • Ruritania's parking by-laws show the other side. They are valid law with no moral test in them at all.

To defeat positivism, you have to show a connection that must always exist. An example is the claim that extreme injustice stops something being law (2.3.2 and section 8). A connection that merely happens to exist is not enough.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

any argument of the form law X contains a moral standard, so positivism fails; Riggs refutes positivism.

2.1.5 Against: Finnis's rubbish heap

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

Finnis doubts that law can be described from a shapeless heap of facts, the so-called rubbish heap, unless you already have some way of deciding which facts matter. That way of deciding involves value judgment. So description already depends on evaluation.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Visiting Researcher

Dr Sato is sent to a town to write a purely factual description of its law. In a week she records a traffic warden's parking fines, a gang's weekly protection fees, the chess club's rules, a temple's dietary rules, a magistrate's eviction order, and a parent's 10 pm curfew. All of them are rules, all are backed by some pressure, and all are obeyed.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Look at what Sato has collected. Nothing in the raw data tells her which of these rules are law. All of them are rules that people follow under some pressure.

To leave out the gang's fees and keep the warden's fines, she needs a test. It might be that law consists of rules which claim to serve the common good, or that law consists of rules which officials accept as binding. Either way, choosing the test is a judgment about what law is and what it is for.

So positivism cannot begin from pure description. It first has to judge which facts matter. That is Finnis's point.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

LP is merely descriptive; jurisprudence is just a description of rules.

32.2 Hart's internal ought

📘 Learn 2.2 in Lesson 2 →
🔑 Trigger words: mere commands, habit, Hart concedes moral evaluation

2.2.1 Law is more than commands obeyed out of habit

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

Austin says law is the command of a ruler who is habitually obeyed and who obeys no one, backed by a punishment. Hart says this misses something important about law: the sense that people ought to follow it, seen from the inside.

A social rule has two sides.

  • The outside. People regularly behave in a certain way. On its own, that is only a habit.
  • The inside. People criticise anyone who departs from the pattern, they demand that others follow it, they accept that the criticism is fair, and they use words like ought, must, right and wrong. Hart calls this the critical reflective attitude.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Saturday Movies and Red Lights

In the town of Bellhaven, most families go to the cinema on Saturday night, and most drivers stop at red lights. One Saturday Jun stays home, and nobody minds. That same night Jun drives through a red light. Other drivers honk, a passer-by shouts that he should have stopped, a police officer fines him, and Jun's friends agree he deserved it.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Both patterns are regular behaviour, but only one of them is a rule.

  • The cinema is a habit. Plenty of people do it, but nobody treats staying home as doing something wrong.
  • The red light is a rule. When Jun breaks it, people criticise him, they demand he comply, everyone accepts that the criticism is fair, and they use the word should.

An account of law as commands obeyed out of habit cannot tell the cinema and the red light apart. Hart's account can, because it looks at how people treat the pattern from the inside.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

law is just commands backed by threats; law is obeyed from habit.

2.2.2 The ought need not be moral

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

The inside view does not have to be a moral view. Hart accepts that officials may follow the rules out of fear, self-interest or habit. What matters is that they use the rule as a standard for judging conduct. So Hart moves past mere habit without having to say that identifying law needs moral judgment. Liu warns against writing that Hart requires moral approval.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Reluctant Tax Judge

Judge Wong of the Ruritanian High Court thinks the new Wealth Levy Act is unfair to small family firms. She applies it anyway because Parliament passed it, and rules against a firm. Privately she says she wants her pension, and that this is how judges here do things. When a junior judge refuses to apply the Act because he dislikes it, Wong criticises his ruling as legally wrong.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Look first at her motives. They are self-interest and habit, not moral approval of the Act.

Now look at what she does. She treats whatever Parliament enacts as the standard. And she criticises the junior judge for departing from it. That is the inside view, and on Hart's account it is enough for a rule identifying the law to exist.

So anyone who says Hart's inside view forces him to admit that law rests on moral approval is wrong. Hart has moved beyond mere habit, but he has not moved into morality.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

Hart's internal point of view concedes that law rests on moral approval.

2.2.3 Dworkin's Nazi dilemma for Hart

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

Dworkin points out that many officials in Nazi Germany obeyed Hitler only out of fear. He says this creates a dilemma for Hart.

  • If obeying out of fear counts as accepting the rules, it becomes hard to see how Hart differs from Austin.
  • If it does not count, then it seems there was no law in Nazi Germany, and that is not how most people use the word law.

The reply is that acceptance, even when it comes from fear, self-interest or habit, still treats the rules as standards (14.4).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Kessland Regime

In Kessland, judges and police enforce the Leader's decrees. Most officials obey only because people who dissent disappear. Yet in court, judges cite the decrees, criticise lawyers who ignore them, and overturn lower-court rulings that depart from them.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Dworkin's dilemma gives two options.

  • First option: if obeying out of terror counts as acceptance, Hart seems to be saying the same as Austin in longer words.
  • Second option: if it does not count, Kessland has no law at all.

The reply takes the first option but denies that Hart collapses into Austin. Kessland's officials do more than obey out of fear. They use the decrees as standards. They cite them, they criticise people who ignore them, and they correct lower courts. That use is what Hart means by acceptance, whatever the motive behind it.

So Kessland had law, and it was wicked law. That is the positivist's point. Calling it law is what lets us condemn it plainly as law that is too evil to obey (8.2).

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

if officials obey out of fear, Hart is no different from Austin; Nazi law.

42.3 Is NLT elitist?

📘 Learn 2.3 in Lesson 2 →
🔑 Trigger words: only the devout, religious faith, any judge strikes down

2.3.1 Natural law is known by reason, not revelation

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

Natural law does not depend on moral truths that only religious believers can see. Unlike divine law, natural law can be understood by human reason (TSH).

Aquinas described four kinds of law:

KindWhat it is
Eternalthe order governing all of creation
Divinewhat is revealed in scripture
Naturalthe part of eternal law that humans can grasp through practical reason
Humanlaw that people lay down in line with natural law

Grotius made natural law secular. He said that it would have the same content even if God did not exist.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Prisoner-Torture Ordinance

Ruritania passes an ordinance that lets guards torture prisoners for entertainment. Two citizens argue that it is not law. Sister Agnes cites scripture. Ben, an atheist philosopher, argues from human vulnerability and from how senseless it is to inflict pain for fun. A columnist writes that natural law is a theory for priests, and that only believers can know what it requires.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Ben reaches the same conclusion as Sister Agnes without relying on any religion. That is exactly what natural law says is possible.

In Aquinas's scheme, scripture belongs to divine law. Natural law is what practical reason can work out, and reason is open to anyone. Grotius went further and said that its content would be the same even if God did not exist.

So the columnist has confused natural law with divine law, and the charge that it is only for believers fails.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

NLT depends on religious faith; only the devout can know natural law.

2.3.2 NLT does not license any judge to strike down any law

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

Natural law comes in different strengths, and none of the serious versions lets judges strike down whatever they dislike.

  • Strong natural law: every rule must embody morality. That would have judges second-guessing tax law.
  • Weak natural law: a rule loses its status as law only when it departs from morality to an extreme degree, such as a law to execute all redheads (Liu).
  • The Radbruch formula: only intolerably unjust statutes are void (8.2 to 8.3). Alexy says no serious writer defends the view that a judge may refuse whatever he considers unfair.
  • Finnis: an unjust law is not simply nothing that you may ignore. It only loses its usual moral force to bind your conscience, and there may still be a duty to obey it so as not to weaken a basically just system.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Judge Tan's Three Files

Judge Tan, a natural lawyer, has three files on her desk.

  • (a) The Income Tax (Amendment) Act raises the top rate from 22% to 24%. She thinks this is unfair to middle-income earners.
  • (b) The Licensing Act bans street hawking near malls. She thinks this is unjust to poor hawkers.
  • (c) The Public Order (Redheads) Act orders the execution of all redheads.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Take each version in turn.

  • Strong natural law would let her refuse file (a) simply because she disagrees with it. No serious natural lawyer holds that view, and it would make law unworkable.
  • Weak natural law and the Radbruch formula leave files (a) and (b) as law. They may be unfair, but they are nowhere near the extreme. Only file (c) departs so far from justice that it stops being law.
  • Finnis on file (b): even if the Licensing Act is unjust, she may not treat it as if it did not exist. It has only lost its usual moral force, and there may still be a duty to comply so as not to weaken a just system.

So anyone who says natural law lets any judge strike down any law she dislikes is attacking a position that nobody actually holds.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

NLT lets judges strike down whatever they consider unjust.

2.3.3 Concede: who decides what natural law requires?

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

Tan Seow Hon admits there is no easy answer to the question of who should decide what natural law requires. Accept that judges' authority is doubtful when the injustice is below the extreme level (12.1). Keep the force of natural law for intolerable injustice.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Sentencing Challenge

Ruritania's Constitution says no one shall be deprived of life or liberty except in accordance with law. Kai was given a mandatory minimum sentence. He argues that the word law here means law that conforms to natural law. He also argues that mandatory sentences are unjust because they stop judges fitting the punishment to the offender. Thoughtful citizens and MPs disagree about whether such sentences are unjust.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Suppose Kai is right that the word law carries natural-law content. Someone still has to decide what that content is.

This issue is disputed, and it is nowhere near the case of executing redheads. On a question like this, an unelected court overruling Parliament has doubtful authority, and TSH admits there is no easy answer. So the honest response is to accept that below the extreme level, judges should hesitate.

At the extreme, as with file (c) in 2.3.2, the worry about authority fades. Alexy's point is that the more extreme the injustice, the more certain we can be about it (8.3).

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

who decides what natural law requires?; NLT gives judges too much power.

52.4 Are Fuller and Dworkin natural lawyers in all but name?

📘 Learn 2.4 in Lesson 2 →
🔑 Trigger words: all but name

2.4.1 Fuller's thin, procedural natural law

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

Fuller and Dworkin are allies of natural law. They are not natural lawyers under another name, because neither of them lets injustice as such stop a rule being law.

Fuller's natural law is a thin one that is only about procedure. Legality requires that there be rules, and that holds whether those rules are fair or unfair.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Well-Drafted Ban

Marovia replaces its Land Decree with a new Act. It says that from 1 January next year no member of the Halani minority may buy farmland. The Act meets all eight of Fuller's requirements (section 3). It is general, covering a class of people rather than named individuals. It is published. It applies only to the future. It is clear. It does not contradict other laws. It is possible to obey. It is kept stable. And officials apply it exactly as written.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Every one of Fuller's requirements is met. So by Fuller's test, Marovia is governing through law, even though what the law says is unjust.

Fuller's morality is about how rules are made and applied. It is not about what they say. If Marovia had kept the ban secret or applied it backwards in time, Fuller's test would catch it. Unjust content alone does not.

Because unjust content does not stop a rule being law for Fuller, it overstates things to call him a natural lawyer under another name. His theory is a procedural one, and that makes him an ally of natural law rather than a full member.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

Fuller (or Dworkin) is a natural lawyer in all but name.

2.4.2 Dworkin's judge must interpret the history he finds

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

Dworkin says a judge must interpret the legal history that she actually finds, and not invent a better one. That means a wicked legal history can produce a wicked answer. So Dworkin leaves the case of intolerable injustice open, and his idea of integrity gives the judge no way out of a wicked past (14.5).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Kessland's Eighty Years

For eighty years, every Kessland statute and case has denied the Doran minority the right to make contracts. A Doran trader sues to enforce a sale. Judge Reyes, a follower of Dworkin, looks for the reading of Kessland's law that best fits and justifies the record.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Reyes has to work with the history he finds. A reading that gives the Doran equal contract rights may be better morally, but it fits almost nothing in the record. If fit rules that reading out, the best answer under integrity is still the wicked one.

Weak natural law says intolerable injustice is not law. Dworkin offers no such rule.

So Dworkin shares natural law's view that moral principle is one of the grounds of law, which makes him an ally. But he is not a natural lawyer under another name, because he leaves the extreme case open. It is Radbruch who guards that outer limit (14.5 and section 8).

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

as for 2.4.1.

2.4.3 Concede: weak NLT fails as an account of how lawyers use law

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

Dworkin finds even weak natural law unpersuasive as an account of how lawyers actually use the word law. In Riggs, Judge Gray seems to have agreed with Judge Earl that the law would be better if it denied Elmer the inheritance. He did not agree that the law therefore did deny it.

Accept this point. Then defend natural law as a theory of what makes something law, and not as a dictionary of how people talk.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
"The Law Is Against Her"

In a Ruritanian appeal, Judge Choo writes that a better law would let the tenant stay, but that the law as it stands says she must go. Lawyers on both sides find the sentence perfectly normal.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Suppose natural law were a claim about how all lawyers use the word law. Then Choo's sentence would contradict itself, because on that claim the morally better reading simply is the law. Yet lawyers say this kind of thing every day.

So accept Dworkin's point: as a dictionary of how people talk, natural law fails. Then shift your ground. Natural law is a theory of what makes statements about the law true, especially in extreme cases where injustice stops something being law. Choo's tenant case is nowhere near that extreme.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

NLT misdescribes how lawyers talk; lawyers routinely call unjust laws 'law'.

62.5 Do judges disagree only about whether to obey?

📘 Learn 2.5 in Lesson 2 →
🔑 Trigger words: only about obeying, plain words, no law to apply
▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

Your sheet lists these terms near the end of 2.5. They come first here because the other blocks depend on them.

2.5.1 Terms: empirical v theoretical disagreement

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

Judges can disagree in two very different ways.

  • An empirical disagreement is about facts. Everyone agrees on what makes something law, and they dispute whether that test is met. Is the statute in the book? Was it amended?
  • A theoretical disagreement is about what makes something law in the first place. Do statutes and past decisions make up the whole of the law?

Two views hide theoretical disagreement.

  • The plain-fact view says law is only what institutions have decided in the past, so every question of law has an answer in the books.
  • Semantic theories say lawyers all share hidden rules for using the word law.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Two Arguments About Speeding Fines
  • (a) In Lee's appeal against a speeding fine, the judges argue about whether the amendment lowering the limit to 60 km/h was officially published before or after the day he was caught.
  • (b) In Dr Kumar's appeal against a fine under a limit that is clearly in force, the judges argue about whether the statute's words are the whole law, or must be read together with a common-law principle (2.5.2).
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Compare what the judges are arguing about in each case.

  • (a) is empirical. Everyone agrees that a published statute is law. They dispute one fact: whether this amendment was published in time.
  • (b) is theoretical. They agree on every fact about the statute. They dispute what counts as law.

The plain-fact view can only see disagreements like (a). It would have to describe (b) as an argument about whether the judges should depart from the law. That misses what the judges are really doing.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

any question about what judges disagree about.

2.5.2 Theoretical disagreement is not defiance

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

It is a mistake to say judges only disagree about whether to obey the law. In Riggs, all the judges accepted the law's authority, but they split over what it required.

It is also a mistake to say there was no law to apply. That assumes the plain-fact view, when the question of which arguments count as law is exactly what is in dispute.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Speeding Surgeon

Ruritania's Road Traffic Act says any driver exceeding 70 km/h shall be fined $500. Dr Kumar, off duty, drives at 110 km/h to reach a cyclist who has collapsed, and saves his life. The Act has no emergency exception, but a long line of Ruritanian cases recognises a common-law defence of necessity to save life. All three appeal judges accept that the Act binds them. Two hold that the Act must be read together with the necessity principle, and they quash the fine. One holds that the words are plain and the fine must stand.

A newspaper headline says the judges have defied Parliament. A professor writes that no law covered this case, and that the majority simply made new law.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Both reactions miss what happened.

  • The headline is wrong. No judge refused to follow the Act. They disagreed about what the law, properly understood, required. The headline mistakes a disagreement about the law for defiance of it.
  • The professor is also wrong. To say no law covered the case assumes the plain-fact view, that only the statute's words count. But whether the necessity principle is part of the law is exactly what the judges were arguing about. Saying there was no law takes the dissenting judge's side. It is not a neutral description of the case.
🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

judges only disagree about whether to obey the law; once the plain words run out, there is no law to apply.

2.5.3 Agreed result, split grounds: the McLoughlin pattern

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

In McLoughlin the Law Lords agreed on the result, but split over whether courts may let policy limit liability. So agreement on an outcome can hide a disagreement about what makes something law.

For lawyers, the sheet gives practical advice: run both policy arguments. That means arguing that:

  1. policy fails on these facts, which suits Wilberforce, Edmund-Davies and Russell;
  2. drawing policy lines is a job for Parliament and not the courts, which suits Scarman.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Video-Call Drowning

Mr Ong's 12-year-old son is on a school trip abroad. A teacher supervising a swim is careless and lets the boy drift out of his depth. At that moment another pupil is on a live video call with Mr Ong, and Mr Ong watches in real time as his son goes under and is dragged out unconscious. The boy survives with a brain injury, and Mr Ong develops a psychiatric illness. Every earlier successful nervous-shock claimant in Ruritania was physically at the scene or there just afterwards.

The top court rules 5 to 0 that Mr Ong can recover, but the judges give different reasons. Three say policy may limit liability, but not here. One says courts cannot decide where to draw policy lines. One says reasonable foreseeability is the test, and that any policy limit must not be arbitrary.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

A headline saying the court was unanimous would hide a deep split. The judges agree on who wins. They disagree about whether policy is a proper ground of law at all. That is a theoretical disagreement showing up in the reasons and not in the result.

For the lawyer, the lesson is to run both arguments for Mr Ong:

  1. even if courts may weigh policy, fear of a flood of claims does not justify refusing this claim;
  2. in any event, drawing lines on policy grounds is for Parliament and not for the courts.

Running both arguments gives judges on each side of the split a reason to rule for your client. Block 2.8.2 takes this case through the full McLoughlin card.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

the judges agreed, so there was no real disagreement; how should a lawyer argue a novel case?

2.5.4 Dworkin: LP's two defences insult the judges

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

Legal positivists have two ways of defending the plain-fact view. Dworkin says each one insults the judges.

  • Pretence. Judges only pretend to disagree about the law, in order to keep the public's faith in it. That paints judges as well-meaning liars.
  • Borderline cases. Judges only disagree about a marginal use of the word law, like arguing over whether Buckingham Palace is a house. That paints judges as simpletons.

Dworkin's answer is that Riggs and McLoughlin were not borderline. They were pivotal cases that tested what law is.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Two Commentators on the Speeding Surgeon

After Dr Kumar's case (2.5.2), two commentators write about it. Commentator X says the judges all knew there was no law, and dressed up a policy choice as legal reasoning so the public would keep believing in the rule of law. Commentator Y says they were only quibbling over whether the word law stretches to a necessity principle at the edges, like arguing over whether a palace is a house.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Each commentator makes the judges look bad, and neither explains the case.

  • Commentator X makes them well-meaning liars. There is no evidence they were pretending, and the dissenting judge obviously meant what he said.
  • Commentator Y makes them simpletons. Sensible people do not take a word game through years of appeals.

The better view is that the case was pivotal. The judges disagreed about what counts as law at all. Dworkin compares this to two groups of critics arguing about whether photography is art, in a way that shows they hold different views of what art is. That is a genuine disagreement about theory.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

judges only pretend to disagree; legal disagreement is merely verbal.

2.5.5 Qualify: Liu thinks Dworkin is unfair to LP

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

Liu thinks Dworkin is unfair to legal positivism. A positivist need not turn every disagreement into a dispute about facts. And soft positivism, which is a version of the theory, lets the accepted test of law include moral tests.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Fairness Clause

Ruritania's Constitution says Parliament's laws are valid only if they are not grossly unjust. The judges accept this as part of the test for what counts as law. In a challenge to a new detention law, they split 3 to 2 over whether the law is grossly unjust.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

A soft positivist can explain this split without calling it fake or a mere dispute about facts.

The accepted test of law is still a social fact, because it is what officials accept. Here, that test has taken in a moral standard. So the judges are disagreeing, in good faith, about whether that moral standard is met. Legal positivism can make room for real disagreement that turns on moral argument.

Use this to limit Dworkin's attack. He defeats the plain-fact view, but he does not necessarily defeat every positivist.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

Dworkin refutes positivism; LP cannot explain moral argument in court.

72.6 Is theory useless to lawyers?

📘 Learn 2.6 in Lesson 2 →
🔑 Trigger words: luxury, optional, irrelevant, no client needed, good dictionary, Jaffa Cakes

2.6.1 Citing theory is not using it (Fish)

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

Fish agrees that there is some truth in the charge that theory is useless. Citing Rawls in court is likely to look like decoration at best and showing off at worst.

But applying rules happens inside an enterprise that has a purpose. Without some strong sense of the overall project, going through the rules is an empty exercise. So anyone who calls theory a luxury has confused citing theory with using it.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Associate Who Quoted Rawls

Priya, a first-year associate, drafts a submission in a dispute over a late steel delivery and opens with a paragraph from Rawls on justice as fairness. The partner deletes it, saying the judge will think they are showing off. A month later the firm acts for food-delivery riders, who argue that a statute giving employees paid sick leave covers them. The partner asks Priya what this statute is for, who Parliament thought needed protecting, and from whom.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

The partner was right the first time. Quoting Rawls in a steel case adds nothing and looks like decoration.

But the partner's second question is theory being used. It asks what the state may do for workers, and why. Without that sense of the overall project, Priya could list all the cases on the word employee, but she could not turn them into an argument. A list like that would be an empty exercise.

So the claim that theory is a luxury is true of citing theorists and false of using theory.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

legal theory is a luxury or irrelevant to practice; a good lawyer needs no philosophy.

2.6.2 Easy cases rest on a shared theory; hard cases on rival ones

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

Easy cases rest on a theory that everyone shares (9.9). Hard cases rest on rival theories. Lawyers agree in easy cases because they share a way of justifying decisions, and not because no theory is involved.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Parking Fine and the Riders

Same firm. On Monday a client asks whether he must pay a parking fine issued under a properly made by-law, and everyone agrees that he must. On Friday the partner turns to the riders' case from 2.6.1, where the two sides read the word employee in rival ways.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Compare the two days.

  • On Monday, nobody argues about theory, but a theory is still at work. Everyone shares the view that properly made by-laws are law and bind people. Since nobody disagrees, nothing needs to be said.
  • On Friday, the shared theory runs out. One side reads the statute as protecting anyone who depends financially on a platform. The other reads it as protecting only people with a traditional employment contract. The case is hard because the theories differ.

So when easy cases involve no talk of theory, that shows people agree on theory. It does not show that theory is irrelevant.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

most cases are routine, so theory doesn't matter; no client needs philosophy.

2.6.3 The cake–biscuit lesson: philosophy turns up in unexpected places

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

In the Jaffa Cakes case (United Biscuits (UK) Ltd), a tax tribunal used four philosophical moves:

  • identifying the core features of a cake and of a biscuit;
  • asking what the clear examples of each class have in common;
  • using thought experiments;
  • looking at social context.

Together these amount to a philosophy of cakes and biscuits. The tribunal held Jaffa Cakes were cakes, because stale cakes go hard and stale biscuits go soft. Both sides agreed on the factors but weighed them differently, and most arguments in legal theory have that same shape (Liu).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Sweet Bun Tax

Ruritania's Food Tax Act charges no tax on bread and taxes confectionery at 10%. A bakery chain sells a soft milk bun with 18% sugar, a custard centre and a glazed top, packed in sixes and shelved in the snack aisle. The tax office says it is confectionery. The bakery says it is bread.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

The tribunal has to make the same four moves.

  1. Core features. What makes bread bread? Perhaps it is a basic dough of flour and yeast. What makes confectionery confectionery? Perhaps sweetness is the whole point of it.
  2. Clear examples. What do a loaf and a doughnut each have in common with their own group?
  3. Thought experiment. Would this still be bread without the custard?
  4. Social context. Do people eat it as a meal or as a treat, and where do shops put it?

Both sides will agree on these factors and then weigh them differently. The tribunal cannot decide without a view on what bread is. So philosophy turns up even in a tax dispute.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

theory is optional; any question that mentions Jaffa Cakes.

2.6.4 A good dictionary is not enough when the word is law

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

Tan Seow Hon says the purpose of a rule may settle what counts as a vehicle. But a contested word like law brings in the debate between legal positivism and natural law, and a dictionary cannot settle that.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Toy Car and the Land Decree
  • (a) A park by-law says no vehicles are allowed in the park. A child rides a battery-powered toy car along the path.
  • (b) Asha (2.1.1) asks whether the Marovian Land Decree is law.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • In (a), the by-law's purpose can settle the question without any theory of law. The aim is to keep the park safe and quiet. A slow toy car threatens neither, so it may well fall outside the word vehicles.
  • In (b), no dictionary and no by-law's purpose can help. Whether a plainly unjust enactment is law is exactly the question that positivists and natural lawyers disagree about.

So a good dictionary may be all you need for the word vehicle, but it is not enough for the word law.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

all a lawyer needs is a good dictionary.

2.6.5 You can't judge law good or bad without knowing what it is (Leff)

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

Leff makes this point: you cannot know that something is being done badly until you know what it is that is being done. So judging whether law is good already depends on a theory of what law is for.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Minister's Scorecard

A minister asks a consultant to grade Ruritania's criminal courts on how well they are doing. Court A has high conviction rates and fast trials. Court B is slower, acquits more often, and gives long reasoned judgments.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

The consultant cannot grade either court until she decides what criminal courts are for.

  • If their point is controlling crime, Court A is doing well.
  • If their point is protecting the innocent and giving reasons citizens can accept, Court B may be doing better.

Every judgment about how well something is done depends on an account of its purpose, and that account is theory. So anyone who says law can be improved without theory actually has a theory. They just have not examined it.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

theory can't tell us whether the law is good; reform is practical, not theoretical.

2.6.6 Against: disagreement among theorists doesn't make theory useless

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

Some people say theory cannot help anyone decide, because theorists disagree. That fails, because disagreement does not show there is no answer (4.7). People have disputed the number of planets, and there was still a correct number. If the statement says the Constitution makes philosophy unnecessary, use 11.7.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
"Ten Professors, Ten Answers"

A senior judge tells a law-school audience that if you ask ten legal philosophers whether the Riggs majority was right you will get ten answers, so theory cannot help a judge decide anything.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

That theorists disagree shows the question is hard. It does not show that the question has no answer. People have argued about the number of planets, and there was still a fact of the matter.

The judge also has to decide hard cases anyway. Refusing theory does not avoid theory. It only means deciding on a theory you have not examined. Answer the statement with 4.7, or with 11.7 if it is about the Constitution.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

theory cannot help anyone decide, because theorists disagree.

82.7 Singapore pragmatism

📘 Learn 2.7 in Lesson 2 →
🔑 Trigger words: prevailing philosophy, pragmatic, no blank slate
▤ IN PLAIN WORDS
The rule, in three steps
  1. Singapore's main philosophy is often called pragmatism. When it kept s 377A in 2007, the Government described its approach as a pragmatic one that kept Singapore's social cohesion.
  2. But pragmatism is itself a theory. Tan Seow Hon says that in a pragmatic society, the view that law is whatever a court says skips over the principles that should guide the court.
  3. So the claim that philosophy is unnecessary here fails. Theory exists to guide practice (TSH).

Against the statement: TSH says that in law, as in life, we cannot avoid the question of right and wrong.

Where the trigger phrase comes from: in 2007 the Government also refused to say what it would do if it were legislating from scratch, saying it was not starting from a blank slate.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Unenforced Hotel-Room Law

The city-state of Port Meridian has an old law making it an offence for unmarried couples to share a hotel room. Some citizens want it repealed, and others want it kept. The Government keeps the law but announces that it will not enforce it, calling this a pragmatic approach that keeps the peace between communities. It refuses to say what it would do if writing the law from scratch. A columnist writes that Port Meridian does not do philosophy, and just does what works.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

The columnist is wrong for three reasons.

  • The Government has ranked values. It has put social peace above legal clarity. It has kept both camps on side instead of deciding the merits. And it has treated the existing law as the starting point. That ranking is a theory, a pragmatic one, and like any theory it can be defended or criticised.
  • Refusing to start from scratch is itself a position. It gives extra weight to whatever already exists.
  • "What works" skips over principles. To say what works, you need to know what you are trying to achieve. If the columnist says law is just whatever works or whatever the court says, TSH's reply applies: that view skips over the principles that should guide the decision.

Theory exists to guide practice and to judge it. So a pragmatic state still needs theory, and it still cannot avoid the question of right and wrong.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

Singapore is pragmatic, so legal philosophy is unnecessary here; Singapore's prevailing philosophy.

92.8 Case cards: Riggs and McLoughlin

📘 Learn 2.8 in Lesson 2 →
▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

Riggs turned on whether a clear statute has unstated exceptions. McLoughlin turned on whether policy may be used to distinguish precedent. In each case, the answer depends on a theory of law.

2.8.1 Applying the Riggs card

▤ IN PLAIN WORDS
The card
RowRiggs v Palmer
FactsElmer, aged 16, poisoned his grandfather so that the grandfather would not change his will. Read literally, the statute of wills let Elmer inherit.
DecisionBy 5 to 2, Elmer took nothing.
MajorityJudge Earl relied on what the legislature must have intended, and on basic legal maxims. He said the decision takes no property away from Elmer.
DissentJudge Gray said this was not a matter for conscience, and that courts cannot add to the penalties the law has fixed.
Legal positivismThree possible readings: Gray applied the text as laid down; or Earl's maxim is itself a common-law rule with moral content, which positivism accepts; or there was a gap, filled by the judges' discretion.
DworkinTwo theories, both grounded in morality. Gray protects a principle of justice, that penalties are fixed in advance. Earl protects the law's coherence.
American legal realismRules can be read in different ways, or chosen from the many available, to fit results reached on other grounds.

Liu's two readings (he chooses neither):

  • (a) Both sides argued about law, and the majority's law included common-law principle, so Dworkin overstates the drama.
  • (b) The real dispute was whether law is always subject to basic moral principles, as Earl's language suggests.

Either way, neither side kept strictly to the four corners of the statute.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Vaccine Payout, revisited (2.0)

Dev deliberately contaminated his own vaccination to claim $500,000 under an Act that says any person seriously injured after a vaccination under the national programme shall be paid. He has been convicted and fined $2,000. The Ruritanian Court of Appeal splits 3 to 2.

✔ APPLICATION · Row by rowDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • The issue. As in Riggs, does a clear statute have an unstated exception for someone who brings about the event by his own wrong?
  • Majority, in the style of Earl. Parliament cannot have meant to pay people who injure themselves in order to claim. So read the Act together with the maxim that nobody may profit from their own wrong. Refusing the claim takes nothing that Dev already owned. It only stops him getting money through his wrong, so it is not an extra penalty.
  • Dissent, in the style of Gray. The words are plain, and Parliament has taken full control of this scheme. The $2,000 fine is the punishment the law fixed. Withholding $500,000 on top of that adds to his penalty, and that is a job for Parliament and not for a court's conscience.
  • Legal positivist reading. There are three options:
    1. the dissent is applying the text as laid down;
    2. the majority's maxim is itself common law with moral content, which positivism accepts (2.1.4), so the majority can be positivist too;
    3. the Act is silent, leaving a gap that the judges fill by discretion.
  • Dworkin's reading. Both sides hold theories of legislation that rest on morality. The dissent protects a principle of justice, that penalties are fixed in advance by the legislature. The majority protects the law's coherence. Their disagreement is about what the law is.
  • Legal realist reading. The judges first decided whether Dev should get the money, and then picked the method of reading that fitted. The rules could be read either way, so the result came from somewhere else.
  • Liu's two readings.
    • (a) Everyone argued about law, and the majority cited a common-law principle as part of the law, so Dworkin overstates the drama.
    • (b) The real split is between the view that law is always subject to basic moral principles, held by the majority, and the view that the law is simply the law, held by the dissent.
    • Either way, neither side kept to the Act's four corners. Even the dissent's point about fixed penalties is an argument of policy and morality.
🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

unstated exception or literal v purposive problems; judges disagree only about whether to obey.

2.8.2 Applying the McLoughlin card

▤ IN PLAIN WORDS
The card
RowMcLoughlin v O'Brian
FactsMrs McLoughlin was not at the scene of the accident. Hours later, in hospital, she saw her injured family still covered in dirt. A daughter died.
Lower courtsThe trial judge said her shock was not foreseeable. The Court of Appeal said it was foreseeable, but policy confines recovery to people at the scene.
DecisionBy 5 to 0, reversing the Court of Appeal, her shock was recoverable.
Majority on the reasonsWilberforce, Edmund-Davies and Russell said policy may limit liability, but not here.
Split on the reasonsNo one dissented on the result. Scarman said courts cannot decide where to draw policy lines. Bridge said stopping at the decided cases would be a failure of the court's duty.
Legal positivismAs Dworkin reads the Court of Appeal: the precedents ran out, so there was no law, and the job was repair by policy.
DworkinThe force of precedent was in dispute. Scarman thought he was bound by the principles embedded in earlier cases.
American legal realismReasons follow results. Yet the grounds split a unanimous House.

Wilberforce's three elements:

  1. Class of person: close ties of love and affection.
  2. Closeness in time and space, including the immediate aftermath.
  3. How the shock came: by sight or hearing, not from someone else's report.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Video-Call Drowning, revisited (2.5.3)

Same facts as the hypo in 2.5.3; reread them first.

✔ APPLICATION · Stage by stageDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Trial judge. He distinguishes the earlier cases. Shock to a parent in another country is not reasonably foreseeable, so the claim fails.
  • Court of Appeal. With live video, the shock is foreseeable. But policy confines recovery to people physically at the scene. Otherwise anyone watching a live stream could sue, with worries about a flood of claims, fraud and insurance costs. So the claim fails.
  • Top court, 5 to 0 for Mr Ong. Wilberforce's three elements:
    1. Class of person: father and son have close ties. Satisfied.
    2. Closeness in time: he saw it as it happened. Satisfied. Closeness in space: he was thousands of kilometres away, and the idea of the immediate aftermath does not obviously cover that.
    3. How the shock came: he saw it with his own eyes rather than from someone's report, but he saw it on a screen. Whether live video counts as sight or is closer to a report is the hard question. So a judge using Wilberforce's approach must decide where the policy line falls.
  • A judge like Scarman. Courts cannot decide where this line goes. The principle of foreseeable harm to a close relative decides the case, and Parliament may limit it.
  • A judge like Bridge. Reasonable foreseeability is the test. A line at physical presence would be arbitrary, and stopping at the decided cases would be a failure of the court's duty.
  • Legal positivist reading (Dworkin's account of the Court of Appeal). The precedents ran out, there was no law either way, and the court's job was repair.
  • Dworkin's reading. The judges dispute the force of precedent. Are they bound by the principles embedded in earlier cases, as Scarman thought, or only by what those cases decided?
  • Legal realist reading. The result came first, out of sympathy for the father, and the reasons followed. But a realist has to explain why judges who agreed on the result split so sharply on the grounds. That split suggests the reasons mattered.
🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

when precedent runs out, judges legislate; floodgates.

102.9 The conclusion, applied

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

The conclusion. The statement is wrong or only partly right. Legal positivism is right to tie law to its sources, and Dworkin is unfair to paint it as blind to theoretical disagreement. But deciding what counts as law involves a value judgment, and rival theories split the judges in Riggs and the Lords' reasons in McLoughlin. So theory is not optional.

Weak natural law is only needed in cases of extreme injustice (section 8). Riggs needed no such extreme. It only needed a choice of theory about what makes something law.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Putting the hypos together

Take this statement: a good lawyer only needs to know what the law says, and legal theory is a luxury.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Here is how the hypos fit together in an answer.

  • Accept what is true. Ravi (2.1.3) is right that lawyers have to know the sources first. And the fairness clause (2.5.5) shows that positivism can handle moral tests.
  • Then show the limit. Professor Lim's supposed description of the Land Decree was really a value judgment (2.1.2). Dev's payout (2.8.1) and Mr Ong's claim (2.8.2) both turn on rival theories of what makes something law. Even the sweet bun (2.6.3) needs a view on what bread is.
  • Finish with the narrow point. Only the Redheads Act (2.3.2, file (c)) needs weak natural law's test of extreme injustice. Dev's case only needs a choice of theory.
