HYPO LESSON 3 · ARCHETYPE 3 · ABOUT 33 MIN · 56 QUESTIONS

Hypos: Rule of law and Fuller

⚡ BIG IDEA

The rule of law is a real but thin kind of morality. It binds rulers and comes in degrees, but it cannot guarantee that laws are just.

The theory behind these hypos is taught in Lesson 3. Do that lesson first if the rules below look unfamiliar.

How to work through a hypo
  1. 1Read the rule (teal box). It puts the sheet's point in plain words. The exact wording to use in the exam is in the Lessons and Sheet tabs.
  2. 2Read the hypothetical (amber box). Before reading on, decide what the rule says about these facts.
  3. 3Tap Application (green box) and compare it with your answer.
  4. 4The exam cue (violet box) lists question words that should send you to this block. Each block ends with a quick check.
Applications:
ℹ NOTE
About these hypos

Each block on this page has three parts: the rule in plain words, a made-up set of facts, and a worked answer. Your exact sheet wording, with its quotations, is still in the Lessons and Sheet tabs.

Fuller's eight requirements come up throughout. A proper system of rules must be: (1) general, meaning there are rules at all; (2) published; (3) forward-looking, not backdated; (4) clear; (5) free of contradiction; (6) possible to obey; (7) reasonably stable; and (8) actually followed by officials. The last one is called congruence: what officials do must match what the rule says.

The Radbruch formula is the idea that a law so unjust it is intolerable stops being law. TSH is Tan Seow Hon.

13.0 The archetype in one line

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

The position. The rule of law is a real kind of morality, but a thin one. It binds rulers, and it comes in degrees, but it cannot guarantee that the laws are just.

The opening. Fuller says that if one of his requirements fails completely, what is left cannot properly be called a legal system at all. Short of that, legality is always a matter of degree. So legality restrains rulers and exposes their aims to criticism. But it cannot turn bad laws into just ones.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Two Islands
  • On Teral Island, the Governor keeps the entire criminal code in a locked safe. No one but him has read it. People are fined and jailed under rules they have never seen.
  • On Brannock Island, the code is published, but a few sections are badly drafted, and one licensing rule is rarely enforced.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Compare the two islands against Fuller's test.

  • Teral has failed completely on publication. Nobody can see any of the rules. For Fuller, that is not a bad legal system. It is not a legal system at all.
  • Brannock has a legal system with some defects. A few unclear sections and one rarely enforced rule make it worse, but they do not end it. Legality here is a matter of degree.
  • The limit of the idea. Suppose Teral published its code tomorrow. That would make it a legal system, but it would not make the code fair. Legality makes rulers announce their rules and keep to them. A published rule can still be wicked.
🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

the rule of law guarantees justice; the rule of law is mere efficiency; X is not a legal system at all.

23.1 Ranking

📘 Learn 3.1 in Lesson 3 →
🔑 Trigger words: rank them; not all equally important

3.1.1 Rank by branch of law and kind of rule

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS
  1. Fuller accepts that which requirement matters most can change with the area of law and the kind of rule. So in criminal law, put the ban on backdating first.
  2. Fuller says that a backdated criminal statute is condemned by everyone. The non-enforcement of s 377A strained the match between rule and practice, but the legal system still stood. So a failure of congruence for one single rule ranks last.
  3. But failures tend to build on each other. An unclear rule can create the need for backdated laws later on. So ranking something low is never a reason to neglect it.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Minister's Audit

Ruritania's Law Minister asks you to rank three defects in its law, worst first.

  • (a) A new offence of online disrespect to officials has been applied to posts made last year, before the offence existed.
  • (b) One old licensing rule for street buskers is no longer enforced, though it stays on the books.
  • (c) The zoning code is so vaguely drafted that builders cannot tell what is allowed.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Go through the three defects.

  • First comes (a). People are being punished for something that was legal when they did it. That is the kind of law Fuller says is condemned by everyone.
  • Last comes (b). It is only one rule. Officials ignoring it does strain the match between rule and practice, but the legal system as a whole carries on.
  • In between comes (c), with a warning. If builders and courts cannot tell what the zoning code means, the government will soon have to pass backdated fixes to sort out the mess. So (c) must not be neglected just because it ranks below (a).

3.1.2 Requirements can conflict: curative retroactivity

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

Liu's slide points out that Fuller's requirements can pull against each other. The standard example is curative retroactivity, which means a backdated law that repairs some other failure of legality.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Missing Stamp

Ruritanian law says a marriage certificate is valid only if it carries a state stamp. For six months the printing office runs out of stamps, so 3,000 couples marry with unstamped certificates, and all those marriages are void. Parliament passes a statute making them valid, with backdated effect.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

This statute does break the rule against backdating. But look at what it repairs. The couples could not have got a stamp, so they could not have complied with the requirement. The backdated law fixes that earlier failure.

So two requirements are pulling in opposite directions here, and the backdated law actually serves legality overall.

This idea has limits. Suppose a regime kills its opponents and then passes a backdated law that validates the killings. That law repairs no defect in form. It is a cover-up, not a cure.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

rank Fuller's requirements; they are not all equally important.

33.2 Unenforced law

📘 Learn 3.2 in Lesson 3 →
🔑 Trigger words: sham; mockery; enforce fully or repeal; moral signpost

3.2.1 Open non-enforcement strains congruence, but isn't a sham

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS
  1. It goes too far to call an openly unenforced law a sham. Open non-enforcement does strain the match between rule and practice. But one rule that is rarely enforced does not bring down a system.
  2. Tan Seow Hon says that the open announcement in 2007 broke Fuller's requirement, but that it also showed a competing value: the symbolic message the law sends.
  3. So the demand to enforce fully or else repeal is too stark. There is a third option. The law itself can say openly that trivial cases are exempt, as s 95 of the Penal Code does for slight harm.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Midnight Noise Rule

Port Meridian's Public Order Act makes it an offence to play music outdoors after midnight. Many residents want it kept as a statement that the city values quiet. Others want it gone. The Minister tells Parliament that the law will stay as a signal of the city's values, but police will not go out of their way to enforce it. A critic writes that this makes the law a sham, and that it should be enforced fully or repealed.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

There are three points to make to the critic.

  • It is not a sham. There is a gap between the rule and what officials do, and that is a real cost. But one rule that is rarely enforced does not collapse the legal system.
  • There is a trade-off. As TSH said about 2007, the announcement breaks Fuller's requirement but shows a competing value, which is the law's symbolic message.
  • There is a middle path. The critic offers only two options, and there is a third. The law could say openly what is exempt, as s 95 does for slight harm. Port Meridian could exempt music below a set volume. Then the rule and the practice would match.

3.2.2 STEELMAN: non-enforcement hands power to officials

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

The best case against non-enforcement comes from Perera, speaking in Parliament in 2022. Keeping a law on the books while promising not to use it puts too much power in the hands of the Government and the prosecutors.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

A year later, the police charge a well-known government critic for playing music at 12.30 am. No one else has been charged since the announcement.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

This is Perera's worry made real. A law that stays on the books while officials choose when to use it gives them a weapon against people they dislike. Nobody else has been charged, so the rule is not really general any more. This is the strongest argument for the critic's demand to enforce or repeal.

3.2.3 Tan Seng Kee and Liu's analysis

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

In Tan Seng Kee (Court of Appeal, 2022), the court held that the Attorney-General's 2018 assurance about s 377A bound him until he gave clear notice otherwise (7.7). Liu splits the analysis into before and after that case.

  • Before the case, non-enforcement was what officials did, and it was not a rule. There was simply a gap between the law and the practice. Treated as a matter of prosecutors' discretion, it also weakened the requirement that rules apply generally.
  • After the case, what officials say can quietly change the law.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

The critic from 3.2.2 argues in court that the Minister's announcement bound the police not to prosecute without first giving clear public notice. The court agrees and stops the prosecution.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

There is a gain and a new cost.

  • The gain. The court has closed the gap. The announcement now has legal force, so what the law says and what officials do line up better.
  • The new cost, on Liu's analysis. A minister's statement has changed what the law means in practice, without any amendment. A citizen reading the Act would have no way of knowing this. That hurts clarity and stability.

3.2.4 CONCEDE: TSH calls it a breach, not a strain

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

Tan Seow Hon is harsher than the sheet's first point. She calls open non-enforcement a breach of Fuller's requirement, and not merely a strain on it. So accept that it is a breach, and defend only the trade-off.

✔ APPLICATION · To the Midnight Noise RuleDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Do not argue that there is no defect. Say that this does break the requirement that officials follow the declared rule, as TSH says. Then make the smaller claim you can actually hold: the breach may be worth it for the symbolic value, and it falls short of making the law a sham.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

an unenforced law is a sham or a mockery; enforce it fully or repeal it; law as a moral signpost.

43.3 The tyrant, and what makes legality moral

📘 Learn 3.3 in Lesson 3 →
🔑 Trigger words: neither inner nor moral; a tyrant could follow it; guarantees justice; one rule fails

3.3.1 Legality is moral, but thin

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS
  1. It is half right to say that a tyrant could follow Fuller's requirements. Legality is moral, but thin. At its minimum it only demands that there be rules, whether fair or unfair.
  2. It is moral for three reasons:
    • it is a two-way bargain, and that reciprocity is what grounds the citizen's duty to obey;
    • it treats people as responsible agents who can plan and choose;
    • it binds even a ruler who only cares about himself.
  3. So the claim that legality guarantees justice fails. Wicked aims can be carried out through clear, public rules. Intolerable injustice needs the Radbruch formula (8.3).
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
General Vos's Decree

General Vos takes power in Kessland and wants to entrench himself. He publishes a clear, general decree that applies only to the future. It says that from 1 March all political parties other than the National Party are dissolved, and that organising for a dissolved party is punishable by two years in jail. Officials enforce it exactly as written.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Work through the three steps.

  • Half right. A tyrant can follow Fuller's requirements. This decree is general, public, clear and forward-looking.
  • But legality is still doing moral work. Because the rule is published in advance, citizens know exactly what will get them jailed. They can choose whether to comply, protest openly or leave. That treats them as responsible agents. Vos has also tied his own hands. If he jails someone who did not organise for a dissolved party, he breaks the bargain his own decree announced. That bargain, called reciprocity, is what grounds any duty to obey.
  • Not a guarantee. The content of the decree is still unjust. If it were intolerably unjust, legality would not save it. That would be a question for the Radbruch formula (8.3).

3.3.2 STEELMAN: the label seems misapplied

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

The best objection comes from Liu's slide. Calling these requirements a morality may be the wrong label. Perhaps the concern is really with how well law works, which is called efficacy.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

A critic says that calling Fuller's eight principles a morality is like saying a poisoner's craft has a morality because a good poisoner uses precise doses.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

This is the best objection, and it deserves an answer. A sharp knife is efficient and not moral, whether it cuts bread or a throat.

Answer it with the two arguments in 3.3.1. Unlike sharpness, legality respects the people it governs as agents who can plan. And it binds the ruler through a two-way bargain. Neither of those is true of a poisoner's precision.

3.3.3 AGAINST: inner and outer morality decay together

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

Fuller says that the inner morality of law (its form) and the outer morality of law (its content) decay together, almost inevitably.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

Two years on, Vos finds his own published rules inconvenient. He sets up special tribunals that ignore the code when it suits him, issues secret orders, and backdates new offences.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

As his aims become more wicked, his respect for legality decays with them. Rulers who pursue evil ends tend to find clear, public, binding rules an obstacle.

Fuller's point is that the two kinds of morality rarely come apart for long. That is why a regime with wicked aims that also obeys all eight requirements perfectly is rarer than the tyrant objection suggests.

3.3.4 When a single rule fails

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

Now take a single rule rather than a whole system.

  • If it is secret or backdated, it creates no moral duty to obey it.
  • If it is unclear, it is less of a law than a clear one.
  • Whether it is actually valid is a question for the Radbruch formula (section 8), and not for Fuller.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

Vos issues three more orders: a secret order banning foreign newspapers; a backdated order making last year's protests a crime; and an unclear order banning disloyal attitudes.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Keep the questions separate.

  • The secret and backdated orders. Citizens owe no moral duty to obey rules they could not have known about, or that did not exist when they acted.
  • The unclear order. It is less of a law than a clear one, because nobody can use it to guide their conduct.
  • Whether any of them is still law. That is a different question. Fuller speaks to whether people are morally bound. Validity is the question for the Radbruch formula (section 8).

3.3.5 CONCEDE: a regime can meet all eight and still be wicked

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

Liu's slide accepts that a regime can meet all eight requirements and still be wicked. Admit that. But do not admit that legality is therefore morally empty.

✔ APPLICATION · To 3.3.1Decide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Vos's party ban meets all eight requirements and is still wicked. Say so openly. Then hold your position: legality's moral value, which lies in treating people as agents and in the two-way bargain, is real even when the content is bad. It is just not enough on its own.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

Fuller's principles are neither inner nor moral; a tyrant could follow them; legality guarantees justice; what if one rule fails?.

53.4 Discretion

📘 Learn 3.4 in Lesson 3 →
🔑 Trigger words: rule of men; unfettered discretion; enforced only against critics

3.4.1 Only uncontrolled discretion becomes rule by men

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS
  1. It goes too far to say every grant of discretion is a small surrender. Only uncontrolled discretion turns law into rule by individuals.
  2. Fuller condemned a 1934 Nazi statute because it was undermined by uncontrolled official discretion. Enforcing a law only against critics comes close to that.
  3. So Singapore's discretion fits with legality as long as it is limited by law and can be reviewed by the courts.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Gatherings Commissioner

Two cities give officials power over public gatherings.

  • Ruritania: the Commissioner may ban any gathering he considers undesirable, his decision is final, and he need give no reasons. In practice he bans only opposition rallies.
  • Brannock: the Commissioner may ban a gathering likely to cause serious public disorder, he must give written reasons, and his decision may be reviewed by the courts.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Ask the same question of each city: is the discretion controlled?

  • Ruritania has uncontrolled discretion. There is no standard, no duty to give reasons and no review, and it is used only against critics. That is rule by individuals dressed up as law. It is close to the 1934 statute Fuller condemned, where prosecution needed the consent of the Leader's representative.
  • Brannock also gives discretion. But it is limited by a legal standard and open to review, so it fits with legality.

The right question is never whether there is discretion. It is whether the discretion is controlled.

3.4.2 JUDGE: review legality, not merits

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

For judges: review whether the decision was lawful, and do not review whether it was wise. Under Art 35(8), prosecutors have discretion, but it is subject to the equality guarantee in Art 12 (Ramalingam). Liu says discretion wears down generality by degrees. Restraint based on principle is fine. Protecting allies and punishing enemies is not.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

Two people commit the same offence together. The prosecutor charges one with a serious offence and gives the other, the son of a minister, a warning. The charged person asks a court to review the decision.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

The judge should not second-guess ordinary charging decisions, because that would be reviewing whether they were wise. But she can ask whether the discretion was used lawfully, and that includes whether it was consistent with equality before the law under Art 12, as Ramalingam holds.

Charging fewer people on a principled basis wears down generality only slightly. Sparing allies and punishing enemies means one law for the favoured, and that is what legality condemns.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

discretion is rule by men; unfettered discretion; the law is enforced only against critics.

63.5 Mandatory sentences and presumptions

📘 Learn 3.5 in Lesson 3 →
🔑 Trigger words: purest expression of the rule of law; like cases alike
▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS
  1. Mandatory sentences can look like the purest form of the rule of law. But what they buy is certainty, and not justice.
  2. Fuller points out that treating like cases alike can be done by good or bad standards, depending on how you define what counts as alike.
  3. So leaving nothing to judges is just only if the line drawn follows real differences in harm or fault.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The $100 Line

Ruritania's Theft (Mandatory Sentences) Act says that any person who steals property worth more than $100 shall be imprisoned for five years. In one week Lina, a jobless mother, steals $110 of baby formula, and Marco, a professional fence, steals $40,000 of jewellery for resale. Both get five years. The Minister says this is the rule of law in its purest form, because like cases are treated alike and judges have no discretion.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Separate what the Act achieves from what it does not.

  • It gives certainty. Everyone knows the sentence in advance.
  • It does not guarantee justice. The Act treats Lina and Marco as alike only because both went over $100. As Fuller says, you can treat people alike by a good or a bad standard of what counts as alike. Here the line ignores the real differences in harm and fault between them.
  • The test. A mandatory rule is just only if its line follows real differences in harm or fault. This one does not. So it buys predictability at the cost of justice.
🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

mandatory sentences are the purest expression of the rule of law; like cases must be treated alike.

73.6 Rules v standards

📘 Learn 3.6 in Lesson 3 →
🔑 Trigger words: same standard for those who cannot meet it; learner driver; clear rules

3.6.1 The reasonable-man dilemma

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS
  1. Holding a learner driver to the ordinary standard is what Fuller calls the reasonable-man dilemma. By comparison with strict civil liability, the law can be seen as adding a kind of extra charge on a risky activity, and that can justify the standard. But it can never justify it in criminal law.
  2. Fuller's tension is this. Justice that keeps its distance is bound at times to be harsh. Justice that looks closely at each person cannot be even-handed. So the law moderates the reasonable-man standard.
  3. So the claim that clear rules are always better goes too far. Standards such as good faith can make things clearer, and a false clarity can do more harm than an honest vagueness.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Sam's Second Lesson

Sam is on his second driving lesson. He panics at a junction, mounts the kerb and injures a pedestrian. Sam did his honest best, and his best was below what a competent driver would do. The pedestrian sues in negligence. Separately, prosecutors consider charging Sam with careless driving.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Treat the two proceedings differently.

  • The civil claim. Holding Sam to a competent driver's standard asks the impossible of him. Fuller's answer is the idea of an extra charge. The law is not commanding Sam to drive like an expert. It is attaching a cost to choosing to enter a risky activity, much as a sales tax attaches a cost to selling. That can justify the ordinary standard in tort.
  • The criminal charge. The extra-charge idea does not carry over. Branding Sam a criminal for falling short of a standard he could not meet is exactly what Fuller warns against.
  • The tension. Judging Sam by his personal limits cannot be even-handed between drivers. Judging everyone by one standard is sometimes harsh. The law has to steer a middle course.

3.6.2 The cases: Nettleship, Cook, Imbree

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

In Nettleship v Weston, a learner driver owed the same standard as an ordinary driver. Cook v Cook lowered the standard where the passenger knew the driver was a learner. That case was later overruled in Imbree v McNeilly (2008).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

Sam's instructor, sitting beside him, is also injured, and knew perfectly well that Sam was a nervous beginner.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Follow the cases in order.

  • Under Nettleship, the ordinary standard applies, even to a claim by the instructor.
  • Under Cook, a passenger who knew the driver was a learner would be owed only the care of a reasonable learner.
  • After Imbree, Cook has been overruled, so the ordinary standard is back.

The swing between these cases shows the dilemma at work. The law kept trying different middle courses.

3.6.3 Clear rules are not always better

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Fog Day

On a foggy morning, there are two possible traffic laws.

  • (a) Do not exceed 50 km/h.
  • (b) Drive with due care for the conditions.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Rule (a) is clear, but in thick fog 50 km/h is dangerous, and drivers who obey the rule may think they are safe. That is a false clarity.

Standard (b) is vaguer, but everyone understands it, and it tells drivers what actually matters. Standards like good faith or due care can be the clearest option. So the claim that clear rules are always better goes too far.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

the same standard for those who cannot meet it; learner driver; clear rules are always better.

83.7 Authority, reciprocity, crisis

📘 Learn 3.7 in Lesson 3 →
🔑 Trigger words: duty springs from authority; goodwill; crisis; simply majority will

3.7.1 The duty springs from reciprocity, not authority

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS
  1. Saying that the duty to obey comes from authority is the command view of law. Fuller says this confuses being faithful to law with deferring to whoever is in charge.
  2. The duty rests on a two-way bargain, or reciprocity. Once a government finally and completely breaks that bargain, nothing is left to ground the citizen's duty.
  3. So goodwill cannot be enough. No single person's intelligence or goodwill can secure the whole enterprise of law. It needs many people cooperating.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Prime Minister's Speech

Ruritania's Prime Minister tells citizens that they must obey the law because the government is lawful and they can trust its good intentions. Meanwhile, building inspectors routinely let the Prime Minister's allies ignore the fire code, while fining everyone else.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

There are three things wrong with the speech.

  • Authority is not the source of the duty. The Prime Minister treats obedience as owed to him. That confuses being faithful to law with deferring to authority. The duty comes from a two-way bargain. The government asks citizens to follow rules, and in return it implicitly promises to judge them by those same rules.
  • The bargain is being broken. Each favour to an ally breaks that promise a little. If the government broke it completely, nothing would be left to ground the citizen's duty.
  • Good intentions do not fix it. However wise the Prime Minister is, no single person's goodwill can secure legality. It needs the cooperation of legislators, inspectors, courts and citizens.

3.7.2 The voter analogy

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

Fuller says that where officials ignore the rules, there comes a point at which obeying is futile. He compares it to casting a vote that will never be counted.

✔ APPLICATION · To the fire codeDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Think about an honest builder who keeps to the code while allies are waved through. He is like a voter who knows the count is rigged. He can still obey, but obeying has become pointless.

3.7.3 AGAINST: majority will, accurately expressed

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

Someone may say that law should simply express the majority's will accurately. But following a shifting majority breaks the requirement of stability, like Rex in Fuller's story, who amended his laws every day.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

A new party promises law by daily poll. Each week, laws change to match the latest survey.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Citizens could never plan, because the rules would keep moving. Like Rex's daily stream of amendments, a law that changes constantly is worse than having no law. So accurately following the majority's will is not the same thing as the rule of law.

3.7.4 QUALIFY: crisis

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

In a crisis, grim necessity may justify hiding the funding of weapons. But Fuller can see no emergency that would justify a secret law creating a new crime.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

During a border crisis, Ruritania's cabinet (i) secretly funds research into a new defence system, and (ii) passes a secret law making it a crime to assist hostile interests, under which several people are arrested.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Ask whether each secret tells anyone how to behave.

  • (i) can be justified by necessity. Secret spending tells no citizen how to behave, so nobody is left unable to follow a rule.
  • (ii) cannot be justified. A secret criminal law punishes people for breaking rules they could never have known. Fuller can think of no emergency that would justify that.

So a crisis may justify some secrecy, but never secret crimes.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

the duty to obey springs from authority; good government needs only goodwill; in a crisis, legality must give way; law is simply majority will.

93.8 Judge-made law

📘 Learn 3.8 in Lesson 3 →
🔑 Trigger words: never fully prospective; announced after the dispute; retrospective overruling
▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS
  1. Decisions by judges are partly backward-looking, because they are announced after the events. So it is true in form that judge-made law cannot be fully forward-looking. But a new rule may only confirm views that were already widely held.
  2. In civil cases, applying an overruling to the past is a price worth paying. If new rulings applied only to the future, a private litigant would have no reason to challenge a bad precedent.
  3. Crime is different. Applying an overruling to the past would leave people branded as criminals for relying on what a court had told them.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Two Overrulings
  • (a) Civil. A 1990 Ruritanian case held that landlords owe no duty to repair dangerous stairs. In 2026 tenant Clara, hurt on her landlord's stairs, persuades the top court to overrule it.
  • (b) Criminal. In 2020 the top court held that the Betting Act does not cover online fantasy leagues, and thousands of people played. In 2026 it changes its mind.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Compare the two situations.

  • Judge-made law is partly backward-looking in form. Any new rule is announced after the events it decides. But if most people already thought landlords should fix dangerous stairs, the ruling in (a) only confirms what was widely believed.
  • In (a), the new rule should apply to Clara herself. If the court changed the law only for the future, Clara would win nothing, and no tenant would bother to challenge a bad precedent. Applying it to the past is the price of letting private litigants fix bad law.
  • In (b), the position is different. Applied to the past, the new ruling would brand people as criminals for doing what the court itself had said was legal. In criminal law, the change should apply only to the future.

3.8.1 Abdul Nasir: constancy, not branded as criminals

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

In Abdul Nasir (Court of Appeal, 1997), life imprisonment was held to mean a prisoner's natural life, but only for future cases (8.6). This is a problem about the law's meaning staying stable. It is not the problem of branding someone a criminal.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

Ruritania's top court rules that life imprisonment means the rest of the prisoner's natural life, and not 20 years as long assumed, and applies this only to future sentences.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Nobody is being turned into a criminal for conduct that was lawful, because the offenders' acts were already crimes. What has changed is what an existing sentence means. That is a problem of stability, because the law's meaning has shifted over time. It is why applying the ruling only to the future is the fair fix. It is not the problem in case (b) in 3.8.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

judge-made law can never be fully prospective; it is announced after the dispute; retrospective overruling.

103.9 Thin v thick; the Marxist challenge

📘 Learn 3.9 in Lesson 3 →
🔑 Trigger words: ruling-class slogan; instrument of power; whims of officials

3.9.1 Legal form binds rulers too

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS
  1. It goes too far to call the rule of law a slogan for class power, because the form of law binds rulers too. Fuller's point is that legal form cannot simply be built on more law: it depends on people actually keeping to it.
  2. Liu's slide answers the Marxist critic: law has a character of its own, and applies legal tests by standards of universality and fairness (on the crits, see 9.3).
  3. So thin legality is better than the whims of officials. Published rules give notice and invite criticism.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Eviction Case

A student activist says that the rule of law is a slogan for the rich, because landlords wrote the eviction laws and the courts enforce them. The same month, Ruritania's largest property company tries to evict 200 tenants without the 60 days' notice the Act requires. The court rules for the tenants.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Accept the true part, then show what it misses.

  • There is some truth here. The content of eviction law may well favour landlords.
  • But the form of law binds the powerful too. Once rules are law, the court applies them by standards of universality and fairness, to the property company as to anyone else. The company is bound by the very notice rule its industry wanted. That is what it means for law to have a character of its own.
  • Published rules beat whims. Because the notice rule is published, the tenants knew their rights and could challenge the company, and anyone can see what the law demands and criticise it. Without published rules, the company and officials could simply do what they liked. So thin legality is worth having, even for people who criticise what the law says.

3.9.2 STEELMAN (Liu): dragging the monster into the light

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

Liu's best point for legality is that law drags the monster into the light. A regime that states its aims openly can be criticised, organised against and escaped from. Arbitrary power shows no pattern at all.

The objection on the other side is that rules make evil look legitimate and help it spread, because people can say that it is the law.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

Compare two regimes persecuting the same minority.

  • Regime A publishes a decree that members of group Z may not hold public office.
  • Regime B has no rule at all. Members of group Z are quietly sacked, or disappear, at random.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Look at both sides.

  • For legality, in Regime A, members of group Z know exactly what is being done to them. Outsiders can quote the decree and condemn it. Opponents can organise around it, and people can decide to leave in time. Under Regime B there is no pattern to criticise and no way of staying safe.
  • Against legality, in Regime A, the decree also lets clerks and neighbours say it is the law, which spreads the persecution and makes it seem normal.

Liu's point is that this is a trade-off, and that the argument from visibility is on legality's side.

113.10 Conclusion, applied

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

The conclusion. The statement is right only in part. Legality binds rulers, respects citizens as agents, exposes rulers' aims to criticism and comes in degrees, so calling something no legal system at all requires a total failure. But legality is thin and cannot guarantee just laws. Dealing with intolerable injustice is the job of the Radbruch formula.

✔ APPLICATION · Applied to the hyposDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Here is where each part of the conclusion was shown.

  • Legality binds rulers: the property company had to give notice (3.9.1).
  • It respects citizens as agents: Vos's published ban let people plan (3.3.1).
  • It exposes aims to criticism: Regime A's decree can be quoted and condemned (3.9.2).
  • It comes in degrees: compare Brannock with Teral (3.0).
  • It cannot guarantee justice: the $100 line (3.5) and Vos's ban are proper in form and unjust in content.

HYPO LESSON 4 · ARCHETYPE 4 · ABOUT 24 MIN · 41 QUESTIONS

Hypos: Moral objectivity and scepticism

⚡ BIG IDEA

The sceptic's case does not succeed, and the sceptic's own demands assume that there is moral truth. Being fallible calls for careful deliberation and provisional judgment. It does not call for tolerance as a dogma, or for silence.

The theory behind these hypos is taught in Lesson 4. Do that lesson first if the rules below look unfamiliar.

How to work through a hypo
  1. 1Read the rule (teal box). It puts the sheet's point in plain words. The exact wording to use in the exam is in the Lessons and Sheet tabs.
  2. 2Read the hypothetical (amber box). Before reading on, decide what the rule says about these facts.
  3. 3Tap Application (green box) and compare it with your answer.
  4. 4The exam cue (violet box) lists question words that should send you to this block. Each block ends with a quick check.
Applications:
ℹ NOTE
About these hypos

Each block on this page has three parts: the rule in plain words, a made-up set of facts, and a worked answer. Your exact sheet wording, with its quotations, is still in the Lessons and Sheet tabs.

Some terms come up throughout. A sceptic doubts that there is any moral truth we can know. A moral realist thinks moral claims can be true or false. TSH is Tan Seow Hon.

14.0 The archetype in one line

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

The position. The sceptic's case does not succeed, and the sceptic's own demands assume that moral truth exists. So the sceptic's conclusion fails. Because we can make mistakes, we should deliberate and hold our judgments provisionally. But that is no reason for treating tolerance as a dogma, or for keeping silent.

The opening. People say morality is just opinion, or a social construct, and offer that as a reason for tolerance, neutrality or keeping morality out of law. But that conclusion is itself a moral demand, and the sceptic has no basis for it. Disagreement and lack of proof do not show there is no moral truth. And believing in moral truth requires deliberation, not imposing your views on others.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Neutral Committee

A Ruritanian parliamentary committee must decide whether to ban commercial surrogacy. Its chair opens by saying that morality is just personal opinion, so the committee must stay neutral and must not impose anyone's values.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Look at the word must. The chair is telling the committee what it ought to do, and that demand binds people who disagree with it. So the chair is making a moral demand.

Now apply the chair's own view to that demand. If morality really were just personal opinion, the demand for neutrality would be only the chair's opinion. It would have no more claim on the committee than anyone else's opinion. So scepticism cannot deliver the neutrality it promises.

The better course is to deliberate, hold conclusions provisionally, and require stronger reasons the more coercive the law is.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

morality is just opinion, so…; keep morality out of law.

24.1 Map

📘 Learn 4.1 in Lesson 4 →
🔑 Trigger words: just opinion; eye of the beholder; durian; nobody has proved; varies by culture

4.1.1 Sort the sceptic's claim first

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS
  1. Statements about morality often run together three different positions:
    • relativism: moral views differ from culture to culture;
    • scepticism: there is no moral standard, or none we can know;
    • non-cognitivism: moral claims only express feelings.
  2. On Hume's non-cognitivism, a moral claim is like saying you dislike durian. It is neither true nor false. Moral realists say a moral claim can be true or false.
  3. So saying that nobody has proved something only has force if proof means strict deduction. Natural science would fail that test too.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Four MPs on the Dog-Meat Bill

Ruritania debates a bill banning the sale of dog meat. Four MPs object.

  • MP A says that whether this is wrong varies from culture to culture.
  • MP B says there is no moral truth here, or if there is, we cannot know it.
  • MP C says that calling it wrong is like saying you dislike durian, because it is just a feeling.
  • MP D says nobody has proved it is wrong.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Sort each MP's claim, because each needs a different answer.

  • MP A is a relativist. Notice that cultures differing does not show that no culture is wrong.
  • MP B is a sceptic, either because no standard exists or because we cannot know it.
  • MP C is a non-cognitivist, following Hume. On this view, saying that something is wrong is neither true nor false, like a taste. A realist answers that it is a claim about the act, and so can be true or false.
  • MP D assumes that proof means deduction. Nobody can deduce that the sun will rise tomorrow, yet science is not mere opinion. If deduction were the only proof, natural science would fail too.

Sorting the claims first lets you answer each one, instead of fighting a blur.

4.1.2 Liu's replies to the stock lines

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

Liu has a reply to two stock lines. Saying there are shades of grey is not an argument at all. And saying these are merely opinions assumes the very point that is in dispute.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

MP E adds that it is not black and white, that there are shades of grey, and that these are merely opinions.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Take the two phrases one at a time.

  • Shades of grey only says that the question is hard. That is no argument that the question has no answer.
  • Merely opinions assumes that moral views cannot be statements of fact. But that is exactly what is being debated, so it begs the question.

4.1.3 TRAP: subjective isn't controversial; moral ≠ legal realism

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

Two traps to avoid.

  • Saying something is subjective is different from saying it is controversial. Whether the earth goes round the sun was once controversial, but it was never subjective.
  • Moral realism has nothing to do with legal realism (Liu, Week 3).
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

A student writes that whether dog meat should be banned is hugely controversial, so it is subjective, and that like the legal realists he thinks there is no objective answer.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

The student makes two mistakes.

  • Controversy is not subjectivity. People once fiercely disputed whether the earth goes round the sun, and there was still a fact of the matter.
  • He has the wrong kind of realism. Legal realism says judges decide by preference and then justify the result. Moral realism says moral facts exist. They are unrelated, and mixing them up costs marks.

4.1.4 STEELMAN: Hume was no extreme relativist

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

Here is the best reading of Hume, who does not seem to be an extreme relativist.

  • When he says reason is the slave of the passions, he may mean that shared human feelings supply the starting points of moral reasoning.
  • He held that the rules of justice are artificial, because humans make them, but that they are not arbitrary.
✔ APPLICATION · To MP CDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Treat MP C's use of Hume fairly. Even if moral claims rest on feelings, Hume thought humans share enough feelings for the rules of justice not to be arbitrary. So saying that it is just a feeling does not get MP C to the conclusion that anything goes.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

morality is just opinion; in the eye of the beholder; nobody has proved it; it varies by culture.

34.2 Self-refutation

📘 Learn 4.2 in Lesson 4 →
🔑 Trigger words: all moral opinions are equally valid; who are you to judge; intolerant; social construct

4.2.1 The sceptic's demand refutes itself

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS
  1. When a sceptic says we must tolerate, or that no one may judge, that is itself an objective moral demand. It is exactly the kind of thing the sceptic says does not exist.
  2. A social construct that binds outsiders has stopped being subjectivism. If the binding rests on everyone's equal moral worth, the sceptic has become a moral realist (TSH).
  3. So the statement defeats itself. And true subjectivism, followed to its end, leaves its supporters with no answer to genocide except force.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Banned Speaker

A university society cancels a talk by a visiting speaker who argues that some cultural practices are morally wrong. The society's statement says that all moral opinions are equally valid, that the speaker has no standing to judge other cultures, and that intolerance must not be given a platform.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Follow the society's own words.

  • The contradiction. If all moral opinions are equally valid, the speaker's opinion is as valid as the society's. Yet the society treats its rule against intolerance as binding on the speaker, who rejects it. That is an objective moral demand.
  • The realist premise. Ask why the speaker must tolerate other cultures. The likely answer is that everyone has equal moral worth. That claim holds for everyone, whatever they believe, so it is moral realism.
  • Where this ends. Imagine the speaker's own culture practised genocide. A consistent subjectivist could only say that your norms do not bind me. The other side can say the same back, and then only force is left.

4.2.2 CONCEDE: self-refutation settles no content

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

Accept that this self-refutation point has limits. It only catches the sceptic who makes demands, and it tells you nothing about which moral views are right. The debate that follows is, in the phrase on your sheet, a squabble within the family of moral realists. So accept that a realist must still argue for each moral norm.

✔ APPLICATION · To the Banned SpeakerDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Winning the self-refutation point does not show that the speaker is right about which practices are wrong. It only shows that both sides are now moral realists, arguing about content. Each still has to give reasons for its view.

4.2.3 TRAP: TSH's domain is persuasion, not proof

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

Here is a trap. Tan Seow Hon's argument is about moral persuasion. It does not prove that moral facts exist (Liu, Week 3). A sceptic who says no one is bound by anything is consistent, but can argue for nothing.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

A different student says that he is a true sceptic. No moral rule binds anyone, so he makes no demands, not even for tolerance.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

TSH's argument has no grip on this student, because he makes no demand that could contradict itself. So do not claim that TSH proves moral facts exist.

Instead, show the cost of his position. He can argue for nothing at all, not even against the society that cancelled the talk. His position is consistent, but useless in a debate about what the law should do.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

all moral opinions are equally valid; who are you to judge?; imposing values is intolerant; morality is a social construct.

44.3 Appeals

📘 Learn 4.3 in Lesson 4 →
🔑 Trigger words: nobody can agree; we have been wrong before; it is safer; imposing values

4.3.1 Disagreement and past error

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS
  1. If nobody can agree, that shows that someone is wrong. It does not show that there is nothing to be right about (4.7).
  2. Tan Seow Hon explains why people disagree:
    • the fashions of the times distort reason;
    • weakness gives way to passion;
    • self-interest, hardened by habit, dulls the conscience.
  3. So saying we have been wrong before is a reason to go slowly, and not a reason to abstain. Calling slavery an error assumes there was a right answer.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Organ-Market Debate

Ruritania debates legalising the sale of kidneys. One MP says nobody can agree on this. He says that fifty years ago people thought homosexuality was a disease, that we have been wrong before, and that it is safer for the law to say nothing.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Answer each of the MP's points.

  • Nobody can agree. If one MP says selling kidneys is wrong and another says it is not, at least one of them is mistaken. Disagreement shows error somewhere. It does not show there is no truth.
  • Why people disagree. TSH points to the fashions of the time, weak will and self-interest. Kidney brokers profit from one answer, and that can dull their judgment.
  • We have been wrong before. Calling a past view an error assumes there was a right answer that we got wrong. So the lesson is to move carefully and keep listening to reasons. It is not to refuse to decide.

4.3.2 STEELMAN: humility

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

The best case on the other side is humility: the law should only force people on matters that are widely agreed. But that is a realist's argument. True realism involves a commitment to deliberation.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Saying that the law should only coerce where there is broad agreement is a sensible principle. But it is a moral principle about the limits of force, and it has to be argued for on its merits. A realist can accept it, because a realist who knows she might be wrong will deliberate before forcing anyone.

4.3.3 Imposition

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

On the charge of imposing values: moral realists are not the only people who can be bigoted and intolerant.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

The MP says realists are dangerous because they impose their values. A sceptic MP then shouts down every speaker who disagrees with legalisation.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Bigotry is a fault of character, and has nothing to do with whether you believe in moral truth. A sceptic can be intolerant, as the MP who shouts people down shows. A realist who holds views provisionally can be very open. So the claim that realism means imposing your views fails.

4.3.4 CONCEDE: the realist's weak point is access

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

Accept the realist's weak point, which is how we know what is right. Consensus can be mistaken. In 2007, both sides of the s 377A debate were people who thought they were right, and absolutely so. So accept that realism does not settle any case on its own. It requires reasons.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Both sides of the organ-market debate may be equally sure they are right. Realism says one of them is wrong, but it does not say which. So the honest answer accepts that being a realist does not settle the kidney question. It only requires both sides to give reasons rather than declaring victory.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

nobody can agree; we have been wrong before; it is safer to stay out; imposing values.

54.4 Is–ought

📘 Learn 4.4 in Lesson 4 →
🔑 Trigger words: Hume showed; no ought from is; biology tells us nothing; studies show; natural; so legislators should

4.4.1 Facts alone settle nothing; facts plus an agreed ought do

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS
  1. Hume's point holds. Biological facts alone cannot settle whether a practice should be legal.
  2. Finnis does not draw any moral conclusion from facts. The basic goods are self-evident, and facts such as embryology only show how those goods apply.
  3. So it goes too far to say facts tell us nothing. Once a moral starting point is agreed, the facts fix what is at stake.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Embryologist's Evidence

A committee on embryo research hears Dr Ihara say that at about 14 days the primitive streak forms. Two MPs react. MP F says the law should therefore allow research up to 14 days. MP G says biology tells us nothing about what the law should be.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Each MP makes a different mistake.

  • MP F jumps from fact to ought. The fact about the primitive streak does not, on its own, tell anyone what to do. MP F needs a moral premise, such as that research is allowed before a human individual exists, and has not stated it.
  • MP G goes too far the other way. Suppose the committee agrees that human life is a basic good that must not be directly attacked, as Finnis says. Then embryology becomes crucial. It tells them when a human life is present, and so what is at stake in each kind of research.
  • Finnis's route. He does not work out that life is good from biology. The good is self-evident, and biology only shows how it applies.

4.4.2 Hume's two arguments, and the replies

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

Hume makes two arguments:

  1. Wrongness lies not in the act but in our feelings, because reason only knows relations of ideas and matters of fact. The slides call this Statement X.
  2. You cannot get an ought from an is.

There are two replies.

  1. Statement X is itself neither a relation of ideas nor a matter of fact. So by its own test, it is neither true nor false.
  2. The gap between is and ought is only a point about logic. If people agree on a moral starting point, such as human dignity, then that plus the facts does produce an ought.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

MP G presses on, saying that Hume showed that only maths and facts can be true, and that morality is neither, so it is just sentiment.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Use both replies.

  • Turn Statement X on itself. The claim that only relations of ideas and matters of fact can be true is not maths, and it is not an observable fact. By its own test it is neither true nor false, so it cannot show anything.
  • The gap is narrow. Hume shows that you cannot deduce an ought from facts alone. He does not show that facts are irrelevant once a moral starting point, such as human dignity, is shared.
🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

Hume showed you can't get an ought from an is; biology tells us nothing; studies show, so legislators should; it's natural.

64.5 Hidden judgement

📘 Learn 4.5 in Lesson 4 →
🔑 Trigger words: consensual and harms no one else; not wrong; victimless; the state should stay neutral

4.5.1 Consensual and harmless, so not wrong is a moral verdict

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS
  1. Saying something is not wrong because it is consensual and harms no one else is a moral verdict. It is not a neutral fact.
  2. The hidden premise is that autonomy comes first, and that rests on everyone's equal worth.
    • Unlimited autonomy would leave everyone equally worthless, because anyone could do anything to anyone.
    • Limited autonomy is a moral law (TSH).
  3. So the claim that the law should stay neutral fails. Where harm stops, and whose consent counts, are moral choices. As Thio said in 2007, there is no Switzerland of ambivalence, meaning no neutral ground to retreat to.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Kidney Contract

Ravi, deep in debt, agrees to sell a kidney to a wealthy buyer for $50,000. A columnist writes that it is consensual and harms no one else, so it is not wrong and the state should stay neutral.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Work through what the columnist has assumed.

  • It is a moral verdict. Saying that it is consensual and harmless, so not wrong, is not neutral. It applies a principle: adults may do as they choose unless they harm others.
  • The hidden premise. That principle puts autonomy first, and autonomy rests on everyone's equal moral worth. If autonomy had no limits, anyone could do anything to anyone, so everyone would be equally worthless. Once we add limits, such as bodily integrity and no exploitation, we have a moral law.
  • The choices hidden in the word neutral. Is Ravi's consent real when he is desperate? Does harm include the long-term risk to Ravi himself, or the pressure on other poor people to sell? Answering those questions takes moral sides. Staying neutral just means accepting the columnist's answers.

4.5.2 Finnis's charge

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

Finnis makes a charge. It is a flat self-contradiction to appeal only to what people subjectively prefer, and then to ground that in the value of self-governance.

✔ APPLICATION · To the columnistDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Suppose the columnist says the law should respect whatever people prefer, because self-governance is valuable. The second half is a claim that something is objectively valuable. So the columnist has undercut the claim that it is all subjective preference, in the very act of defending it.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

consensual and harms no one else; victimless; not wrong; the state should stay neutral.

74.6 Whatever is enacted?

📘 Learn 4.6 in Lesson 4 →
🔑 Trigger words: law is whatever people say is law; whatever Parliament enacts; separation is safer

4.6.1 Nothing above the lawgiver

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS
  1. If law is whatever is enacted, nothing stands above the lawgiver. Liu asks whether that makes one group of people the final lawgiver over everyone else.
  2. Saying citizens are safer if law can have any content is itself a moral claim about safety, liberty and power.
  3. So natural law remains a standard for criticising what is enacted, without denying that merely unjust enactments are still law.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Citizenship Act

A commentator argues that law is whatever Parliament enacts, and that keeping law separate from morality keeps citizens safe from moralising judges. Parliament then passes, by proper procedure, an Act stripping citizenship from anyone who criticises the government three times online.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Apply the three points.

  • Nothing stands above Parliament. On the commentator's view the Act is law, and there is no higher standard by which to call it a defective law. The legislators become the final lawgivers over their fellow citizens.
  • Safer is a moral claim. Safer for whom? The critics who lose their citizenship are not safer. The commentator is weighing safety, liberty and power, and that is moral argument and not neutral description.
  • The standard. Natural law lets us say the Act falls short of what law should be. That does not mean every merely unjust law stops being law. Only the extreme case might (section 8).

4.6.2 Alexy: only the strong connection thesis risks legitimation

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

Alexy says that only the strong version of the link between law and morality risks making people accept laws uncritically. The weak version, which is the Radbruch formula, keeps law open to criticism. For Hart's case for keeping law and morality separate, see 8.2.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

The commentator replies that if you tie law to morality, people will think every law is moral and will stop criticising.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Separate the two versions.

  • It is true of the strong version. If every law were necessarily moral, then calling something law would bless it.
  • It is not true of the weak version. The Radbruch formula says only that intolerable injustice is not law. Everything below that line is law and is fully open to moral criticism. So the weak version does not silence critics. For Hart's own case, use 8.2.
🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

law is whatever people say is law; whatever Parliament enacts; separating law and morality is safer.

84.7 The objectivity anchor (the reusable paragraph)

📘 Learn 4.7 in Lesson 4 →
▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

The paragraph you can reuse has five moves.

  1. Demanding tolerance or deference because morality is just opinion, or personal, or a social construct, defeats itself. The demand binds others, and that abandons subjectivism.
  2. If the demand rests on equal moral worth, the sceptic is a moral realist.
  3. Disagreement no more disproves moral facts than disputes over the number of planets do. Something unproven is not therefore false.
  4. Refusing to act on a moral judgment may amount to acting on its opposite. So keeping morality out is itself a moral choice.
  5. Realism requires deliberation and provisional judgment, not imposing your views (TSH).

Where the sheet uses it: 4.1 to 4.3 and 4.5 (just opinion, nobody can agree, it is safer); 11.7 (personal morality, private conscience); 6.10 (equally valid); 7.5 (neutral); and 10.4 (no one can say objectively).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Judge Who Keeps Morality Private

A judge hears a challenge to a law allowing landlords to refuse tenants of a particular religion. He writes that morality is personal and that judges may not disagree with Parliament about it, so he takes no moral position. He upholds the law.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Run the paragraph's moves on him.

  • It defeats itself. That judges may not impose their morality is itself a moral rule, binding on every judge whatever they believe.
  • The realist premise. Why must judges not impose? If the answer is that citizens have equal moral worth and deserve equal respect, he is a moral realist.
  • Disagreement. That people disagree about religious discrimination does not show there is no answer.
  • Refusing to judge is judging. By taking no position and upholding the law, he lets the discrimination stand. That is acting as if it were acceptable.
  • The better path. He should deliberate, give reasons, and hold his judgment provisionally.
🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

any statement that relies on morality being subjective in order to reach a practical conclusion.

94.8 Conclusion, applied

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

The conclusion. The statement fails or is overstated. Scepticism cannot deliver the tolerance, safety or neutrality it promises, because that promise is itself a moral norm. The sceptic's reasons are also inconclusive, though that does not prove any moral fact. The realist's weak point is how we know what is right, not whether there is a right answer. Consensus can be wrong, and in 2007 both sides claimed moral truth. So hold moral judgments provisionally, and require more of them the more coercive the law is.

✔ APPLICATION · Applied to the hyposDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Here is where each part of the conclusion was shown.

  • The promise is a moral norm: the Neutral Committee (4.0) and the Banned Speaker (4.2.1).
  • Inconclusive reasons prove no fact: accept, with TSH's limit (4.2.3), that refuting the sceptic does not prove moral facts exist.
  • The problem of knowing: in the organ-market debate (4.3.4), both sides were sure.
  • More force needs more reason: a criminal ban on selling kidneys needs stronger reasons than a licence would.
