Hypos: Finnis for law-makers

⚡ BIG IDEA

Finnis gives law-makers real limits on what they may do, and leaves much else to careful judgment.

The theory behind these hypos is taught in Lesson 5. Do that lesson first if the rules below look unfamiliar.

How to work through a hypo
  1. 1Read the rule (teal box). It puts the sheet's point in plain words. The exact wording to use in the exam is in the Lessons and Sheet tabs.
  2. 2Read the hypothetical (amber box). Before reading on, decide what the rule says about these facts.
  3. 3Tap Application (green box) and compare it with your answer.
  4. 4The exam cue (violet box) lists question words that should send you to this block. Each block ends with a quick check.
Applications:
ℹ NOTE
About these hypos

Each block on this page has three parts: the rule in plain words, a made-up set of facts, and a worked answer. Your exact sheet wording, with its quotations, is still in the Lessons and Sheet tabs.

Practical reasonableness is Finnis's term for thinking well about what to do. A number in brackets, such as [7], refers to one of his nine requirements, which are listed in block 5.2. TSH is Tan Seow Hon.

15.0 The archetype in one line

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

The position. Finnis gives legislators real limits, and leaves much else to careful judgment, which he calls prudence.

The opening. The statement assumes that a theory of what is good must either dictate how citizens live or offer no guidance at all. Finnis shows a third way.

  • Seven basic goods and nine requirements for thinking well produce a few absolute limits, such as never intending to kill an innocent person.
  • They also produce a common good that is a framework for people's lives, and not a plan for how each person must live.

Within those limits, legislators choose prudently, and reasonable people may differ.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Three Bills on the Order Paper

Ruritania's Parliament has three bills before it:

  • (a) the Assisted Dying Bill, letting doctors give lethal injections on request;
  • (b) the Online Falsehoods Bill, letting a minister order corrections to false online statements;
  • (c) the Museums Bill, funding free entry to national museums.

A commentator says that Finnis either tells Parliament exactly how everyone must live, or is no help at all.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Finnis does neither. Take the bills one by one.

  • (a) hits an absolute limit. Allowing doctors to kill intentionally, even on request, chooses directly against the basic good of life. So it is ruled out.
  • (b) is a matter for prudence. Truth is a basic good, and deliberate lies damage it, so the state may act. How it should act, given the risk of chilling free speech, is a judgment on which reasonable legislators can differ.
  • (c) is about helping people. Free museums help citizens take part in knowledge and in the experience of beauty. Whether to fund them, and how much, is a prudent choice and not a duty.

So the theory gives a real limit in (a), and leaves wide room for prudence in (b) and (c).

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

Finnis would have the state dictate how citizens live; Finnis offers law-makers no guidance.

25.1 Goods and priorities

📘 Learn 5.1 in Lesson 5 →
🔑 Trigger words: basic goods; obviously good; just taste; rank the goods; golfer

5.1.1 Self-evident goods, no objective ranking

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS
  1. Finnis's seven basic goods are self-evident. They are not worked out from other facts. Anyone who reflects on why they act can see that something like knowledge is good in itself.
  2. The goods are all equally basic, though each person can give some more priority than others. There is no objective order among them.
  3. So life-plans, and not the state, rank the goods. It does not follow that the state must do the ranking.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Culture Minister's Ranking

Ruritania's Culture Minister announces that knowledge matters more than play. From next year, all public arts and sport funding will go to universities. Playing football, he says, is a waste of a citizen's time.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Apply the three points.

  • There is no objective ranking. For Finnis, knowledge and play are both basic goods, and they are equally fundamental. Neither is objectively higher.
  • Priorities belong to life-plans. A scholar may reasonably put knowledge first, and a footballer may reasonably put play first. The ranking depends on each person's temperament, abilities and opportunities.
  • So the Minister's premise fails. He assumes that because goods have to be ranked, the state must rank them for everyone. Finnis gives the ranking to each person's plan of life. The state's job is to maintain the conditions in which people can pursue their own plans (5.5).

5.1.2 The golfer

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

Finnis's example of the golfer: walking past a drowning stranger shows indifference to the good of others whom one could easily help.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

Ah Seng loves golf, and has made play his top priority. On the 7th hole he sees a child struggling in the water hazard. Helping would cost him two minutes. He plays on, saying that golf is his priority and that this is his life-plan.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Having priorities is fine. Using them to ignore someone you could easily save is not.

Ah Seng is showing indifference to the good of someone he could easily help, and that breaks requirement [3], which forbids arbitrary preference among persons. A life-plan ranks your own pursuits. It does not let you treat another person's life as worthless.

5.1.3 The seven goods, and Liu's test

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

The seven goods are life, knowledge, play, aesthetic experience, sociability, practical reasonableness and religion. Religion here includes agnostic or negative answers to questions about ultimate reality.

The goods are pre-moral. They are not moral rules themselves. Morality comes in with the nine requirements.

Liu's test for whether something is a basic good: strip away every use it has for the other goods. Is anything still left?

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

A student says play is not a basic good, because it is just a way of keeping healthy and making friends.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Run Liu's test. Picture someone alone, playing a card game at midnight. It does nothing for their health and involves no friends, yet it still has a point, because the game is enjoyed for its own sake. Something is left after the other uses have been stripped away, so play passes the test.

Notice also that religion here does not mean church membership. An atheist who has thought hard about their place in the universe, and has concluded there is no God, is taking part in this good.

5.1.4 QUALIFY: Liu's answers to four objections

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

Liu answers four standard objections.

  • Gossip is low-grade knowledge, but it is still knowledge.
  • Suicide shows that someone has been deprived of the good of life, and not that they have rejected it.
  • Lacking a good does not stop it being a good.
  • Pleasure is one aspect of the goods, and not their point.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

At a seminar, four objections are raised.

  • (i) People love gossip, so is that really the good of knowledge?
  • (ii) Some people choose to die, so life is not good for everyone.
  • (iii) An uncle has severe dementia and cannot reason, so practical reasonableness is not a universal good.
  • (iv) Play is just pleasure.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Answer each objection in turn.

  • (i) Gossip is still knowledge, just a low grade of it. Taking part in a good at a low level is still taking part.
  • (ii) People who want to die are usually suffering and are already deprived of the good of life. That does not show that a fuller life would not be good for them.
  • (iii) The uncle lacking the good does not stop it being a good. That is exactly why the goods need protecting.
  • (iv) Play is enjoyable, and pleasure is one aspect of it. But a game can still be worth playing on a day when it is not fun, so pleasure is not the point.
🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

who says these are goods?; it's just taste; the state must rank the goods; the golfer.

35.2 The nine requirements as structure

📘 Learn 5.2 in Lesson 5 →
🔑 Trigger words: plan of life; detachment; commitment; efficiency; transpose to a legislature
▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS
  1. Nine requirements of practical reasonableness structure how we pursue the goods. Most of them carry over to a legislature, though a state has no single life-plan (5.5).
  2. All nine bind together, and each is basic and cannot be reduced to the others. To Liu they read as prudent advice: failing requirements (4) or (5) looks unwise rather than immoral.

The nine requirements are:

  1. a coherent plan of life;
  2. no arbitrary preference among values;
  3. no arbitrary preference among persons, which is the Golden Rule;
  4. detachment, meaning no fanatical policy;
  5. commitment, meaning keeping faith with what you have begun;
  6. efficiency, within reason (5.4);
  7. respect for every basic value in every act (5.3);
  8. the common good (5.5);
  9. following your conscience.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Parliament's Year

Ruritania's Parliament, over one year:

  1. adopts a five-year legislative programme;
  2. passes a budget that funds roads and factories but cuts every library and park, with no stated reason;
  3. exempts MPs from a new tax that applies to everyone else;
  4. pursues "zero road deaths at any cost", banning all driving after dark;
  5. abandons a promised pension reform the moment it becomes unpopular;
  6. buys the cheaper of two equally good hospital IT systems;
  7. authorises police to torture a suspect to find a bomb;
  8. maintains courts, roads and schools so citizens can pursue their own plans;
  9. lets MPs vote against the whip where conscience forbids a bill.
✔ APPLICATION · Requirement by requirementDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Match each thing Parliament does to a requirement.

  1. Plan. The five-year programme is the state's version of a coherent plan. But it is only a framework, because a state has no single life-plan for its citizens.
  2. Values. Cutting every library and park with no reason arbitrarily downgrades knowledge and the experience of beauty.
  3. Persons. Exempting MPs is favouring themselves. They would not accept it if others did it to them.
  4. Detachment. Seeking zero road deaths at any cost is fanaticism. It gives one project a weight that only a basic value deserves, and it crushes everything else.
  5. Commitment. Dropping the pension reform at the first sign of resistance fails to keep faith.
  6. Efficiency. Choosing the cheaper of two equal systems is efficiency within reason.
  7. Every value in every act. Torture chooses directly against a basic good, and that is ruled out whatever is at stake (5.3).
  8. Common good. Maintaining the conditions for citizens' own pursuits is the common good as a framework (5.5).
  9. Conscience. No MP should vote for what they judge to be wrong.

Liu's doubt. Breaking requirements (4) and (5) looks unwise rather than immoral. Finnis would answer that each requirement is basic and cannot be reduced to the others, and that all of them bind.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

apply Finnis's requirements to a legislature; detachment; commitment; plan of life.

45.3 Absolutes and double effect

📘 Learn 5.3 in Lesson 5 →
🔑 Trigger words: shoot one hostage; scientist; a foreseen death is just as dead

5.3.1 Never take life directly as a means

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS
  1. The seventh requirement produces absolute rules, such as never taking a life directly as a means to something else. So shooting one hostage to free ten is ruled out.
  2. An act is defined mainly by what is intended. Damaging a good as a means or an end is different from damaging it as a side effect. But you cannot simply redescribe your plan however you like.
  3. So saying that a foreseen death is just as dead misses the point. Side effects are judged too, but by fairness and by your commitments, and not by adding up results.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Bank Siege

A gunman holds eleven hostages in a bank. He tells the police commander to shoot one hostage, and promises to release the other ten if she does. If she refuses, he will kill all eleven. The commander refuses. Later the same day, in a separate incident, police shoot at a getaway car to stop it, knowing the hostage in the back seat may well be hit.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Compare the two shootings.

  • The demand to shoot is ruled out. Shooting the hostage does nothing by itself except kill an innocent person. The release of the ten would come from a separate, later act, which is the gunman's own free choice. Killing as a means is absolutely ruled out, whatever the numbers.
  • The car is different. The police intend to stop the car. The risk to the hostage is a side effect and not their aim. They cannot simply redescribe their plan, though. If they aimed at the hostage to make the car stop, that would be killing as a means.
  • A foreseen death is just as dead. That is true, but it misses the point. Side effects are not free, and shooting at the car must still be fair. Would the commander think it reasonable if she were in the back seat? Was there another way? The shooting is judged by those tests, and not by adding up lives.

5.3.2 The scientist

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

Finnis's example of the scientist: intending only to gain knowledge, a scientist takes a living person's heart. Even if the death is treated as a side effect, it is impermissible because it is unfair.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

Dr Reyes wants to study a healthy beating heart. He removes one from a living patient who has not consented. He says he does not intend the death, that he only wants the knowledge, and that the death is a side effect.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Grant him his description. His aim is knowledge, his means is removing the heart, and death is a certain side effect.

It still fails, because side effects are judged by fairness. Nobody would accept being killed for someone else's research, so the act is unfair and impermissible. The doctrine of side effects is not a loophole.

5.3.3 The pregnancy cases

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

The pregnancy cases, as the sheet applies them:

  • chemotherapy, or removing a cancerous womb, treats the mother, and the death of the unborn child is a side effect;
  • direct termination intends the death;
  • pre-eclampsia is hard, on the sheet's own reading.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

A hospital ethics committee has four files:

  • (i) a pregnant woman with aggressive cancer needs chemotherapy that will probably end the pregnancy;
  • (ii) a woman has a cancerous womb that must be removed while she is pregnant;
  • (iii) a woman requests a termination because the pregnancy is unplanned;
  • (iv) a woman has severe pre-eclampsia, and only delivery or termination will save her.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Ask what each procedure is aimed at.

  • Files (i) and (ii) treat the mother's disease. The death of the unborn child is foreseen but not intended, so these are permissible if fair.
  • File (iii) intends the death as the means of ending the pregnancy, so it is ruled out.
  • File (iv) is hard. The treatment is the ending of the pregnancy itself, so it is difficult to call the death merely a side effect. Say so in the exam, rather than forcing an answer.

5.3.4 QUALIFY: Liu's verdict

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

Liu says the line between means and side effects is honestly rather artificial.

  • It is out of step with our intuitions, which is odd for principles claimed to be self-evident.
  • It is a poor guide when you are facing an attacker.
  • It limits autonomy heavily, because consent cures nothing.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

A homeowner is attacked with a knife at 2 am. Finnis says she may act to disarm or deter, even foreseeing that the attacker may die, but she may not aim to kill. Separately, a terminally ill man begs his doctor for a lethal dose, and is refused.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

These two situations bring out Liu's three criticisms.

Can the homeowner really sort aiming to disarm from aiming to kill, in two seconds? And for Finnis the dying man's consent changes nothing.

Use these points to evaluate Finnis. Keep your explanation of his view separate from your criticism of it.

5.3.5 TRAP: double effect is Aquinas's; intention, not foresight

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

Two traps to avoid.

  • Double effect comes from Aquinas. For Finnis, doctrines of this kind are useful summaries, but they are not themselves principles of practical reasonableness.
  • The line is about intention, not foresight. A certain death can still be a side effect.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

There are two errors to avoid in the exam.

  • Do not call double effect one of Finnis's requirements, or say that it is the same as requirement [7]. It is an older summary of hard cases, which Finnis treats as a useful reminder and not as a principle.
  • Do not say that a side effect must be uncertain. The scientist (5.3.2) knew the death was certain, and it was still a side effect. What made it wrong was that it was unfair.
🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

shoot one hostage to save ten; a foreseen death is just as dead; the scientist; abortion and medical cases.

55.4 Against utilitarianism

📘 Learn 5.4 in Lesson 5 →
🔑 Trigger words: greatest happiness; whatever makes them happy; maximise preferences; healthcare savings

5.4.1 Not so much false as senseless

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS
  1. Finnis says the idea of the greatest happiness makes no sense outside limited technical settings. The goods cannot be measured on one scale, so utilitarianism is not so much false as senseless.
  2. So maximising satisfied preferences is reasonable only inside the other requirements, as a form of efficiency. It is never the measure of what is right.

Your sheet adds this. Over a wide range of preferences, maximising is reasonable. But sadists' preferences do not count, and some acts, such as certain intentional killings and frauds, are excluded altogether.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Happiness Ministry

Ruritania creates a Happiness Ministry with one rule: adopt whatever policy produces the greatest total satisfaction of citizens' preferences. In its first month it faces three choices:

  • (i) which of two equally good bus routes to build;
  • (ii) whether to let a popular TV show stage real fights in which unwilling prisoners are hurt, because millions enjoy watching;
  • (iii) whether to secretly poison one terminally ill patient so his organs can save five others.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Look at each choice.

  • (i) Maximising is fine. The goal is definite, which is getting people to work. Comparing routes by how many people they serve is a technical calculation that Finnis accepts.
  • (ii) The viewers' preferences do not count. They are sadistic, and the requirements discount them. No number of viewers changes that.
  • (iii) This is excluded altogether. It is an intentional killing, so it is outside what any cost-benefit calculation may consider.
  • The deeper point. The Ministry's rule assumes life, friendship and knowledge can all be turned into one currency of satisfaction and added up. Finnis says that is like adding the size of a page, the number six and the mass of a book. The goods cannot be compared on one scale, so the calculation is not false but senseless.

5.4.2 The experience machine

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

Nozick's experience machine is used against the idea that pleasure is the point of everything. A sensible person would not choose to plug into the machine, because we want to actually do things.

A limit from Liu: his class split about 14 to 10, so intuition is a fragile proof. Finnis only needs to show that turning the goods into units of pleasure loses something.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

A start-up offers the LifePod. Plug in for life and you will feel you are living a perfect life, writing novels and making friends, but none of it is real. A poll of law students finds 58% would plug in.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Take the three steps.

  • Finnis's claim. No sensible person would plug in, because we want to actually do things and be a certain kind of person. We do not just want the experiences.
  • Liu's worry. If 58% would plug in, the supposedly obvious intuition is not obvious, and relying on it is risky.
  • The rescue. Finnis does not need everyone to refuse. He only needs it to be true that something is lost when friendship or real achievement is turned into units of pleasure. Even a student who plugs in can accept that.

5.4.3 STEELMAN: efficiency is real, but life is not a cost

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

The best case on the other side is that efficiency really is a requirement, so savings in healthcare matter. But life is a basic good, and not a cost to be set off against other costs.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

The Health Ministry proposes (a) switching to a cheaper but equally effective cancer drug, and (b) a rule that patients over 80 are never offered dialysis, because the money saves more years of life elsewhere.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Compare the two proposals.

  • (a) is efficiency within reason, which Finnis accepts. Resources are limited.
  • (b) treats some people's lives as a cost to be set off against others' lives. That turns life into units and drops a whole class of people from consideration. So it goes beyond the limits of efficiency, and it breaks requirement [3], which forbids arbitrary preference among persons.
🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

the greatest happiness of the greatest number; give people whatever makes them happy; maximise preferences; healthcare savings.

65.5 From person to state

📘 Learn 5.5 in Lesson 5 →
🔑 Trigger words: transpose to the state; common good; minimal framework; online falsehoods; closer to liberalism

5.5.1 The common good is a set of conditions

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS
  1. Finnis's common good is a set of conditions that let members achieve reasonable goals for themselves.
  2. A state is not a ship bound for one port. Committing to a life-plan is nothing like setting out to bake a cake, because there is no single end product.
  3. Yet the common good is definite enough to rule out many kinds of political arrangement and law. So it understates Finnis to say he gives almost no guidance.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Ship of State

A Ruritanian party proposes a National Life Plan. Every citizen is assigned a career at 16, must attend state cultural events monthly, and must marry by 30. Its leader says that a state is like a ship, and must steer everyone to one destination.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Apply the three points.

  • There is no single destination. Finnis's common good is the conditions in which each person can pursue their own reasonable goals, such as courts, roads, schools and public order. It is not a destination the state steers everyone towards.
  • It is not like baking a cake. A life-plan is not a project with one finished product, so there is no single plan the state could impose.
  • It is still definite. The common good is definite enough to rule out the National Life Plan. Assigning careers and forcing marriage destroy the very conditions in which people pursue their own goods. So Finnis does give real guidance, because he excludes many kinds of law.

5.5.2 LEGISLATOR: Liu's working summary

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

Liu's working summary for law-makers:

  1. law is a framework;
  2. it should help people pursue the goods;
  3. public authorities must never intend to damage the goods;
  4. they may prohibit acts that do;
  5. the rest is prudence, as with hate speech or fake news, weighing the risk of chilling speech in the particular place concerned.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Online Falsehoods Bill

Port Meridian proposes a law letting a minister order the takedown of false statements of fact online.

✔ APPLICATION · Step by stepDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Follow Liu's five steps.

  1. Framework. The state is not deciding what citizens should believe. It is protecting the conditions for public knowledge.
  2. Help. A healthy flow of true information serves knowledge, friendship and practical reasonableness.
  3. Never intend damage. The state itself must not spread falsehoods or suppress the truth.
  4. May prohibit. Deliberate lies spread to deceive damage knowledge, so prohibiting them can be justified in principle.
  5. Prudence. A broad power in a minister's hands may chill honest speech. Whether that risk is serious depends on the particular place: how independent the courts are, how the power is likely to be used, and what review exists.

Finnis gives the frame. The final decision is one of prudence.

5.5.3 CONCEDE: Finnis is less liberal than he looks

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

Accept that Finnis is less liberal than he looks. He says the state must favour the basic forms of good and discourage their opposites. So concede that he is not neutral. Even so, the state's job remains only to keep peace and justice.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

A liberal critic says Finnis's state is basically neutral. Then Port Meridian taxes casinos heavily, funds marriage counselling and bans the sale of hard drugs, citing the goods.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Finnis would let the state favour the goods and discourage what damages them. So he is not neutral, and you should concede that.

But even so, the role of his state is limited to peace and justice. It is not making citizens fully good, which is the job of families and churches. So Finnis sits between strict liberal neutrality and a state that dictates virtue.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

transpose Finnis to the state; the common good; a minimal framework; online falsehoods; Finnis is closer to liberalism than he seems.

75.6 Human nature: urges or ends?

📘 Learn 5.6 in Lesson 5 →
🔑 Trigger words: human nature; follow nature; urges; live in the moment

5.6.1 Urges are not goods

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS
  1. Following nature can mean obeying your urges, or pursuing your proper ends. The Stoics saw humans as having natural ends, known through reflection.
  2. Finnis draws nothing from urges. Many urges, such as the urge to be cruel for no reason, correspond to no good at all. And no value can be worked out from a fact.
  3. So saying that law should give people what they want mistakes urges for goods. It is unreasonable to live from moment to moment, following immediate cravings.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The 24-Hour Licence

A minister proposes letting bars serve alcohol 24 hours a day. He says people clearly want to drink late, that this is human nature, and that the law should follow nature and give people what they want.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Apply the three points.

  • Urges and ends are different. The minister reads nature as meaning urges. The classical tradition reads it as the ends that reason can grasp.
  • Nothing follows from urges. That people want something does not make it good. Some urges, like the urge to be cruel for no reason, correspond to no good at all. And Finnis draws no ought from facts about wanting.
  • Living in the moment. A law built on immediate cravings encourages the life Finnis calls unreasonable: living from moment to moment instead of by a coherent plan. The minister has to argue that late drinking serves a good, such as play or friendship, and that the costs to others are justified. Saying that people want it is not an argument.

5.6.2 Seligman and Tierney; Liu on the life-plan

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

Seligman and Tierney say human minds are built to look ahead. That fits Finnis's idea of a life-plan judged from the end of one's life, but it cannot justify it.

Liu adds that the plan works through general policies, such as having greens at every meal. It is not a deathbed test for each lunch. Finnis borrows from Rawls the idea of a rational plan of life.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

A student says that Finnis wants him to imagine his deathbed every time he chooses lunch, and that this is absurd.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Liu's answer is that the plan works through general policies. Decide once that you eat healthily, so that every meal includes greens, and lunch settles itself.

The psychology also fits, since humans are built to steer by imagined futures. But fitting our psychology does not prove the plan is reasonable. Facts about how minds work cannot give you an ought (5.6.1).

5.6.3 CONCEDE: Harris on facts and reflection

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

Accept Harris's point. He asks whether assumptions about human nature will inevitably form part of what we reflect on when we consider our inclinations. Admit that there is such a mixture. Harris still calls this process reasoning.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Finnis says we grasp the goods from the inside, through our inclinations, without working them out from facts. Harris's point is that facts about human nature inevitably feed into that reflection.

Accept this. Finnis's method is not free of facts. But it is still a form of reasoning and not mere feeling.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

follow human nature; give people what they want; live in the moment.

85.7 Finnis tested

📘 Learn 5.7 in Lesson 5 →
🔑 Trigger words: critically evaluate; self-evident; who decides; is gambling play?
▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS
  1. Finnis's weak points are his method and the seventh requirement:
    • self-evidence rests on intuitions shaped by upbringing;
    • the line between means and side effects looks artificial (Liu);
    • being open to everyone's reason is not the same as being accepted by everyone. For example, is casino gambling play?
  2. He replies that there is nothing magic about the number seven. He also says that those who dissent may be innocently mistaken, which is not the same as being perfectly reasonable.
  3. So concede to Rawls that reasonable disagreement limits what the state may force, even where Finnis is right about the good.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Casino Licence

Port Meridian considers licensing a second casino. Supporters say gambling is play, which is a basic good, so Finnis would back it. Opponents say it is addiction and greed, so Finnis would ban it. Both sides claim that the answer is self-evident.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Work through the weak points and the replies.

  • Self-evidence under strain. Both sides find different things obvious, partly because of how they were brought up. That is the weakness in Finnis's method.
  • Open to reason is not the same as accepted. The goods may be open to everyone's reason, but citizens plainly do not accept the same view of whether casino gambling is play.
  • Finnis's replies. The list is flexible. And people who disagree may simply be mistaken without being at fault.
  • The concession to Rawls. Even if Finnis is right that compulsive gambling damages the goods, the depth of reasonable disagreement counsels restraint in using the criminal law. Regulating, through licences, limits and levies, may be easier to defend than banning.
🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

critically evaluate Finnis; are the goods really self-evident?; who decides?; is gambling play?.

95.8 Conclusion, applied

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

The conclusion. Finnis gives legislators real limits: never intend to destroy a basic good, never treat one as worthless, and secure the conditions in which each citizen can pursue their own plan. Beyond that, the issue is one for prudence. And because his self-evidence rests on disputed intuitions, and his line between means and side effects is, for Liu, artificial, disagreement about the goods counsels restraint in using force. The statement is overstated: Finnis guides law-makers without dictating to them.

✔ APPLICATION · Applied to the hyposDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Here is where each part of the conclusion was shown.

  • Never intend to destroy a good: the Assisted Dying Bill (5.0) and the bank siege (5.3.1).
  • Never treat one as worthless: the Culture Minister (5.1.1) and the over-80s dialysis rule (5.4.3).
  • Secure the conditions: the Ship of State (5.5.1).
  • Prudence: the Online Falsehoods Bill (5.5.2).
  • Restraint in using force: the Casino Licence (5.7).

HYPO LESSON 6 · ARCHETYPE 6 · ABOUT 36 MIN · 55 QUESTIONS

Hypos: Pluralist legislation, Rawls v Finnis

⚡ BIG IDEA

No law on a contested moral issue is neutral. Its reasons must be open to every citizen, sound on the merits, and suited to the circumstances.

The theory behind these hypos is taught in Lesson 6. Do that lesson first if the rules below look unfamiliar.

How to work through a hypo
  1. 1Read the rule (teal box). It puts the sheet's point in plain words. The exact wording to use in the exam is in the Lessons and Sheet tabs.
  2. 2Read the hypothetical (amber box). Before reading on, decide what the rule says about these facts.
  3. 3Tap Application (green box) and compare it with your answer.
  4. 4The exam cue (violet box) lists question words that should send you to this block. Each block ends with a quick check.
Applications:
ℹ NOTE
About these hypos

Each block on this page has three parts: the rule in plain words, a made-up set of facts, and a worked answer. Your exact sheet wording, with its quotations, is still in the Lessons and Sheet tabs.

Some terms come up throughout. Public reason means giving reasons that every citizen could accept, rather than reasons that depend on one faith or philosophy. A comprehensive doctrine is a full view of life, such as a religion or a secular philosophy. The overlapping consensus is when people with different doctrines each support the same political principles, for their own reasons. TSH is Tan Seow Hon.

16.0 The archetype in one line

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

The position. No law on a contested moral issue is neutral. Its reasons must be open to every citizen, sound on the merits, and suited to the circumstances.

The opening. The statement asks Parliament to take no side, or to rely only on grounds that every citizen shares. Rawls is right to require reasons that each citizen could accept. But his neutrality is about how a law is justified, and not about its result. Allowing something still takes a moral side. Being open to everyone is not the same as being accepted by everyone. And any fair process rests on some substantive values. So a law's reasons must be open to all, sound, and carefully suited to the circumstances.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Surrogacy Bill

Ruritania is deciding whether to allow commercial surrogacy. The Minister says that citizens deeply disagree, so Parliament will take no side. It will simply allow it, and each citizen can decide for themselves.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Work through what the Minister has said.

  • Allowing it is a side. Permitting commercial surrogacy settles, for the law, that paying a woman to carry a child is acceptable. Opponents will see the supposedly neutral option as a defeat.
  • What Rawls can rightly demand. Whatever Parliament decides, its reasons should be ones every citizen could accept. Protecting women from exploitation and protecting children's welfare are such reasons. Saying that my faith forbids it, or that my philosophy of autonomy requires it, is not.
  • What else is needed. The reasons must also be sound, meaning true claims about exploitation and welfare. And they must be suited to Ruritania's circumstances, meaning how its clinics and courts actually work.
🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

the state should take no side; only grounds every citizen can share.

26.1 Rawls

📘 Learn 6.1 in Lesson 6 →
🔑 Trigger words: grounds every citizen can share; majority; civility

6.1.1 More than a majority, less than unanimity

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS
  1. Rawls asks for more than a majority and less than unanimity. Political power is legitimate only under basic constitutional arrangements that all citizens could reasonably be expected to accept.
  2. Public reason binds these people:
    • judges, more strictly than others;
    • officials and candidates;
    • citizens, when voting as if they were legislators;
    • on constitutional basics and basic justice, as far as possible. It never binds churches or the media.
  3. So it gets Rawls backwards to say civility replaces justification. Civility is a moral duty to justify. When officials and citizens follow public reason, what the majority enacts is legitimate law.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Who Must Give Public Reasons?

During Ruritania's surrogacy debate, five people speak:

  • (i) a bishop, in a sermon, says surrogacy offends God;
  • (ii) a newspaper editorial mocks the opponents;
  • (iii) an MP, in the House, argues it exploits poor women;
  • (iv) a judge, striking down a regulation, cites her religious convictions;
  • (v) a citizen, alone in the voting booth, votes in a referendum based only on his faith's teaching.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Ask who is bound by public reason.

  • (i) and (ii) are free. Churches and the media belong to the wider culture, which public reason does not bind.
  • (iii) is doing it right. Exploitation of poor women is a political value any citizen could accept.
  • (iv) breaks it most seriously. Public reason binds judges more strictly than anyone else.
  • (v) breaks it too. When voting, Rawls asks citizens to think as if they were legislators and to give only public reasons.
  • The result. If officials and voters do follow public reason, then what the majority enacts is legitimate law, even for those who lost. That is not unanimity, because some people will still disagree. But it is more than a bare majority, because the reasons must be ones all could reasonably accept.

6.1.2 AGAINST: Finnis's dilemma

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

Finnis poses a dilemma for Rawls's test about what citizens may reasonably be expected to accept.

  • Read as a prediction, the test gives anyone a veto, which Finnis calls a gross form of veto.
  • Read as a moral standard, the test has to judge the merits of each objection, as calling some believers mistaken does.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

A small, loud group says it will never accept any surrogacy law at all.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Try each reading.

  • As a prediction. If the test means that people will in fact agree, this group has a veto over the law, which is absurd.
  • As a moral standard. If the test means that people ought to agree if they are reasonable, then Rawls has to judge whether the group's objection is any good. That is a judgment on the merits, and his theory claimed to avoid that.

Either way, Rawls's test is in trouble.

6.1.3 QUALIFY: TSH and Finnis on majorities

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

Two limits on the majority's role.

  • Tan Seow Hon says Rawls cannot mean that public reason just is what the majority thinks. So he has to show that the votes on the losing side were unreasonable.
  • Finnis says that keeping moral truth out leaves the gravest questions to the sheer power of numbers (14.10).
✔ APPLICATION · To surrogacyDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Suppose the bill passes 60 to 40. That alone does not show it rests on public reason. Rawls still has to show that the losing side's arguments were not reasonable. Otherwise, as Finnis says, it is just numbers.

6.1.4 The basis of Rawls's view

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

Rawls's deepest divide is between the older view that there is one reasonable idea of the good, which he calls the dominant tradition from Plato to Aquinas, and the view that reasonable people will always hold different ideas of the good. On his view, political power is the power of free and equal citizens acting together.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Rawls's whole test starts from the claim that reasonable people will always disagree about the good life. If you hold the older view, that reason can find one true good, you will find his test too timid. That divide, more than any single issue, is where Rawls and Finnis really part.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

only grounds every citizen can share; the majority decides; civility.

36.2 Not neutral

📘 Learn 6.2 in Lesson 6 →
🔑 Trigger words: takes no side; neutral fact

6.2.1 Taking no side takes a side

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS
  1. Saying that the state takes no side is itself a moral position. Even Rawls accepts that what we do has implications for views about salvation.
  2. Even Rawls's filter is moral. Calling someone unreasonable means they refuse fair terms of cooperation. It does not mean they are wrong. And who counts as reasonable is the very point in dispute (6.11).
  3. So neutrality cannot be achieved. Even Singapore's supposedly secular sexuality curriculum reflects a national stance on the family, as Minister Masagos said in 2022.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Religion-Free Curriculum

Port Meridian's schools decide to stay neutral by never mentioning religion in class. There is no teaching about any faith, and no religious holidays are marked.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Apply the three points.

  • It is not neutral in its effect. A child taught for twelve years as if religion did not matter learns something about religion. Rawls himself accepts that what the state does has implications for views about salvation, even if none are intended.
  • The filter is moral. If a group objects and Port Meridian calls it unreasonable, that judgment rests on a moral standard: being willing to accept fair terms.
  • Every curriculum has a stance. As Masagos's remark shows, even a secular curriculum reflects some view, in that case a view of the family.

6.2.2 AGAINST: Finnis on method

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

Finnis objects to Rawls's method. Rawls's thin theory of the good is arbitrary and leaves out most of what makes human life good. And the fact that people in the Original Position would reject something does not make it unjust.

(The Original Position is Rawls's thought experiment, in which people choose principles without knowing their place in society.)

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

A Rawlsian planner says that behind the veil of ignorance no one would choose principles that favour friendship or art, so the state may give them no special value.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Finnis has two replies.

  • The thin theory. Counting only liberty, opportunity, wealth and self-respect as goods, and treating knowledge, play and friendship as unimportant, is not neutral. It is an impoverished picture of what is good.
  • The veil proves less than is claimed. Even if the principles chosen behind the veil are fair, that does not show that principles not chosen there are unjust.

6.2.3 TRAP: unreasonable ≠ false

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

Two traps to avoid.

  • A doctrine that says there is no salvation outside the church may be true. It is unreasonable only because it proposes to use the state's power to enforce itself.
  • Tolerance does not have to be part of a doctrine's teaching. The doctrine only has to not be hostile to fair and reciprocal terms (Liu, Week 6).
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

Two churches in Port Meridian each teach that there is no salvation outside their own church. Church A campaigns to make its doctrine the law. Church B teaches it to members but accepts equal rights for all.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Do not write that Rawls calls Church A's doctrine false. He does not.

Church A is unreasonable because it wants the state's power to enforce its doctrine on others. Church B holds the same belief and is reasonable. It does not preach tolerance as a doctrine, but it is not hostile to fair terms.

6.2.4 AGAINST: liberal neutrality favours the already-established

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

Another objection is that liberal neutrality favours views that are already built into institutions and social life. Rawls himself accepts that political liberalism is a moral view.

✔ APPLICATION · To the curriculumDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

A supposedly neutral curriculum built around individual choice suits the views already at home in Port Meridian's institutions, and the people who value choosing among ways of life. Faiths that see life as received rather than chosen are disadvantaged. Rawls's own reply accepts that his view is a moral one.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

the state takes no side; permitting it is neutral; it's a neutral fact.

46.3 Overlapping consensus v modus vivendi

📘 Learn 6.3 in Lesson 6 →
🔑 Trigger words: what the faiths share; overlap of convictions; modus vivendi

6.3.1 The OC is not Devlin's shared morality, and not a truce

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS
  1. Legislating what the faiths share is Devlin's idea of shared morality. It is not Rawls's overlapping consensus. The consensus is among reasonable doctrines, and it is about a political idea of justice.
  2. Each doctrine supports that idea on its own moral grounds. So the consensus holds even if political power shifts, and a mere truce cannot do that.
  3. So the overlapping consensus is not just a truce in philosophical dress, though the word reasonable decides who gets to belong.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Two Settlements on Kessland Island

Kessland Island has two faith communities, the Arans and the Belts.

  • In 1950, after a civil war, they sign a treaty giving each equal worship rights. Each side signs only because it cannot win. Each says privately that it would suppress the other if it could.
  • In 2026, both communities teach equal religious liberty. The Arans say God gave everyone free conscience. The Belts say forcing belief is unfair. A census shows the Arans will soon be 70% of the population, and they say nothing would change.

A politician proposes making law out of whatever the two faiths' teachings share.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Compare the two periods, then look at the politician's idea.

  • 1950 is a truce, which Rawls calls a modus vivendi. It rests on a balance of power, and it would collapse when power shifts.
  • 2026 is an overlapping consensus. Each community supports equal liberty on its own moral grounds. The test is whether it survives a shift in power, and the Arans' answer shows that it does.
  • The politician is describing Devlin and not Rawls. Whatever the faiths share is shared morality, and that could include all sorts of moral rules. Rawls's consensus is only about a political idea of justice.
  • The catch. Who counts as a reasonable doctrine, eligible to join the consensus, is decided by Rawls's own standard (6.11).

6.3.2 QUALIFY: Finnis on the abortion consensus

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

A limit from Finnis. The pro-choice writers share no view about the unborn, so there is no overlapping consensus among them except in the result they reach.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Suppose three pro-choice writers reach the same law by three incompatible routes about what the unborn is. They agree only on the outcome. That is closer to a coalition than to a consensus on principle.

6.3.3 The OC is on principles, not reasons; tolerance works outside it

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS
  • The overlapping consensus is on principles, and not on reasons. The Golden Rule can be held as divine teaching or as reciprocity. Secular doctrines, such as those of Kant or Mill, can join as well (Liu).
  • Tolerance works outside the overlap. It says: I may be right, but making this law would be unfair (Liu).
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

An Aran also believes alcohol is sinful, a view the Belts do not share.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Separate what is inside the overlap from what is outside it.

  • Inside the overlap, both communities agree on equal liberty, though for different reasons. That is enough.
  • Outside it, the Aran's view on alcohol is not in the overlap. Tolerance means saying: I may be right that drinking is wrong, but making it a crime would be unfair to the Belts. So the Aran keeps the belief, but does not try to legislate it.
🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

legislate what the faiths share; an overlap of convictions; it's just a modus vivendi.

56.4 Sorting reasons

📘 Learn 6.4 in Lesson 6 →
🔑 Trigger words: whose morality is admissible; four MPs

6.4.1 By kind, by motive, by merit

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS
  1. Rawls and Finnis differ on more than whose morality can be used:
    • Rawls sorts reasons by their kind;
    • Chua, Singapore's Health Minister in 1969, sorted them by motive;
    • Finnis and Tan Seow Hon sort them by merit.
  2. Rawls treats secular full philosophies the same way as religious ones. But he accepts Catholic arguments about the common good when they are put in terms of political values.
  3. So the lines blur. TSH points to a catch-22: religious reasons would fail Rawls's test, and Chua dismissed medical reasons as a mere front for religion. That test goes further than Rawls's.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Four MPs on Assisted Dying

Ruritania debates legalising assisted dying. Four MPs oppose it.

  • MP A says scripture teaches that life is God's gift and only God may take it.
  • MP B, a strict Kantian, says killing is always wrong because persons are ends in themselves.
  • MP C, a Catholic, says legalising it will pressure the elderly and disabled to die, and weaken trust between doctors and patients.
  • MP D, a devout believer, cites medical studies on palliative care. The Minister dismisses her studies as a front for her religion.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Sort the reasons in each of the three ways.

  • Rawls, sorting by kind. A and B both argue from full doctrines, one religious and one secular, and both fail public reason equally. C passes. Although C is Catholic, the argument is put in political values: protecting vulnerable citizens, and the relationship between doctor and patient. D's studies are public reasons too.
  • Chua, sorting by motive. The Minister rejects D because of D's faith, whatever her argument. That excludes even public reasons, so it goes further than Rawls. This is TSH's catch-22: religious arguments fail, and non-religious arguments from religious people are written off as a front.
  • Finnis and TSH, sorting by merit. Ask whether each argument is good. Are C's and D's claims about pressure and palliative care true?

6.4.2 CONCEDE: merit-sorting rests on disputed premises

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

Accept this point from Rawls: sorting reasons by merit rests on disputed premises. Tan Seow Hon replies that process also rests on substantive values. Accept that merit settles what is true, and not whether it may be enforced (5.7).

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Even if MP B's Kantian argument is sound, deciding that it is sound is a contested call, which is Rawls's point. TSH's reply is that Rawls's own process also rests on contested values. Accept both points. Being right about the merits does not, by itself, justify forcing those who disagree.

6.4.3 Liu on what public reason is not

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

Liu adds four points about what public reason is not:

  • a bad reason is not the same as a non-public one;
  • a motive is not the same as a justification;
  • a Kantian's claim that all lying is wrong is excluded too;
  • public reason shifts as the wider culture shifts.
✔ APPLICATION · To the four MPsDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Apply each of Liu's points.

  • MP C's argument might be weak, but being weak does not make it non-public.
  • MP D's motive is her faith, but her justification is the studies.
  • MP B is excluded just like MP A, so public reason is not anti-religious.
  • As views in the wider society shift, what counts as a public reason can shift too.

whose morality is admissible?; four MPs; religious arguments in Parliament.

66.5 Abortion

📘 Learn 6.5 in Lesson 6 →
🔑 Trigger words: nobody can say when life begins; stand aside; free not to have one; slavery; compromise

6.5.1 A permissive law is not neutral

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS
  1. It fails to say a permissive law is neutral. Chua said learned men had not been able to agree, and then declared that an early conception is not a human being.
  2. If nobody can say when life begins, then TSH's hunter, who is unsure what is moving behind a bush, should not fire.
  3. So Parliament cannot stand aside, because allowing abortion settles the question of what the unborn is. Argue for limits from consequences that everyone can assess.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Late-Limit Bill

Ruritania's Health Minister proposes allowing abortion on request up to 24 weeks. In the debate she says that experts cannot agree when life begins, so Parliament will take no view, and women who object are free not to have one. In the same speech she adds that a 12-week foetus is not yet a human being.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Work through the Minister's speech.

  • She settled what she said could not be settled. Like Chua in 1969, she says no one can say when life begins, and then says a 12-week foetus is not a human being.
  • The hunter. If we really do not know whether the foetus is a person, the cautious course is not to fire. A hunter who shoots at movement in a bush without checking it is not a person is irresponsible.
  • Allowing it settles the question. The law forbids killing the innocent. So allowing abortion treats the foetus as not an innocent person in the relevant sense. Standing aside is not available.
  • The constructive route. An opponent can still argue for limits from reasons any citizen could accept: health risks, how often late terminations are really needed, and support for adoption.

6.5.2 Rawls's two positions, and Finnis's reply

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

Rawls first said that a doctrine denying the first-trimester right was to that extent unreasonable. He later said Catholics need not exercise the right, and by then he accepted that arguments against the right, in political values, were public reason. Finnis says that telling objectors they need not exercise the right is like a slave-owner's reply, and shows impudence or thoughtlessness.

✔ APPLICATION · To the Minister's "free not to have one"Decide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Finnis's point is that this answers nothing for someone who believes the foetus is a person. It is like telling someone who opposes slavery that they need not own slaves. The objector's concern is not their own conduct. It is the victim.

6.5.3 AGAINST: TSH on Macedo's middle ground

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

Tan Seow Hon objects to Macedo's idea of a middle ground. Treating abortion as a close call is not a neutral midpoint. It comes from non-cognitivism, the view that moral claims only express feelings. And a pro-life middle, which is a ban with help for women, easier adoption, and penalties on providers rather than women, would be rejected by pro-choice people, as she reports Wolfe and George as saying.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

A backbencher proposes a compromise: abortion on request to 16 weeks, then only for medical reasons. Another MP proposes a different compromise: a ban, plus full support for pregnant women, easier adoption, and penalties only on providers.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Each side calls its own proposal the middle. TSH's point is that any middle assumes how much the unborn's life weighs against the woman's choice. So splitting the difference is not a neutral position. It already takes a view of the question.

6.5.4 AGAINST: Finnis turns reciprocity on Rawls

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

Finnis turns the idea of reciprocity against Rawls. Children raised to be abused and killed painlessly in their sleep plainly fail to count under reciprocity. So he asks why Rawls draws the boundary of justice and fairness at birth, and why the child a week before birth faces the ultimate coercion.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Rawls's idea of reciprocity is meant for free and equal citizens. But Finnis's horrifying example shows that we think justice covers people who cannot yet take part, such as young children. So why stop at birth? A foetus a week before birth and a newborn a week after differ mainly in where they are. Rawls owes a reason for the line.

6.5.5 CONCEDE: TSH on who counts as human

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

Accept this from Tan Seow Hon: our agreement on human worth does not yet extend to the details of who is entitled to be treated as human. So argue for caution, and not for victory.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Even a strong pro-life argument cannot claim that the debate has been won. Everyone agrees humans have equal worth, but they disagree about who counts. So the honest conclusion is caution: hesitate before declaring the question settled, either way.

6.5.6 TRAP: Finnis's article is not an argument that abortion is wrong

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

Here is a trap (Liu). Finnis's article is not an argument that abortion is wrong. It tests Rawls's promise of fair terms that do not settle deep questions. Rawls and Reiman assume the unborn is not a person. If it were, it would be owed fair terms too.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

In an exam, do not write that Finnis proves abortion is murder. Write that Finnis shows Rawls's supposedly neutral permissive answer quietly assumes that the unborn is not a person, so it does not avoid the deep question. That is the point about method the article makes.

6.5.7 Slide 7's decision tree

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

The slide gives a decision tree:

  1. Is the unborn a clump of cells?
  2. If not, must the woman provide for it, as in Thomson's example of the violinist?

Either branch settles a moral question. Finnis says Thomson's argument gets treated as more reasonable than it is.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

A pro-choice MP says that even if the foetus is a person, nobody can be forced to use her body to keep another alive. If you woke up plugged into a famous violinist's kidneys, you could unplug.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Look at the two branches.

  • The first branch, that it is just cells, answers the question of what the unborn is directly.
  • The violinist argument tries to avoid that question. But it still makes a moral claim: that the woman has no duty to provide for even a person. Either way, a moral answer is being given.
  • Finnis adds that Thomson's argument, which he calls a bald assertion, gets treated as more reasonable than it is.

The sheet only says to see section 5. Use the section 5 material here: absolute limits (5.3), no state ranking of the goods (5.1), and prudence (5.5).

Quick hypothetical

86.7 Religion

📘 Learn 6.7 in Lesson 6 →
🔑 Trigger words: religious arguments; faith condemns it; exemption

6.7.1 Religious arguments aren't barred for being religious

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS
  1. Public reason does not exclude any argument for being religious. The Good Samaritan may be cited, if public reasons follow in due course.
  2. Finnis's basic good of religion, which includes agnostic or negative answers, supports religious freedom. Rawls protects it because denying basic liberties normally breaks reciprocity.
  3. So banning something because a faith condemns it fails. But Tan Seow Hon warns that a national-interest test may leave religion with little practical effect.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Bystander Bill and the Tattoo Ban
  • (a) An MP introduces a bill requiring bystanders to call emergency services when they see someone injured. She opens with the parable of the Good Samaritan, then argues that it would save lives and cost bystanders almost nothing.
  • (b) Another MP proposes banning tattoo parlours because his faith teaches that marking the body is sinful.
  • (c) A religious minority asks for an exemption from a new law, so it can keep its traditional head-coverings in court.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Take each proposal in turn.

  • (a) passes. Citing scripture is allowed, as long as public reasons follow. Here they do: lives saved, at very little cost.
  • (b) fails. That a faith condemns something is not a reason every citizen could accept.
  • (c) has support from both theorists, for different reasons. For Finnis, religion is a basic good, including agnostic answers, that the state should respect. For Rawls, denying basic liberties like religious freedom normally breaks reciprocity.
  • TSH's warning. If every law must serve the national interest, religious views may in the end have little practical effect, even when people are allowed to voice them.

6.7.2 TSH: is this begging the question?

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

Tan Seow Hon says political values make religious views count for nothing wherever an issue is labelled metaphysical. Whether an issue is political is itself disputed, as with polygamy. Liu's slide asks whether this begs the question.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

A man asks Ruritania to recognise his polygamous marriage. The government says marriage is a political matter, the orderly raising of the next generation, so only political values count. He replies that for him marriage is a religious matter, and that his faith permits it.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Whether marriage is political is exactly what is in dispute. Labelling it political settles the question against the religious view before any argument begins. That is TSH's point, and it is the question Liu's slide is asking.

religious arguments have no place; ban it because a faith condemns it; exemption.

96.8 The whip

📘 Learn 6.8 in Lesson 6 →
🔑 Trigger words: party discipline; conscience; one clear voice
▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS
  1. A whipped House may not represent the majority's opinion (TSH). So speaking with one clear voice need not show what justice requires.
  2. For TSH, lifting the whip on certain occasions is an option, with each member encouraged to see their role in working out higher law. Another option is for courts to act.
  3. So a free vote serves conscience, but not necessarily public reason. Treating s 377A as policy rather than conscience, as Shanmugam did in 2022, is itself a moral judgment.

There is also a precedent: abortion free votes in 1969 and 1974, which TSH says arguably endorsed considering religious perspectives.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Euthanasia Vote

Ruritania's ruling party holds 80% of seats. Its leaders whip MPs to vote for an assisted dying bill, saying the House must speak with one clear voice. Several MPs privately believe the bill is gravely wrong. The leader says this is health policy and not a matter of conscience.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Work through the four points.

  • One voice is not the majority's voice. A whipped 80% may not reflect what most MPs or citizens actually think, so the result does not show what justice requires.
  • Lifting the whip is an option. TSH suggests letting MPs vote freely on certain occasions, each considering their role in working out what higher law requires. Singapore did this on abortion in 1969 and 1974.
  • A free vote serves conscience. It does not guarantee public reason, because MPs voting freely might still give only religious reasons.
  • Calling this policy is itself a judgment. Calling the bill mere health policy decides that it raises no grave moral question, and that is a moral call.

106.9 Close

🔑 Trigger words: make people better
▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

Moral truth, and not neutrality, limits legislation. But saying that the law's task is to make people better goes too far.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Improvement Act

A minister proposes an Improvement Act. Every adult must read one approved book a month and attend a monthly ethics class, because the law's job is to make people better.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Two points answer the minister.

  • Moral truth does limit law. Finnis's absolute limits are real (5.3), and neutrality is impossible anyway (6.2).
  • But this goes too far. Even Finnis's tradition gives the state a limited role: to keep peace and justice, and not to make people fully good. That job is for families, churches and individuals. And forcing virtue undercuts the very practical reasonableness it aims at, because you cannot make someone good by compulsion.

116.10 Aim and mechanism

📘 Learn 6.10 in Lesson 6 →
🔑 Trigger words: equally valid; objectively necessary; wrongdoer; only then; fixed conception of the good life

6.10.1 The aim and the mechanism come apart

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS
  1. The statement's aim, which is not imposing one fixed idea of the good life, and its mechanism, which is the harm-to-others test, are separate things.
  2. The mechanism is:
    • not necessary, because Hart's paternalism responds to defective consent and not to immorality (7.2);
    • not neutral, because Rawls counts Mill's liberalism among the full doctrines.
  3. So the statement can keep its aim only by dropping its mechanism. Finnis supplies substance, Rawls supplies discipline, and Hart supplies a presumption against force.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Draft Constitutional Clause

A reform commission proposes this clause: because all moral opinions are equally valid, the state shall not impose any fixed idea of the good life. Only when conduct harms others is force objectively necessary against the wrongdoer, and only then may the law intervene.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Separate the aim from the mechanism.

  • The aim is fine. Not imposing one way of life on everyone is a reasonable goal.
  • The mechanism is not needed for it. The state can avoid imposing a way of life and still pass some protective laws, such as a cooling-off period for payday loans. As Hart shows, that kind of paternalism protects people whose consent may be defective. It does not impose a view of the good life (7.2).
  • The mechanism is not neutral. Saying only harm to others counts is Mill's liberal philosophy, which Rawls himself classes as one full doctrine among others.
  • Keep the aim and drop the mechanism. Use Finnis for what law protects, Rawls for the discipline of giving public reasons, and Hart for a presumption against force.

6.10.2 The loaded words

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

The statement's own words carry hidden commitments.

  • Objectively assumes moral realism.
  • Wrongdoer assumes there is a wrong.
  • Others raises the question of who counts (6.5).
  • Equally valid defeats itself (4.7).
✔ APPLICATION · To the clauseDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

The clause says opinions are equally valid, and then speaks of what is objectively necessary against a wrongdoer. That assumes there are objective wrongs. And harming others leaves open whether the unborn, animals or future generations count as others. Each of these words assumes what the clause's first sentence denies.

6.10.3 Liu's model: read the sentences as a chain

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

Liu's model is to read the sentences as a chain. The second sentence is the means to the first, and the words only then make it the only means.

  • Finnis says there is a range of valid opinions rather than one, and that protecting others is a ground for force but not the only one.
  • Rawls says equal validity holds in advance, but not for unreasonable doctrines.
  • Critics say toleration is itself imposed.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Answer the clause link by link.

  • Is not imposing a way of life best served by the harm-only rule?
  • Is the harm-only rule the only way to do that?
  • Finnis says there are other grounds.
  • Rawls says equal validity cannot extend to unreasonable doctrines.
  • Critics say the clause imposes toleration while claiming to impose nothing.
🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

multi-sentence statements with equally valid, objectively necessary, only then, wrongdoer, fixed conception of the good life.

126.11 Freestanding yet overriding

📘 Learn 6.11 in Lesson 6 →
🔑 Trigger words: freestanding; overriding; contradictory
▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS
  1. Freestanding means not derived from any full doctrine. It does not mean free of values. The idea is political, but it is still moral.
  2. On constitutional basics and basic justice, political values normally win, because they are very great values and they govern the basic framework of social life. Reasonable doctrines can support them, and the virtues of cooperation are valuable to everyone.
  3. So there is no contradiction for the reasonable. But for dissenters, the label reasonable does the overriding, and Tan Seow Hon asks what standard supports that label.

The best case for Rawls: Masagos echoed him in 2022, saying decisions apply secular, universal values and not individual religious beliefs. Finnis partly agrees (14.10).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Overridden Believer

Jun, a devout citizen, says Rawls claims his political values are freestanding, independent of Jun's faith. Yet on basic questions they override his faith. How can something independent of his beliefs have authority over them? He says it is contradictory.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Work through the three points.

  • Freestanding does not mean free of values. The political idea does not come from any one religion or philosophy, but it is openly moral.
  • Why it overrides. It governs the basic framework within which everyone lives together, and the values at stake, such as fair cooperation and equal liberty, are very great. Jun's own faith may well support them for its own reasons, which is the overlapping consensus. Then there is no contradiction, because Jun accepts the override from inside his faith.
  • The real problem. If Jun's faith does not support them, Rawls calls him unreasonable, and that label does the overriding. TSH asks what standard justifies the label. If it is not just majority opinion, it looks like an objective moral standard of the kind Rawls says he avoids.
  • The best case. Singapore's ministers speak in the same way, so the idea has real-world appeal.
🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

freestanding; overriding; Rawls's view is contradictory.

136.12 Conclusion, applied

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

The conclusion. The statement is wrong, overstated or partly right. Rawls is right to demand that force be justifiable to every citizen, and his word unreasonable condemns refusing fair terms, and not being mistaken. But neutrality cannot deliver what is promised, because any law on the issue takes a moral side, as Finnis's abortion example shows. Pluralism asks for equal respect for persons, and not equal validity for opinions. Reasons must be open to all, sound, and carefully suited to the circumstances.

✔ APPLICATION · Applied to the hyposDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Here is where each part of the conclusion was shown.

  • Justifying force to everyone: who must give public reasons (6.1.1).
  • Unreasonable does not mean wrong: Church A and Church B (6.2.3).
  • Neutrality fails: the Surrogacy Bill (6.0) and the Late-Limit Bill (6.5.1).
  • Persons and not opinions: Jun (6.11) deserves respect even if his view is rejected.
  • Open, sound and suited: MP C's argument (6.4.1), tested on its merits and on Ruritania's facts.
