HYPO LESSON 7 · ARCHETYPE 7 · ABOUT 35 MIN · 61 QUESTIONS

Hypos: Enforcement of morals

⚡ BIG IDEA

Every answer to whether law should enforce morality, repeal included, takes a moral side. The real question is which reasons justify how much force.

The theory behind these hypos is taught in Lesson 7. Do that lesson first if the rules below look unfamiliar.

How to work through a hypo
  1. 1Read the rule (teal box). It puts the sheet's point in plain words. The exact wording to use in the exam is in the Lessons and Sheet tabs.
  2. 2Read the hypothetical (amber box). Before reading on, decide what the rule says about these facts.
  3. 3Tap Application (green box) and compare it with your answer.
  4. 4The exam cue (violet box) lists question words that should send you to this block. Each block ends with a quick check.
Applications:
ℹ NOTE
About these hypos

Each block on this page has three parts: the rule in plain words, a made-up set of facts, and a worked answer. Your exact sheet wording, with its quotations, is still in the Lessons and Sheet tabs.

Some blocks (7.4 to 7.7, and 7.11) are about Singapore's real debates on s 377A, the old offence covering sex between men. For those, the facts are either an invented law from Ruritania (an old ban on unmarried couples living together), with a Singapore link in the answer, or a columnist's claim about the real events that you test against what happened.

Coercion means the state using force or the threat of force, such as punishment. TSH is Tan Seow Hon. A dagger (†) marks a point from the slides. The coverage table is the last section.

17.0 The archetype in one line

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

The position. Every answer to whether law should enforce morality, repeal included, takes a moral side. The real question is which reasons justify how much coercion.

The opening. The statement treats harm, personal choice or the majority's feeling as a neutral test of when law may use force. None of these is neutral. What counts as harm, and whose feelings count, are moral questions. So the issue is which reasons justify how much coercion.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Veridine

A new hallucinogen called veridine becomes popular in Ruritania. Parliament has three options:

  • (a) jail anyone who uses it;
  • (b) allow sale only on prescription;
  • (c) do nothing, because the state should take no side.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Take the three options together.

  • Every option takes a side. Option (a) says the state may punish people for what they do to themselves. Option (b) says the state may protect people whose choices may be impaired, without punishing them. Option (c) says neither of those reasons is good enough. Each answer rests on a moral view, including doing nothing.
  • Match the reason to the force used. Jail needs the strongest justification. Prescription-only needs a lesser one. So the useful question is not whether to enforce morality, yes or no. It is which reason supports which level of coercion.
🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

should law enforce morality?; harm is the only neutral test.

27.1 Harm as plain fact

📘 Learn 7.1 in Lesson 7 →
🔑 Trigger words: Wolfenden got it right; only harm to others; plain matter of fact; a sham

7.1.1 Harm is not a plain fact

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS
  1. The claim that harm is a plain matter of fact fails. What counts as harm, and who counts as another person affected, are moral questions.
  2. Hart's real question is whether the bare fact that a society's accepted morality condemns something is any reason to punish it.
  3. So the claim that the Hart and Devlin quarrel is a sham fails. Both sides do argue morally. But they hold different critical principles (the standards used to test a society's morals), and not merely rival moral codes.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Bare-Knuckle Club

In a warehouse, consenting adults hold private bare-knuckle fights. Broken jaws and concussions are common. No one under 21 is admitted, and no spectators are allowed. A committee member says that Wolfenden got it right. Harm to others is a plain matter of fact, and there is none here, so the law has no business here. The member adds that the rest of the debate is a sham, because everyone is only moralising.

(The Wolfenden report was the 1957 English report that said private consensual conduct should not be a crime.)

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Answer the committee member one step at a time.

  • Harm is not a plain fact. Is a broken jaw that the fighter agreed to harm to others? What about the fighter's children, who depend on the fighter's income, or the public hospital that gives treatment? Whether those count is a moral choice. It is not something you can simply observe.
  • Hart's real question. It is not whether the fights are wrong. It is whether the bare fact that most Ruritanians condemn them is any reason to punish them.
  • It is not a sham. Both sides do argue morally. But they disagree about critical principles, such as whether liberty may be restricted when nobody is harmed. That is a real dispute, and more than a clash over which acts are wrong.

7.1.2 STEELMAN: liberty as a value

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

The strongest case for the other side. Mill says that over their own body and mind, each person is sovereign†. Hart says liberty may be a value in itself.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

The strongest case for the fighters is that it is their bodies and their risk. Freedom to choose, even to choose badly, has value of its own. It also lets people try out different ways of living. Make this case fully before you attack it.

7.1.3 AGAINST: what concerns others?

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

Points against.

  • Liu asks what really concerns others, and whether that is everything†.
  • The Wolfenden report itself protected public decency and vulnerable people.
  • Devlin says Wolfenden's own bans on corrupting the young take a public morality for granted.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

The club's defenders also want the law to ban anyone under 21 from fighting, and to ban recruiting vulnerable young men from homeless shelters.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Two points follow.

  • Almost everything concerns others, at some distance. Families, hospitals and the young men who look up to the fighters are all touched. So the test of harm only to others does not draw a sharp line.
  • Even the defenders are protecting morality. Their own rules, protecting the young and banning the exploitation of vulnerable recruits, are what Wolfenden did. Devlin's point is that banning the corruption of the young makes sense only if society has a view about what is corrupt. So Wolfenden's approach already relies on a public morality.

7.1.4 TRAP: this is not a debate about positivism

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

A trap. This is not a debate about legal positivism. Hart and Devlin agreed that the laws in question were law. They argued about what the law should be. Hart's ideas can be taken separately, so a legal positivist could side with Devlin (Liu, Weeks 7 and 9).

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Do not write that Hart, being a positivist, rejects the idea of enforcing morality. Legal positivism is a theory about how to identify what the law is. Whether the club should be banned is a question about what the law should be. A positivist could take either side.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

Wolfenden got it right; only harm to others; harm is a plain matter of fact; the Hart–Devlin quarrel is a sham.

37.2 Paternalism, and the offence line

📘 Learn 7.2 in Lesson 7 →
🔑 Trigger words: protect adults from themselves; sale and consumption; offensive; public decency

7.2.1 Hart's paternalism protects defective consent

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS
  1. The idea that adults must never be protected from themselves is Mill's anti-paternalism. (Paternalism means restricting someone for their own good.) Hart says Mill pushed this so far that it may now look fantastic.
  2. Hart's paternalism protects people whose consent is defective. It does not aim to make them virtuous. It supports restricting sale. It does not obviously support jailing the very user it is meant to protect.
  3. So the claim that the line is easy to draw fails. Paternalism and offence both depend on whose choices and feelings count.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Veridine, revisited (7.0)

Parliament debates two clauses. Clause 1 bans the sale of veridine except on prescription. Clause 2 makes using it punishable by jail. An MP who follows Mill says adults must never be protected from themselves, so both clauses are wrong.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Take the MP's view, then each clause.

  • The Millian view looks extreme today. Hart's point is that people often choose on passing desires, with clouded judgment, or under subtle pressure. Consent given in that way is defective.
  • Clause 1 fits Hart. Restricting sale protects buyers whose consent may be impaired, and it does not punish them.
  • Clause 2 does not obviously fit. Jailing the very user you claim to protect is hard to defend as protection. It looks more like punishment.
  • The line is contested. Whose consent counts as defective is a judgment call. That is why the line is not easy to draw.

7.2.2 FOR: Hart on drugs

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

In support. Hart says that punishing the supply of drugs, even to adults, except on a doctor's prescription, can be explained as protecting the buyers. Passing desires, clouded judgment and subtle pressure all weaken consent.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

This is Hart's own example, and it matches Clause 1. Use it to show that paternalism is different from enforcing morality. The law here protects the buyer. It does not punish wickedness.

7.2.3 AGAINST: TSH on targets, and the offence line

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

Points against.

  • Tan Seow Hon says morals pick which risks get banned. Compare apotemnophilia (a desire to have a healthy limb removed) with dangerous sports.
  • Hart's offence ground covers indecency in public. It does not cover distress at the bare knowledge of what others do in private.
  • For the teetotallers, see 12.6.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist
  • (i) Ruritania bans surgeons from amputating a healthy limb at the request of a person with apotemnophilia, but allows free solo climbing, which kills more people.
  • (ii) Residents complain that they are distressed just to know that veridine parties happen in private homes.
  • (iii) Teetotallers complain about public drinking at outdoor festivals.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Take each complaint in turn.

  • (i) Morals pick the targets. Both activities involve agreeing to serious harm to yourself. So why ban one and not the other? Tan Seow Hon's answer is that a moral view picks the target: one is seen as degrading and the other as admirable. So paternalism is not morally neutral either.
  • (ii) Bare knowledge is not enough. Hart's offence ground covers public acts that affront decency. It does not cover distress at merely knowing what others do in private. If bare knowledge counted, the only freedom left would be to do what nobody objects to.
  • (iii) The teetotallers. Public drinking does offend teetotallers, yet the law ignores them. Deciding which public offences count needs majority opinion or morality. So even the offence line is not neutral (12.6).
🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

never protect adults from themselves; punish sale but not consumption; it's offensive; public decency.

47.3 Devlin's jury box, rightly read

📘 Learn 7.3 in Lesson 7 →
🔑 Trigger words: majority disgust; revulsion; act swiftly; behind closed doors; Clapham omnibus; right-minded man

7.3.1 Devlin's premise without his safeguards

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS
  1. The claim that majority disgust is reason enough borrows Devlin's premise but drops his safeguards.
  2. Devlin refuses to count heads. He wants slowness and, more tentatively, respect for privacy. He does not want a majority to act quickly, or to ignore what happens behind closed doors.
  3. So the claim that majority feeling is the voice of the community fails. For Devlin, disgust is only a good indication. He also demands a deliberate judgment that the practice injures society.

From Devlin's text:

  • Page 15. For the law-maker, majority opinion is not enough. The standard does not depend on counting heads. It is what twelve people chosen at random could be expected to agree on unanimously after discussion. (He takes this idea of practical morality from Pollock.)
  • Page 17. It is far from enough that a majority dislike a practice. Disgust counts only if it is deeply felt and not manufactured. Those swayed simply by disgust would be wrong.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Suspension Parties

A viral video shows a private party where consenting adults are suspended from hooks through their skin. A snap poll finds 65% of Ruritanians are disgusted. An MP says that the ordinary person on the Clapham omnibus is revolted, that majority disgust is reason enough, and that Parliament should ban the parties this week, private ones included.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Check the MP against what Devlin actually said.

  • Devlin does not count heads. He rejects a 65% poll as the test. He asks what twelve randomly chosen jurors would be unanimous on after discussion. A deeply divided issue may fail that test.
  • Disgust is a sign and not the test. It must be deeply felt, and not stirred up by a viral video. Even then it is only an indication. Devlin also demands a calm, deliberate judgment that the practice injures society.
  • Slowness and privacy. Banning it this week ignores Devlin's caution about acting quickly on a new matter. Reaching into private parties ignores his tentative respect for privacy.

So the MP is using Devlin's name while throwing away his safeguards.

7.3.2 STEELMAN: no society can do without disgust

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

The strongest case for the other side. Devlin says no society can do without intolerance, indignation and disgust (page 17).

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

The best case for the MP is that moral feelings carry information. Real and widely shared revulsion can be a sign that a basic norm is at stake. Grant that much before you show that the MP has gone too far.

7.3.3 AGAINST: no unanimity, and critical morality

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

Points against.

  • On a contested issue, you cannot expect a unanimous jury.
  • Hart says critical morality must test that judgment. His example is a racist society.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

In a different society, juries would be unanimously disgusted by mixed-race couples.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

There are two separate problems.

  • The unanimity test cuts against banning contested practices. On the suspension parties, twelve random jurors would probably split. So Devlin's own test is not met.
  • Unanimity is not enough anyway. Where a whole society shares a prejudice, as with mixed-race couples, unanimous disgust shows only what that society feels. Hart's point is that we need critical principles to test whether the feeling is a good reason.

7.3.4 What Devlin actually attacked

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

Devlin attacked Wolfenden's approach, and not its conclusion. He gave no opinion either way (page 2), and eventually supported decriminalisation (Shanmugam, 28 November 2022; Liu, Week 9). But in 1959, he said the difficulty of repeal weighed strongly against change (page 18).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

A student writes that Devlin opposed decriminalising homosexuality, so he would support the ban on suspension parties.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

The student makes two mistakes.

  • Devlin's lecture argued only that protecting society is an acceptable kind of reason for law. He declined to give a view on Wolfenden's conclusions, and he later supported decriminalisation.
  • His 1959 remark was about how difficult repeal would be. It was not a verdict that the conduct must stay criminal.

So do not assume that Devlin's theory requires a ban.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

majority disgust is enough; revulsion; act swiftly; even behind closed doors; the man on the Clapham omnibus; the right-minded man.

57.4 Disintegration

📘 Learn 7.4 in Lesson 7 →
🔑 Trigger words: chain reaction; inevitably; end of society; slippery slope

7.4.1 Trivial or unproven

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS
  1. The claim that repeal begins the end of society is trivial if a society simply is its present morality. And as a prediction, it is unproven.
  2. Hart says nothing shows that private deviation threatens society in the way treason does, and there is much evidence against it.
  3. So the word inevitably overstates the case. Only the principled slope has real force, and Article 156 now shields Singapore's marriage laws from challenge under the fundamental liberties.

Liu's four readings of disintegration†:

ReadingVerdict
Society is its moralityTrivial. Hart calls this absurd. Change is more like a peaceful change of constitution.
Society actually collapsesHart says there seems to be no such drift towards permissiveness in Europe.
Personal bonds loosen (George)Those who reject a shared way of life may not regret the loss.
The principled slopeFrom Lawrence to Obergefell, and on to Masterpiece Cakeshop and Bull v Hall†. Contrast Article 156.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Cohabitation Law

Ruritania has an old law making it a crime for unmarried couples to live together. A bill proposes repealing it. An opponent says repeal will start a chain reaction and will inevitably lead to the end of society.

✔ APPLICATION · Reading by readingDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Go through Liu's four readings.

  1. Society is its morality. If our society only means our current moral code, then any change ends it, but only by definition. That is trivial. Changing a rule is more like a peaceful constitutional amendment: the same society, moving on.
  2. Actual collapse. The opponent must show that countries which allowed cohabitation fell into lawlessness. Hart's point is that there is no such evidence.
  3. Loosened bonds. Perhaps people will share less of a common way of life. But couples who do not share that ideal will not see this as a loss.
  4. The principled slope. This is the strong version. If repeal rests on the principle that cohabitation is not wrong, the same principle may later be used to demand equal treatment with marriage in tax, adoption and the courts. A constitutional shield for marriage laws would stop the slope at that point.

Singapore link. This is the s 377A debate. The principled slope runs from Lawrence (decriminalisation) to Obergefell (marriage), and on to Masterpiece Cakeshop and Bull v Hall (service providers). Article 156 now shields Singapore's marriage laws from challenges based on fundamental liberties.

7.4.2 STEELMAN: immorality is like subversion

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

The strongest case for the other side. Devlin says immorality, like subversion, is by its nature capable of threatening the existence of society. The reply: that gives the law jurisdiction. It does not give a reason to punish this particular conduct.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Grant Devlin that society may in principle legislate against some immorality, as it does against treason. That does not show that cohabitation is the kind of immorality that threatens society. Having the power to act is different from having a reason to act here.

7.4.3 QUALIFY: whose morality?

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

A qualification: whose morality? The origin of s 377A looked like happenstance, as Shanmugam said in 2022. It dates only from 1938. But keeping it in 2007 was a choice.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

Historians show that Ruritania's cohabitation law was copied from a colonial statute in 1931, after a two-minute debate.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

That weakens any claim that the law expresses Ruritania's deep morality. But keeping the law today is a fresh choice, and it must be defended on its merits. An accidental origin neither condemns the law nor saves it.

7.4.4 QUALIFY: Liu on change and fragmentation

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

A qualification from Liu (Week 9).

  • If the thesis is recast as mere change, it cannot justify harsh sanctions.
  • Devlin's real fear is fragmentation, where society splinters into many views.
  • He assumes a consensus. Plural Singapore, unlike 1950s England, may not have one, or may keep one only through coercion.

Most jurists, Liu thinks, side with Hart.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

If the opponent falls back on saying that repeal will change society, that is true. But it cannot justify jailing cohabiting couples, because change is not a disaster. Devlin's real fear, a society splintering into many views, assumes one shared view to begin with. A society of many faiths may never have had one, or may hold one only through the very law in dispute.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

a chain reaction; inevitably; the end of society; a slippery slope.

67.5 Is repeal neutral?

📘 Learn 7.5 in Lesson 7 →
🔑 Trigger words: takes no side; neutral; stands aside; leaves each citizen free
▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS
  1. The claim that repeal takes no side fails. Withdrawing the criminal law rests on a moral judgment about what the state may punish.
  2. Finnis says every society takes a public stand on abortion. And Shanmugam called repeal the right thing to do, which is itself a verdict.
  3. So repeal is neutral only in a weak sense. Withdrawing a crime is not the same as endorsing the conduct, but the reasons for withdrawing it are never neutral.

In support. Shanmugam said in 2022 that a crime generally needs a public order or public interest issue (16.3). Private consensual acts between adults raise no law-and-order concerns. Faishal said the same.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Minister's Repeal Speech

Ruritania's Minister repeals the cohabitation law. In one speech the Minister says two things: that by repealing, the state takes no side and leaves each citizen free; and that repeal is the right thing to do.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Compare the two statements.

  • The Minister took a side. Saying repeal is the right thing to do is a moral verdict. And repeal rests on a judgment that cohabitation is not the kind of conduct the state may punish.
  • The weak sense in which the Minister is right. Repealing a crime is not the same as endorsing cohabitation. The law withdraws. It does not celebrate.
  • The Minister's best reason. It is Shanmugam's: a crime generally needs a public order or public interest issue, and private consensual conduct between adults raises none. That reason is a principle. It is not neutrality.
🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

repeal takes no side; the state stands aside; leaves each citizen free.

77.6 2007

📘 Learn 7.6 in Lesson 7 →
🔑 Trigger words: majority opinion; what prevailed; the 2007 compromise; live and let live
▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS
  1. In 2007, majority feeling prevailed, with Devlin's slowness and privacy. S 377A was kept, but the government said it would not actively enforce it.
  2. Those who wanted to keep it answered the objections that it caused no harm and that the reasons were only religious. They gave other grounds and spill-over arguments. They largely avoided Devlin's treason and disintegration ideas, though perhaps two speeches came closer.
  3. So saying that majority feeling decides describes the result of 2007, and not its reasons:
    • the debate had moved from toleration and privacy to arguments about rights;
    • the motive, whether deferring to the majority or protecting what was right, was what Tan Seow Hon calls a point of equivocation, meaning it was left unclear;
    • by 2022, tolerance had shifted.

Points against.

  • The spill-over to marriage and adoption was, as Tan Seow Hon puts it, a real harm in the form of public consequences.
  • Thio said harm can be both physical and intangible. According to Tan Seow Hon, she explained that homosexuality could be seen as contrary to biological design.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Columnist's Claim

A columnist writes that in 2007 Singapore simply let majority feeling decide s 377A. MPs said most people were disgusted, and that was that. The columnist calls it pure Devlin.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Test the claim against the record.

  • Partly right about the result. The majority view did prevail, and in a way Devlin would recognise: slowly, by keeping the law, and with respect for privacy, by not actively enforcing it.
  • Wrong about the reasons. Those who wanted to keep it did not mainly argue from disgust or disintegration. They answered the objections with other grounds, chiefly spill-over: keeping the law protects marriage and adoption from later challenge. Tan Seow Hon calls that a real harm in the form of public consequences, and Thio said harm can be intangible.
  • The debate had changed. It was not the old Hart and Devlin debate about toleration and privacy. It was a debate about rights. Was the government deferring to the majority, or defending what it thought right? Tan Seow Hon says that was left unclear.
  • It did not last. By 2022 tolerance had shifted, and the law was repealed.
🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

majority opinion prevailed in 2007; the 2007 compromise; live and let live.

87.7 Consistency and non-enforcement

📘 Learn 7.7 in Lesson 7 →
🔑 Trigger words: arbitrary; inconsistent; sham; enforce fully or repeal; unenforced; moral signpost
▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS
  1. Neither inconsistency nor non-enforcement, taken alone, makes s 377A arbitrary or a sham.
  2. Devlin admits there is no logic to be found in this. Each crime is weighed on its own, so the fact that adultery is legal proves nothing.
  3. So the demand to enforce it fully or repeal it is too stark. Announcing non-enforcement breached Fuller's requirement of congruence (that officials act on the rules as stated), yet the law still sent a symbolic message.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Adultery Is Legal

Ruritania keeps its cohabitation law but announces that police will not actively enforce it. Adultery, which arguably breaks up more families, is not a crime at all. A critic says this is arbitrary and inconsistent, that the state should either enforce the law fully or repeal it, and that an unenforced law is a sham.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Take the two complaints in turn.

  • Inconsistency proves little. Devlin admits the criminal law follows no logic across offences. Adultery is left alone largely because it is too hard to police. Each offence must be judged on its own merits, so the fact that adultery is legal does not show that the cohabitation law is arbitrary.
  • Non-enforcement is not a sham, but it has a cost. It breaches congruence (3.2). Yet the law still sends a symbolic message about the value placed on marriage. That is the trade-off (3.2).

7.7.1 AGAINST: the sword hanging over people

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

Points against. Hart says an unenforced law gives police and prosecutors formidable powers to discriminate. Shanmugam called it a sword hanging over gay men.

✔ APPLICATION · To RuritaniaDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

A cohabiting couple cannot be sure that the policy will not change, or that a particular officer will not act. That standing threat, and the power it gives officials to pick targets, is the strongest objection to keeping the law unenforced.

7.7.2 QUALIFY: policing varies

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

A qualification. Tan Seow Hon says policing varies with the offence. An MP in 2007 said some laws, such as the ban on nudity visible to the public, are hard to police.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

The critic assumes that a law is a sham unless it is fully enforced. But many laws are enforced patchily because of their nature, such as the ban on public nudity, and no one calls them shams. Difficulty of enforcement does not, alone, settle whether a law should exist.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

arbitrary; inconsistent; a sham; enforce it fully or repeal it; an unenforced moral signpost.

97.8 Wrong before; order v good

📘 Learn 7.8 in Lesson 7 →
🔑 Trigger words: we were wrong before; slavery; keep order, not make people good; how severely

7.8.1 Past error doesn't mean abstention

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS
  1. The claim that we were wrong before defeats itself. Calling a past law an error assumes there is a right answer.
  2. As Siew argued in 2007, disgust once defended slavery. That supports Devlin's slowness and Hart's demand for reasons. It does not support giving up on moral judgment.
  3. So the idea that law should keep order and not make people good fits Devlin's legal minimum. Stephen would punish vice as such, and Finnis aims at the common good.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Campaigner's Speech

A campaigner against the cohabitation law says that Ruritania once banned interracial marriage, and that the majority were disgusted by such marriages then. The campaigner says we were wrong before, so we can never trust moral judgments in law, and the law should keep order and not make people good.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Take the campaigner's argument apart.

  • It defeats itself. Calling the old ban wrong assumes there was a right answer. So past error cannot mean never judge. It means judge carefully.
  • What it does support. Disgust has backed injustice before, which is Siew's point about slavery. That supports Devlin's slowness and Hart's demand for real reasons before making something a crime. It does not support abandoning moral judgment altogether.
  • Keep order, not make people good. Each theorist reads this differently:
    • Devlin: the criminal law sets a minimum, and not the highest standard of good conduct;
    • Stephen: the law should punish vice as such;
    • Finnis: law aims at the common good, the conditions in which people can flourish.

7.8.2 Whether to punish and how severely

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

Hart says that whether to punish and how severely to punish are separate questions. So a harsh penalty needs its own justification.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

Instead of repealing, Ruritania raises the cohabitation penalty from a $500 fine to two years in jail.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Even if some penalty were justified, the jump to jail needs a justification of its own. The fact that something may be punished does not show that it may be punished harshly.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

we were wrong before; slavery; law should keep order, not make people good; how severely?.

107.9 The coercion gradient: punish, regulate, promote

📘 Learn 7.9 in Lesson 7 →
🔑 Trigger words: enforce morality; regulate private behaviour; their own lives; promote; defend marriage
▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS
  1. Enforcing morality can mean punishing, regulating or promoting. The justification needed rises with the amount of coercion used.
  2. Hart says coercion starts out as something objectionable. It punishes offenders, it restricts everyone else, and in sexual matters it may cause misery of a very special degree.
  3. So the claim that legislators should not enforce morality fails as stated, because all law promotes some morality. But it does hold for punishing private consensual conduct for immorality alone.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Three Gambling Laws

Ruritania considers three responses to gambling:

  • (a) jail anyone who plays private poker for money;
  • (b) license casinos and charge citizens an entry levy;
  • (c) fund school lessons on the risks of gambling.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Place each response on the scale.

  • The gradient. (a) punishes, (b) regulates, and (c) promotes. The justification needed is highest for (a) and lowest for (c).
  • Hart on (a). Jail punishes the players and restricts everyone else who might play. And as Hart notes, criminal law in intimate or personal matters can cause special misery. So it needs strong reasons.
  • The statement fails as stated. Even (c) promotes a moral view, that gambling is risky and unwise. So a rule against ever enforcing morality would ban almost all law. Its true core is narrower: do not punish private consensual conduct merely because it is thought immoral.

7.9.1 CONCEDE: promotion coerces too

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

A concession. Promotion also coerces, through school curricula, media rules and adoption. Rawls says that appeals to monogamy as such reflect full doctrines (complete views of life), though he leaves the question open. Concede that promotion needs public reasons, meaning reasons every citizen could accept (6.1). Liu reads the 2022 package as arguably Rawlsian (13.2).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

Ruritania's curriculum teaches that marriage is the ideal family. Media rules restrict scenes showing cohabiting couples, and adoption favours married couples.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Promotion is not free of coercion. Children must sit the lessons, broadcasters must obey the rules, and cohabiting couples lose out in adoption. So promotion also needs public reasons, the kind any citizen could accept. Saying that marriage as such is better, on the basis of a faith or a philosophy, is not one. Arguments about child welfare might be. Liu's view is that Singapore's 2022 package (repeal plus Article 156) can be read as Rawlsian in this sense.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

legislators should not enforce morality; regulate private behaviour; people should live their own lives; promote; defend marriage.

117.10 Sin, crime and religion

📘 Learn 7.10 in Lesson 7 →
🔑 Trigger words: religious grounds; sin; a faith condemns it; without exception
▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS
  1. In any secular society, as Pritam Singh said in 2022, sin and crime are separate categories.
  2. Even Devlin accepts that law can no longer rely on doctrines that citizens are entitled to disbelieve. So a ban based on a faith needs a secular reason.
  3. So a ban without exception fails twice. One faith cannot alone justify coercing others, and the ban would also catch sacramental or temple use.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Alcohol Petition

A large faith group in Ruritania petitions for a total ban on alcohol. It says its faith teaches that drinking is a sin, so the law should forbid it, without exception.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Work through the petition.

  • Sin is not crime. That a faith calls something a sin does not make it a crime in a secular state. Citizens of other faiths, or of none, are entitled to disbelieve the doctrine, and even Devlin accepts that the law cannot rest on it.
  • A secular reason is needed. Drink-driving deaths or liver disease would be examples. That reason would then have to justify the specific measure.
  • A ban without exception fails twice.
    • One faith's teaching cannot justify coercing everyone else.
    • A total ban would also catch communion wine and religious offerings, so it would burden other faiths' practices.
🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

ban it on religious grounds; it's a sin; a faith condemns it; without exception.

127.11 Polls are not a mandate

📘 Learn 7.11 in Lesson 7 →
🔑 Trigger words: poll; 85% at least somewhat support; most citizens; let the people decide
▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS
  1. A poll showing disapproval is no mandate to make something a crime. In 2007, as Hri Kumar noted, the 70% who frowned on the conduct were never asked about making it a crime.
  2. Tan Seow Hon's dilemma: if there is a right to the conduct, then following the majority is oppression; if there is not, it is democracy. So the moral question comes back.
  3. So majority support is evidence to weigh. It is never a reason that settles what the law should be.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The 85% Survey

A survey finds that 85% of Ruritanians at least somewhat support keeping the cohabitation law. An MP says that the people should decide, and that the survey settles it.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Three points answer the MP.

  • What was actually asked? Somewhat supporting the law may mean only mild disapproval of cohabitation. It need not mean support for prosecuting couples. Like the 70% in 2007 who frowned on homosexual conduct, these people may never have been asked whether it should be a crime.
  • Tan Seow Hon's dilemma. If cohabiting couples have a right to live together, letting 85% override it is oppression. If they have no such right, deferring to the majority is democracy. Either way, you must answer the moral question first, so the poll cannot settle it.
  • So treat the poll as evidence of what people think, to weigh alongside other reasons. It is never decisive on its own.

7.11.1 STEELMAN: majority rule treats citizens as equals

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

The strongest case for the other side. Majority rule treats citizens as equals (Indranee, 2007; see 16.3 and 12.3).

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

The best case for the MP is that counting every citizen's view equally is itself a form of respect. Accept the value of that. Then show that it does not answer whether a right is being overridden.

7.11.2 CONCEDE: consensus gauges, not grounds

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

A concession. Consensus can act as a gauge, but it is not the ground. In Liu's map of the 2007 replies, majority opinion can be an indication of objective morality†. Yet majorities were wrong on slavery, and Tan Seow Hon admits there is a catch.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

An 85% view may be tracking something true about the moral question, so it is not worthless. But majorities have backed slavery. So use consensus as a gauge of where moral truth may lie. Never treat it as the ground that makes something right.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

a poll shows…; 85% at least somewhat support; most citizens; let the people decide.

137.12 Conclusion, applied

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

The conclusion. The statement is right, wrong, or only partly right. No answer, repeal included, is neutral, and Hart against Devlin is a moral quarrel, and not one about legal positivism. Harm, defective consent or public offence may justify punishment. Majority feeling is evidence and never the reason. Devlin's disintegration thesis suits a society in deep agreement, and not a plural one. Promotion needs public reasons. Singapore's 2022 package fits this: a presumption like Wolfenden's, needing public order or public interest, for crime, and Article 156 for marriage.

✔ APPLICATION · Applied to the hyposDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Here is where each part of the conclusion was shown.

  • No answer is neutral: Veridine (7.0) and the Minister's repeal speech (7.5).
  • A moral quarrel, and not one about positivism: the trap in 7.1.4.
  • Harm, defective consent, offence: the Bare-Knuckle Club (7.1), Clause 1 (7.2) and the teetotallers (7.2.3).
  • Majority feeling is evidence only: the Suspension Parties (7.3) and the 85% Survey (7.11).
  • Disintegration needs consensus: the Cohabitation Law (7.4.4).
  • Promotion needs public reasons: the curriculum twist (7.9.1).

HYPO LESSON 8 · ARCHETYPE 8 · ABOUT 35 MIN · 56 QUESTIONS

Hypos: Unjust laws, Radbruch and retroactivity

⚡ BIG IDEA

An unjust law stays law unless it is intolerably unjust. But whether a law is valid never settles whether the judge or the citizen should obey it.

The theory behind these hypos is taught in Lesson 8. Do that lesson first if the rules below look unfamiliar.

How to work through a hypo
  1. 1Read the rule (teal box). It puts the sheet's point in plain words. The exact wording to use in the exam is in the Lessons and Sheet tabs.
  2. 2Read the hypothetical (amber box). Before reading on, decide what the rule says about these facts.
  3. 3Tap Application (green box) and compare it with your answer.
  4. 4The exam cue (violet box) lists question words that should send you to this block. Each block ends with a quick check.
Applications:
ℹ NOTE
About these hypos

Each block on this page has three parts: the rule in plain words, a made-up set of facts, and a worked answer. Your exact sheet wording, with its quotations, is still in the Lessons and Sheet tabs.

Most of the facts use Valdoria, an invented state that was ruled by a Junta from 2005 to 2015 and is now a democracy.

The Radbruch formula says a statute stops being law once its injustice is intolerable. Legal positivism says whether something is law depends on its source and not on its merit. TSH is Tan Seow Hon. A dagger (†) marks a point from the slides. The coverage table is the last section.

18.0 The archetype in one line

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

The position. An unjust law stays law unless it is intolerably unjust. But whether it is valid never settles whether the judge or the citizen should obey it.

The opening. The statement runs two questions together:

  1. Is the statute law?
  2. Must anyone obey it?

Answer them separately. An unjust law stays law unless it is intolerably unjust (Radbruch, Alexy). And validity never settles obedience (Hart).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Curfew Decree

During the Junta years, Valdoria passed a Curfew Decree: anyone outdoors after 9 pm could be jailed for a year. A student writes that the Decree was valid law, so citizens had to obey it.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Take the two questions one at a time.

  • Question 1: was it law? On Radbruch's and Alexy's view, a harsh injustice that is not intolerable stays law. A one-year curfew penalty is harsh, but it is probably below that threshold. So it was law.
  • Question 2: did citizens have to obey? Validity does not answer this. Hart says that whether to obey a valid law is a separate moral question. A citizen who shelters a fleeing protester after 9 pm might be morally right to break the curfew.

The student ran the two questions together.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

an unjust law is no law; if it is law, it must be obeyed.

28.1 The grudge informer

📘 Learn 8.1 in Lesson 8 →
🔑 Trigger words: Nazi statute; denounced her husband; could never shelter

8.1.1 Who bears the cost of past injustice

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS
  1. Whether the Nazi statute was law decides who bears the cost of past injustice.
  2. Hart left two honest options: let her go, or punish her under an openly retrospective law. Fuller replies that the second option itself treats the Nazi laws as void, as applied to informers, at least for the purposes of that statute.
  3. So the claim that she could never shelter behind a Nazi statute can hold even if the statute was law. On Alexy's reading, the Bamberg court did not declare any statute void.

The facts: in 1944 she reported her husband's remarks against Hitler. He was sentenced to death, but was sent to the front instead. In 1949 she was convicted under the 1871 Criminal Code.

Fuller defends the courts:

  • if all the Nazi statutes were law, the informers were guiltless;
  • the real issue seems to be who does the dirty work;
  • the courts were living participants in an emergency, so they could not wait, and waiting risked people taking revenge themselves.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Landlord Who Informed

In 2012, under the Junta's Insult Decree (death for disparaging the Leader, even in private), the landlord Kovač reported his tenant for joking in his own flat that the Leader was a fool. Kovač wanted the flat back. The tenant was sentenced to death, later reduced to ten years' hard labour. In 2020, democratic Valdoria prosecutes Kovač for unlawfully depriving a person of liberty, under the Criminal Code of 1900, which was never repealed. Kovač's defence is that he acted lawfully under the Insult Decree.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

There are three routes to an answer.

  • Radbruch. The Insult Decree was so intolerably unjust that it was not law. So Kovač's act was never lawful, and he can be convicted under the 1900 Code.
  • Hart. Be honest about the dilemma. Either let Kovač go, because what he did was lawful at the time, or pass a statute that openly makes his conduct punishable after the fact. Fuller's reply is that this second option itself treats the Insult Decree as void, at least for informers. So the real question is who does the dirty work, the courts or Parliament. And Valdoria's courts, facing angry victims now, may not be able to wait.
  • Alexy's reading of the real case. A court could convict without declaring the Decree void at all. It could use a criminal-law route: Kovač indirectly caused an unlawful deprivation of liberty. So saying that he cannot shelter behind the Decree does not require denying that it was law.

Here is what is at stake. If the Decree was law, the tenant bears the cost of the injustice. If it was not, Kovač does.

8.1.2 QUALIFY: Alexy on Bamberg

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

A qualification from Alexy. The Bamberg court convicted her on what he calls a controversial criminal-law construction, and he leaves that question open.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

If you rely on Alexy's version of the real case, say that the legal reasoning was controversial. That reasoning was an indirect deprivation of liberty, punishable even though the court that sentenced the husband acted legally. Do not present it as settled law.

8.1.3 Liu on the open statute; Alexy's evident reply

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

Liu (Week 10):

  • any open form of retroactive statute will do, for example a statute saying that it is no defence to rely on the named Nazi laws;
  • though she did report under what was procedurally law.

Alexy's reply about evident injustice fits here. The formula defeats a defence, and it creates no new liability.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

Valdoria's Parliament passes a statute saying that in any prosecution under the 1900 Code, it is no defence to rely on the Insult Decree.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Look at this from both sides.

  • Liu. This is an honest, open way of doing what Hart asks. It admits that it looks back in time, so the exact wording does not matter. But notice the unfairness from Kovač's side: when he acted, he was using what was procedurally law.
  • Alexy. The Radbruch formula is not inventing a new crime. The 1900 Code already made the act a crime. The formula only removes a defence based on an evidently unjust decree. And because the injustice was evident, Kovač could have known.
🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

the Nazi statute was law, so she was innocent; she denounced her husband; she could never shelter behind it.

38.2 Hart's best case

📘 Learn 8.2 in Lesson 8 →
🔑 Trigger words: law is law; no law at all; speak plainly; simply refuse; considers unfair

8.2.1 Validity leaves the moral question open

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS
  1. Hart answers the claim that judges raised to believe law is law will never resist. Validity leaves open the final moral question of whether to obey.
  2. Speaking plainly, the decree is law, but too evil to be obeyed. Everyone can understand that condemnation.
  3. So the claim that a judge should simply refuse whatever he considers unfair states the strong connection thesis, meaning that any unfair law is no law. Alexy says no serious non-positivist defends that.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Judge Varga's Training

Judge Varga trained under a professor who taught that law is law. One commentator says positivist judges like Varga will never resist the Junta's laws, because if you are told law is law, you obey. Another commentator says Varga should simply refuse to apply any Junta law she considers unfair.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Each commentator needs a different answer.

  • To the first (Hart). Knowing that the Insult Decree is law does not tell Varga whether to apply it. That is the final moral question, and she must answer it as a moral person. The plain verdict is that it is law but too evil to be obeyed, and everyone can understand that condemnation.
  • To the second. Refusing whatever you consider unfair is the strong connection thesis, that any unfair law is not law. Even non-positivists like Alexy reject it. Only extreme injustice defeats legality.

8.2.2 STEELMAN: honesty

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

The strongest case for the other side. Hart's best point is honesty. Denying evil law the name of law breeds a romantic optimism that all values fit into one system. It also breeds insincerity about a real dilemma.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

If Varga says the Insult Decree is not law and refuses it, she hides the hard choice. She is overriding something that worked as law. Hart wants her to say openly that she is disobeying a law for moral reasons, and to accept what follows. That honesty is his strongest card.

8.2.3 Fuller's reply

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

Fuller's reply is that Radbruch did see the dilemma. Legal positivism gives fidelity to law no coherent meaning, and Hart's dilemma, as Fuller states it, makes no sense.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Hart's picture is of a valid law that you must obey as law but may disobey as a moral person. Fuller would say this leaves fidelity to law empty. If law can have any content at all, what exactly is Varga being faithful to? For Fuller, fidelity makes sense only towards a system that meets the inner morality of law.

8.2.4 AGAINST: an extraordinary naïveté

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

A point against. The claim that legal positivism disarmed German lawyers is, Hart says, an extraordinary naïveté. Elsewhere, the slogan law is law went along with the most enlightened liberal attitudes.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Blaming Varga's positivist training for the Junta's success ignores other countries, where the same slogan sat comfortably with liberal politics. The cause of the judges' compliance lies elsewhere, such as fear, careerism or sympathy with the regime. It does not lie in a theory about how to identify law.

8.2.5 QUALIFY: purpose and cross-purposes

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

Qualifications.

  • Radbruch, in 1946, wrote to arm judges against the next tyranny. Hart, in 1958, said the formula is useless during the regime and unnecessary after it (Liu, Week 11).
  • Hart and Fuller talk at cross purposes. A wicked regime that meets all eight of Fuller's requirements leaves the Radbruch question open (Liu, Week 10).
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

There are two separate points.

  • Timing. Radbruch's aim was to give future judges like Varga a legal ground to refuse. Hart's reply is that during the Junta no court would accept it, and after the Junta a new Parliament can simply legislate.
  • Cross purposes. Imagine the Junta had published every decree clearly and in advance. Fuller's argument that it was not real law would not apply, and the Radbruch question would still be waiting. So Fuller and Hart are not quite answering the same question.
🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

law is law; it was no law at all; speak plainly; the judge should simply refuse whatever he considers unfair.

48.3 Alexy's replies

📘 Learn 8.3 in Lesson 8 →
🔑 Trigger words: how the word is used; any neutral standpoint; eye of the beholder; reaching back; determined tyranny

8.3.1 Observer v participant

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS
  1. Alexy accepts that this is simply how the word law is used, but only by observers. A judge applying Ordinance 11, a citizenship decree, joins a procedure that claims to be correct.
  2. So the claim that the decree is law holds only for observers. A judge refusing it on legal grounds must call it law at first sight, but in the end not law at all.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Citizenship Ordinance

In 2008, the Junta issued an Ordinance taking away citizenship from every member of the Kel minority living abroad, and seizing their property. In 2021, Kel exiles sue to get their property back.

  • A foreign historian writes that in 2008, the Ordinance was Valdorian law.
  • Judge Petrov must decide the exiles' claim.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

The two speakers are in different positions.

  • The historian is an observer. Describing what Valdorian officials treated as law, the historian can call it law. Alexy accepts this.
  • Petrov is a participant. When Petrov decides, the ruling claims to be correct. If the Ordinance's injustice is extreme, Petrov cannot correctly apply it. So Petrov says it was law at first sight but in the end not law at all, and rules for the exiles.

8.3.2 The five objections, applied

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

Alexy replies to five objections. (Liu says to use two of them in an answer. The language objection is the weakest, and effectiveness is speculative both ways.)

ObjectionAlexy's replyApplied to the Citizenship Ordinance
ClarityBeing adequate comes before being simple. At the extreme, the ethical problem is also a legal one.Saying it was law but evil is simpler. But for Petrov, whether the exiles own their property is a legal question, so a purely moral verdict will not decide the case.
EffectivenessLargely accepted. If lawyers share a consensus, resistance gains legal grounds, and the risk of later liability has some effect (12.5).The formula would not have stopped the Junta. But if Valdorian lawyers had shared the Radbruch formula, an official refusing the Ordinance would have had a legal argument. The risk of later liability might have deterred some.
CertaintyThe more extreme the injustice, the more certain our knowledge of it. Only an absolutist objects.Taking citizenship from a whole minority is not a borderline case. The formula only applies where injustice is obvious, so certainty is barely affected.
RelativismIn states steeped in rights, a consensus on rights should stop Hoerster's judge with Nazi morals. The minimum core is not argued for here.Could a judge with Junta values call the new democratic laws unjust? In a state steeped in rights, the shared consensus checks that judge. But Alexy does not fully argue for the minimum core.
Democracy, and being unnecessaryIt applies to the core area only, otherwise there would be no judicial review. The rule against punishment without a prior law may be unamendable (Article 79(3), page 57). For Singapore, see 11.7.The Radbruch formula applies only to the core of extreme injustice, so it does not let judges override ordinary democratic choices.

8.3.3 CONCEDE: candour is the strongest objection

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

A concession. Hart's candour objection is the strongest argument against non-positivism, but it is not its downfall (Alexy). There are two answers:

  • exempt past actors through nulla poena, the rule against punishment without a prior law; or, better,
  • say the injustice was so evident that the legal position was simply determined.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

For a Junta official who enforced the Ordinance, Petrov's ruling looks like judging after the fact, which is Hart's point. Concede it. Alexy's best answer is that the Ordinance was evidently unjust, so the official could have known it had no legal force. Nothing was sprung on the official later. Another answer is to protect past actors from punishment through nulla poena, while still denying the Ordinance any effect today, for example in the property claim.

8.3.4 The real Ordinance 11

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

Ordinance 11 (under the Reich Citizenship Law) took away people's citizenship on racist criteria (Week 10, slide 9†). The Federal Constitutional Court, in 1968, found its injustice intolerable and evident. It said such destruction has nothing in common with law and justice. This is not the informer statutes of 1934 and 1938, which Liu once confused it with (Week 10).

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Keep your examples straight in the exam:

  • the informer case (8.1) involves the 1934 and 1938 statutes;
  • Ordinance 11 is Alexy's citizenship example, and the Valdorian Ordinance above is modelled on it.
🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

that is simply how the word 'law' is used; from any neutral standpoint; in the eye of the beholder; reaching back; against a determined tyranny.

58.4 Does the label matter?

📘 Learn 8.4 in Lesson 8 →
🔑 Trigger words: a quarrel about words; his conscience belongs to his private life; lawbreaker

8.4.1 It decides who may refuse, and who may shelter

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS
  1. The label is a dispute about definitions, and neither side is less honest. Hart judges by effect, and Alexy by concept (Liu, Week 11). But it is no mere quarrel about words. It decides who may lawfully refuse, and who may shelter behind the statute.
  2. Even Hart, although the wife's fate might be the same either way, holds that candour is more than one minor virtue among many.
  3. So saying that his conscience belongs to his private life repeats Radbruch's pre-war view, which Hart says Radbruch recanted.

How each person fares, depending on the label:

PersonIf it is law (legal positivism, Hart)If it is not law (Radbruch, Alexy)
Judgeapplies it, or refuses on moral grounds, which Fuller calls confusion at its heightrefuses on legal grounds (Alexy)
Legislatorbound only by the master rule (Week 13†)legislates to a higher standard
Lawyermay refuse, but what is refused is still the law (Alexy, page 44, on legal positivism)should denounce it as having no legal character (Hart on Radbruch)
Citizena person who refuses is a lawbreaker; a person who obeys acted lawfully, but is morally open to criticisma person who refuses is still punished (8.7); a person who obeys has no shelter if the injustice was evident (Alexy)
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Ordinance, Four Ways

Take the Citizenship Ordinance (8.3.1) in 2008. Four people face it:

  • Judge Horvat, asked to confirm a seizure;
  • MP Novak, voting on an amendment;
  • lawyer Babić, asked to draft eviction notices;
  • clerk Jurić, ordered to stamp the seizure orders.

A commentator says that whether we call it law is just a quarrel about words, and that each person's conscience is a private matter.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Take each person under each label.

  • Judge Horvat. If it is law, the judge either applies it or refuses on purely moral grounds. Fuller calls a court refusing what it admits is law moral confusion at its height. If it is not law, the judge refuses on legal grounds.
  • MP Novak. If it is law, the MP is bound only by the rule of recognition (the test a system uses to identify its laws). On the non-positivist view, the MP must legislate to a higher standard.
  • Lawyer Babić. If it is law, the lawyer may refuse, but what is refused is still law. On Radbruch's view, the lawyer should denounce it as having no legal character at all.
  • Clerk Jurić. If it is law, refusing makes the clerk a lawbreaker, while stamping is lawful, though morally open to criticism. If it is not law, refusing is still punished while the Junta lasts, and stamping gives no later shelter, because the injustice was evident.

So the label changes legal outcomes, and it is more than words. And treating conscience as private is the pre-war view that Radbruch himself abandoned.

8.4.2 AGAINST: words shape attitudes

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

Points against, from Fuller.

  • Words here have a powerful effect on human attitudes.
  • Nazi law failed legality itself, as with the Roehm statute and what he calls the party in the streets.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Calling the Ordinance law gives it dignity in the eyes of officials. And for Fuller, the Junta's system had secret orders, retroactive validations and party thugs acting outside any rule. It may have failed the inner morality of law so badly that law was hardly the right word anyway.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

this is a quarrel about words; his conscience belongs to his private life; the refuser is a lawbreaker.

68.5 A stable democracy

📘 Learn 8.5 in Lesson 8 →
🔑 Trigger words: unelected veto; substitutes his own morality; for Parliament to repeal; must never invalidate

8.5.1 A narrow check, tested by broad consensus

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS
  1. In a stable democracy, the Radbruch formula is a narrow check. It is not an unelected veto. Legislation stands unless it is intolerably unjust (Tan Seow Hon).
  2. For Tan Seow Hon, judges must show intolerable injustice by broad historical consensus, meaning widespread agreement over time. Racial genocide and slavery qualify. Abortion limits did not qualify in 1973. Nor, for now, do laws limiting marriage to opposite-sex couples.
  3. So the claim that judges must never invalidate a law on grounds of justice holds for ordinary injustice, which is for Parliament to repeal. It does not hold for genocide.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Judge Lim's Four Challenges

Ruritania is a stable democracy. Judge Lim is asked to strike down four laws on grounds of injustice:

  • (a) a law raising the voting age from 18 to 21;
  • (b) a law allowing creditors to keep defaulting debtors as unpaid servants until the debt is worked off;
  • (c) a law restricting abortion after 12 weeks;
  • (d) a law defining marriage as between a man and a woman.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Test each law against broad historical consensus.

  • (a) is ordinary injustice, if it is any injustice at all. It is for Parliament to repeal. A judge substituting a personal view would be an unelected veto.
  • (b) is slavery in substance. Broad historical consensus condemns it as intolerably unjust, so the formula applies.
  • (c) and (d) are matters on which, by Tan Seow Hon's test, there is no broad historical consensus that they are intolerably unjust. Abortion limits were not in 1973, and opposite-sex marriage laws are not now.

So only (b) can be struck down on these grounds. The statement that judges must never invalidate is right for (a), (c) and (d), and wrong for (b).

8.5.2 AGAINST: TSH on Arts 9 and 12

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

Points against, from Tan Seow Hon.

  • Constitutional supremacy rests most soundly on equal moral worth. So Articles 9 and 12 may legitimately bring in a higher law, including the Radbruch formula.
  • Consensus generally checks judges' personal ideologies.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

In a system like Singapore's, Judge Lim need not treat the Radbruch formula as a foreign import. Constitutional guarantees of life, liberty and equality can carry it. And the need for consensus stops the judge from using it to impose personal politics.

8.5.3 CONCEDE: TSH's catch, and judicial oligarchy

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

A concession: Tan Seow Hon's catch.

  • Decades on, the formula could be used to impose a worldwide trend on same-sex marriage.
  • Where consensus has, for realists, gone badly wrong, while a local legislature tries to do right, using the formula is a real problem, and more than just ineffective.

A further concession. Among judicial oligarchies, consensus may only reflect the views of selected groups of judges.

Concede both. Then accept Tan Seow Hon's reply: an autocrat, a few oligarchs, or even a brute majority would do no better.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

Forty years on, most of the world's top courts hold that law (d) is intolerably unjust. Ruritania's Parliament still disagrees.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Work through the two risks and the reply.

  • The catch. The consensus test would now point Judge Lim towards striking down (d). If the global consensus were mistaken, the formula would be imposing an error on a legislature trying to do right.
  • Oligarchy. The so-called consensus might really be the view of a small circle of judges citing each other.
  • The reply. Concede both risks. But every other decision-maker, whether an autocrat, a few oligarchs or a brute majority, can also get it wrong. Broad consensus remains the best available check.

8.5.4 QUALIFY: Liu on the formula's role

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

A qualification from Liu (Week 11, drawing on Alexy). Because it draws on common morality, the formula is a safeguard for times of transition. It is mainly a tool of resistance. It has nothing to do once morality has fully shifted.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

The formula is built for the moment when a regime breaks sharply with shared morality, as the Junta did. In a stable democracy, where laws follow the public's moral views, it has little to do. So it is mainly a tool of resistance, and not a tool of routine review.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

an unelected veto; the judge substitutes his own morality; it's for Parliament to repeal; judges must never invalidate.

78.6 Retroactivity

📘 Learn 8.6 in Lesson 8 →
🔑 Trigger words: retrospective laws are always unjust; life imprisonment; overnight
▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS
  1. The claim that retrospective laws are always unjust confuses a cost with a verdict. A curative statute, one that repairs a past defect, may be essential to advance the cause of legality.
  2. The core case is the new crime, which commands a person today to have done something yesterday. Even Hart accepts that this may be odious.
  3. So the statement nearly holds for new crimes. But a longer sentence is less bad, and civil overruling is a price worth paying (3.8).

Also on the sheet:

  • Keep these apart. Being branded as criminals concerns overruling a reading under which the conduct was not criminal. Abdul Nasir† (3.8) raises constancy, meaning the law staying stable over time.
  • Liu's test (Week 2). Retroactivity is abuse when it undermines guidance, through bad faith, frequency, or punishment after the fact. Leniency, such as re-sentencing under the Misuse of Drugs Act, is not abuse, though fairness to prisoners is external morality. The common law is retroactive by default.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Four Retroactive Laws

In one session, Ruritania's Parliament passes four laws with retroactive effect:

  • (a) validating wills witnessed by only one person during a pandemic lockdown, when two witnesses were impossible;
  • (b) a new crime of panic buying, applied to purchases made last March;
  • (c) raising the maximum sentence for burglary from 5 to 7 years, applied to burglaries already committed;
  • (d) letting prisoners serving mandatory death sentences apply for re-sentencing under a new, lighter regime.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Sort the four laws.

  • (a) is curative. It repairs a failure of possibility, because no one could find two witnesses. So it advances legality.
  • (b) is the core abuse. It commands people today to have done something differently yesterday. Even Hart calls this odious.
  • (c) is less bad. Burglary was already a crime, and people had notice of that. It still punishes after the fact, so it needs strong justification, but it is not the same as (b).
  • (d) is leniency. It does not undermine anyone's ability to plan, so it is not abuse. But the reason for it, fairness to prisoners, comes from external morality, so say so.
  • Keep the labels apart. Being branded as criminals is about a court overruling a reading under which conduct was legal. A change to what an existing sentence means, as in Abdul Nasir, is a problem of constancy.

So the claim of always unjust nearly holds for (b), and fails for (a) and (d).

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

retrospective laws are always unjust; life imprisonment; overnight.

88.7 Obey or disobey?

📘 Learn 8.7 in Lesson 8 →
🔑 Trigger words: obligation to obey; has done nothing wrong; will they be punished; fidelity means deference; highest court

8.7.1 Three questions, five theorists

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS
  1. The statement merges three questions: a legal duty to obey, a moral duty to obey, and a moral duty to disobey.
  2. Fidelity is not deference. Rex's subjects stayed faithful to him as king, and not to his law, because he never made any.
  3. So the claim that the citizen who obeys has done nothing wrong holds legally for Hart, and for Radbruch only below the threshold. Morally it stays open.
TheoristLegal dutyMoral duty to obeyMoral duty to disobey
Hartyesnot settled by validitypast a certain degree of iniquity (Bentham, Austin)
Fullerby degree; none on total failurefrom reciprocity; none once finally and completely rupturedno simple principle short of rupture, as under Hitler
Radbruch, Alexynone past intolerable injustice or betrayed equality†below that, law is open to moral criticismjudges and lawyers should deny it legal character
Aquinasnone, as it is a corruption of lawnone, except perhaps to avoid scandal or some particular dangernot stated in Harris
Finnisit is not a nullitynot at first sight; a duty can arise so that a system that is just on the whole is not weakenedapplied: never choose directly against a basic value
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Radio Decree

The Junta's Radio Decree required citizens to report any neighbour who listened to foreign radio. Petra refused to report her neighbours. Tomas reported his. After the Junta falls, Tomas says he obeyed the law and did nothing wrong.

✔ APPLICATION · Theorist by theoristDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Go through the theorists.

  • Hart. The Decree was law, so Tomas had a legal duty, and Petra broke the law. But validity does not settle the moral question. Past a certain degree of iniquity there is a moral duty to resist, and Petra may have been right.
  • Fuller. If the Junta's legal system was badly degraded, through secret orders and retroactive decrees, any duty to obey weakened with it. If the government had wholly ruptured reciprocity, nothing was left to support the duty.
  • Radbruch and Alexy. If the Decree was intolerably unjust, it imposed no legal duty at all. Tomas cannot shelter behind it.
  • Aquinas. An unjust law is a corruption of law. Obedience is owed, perhaps, only to avoid scandal or danger.
  • Finnis. The Decree is not a nullity, but it carries no moral force at first sight. Reporting neighbours for persecution may well be choosing directly against basic goods, which Tomas must never do.

So Tomas's claim holds legally on Hart's view, and on Radbruch's only if the Decree was below the threshold. Morally, it is very much open.

Fidelity is not deference. Suppose Tomas says being faithful to law means obeying whoever rules. Fuller's reply is that Rex's subjects stayed loyal to Rex as king, but could not be faithful to his law, because he never made any. Fidelity to law is owed to a system of rules, and not to the person in charge.

8.7.2 CITIZEN: will they be punished?

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

The citizen: will they be punished? While the regime lasts, yes, either way. As Hoerster says, a person who refuses must expect the usual consequences.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Whatever the theory says about legal validity, the Junta will still jail Petra for refusing. Calling the Decree not law does not protect her during the regime. That is Hoerster's point.

8.7.3 JUDGE: the highest court says law

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

The judge: what if the highest court says it is law?

  • For observers and for legal positivism, it is law.
  • For participants, the court's ruling lays claim to correctness (Alexy). So at extreme injustice, a later court or a lawyer may call it legally wrong. Below that, it is law.
  • For lower courts, see 15.10.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

In 2010, the Junta's Supreme Court upheld the Radio Decree as valid.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

A historian can record that the Decree was law, because the top court said so. But the court's ruling claimed to be correct. Because the Decree was extremely unjust, a court in 2021 or a lawyer can say the 2010 ruling was legally wrong, and more than merely immoral. For an ordinary unjust law, the top court's ruling would simply settle the matter.

8.7.4 STEELMAN: why obey at all? (Liu's pigeon feeder)

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

The strongest case for the other side: why obey at all? This is Liu's example of the pigeon feeder (Week 10).

  • Deterrence makes her comply, but it is not a moral reason.
  • The point that others will copy her justifies punishing her. It does not justify her obeying.
  • Fair play does give a reason. She gains from institutions that others uphold, and fairness between citizens (Rawls) asks her to keep laws she rejects.

Assume the duty, because the topic is its exceptions. Every reason to obey is moral. Legality only says that the rule is law, so a legal positivist has the same reasons (Week 10).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

Mrs Goh feeds stray cats, in breach of a town by-law, because she believes she has a moral duty to them. She is willing to pay any fine.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Sort what counts as a reason.

  • Not reasons. Rising fines may stop her, but that is not a reason to obey. And the point that others will copy explains why the town fines her. It does not explain why she should obey.
  • A real reason: fair play. She benefits every day from rules that others keep even when they disagree, such as clean streets and traffic order. So fairness asks her to keep this one too.
  • The positivist point. That reason is moral. Knowing the by-law is valid only tells her that it is law. So legal positivists and natural lawyers have exactly the same reasons to obey.

is there an obligation to obey?; the citizen who obeyed did nothing wrong; will they be punished?; fidelity means deference; the highest court has spoken.

98.8 Radbruch's betrayal-of-equality limb†

📘 Learn 8.8 in Lesson 8 →
🔑 Trigger words: racist statute; discriminates by race or faith; not even an attempt at justice

8.8.1 Does it even attempt justice?

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS
  1. Radbruch's second limb does not ask how unjust the statute is. It asks whether the statute even attempts justice. Where equality is deliberately betrayed, the statute completely lacks the very nature of law†.
  2. So the claim that the judge must apply it fails for a statute aimed at one race. Morally too, no role excuses applying a law that is racist on its face (Thunder).

Radbruch's tiers (Week 10, slide 2†):

  1. positive law prevails, even when its content is unjust;
  2. at an intolerable level, it is flawed law that must yield to justice;
  3. where equality is betrayed, it is no law at all.

Liu (Week 10) says tier 2 is not a nullity, but the outcome is the same.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Residence Act

Ruritania's Parliament passes a Residence Act saying that no member of the Halani race may live in the capital. It carries no penalty beyond eviction. Judge Tan is asked to grant an eviction order against a Halani family.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Do not start with how harsh the Act is.

  • The question is not one of degree. Eviction is less harsh than death. But the Act does not even attempt justice. It singles out a race and deliberately betrays equality, which is the core of justice. On Radbruch's third tier, it completely lacks the nature of law. So Judge Tan has no law to apply.
  • The tiers compared. Under tier 2, the Act would be flawed law that yields to justice, and not a nullity. Either way, as Liu notes, Judge Tan refuses the order.
  • Morally. Thunder says no professional role, whether judge or lawyer, excuses applying a law that is racist on its face.

8.8.2 CONCEDE: equality is contested

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

A concession. Equality is a contested idea (Westen, as the Court of Appeal noted in LMS). Keep this limb to deliberate betrayal on the face of the law, tested as in 8.5. For unjust outcomes, see 1.3(10).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

A different Act requires all civil servants to pass a test in the national language. Halani citizens fail at higher rates, and they claim that this betrays equality.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

This law does not single out a race on its face. Its unequal outcome comes from a neutral rule. Because equality means many contested things, Radbruch's limb should be kept to deliberate betrayal on the face of the law, like the Residence Act, tested by broad historical consensus as in 8.5. Unequal outcomes from neutral rules belong to other arguments (1.3(10)). They do not support the claim that the law has no legal character.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

a racist statute; it discriminates by race or faith; not even an attempt at justice.

108.9 Conclusion, applied

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

The conclusion. The statement is overstated. Validity never settles what a person should do. A law that survives the formula has been shown not to be intolerably unjust. It has not been shown to be just, and that question stays with Parliament and conscience. Departing from the law can be unjust too. The judge's morality may be wrong (Hoerster's judge with Nazi morals), and Radbruch himself warned of frightful dangers.

✔ APPLICATION · Applied to the hyposDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Here is where each part of the conclusion was shown.

  • Validity does not settle obedience: the Curfew Decree (8.0) and Petra and Tomas (8.7).
  • Surviving the formula does not make a law just: the voting-age law (8.5.1(a)) is still open to criticism in Parliament.
  • Departing from the law can be wrong too: imagine a former Junta judge, still on the bench, refusing to apply Valdoria's new equality laws because that judge thinks they are unjust. That is Hoerster's worry. Radbruch's own warning shows that the formula must stay narrow.
