Hypos: Adjudication (Dworkin, ALR, CLS)

⚡ BIG IDEA

The statement overstates. Judges justify their decisions by fit and political morality, and rules leave some cases open, but not all.

The theory behind these hypos is taught in Lesson 9. Do that lesson first if the rules below look unfamiliar.

How to work through a hypo
  1. 1Read the rule (teal box). It puts the sheet's point in plain words. The exact wording to use in the exam is in the Lessons and Sheet tabs.
  2. 2Read the hypothetical (amber box). Before reading on, decide what the rule says about these facts.
  3. 3Tap Application (green box) and compare it with your answer.
  4. 4The exam cue (violet box) lists question words that should send you to this block. Each block ends with a quick check.
Applications:
ℹ NOTE
About these hypos

Each block on this page has three parts: the rule in plain words, a made-up set of facts, and a worked answer. Your exact sheet wording, with its quotations, is still in the Lessons and Sheet tabs.

Some terms come up throughout. American legal realism says cases turn on more than rules, and that rules often do not decide them. Critical legal studies (the crits) says law hides political choices and serves those in power. Fit is how well a reading matches the existing law. Canons are standard rules for interpreting a text. A ratio is the legal reason a case was decided as it was.

The Radbruch formula says a statute stops being law once its injustice is intolerable. TSH is Tan Seow Hon. A dagger (†) marks a point from the slides. The coverage table is the last section.

19.0 The archetype in one line

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

The position. The statement overstates. Judges justify their decisions by fit and political morality, and rules leave some cases open, but not all.

The opening. The statement treats judging as politics in robes.

  • The realists rightly show that canons and ratios leave some cases open.
  • The crits rightly show that each principle meets a counterprinciple.
  • But a judge cannot predict the judge's own ruling. A judge must justify it, by the reading that best fits and justifies the law (Dworkin).

So rules leave some cases open, but not all. And political morality, not personal preference, closes them.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Two Cases in One Morning

Judge Koh of the Ruritanian High Court hears two cases.

  • (a) A driver was clocked at 92 km/h in a clearly marked 60 zone. The driver has no defence.
  • (b) A rider for a delivery app claims to be an employee under the Employment Act, which does not define the word for platform work.

A commentator says judging is just politics in robes, and that judges decide what they want and then dress it up.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Take the two cases separately.

  • (a) is closed by the rule. No honest reading lets the driver off. So rules do not leave every case open.
  • (b) is truly open. The canons point different ways, and the precedents can be read narrowly or widely, as the realists say.
  • Even in (b), Koh must justify. Koh has to give the reading of employee that best fits the Act and the case law and best justifies them. One such reason is the Act's purpose of protecting dependent workers. That is political morality, argued in public reasons. It is not Koh's private preference about riders.
🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

judging is politics; judges decide first and rationalise after.

29.1 American legal realism

📘 Learn 9.1 in Lesson 9 →
🔑 Trigger words: decide first, prediction, canons, ratios read narrowly or widely

9.1.1 A judge must justify, not predict

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS
  1. Realism rightly says that canons and ratios leave hard cases open. But a judge must justify, and cannot simply predict.
  2. Practitioners may predict, but judges themselves cannot. They must at least claim to justify. A judge who writes, Alas, I must find for the defendant, is predicting nothing on the face of it.
  3. So the claim that law is prediction holds at most for lawyers advising clients. Llewellyn called realism a method and nothing more.

In support: Cheng San GRC (General Election 1997)†.

  • Candidates stood inside polling stations.
  • Section 82(1)(d) barred waiting outside, and (e) barred loitering within 200 metres (before 2023).
  • Read literally, only outside was barred. Read for its purpose (the mischief it aimed at, and the words at or near), being inside was barred too.
  • The Attorney-General advised that no offence had been committed.

The canons were precise, but the outcome was uncertain (Liu, Week 11).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Candidate in the Polling Hall

Ruritania's Elections Act says two things: (a) no person shall wait outside a polling station; (b) no person shall loiter within 100 metres of one. On polling day, candidate Tan stands all day inside the polling hall, smiling and nodding at voters. Tan is charged.

  • Tan's lawyer predicts an acquittal under the literal rule, because outside means outside.
  • The prosecutor argues the purposive rule: the mischief is candidates influencing voters at the booth, and being inside is worse than being outside.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Work through the four points.

  • The realists are right that the canons conflict. The literal rule and the mischief rule are both respectable canons, and they give opposite answers. The rules alone do not settle it.
  • The lawyer may predict, but the judge may not. A lawyer's job is to forecast. A judge cannot decide by forecasting the judge's own decision. The judge must give reasons: which canon fits this Act, and why, such as the purpose of free voting.
  • Alas. If the judge writes, Alas, I must convict, the conviction is presented as compelled by law, and not as predicted. A realist can call that a pose, but the duty to justify is real.
  • Realism as method. Llewellyn himself called realism a method. It is a way of studying courts, and not a theory that tells judges what to do.

9.1.2 QUALIFY: flimsy rulings are costly

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

A qualification from Liu. American legal realism oversimplifies. A judge can write any decision, but reputation, the risk of reversal on appeal, time and credibility (consider Denning) make a flimsy one costly.

Kennedy's correction. Law is a medium that constrains like bricks, relative to what you are trying to build. Moving it costs work and puts credibility at risk.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

The judge personally thinks Tan should be convicted. The judge could write two lines: that inside is near enough to outside, and that Tan is convicted.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

There are two reasons why the judge cannot simply do this.

  • Liu's costs. A two-line ruling invites reversal on appeal, damages the judge's reputation, and uses up credibility. Denning was admired, but he was seen as always pushing the limits.
  • Kennedy's bricks. The statute's words are like bricks. The judge can build different things with them, but turning outside into inside takes real work in argument, and it carries a risk to credibility.

So the realists' idea that anything goes is too quick.

9.1.3 QUALIFY: weak and strong realism

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

Qualification: the weak and strong readings.

  • On Harris's minimal reading, rules are not all that matter.
  • In its extreme form, all legal reasoning is mere surface talk.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

The weak reading is plainly true of Tan's case. The judge's sense of the Act's purpose matters, and not just its words. The strong reading would say the judge's reasons are only decoration. That is much harder to believe, given the costs in 9.1.2. So concede the weak form and reject the strong one.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

judges decide first; law is a prediction of what courts will do; canons cancel out; ratios can be read narrowly or widely.

39.2 Dworkin v ALR

📘 Learn 9.2 in Lesson 9 →
🔑 Trigger words: precedent runs out, judges legislate, floodgates, social goals

9.2.1 A theoretical disagreement, not a gap

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS
  1. Saying that the judge legislates once precedent runs out mistakes a theoretical disagreement about the grounds of law for a gap in the law.
  2. In McLoughlin, all five Lords allowed the appeal, yet they split. Scarman held that the policy of where to draw the line could not be decided by courts. Edmund-Davies called that as novel as it was startling.
  3. So leaving the floodgates worry to Parliament is Scarman's contested view. Defend it as a choice, and not as the lesson of the case. (The floodgates worry is the fear of too many claims.)
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Rescue Volunteer

A train derails. Ravi, a passer-by with no relation to anyone on board, spends three hours pulling injured passengers from the wreck, and develops severe post-traumatic stress. No Ruritanian case has allowed a claim by an unrelated rescuer who was not in personal danger. The rail company argues that if Ravi can sue, every bystander can, and the floodgates will open.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Work through the three points.

  • There is no gap. A realist says precedent has run out, so the judges will simply legislate. But the judges are really disagreeing about what the grounds of the law are. Are earlier cases bound by an underlying principle, such as foreseeable harm to those drawn into the danger? Or only by their facts?
  • The McLoughlin split. One judge, like Scarman, may say that the principle covers Ravi, and that limiting it for floodgates reasons is for Parliament. Another, like Edmund-Davies, says courts may weigh policy, but carefully.
  • Scarman's view is a choice. You can defend it. But present it as your view of the judicial role, and not as what McLoughlin decided.

9.2.2 AGAINST: is floodgates policy or principle?

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

A point against: is floodgates policy or principle (Week 1b, slide 3†)?

  • As policy: court congestion and insurance costs, which lie beyond the limits of the court process (Scarman).
  • As principle: liability out of proportion to fault.
✔ APPLICATION · To RaviDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Look at what the rail company actually says.

  • If it says courts will be swamped and premiums will rise, that is policy. On Scarman's view that is not for judges.
  • If it says it is unfair to make the company liable to an unlimited number of strangers for one moment's carelessness, that is principle. It is a claim about justice between the parties, which courts may weigh.

How you classify the argument decides whether the court can consider it.

9.2.3 QUALIFY: Bridge

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

A qualification. Bridge weighed the policy grounds offered, found them wholly insufficient, and said that stopping at decided cases would be an unwarranted abdication.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

A judge like Bridge would hear the rail company's floodgates argument and find it far too weak to deny Ravi a remedy. That judge would say that refusing to go beyond existing cases, simply because they are the existing cases, gives up the judicial role.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

when precedent runs out, judges legislate; floodgates; courts should pursue social goals.

49.3 CLS v Dworkin

📘 Learn 9.3 in Lesson 9 →
🔑 Trigger words: neutral framework, exceptions prove the rule, drawn up by an elite, tear it down

9.3.1 Principles meet counterprinciples

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS
  1. Unger rightly denies that contract law is a neutral framework. Each principle meets a counterprinciple, which the dominant view files away as an anomaly.
  2. With its exclusions, exceptions and repressions, the dominant theory of contract governs far less than it claims (Unger).
  3. Yet the call to tear it down goes too far. Condemning hidden interests needs a standard that is not merely subjective, and Finnis's basic goods supply one (5.1).
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Deactivated Rider

A delivery platform's standard terms let it deactivate any rider at any time without reasons. Suri, a rider for five years who depends on the app for all her income, is deactivated the day after complaining about pay. She argues that the term is unconscionable (so one-sided that it should not be enforced), given the great inequality of bargaining power. The platform says contract law is a neutral framework, that she agreed, and that unconscionability is a narrow exception that proves the rule.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Set the two principles side by side.

  • The principle: freedom of contract. Parties choose their terms.
  • The counterprinciple: unfair bargains should not be enforced. Duress, undue influence, unconscionability and inequality of bargaining power all belong here.
  • Unger's point. Nothing in the doctrine says which is the rule and which is the exception. Calling fairness an exception reflects the existing power structure, which treats the platform's control as normal. The theory's own exclusions (labour law), exceptions (fiduciary duties) and repressions (long-term relationships like Suri's) show that it governs far less than it claims.
  • But tearing it all down goes too far. To say the platform's control is unjust, and more than just one interest among others, you need a standard that is not merely subjective. Finnis's basic goods, such as Suri's livelihood and her sociability as a worker, can supply one.

9.3.2 FOR: doctrine legitimates hierarchy

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

In support. Doctrine legitimates hierarchy even when it is used by someone who thinks they are advancing progressive causes. It hides interests (Week 1b, slide 17†). The crits generally distance themselves from Marxist instrumentalism, the idea that law is simply a tool of the ruling class.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Even Suri's lawyer, arguing unconscionability, accepts that the platform's terms are the normal starting point, and asks only for an exception. That framing makes the platform's control look legitimate. The crits do not say that law is simply the capitalist's tool, which would be Marxist instrumentalism. They say that it makes these arrangements look natural.

9.3.3 STEELMAN: fit crowns the past

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

The strongest case for the other side. The crits' best point is conservatism. Fit crowns the dominant principle of the past, and files fairness (duress, undue influence: Week 11, slide 14†) away as exceptions. The fixes become, as Unger says, arbitrarily selective.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

The court rescues Suri on unconscionability. A month later, another rider, Hamid, with almost identical facts but a slightly better-paid contract, loses.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

A Dworkinian judge asks which reading best fits the past cases. If most past cases favour freedom of contract, fit keeps that principle on top and treats fairness as an occasional repair. So relief is patchy: Suri wins and Hamid loses, for no principled reason. That is what Unger means by arbitrarily selective, and it is the crits' strongest charge against Dworkin.

9.3.4 AGAINST: Harris on incremental justice

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

A point against. Harris says the liberal must show that reformed legalism yields more step-by-step justice than deconstruction for its own sake.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

The liberal reply to the crits is practical. Suri did win, through ordinary doctrine. The challenge for the liberal is to show that steady reform within legal reasoning helps more riders than exposing contradictions without offering a working alternative.

9.3.5 QUALIFY: ALR v CLS

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

A qualification: the realists and the crits (Liu, Week 1). Both give the same description, that law is politics. They split on what comes next:

  • the realists keep the system, given good judges;
  • the crits would remake it, exposing class interests.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Compare what each would say about Suri's case.

  • A realist says the judge's sympathies decided it, and that the answer is to get good judges.
  • A crit says the whole structure of contract law favours platforms, so we must change the structure and not just the judges.
🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

contract law is a neutral framework; the exceptions prove the rule; law is drawn up by an elite; tear it down.

59.4 Precedent and theory

📘 Learn 9.4 in Lesson 9 →
🔑 Trigger words: like cases alike, stare decisis, authority for argument
▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS
  1. Precedent cannot replace theory. Treating like cases alike needs a test of which differences matter, and that test is moral.
  2. Was a mother who reached hospital two hours later like one who was at the scene? Only a principle, such as foreseeability or physical risk, can say.
  3. So the claim that precedent, and not justice, makes law fair fails. Stare decisis (the practice of following earlier decisions) is itself contested, as strict or relaxed, and it needs justification.

A point against. Relaxed precedent gives way when an earlier decision is sufficiently wrong (Law's Empire). Any interpretation must include a doctrine of mistake.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Two Mothers
  • The precedent: a mother who watched her son drown in front of her recovered damages for nervous shock.
  • The new case: Mrs Wee was at work when her daughter drowned at a public pool. She arrived 90 minutes later and saw her daughter's body.

The pool's lawyer says precedent requires treating like cases alike, and that these cases are unlike because she was not there.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Whether the cases are alike depends on the principle behind the precedent.

  • Like or unlike?
    • If the principle is foreseeable psychiatric harm to close relatives, the cases are alike. A mother seeing her dead child is foreseeable shock, wherever she was standing.
    • If the principle is being in physical danger or at the scene, they are unlike.
  • The choice is moral. Choosing the principle means asking what makes a claim deserve compensation. That is a moral question, and precedent alone cannot answer it.
  • Stare decisis is contested too. Should the court follow a precedent it thinks wrong (strict), or only give it weight (relaxed)? That question itself needs a justification. On Dworkin's relaxed view, a precedent that is sufficiently wrong may give way. So any theory of precedent needs a doctrine of mistake.
🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

treat like cases alike; stare decisis makes law fair; precedent, not justice.

69.5 The right answer

📘 Learn 9.5 in Lesson 9 →
🔑 Trigger words: single right answer, whatever coheres, never refuse an unjust statute

9.5.1 Possible in principle, but no threshold

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS
  1. A single right answer is possible in principle. Interpretation neither finds law ready-made nor invents it, so one reading can be the best.
  2. But fit will often fail to produce one unique interpretation, and then substantive political theory decides.
  3. So the claim that a judge need never refuse an unjust statute fails. Dworkin gives no threshold. The Radbruch formula does, gauged by Tan Seow Hon's broad historical consensus (15.13).
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Judge Reyes and the Strikers' Pensions

Ruritania's Parliament passes an Act taking away the pensions of all public workers who took part in a lawful strike. Two readings of an unclear section fit the Act equally well. One applies it only to future strikes, and the other to strikes in the last ten years. Judge Reyes, a follower of Dworkin, says there is always a single right answer, and that no judge need ever refuse a statute, however unjust.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Work through Reyes's claim.

  • A right answer is possible. If fit narrows the field, the best reading may be the one that shows the Act in its best light. Perhaps that means applying it only to future strikes, since that fits the law's wider respect for reliance.
  • Fit runs out. Here both readings fit. Reyes must use political theory, such as fairness and reliance, to choose. That is what Dworkin says happens.
  • Never refusing is the weak point. If the Act were intolerably unjust, Dworkin gives Reyes no threshold at which to refuse it. The Radbruch formula does: refuse only if the injustice is intolerable, judged by broad historical consensus (15.13). Taking pensions for a lawful strike is unjust, but it is probably not intolerable on that test.

9.5.2 CONCEDE: beliefs other judges need not share

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

A concession. Dworkin says a judge's best reading rests on beliefs other judges need not share. Concede that there is no answer that can be proved. Insist that the choice is political, and not personal (9.8).

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Another judge might honestly prefer the ten-year reading. Concede that Reyes cannot prove that reading wrong. But Reyes's choice rests on public principles, such as reliance and fairness, and not on personal tastes. That is the difference between political and personal judgment.

9.5.3 QUALIFY: when the practice includes the formula

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

A qualification from Liu (Week 11).

  • Where the practice itself includes the formula, a Dworkinian judge can fit and still refuse extreme injustice.
  • Fit is a matter of degree (Denning; the German courts that declared Nazi laws void).

For Tan Seow Hon's catch, see 8.5.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

Ruritania's courts have long held that statutes are read subject to fundamental principles of justice, and they once refused to apply a racist statute.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

In that legal culture, refusing an extremely unjust statute fits the practice. So Reyes can be both a Dworkinian and a judge who refuses at the extreme. Fit is a matter of degree. Denning, and the post-war German courts that declared Nazi laws void, claimed to fit deeper principles of justice. Tan Seow Hon's catch (8.5) still applies, because the consensus behind the formula could itself go wrong.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

there is a single right answer; whatever coheres is law; a judge need never refuse an unjust statute.

79.6 Judge-variance study

📘 Learn 9.6 in Lesson 9 →
🔑 Trigger words: outcomes vary by judge, change the bench
▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS
  1. A realist reads studies of differences between judges as fact scepticism confirmed. But such findings are a criticism of judges who fail to justify. They are not a criticism of Dworkin's theory of how judges ought to decide.

On rule scepticism and fact scepticism (Week 11, slide 8†):

  • Llewellyn's paper rules (rules as written, which may not decide cases);
  • Frank's upper courtitis, the mistake of looking only at appeal courts, when the fact-finder decides whether a rule applies;
  • Liu says appeal only moves the discretion up a level (Week 11).
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Asylum Study

A study of Ruritania's immigration tribunal finds that, for similar cases, one adjudicator grants asylum 12% of the time and another 78%. A columnist says this proves law is whatever the judge you draw wants, and that if you change the bench you change the law.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Go through what the study can and cannot show.

  • The realist reading. This looks like fact scepticism. Adjudicators decide whether an applicant's story is credible, so how the rule applies turns on the fact-finder.
  • Rule scepticism and fact scepticism. Llewellyn's rule scepticism says the paper rules do not decide cases. Frank's fact scepticism says that even if rules were clear, the fact-finder controls whether they apply, and that looking only at appeal courts is upper courtitis.
  • What the study really shows. Some adjudicators are failing to decide by justified standards. That is a criticism of them, judged by the very standard Dworkin sets: decide by the best justification. It does not refute his account of how judges ought to decide.
  • Liu's point on appeal. Appeal does not remove the discretion. It moves it up a level, to the appeal judges.
🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

outcomes vary by judge; change the bench, change the law.

89.7 Synthesis

📘 Learn 9.7 in Lesson 9 →
🔑 Trigger words: answers the realists, victory to the crits
▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS
  1. Dworkin's judge answers the realists. The judge must justify by fit and value, and cannot predict the judge's own ruling.
  2. But fit may crown freedom of contract and file fairness away as an anomaly. Harris reads Unger's mockery of a pre-established harmony as aimed at Dworkin.
  3. So victory for the crits follows only if value is subjective. Liu's third option, natural law, would say which principle should win (Riggs?: Week 11, slide 15†).

A qualification from Liu (Week 11). Dworkin is text-first. The judge brings a political theory, but owes a duty to that law, which is close to Fuller's fidelity. The crits are goal-first, moulding the text to their transformative aim. The work can overlap, but the starting point differs.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Suri on Appeal

Suri's case (9.3) reaches the Court of Appeal. Three judges write.

  • Judge A (a Dworkinian) says the task is to find the reading of contract law that best fits and justifies it. Fit favours freedom of contract, and fairness protects only the vulnerable in extreme cases. Suri wins narrowly.
  • Judge B (a crit) says the goal is to shift contract law towards protecting workers, and reads the authorities to make fairness the governing principle.
  • Judge C (a natural lawyer) says contract law exists to serve human goods, and a term that lets one party destroy another's livelihood on a whim fails that purpose.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Compare the three judges.

  • A answers the realists. A does not predict. A justifies.
  • The crits' objection to A. Fit with the past keeps freedom of contract on top and treats fairness as a convenient anomaly. That is Unger's pre-established harmony, the assumption that the law already hangs together.
  • Do the crits win? Only if choosing between freedom and fairness is just preference. C shows the third option. An objective account of the good can say which principle should win, as the Riggs majority's appeal to principle suggests.
  • Text-first and goal-first. A and B may reach the same result. But A starts from the law and is bound by it, while B starts from the goal and works the law towards it.
🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

Dworkin answers the realists; victory goes to the crits.

99.8 Is theory necessarily implicated?

📘 Learn 9.8 in Lesson 9 →
🔑 Trigger words: necessarily, always, every case, common law and statutes, constitutional democracy
▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS
  1. Theories of law are always involved. A judge who claims simply to apply the statute has already taken a side on what counts as law.
  2. Morality is always presupposed, as with legality and the reasons to defer to clear words. But it is an operative ground, one that actually decides a case, only in hard cases and at intolerable injustice.
  3. So the claim that they are necessarily involved holds for theory, and for morality as a presupposition. It does not hold for morality as the ground of every decision.

Where morality enters, for each theorist:

  • Hart: at most, where the rules run out;
  • Fuller: in fidelity, seen together with the judge's responsibility for making law what it ought to be;
  • Dworkin: in every proposition of law (Core 14.5; Theorist 15.9).

In support: Riggs. There were two morally grounded theories of one statute. Earl relied on the intention of the makers. Gray asked what power the courts had to add to the respondent's penalties.

The strongest case for the other side. Hart says rules have a core of central meaning, where morality sits idle. The court in LMS refused to judge a law's object without legal standards (Tan Seow Hon). The reply: restraint is itself a theory of judging.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
"I Simply Apply the Statute"

Judge Ng says at a conference that theory and morality never come into it in that court, and that the judge simply applies the statute. That week the judge decides:

  • (a) a parking fine under a clear by-law;
  • (b) a case where a son who assaulted his mother claims under her insurance policy as next of kin.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Test Judge Ng's claim against the two cases.

  • Theory is always there. Even in (a), applying the statute assumes a theory of what counts as law: that validly made by-laws are law, and that clear words govern. In (b), deciding whether the plain words or the purpose governs is taking a side, as in Riggs (Earl's intention of the makers against Gray's refusal to add to the penalty).
  • Morality is presupposed in (a), but it does not decide it. Judge Ng's deference to clear words rests on moral reasons, such as fair notice and democratic authority. But the by-law decides the parking case.
  • Morality is operative in (b). It is a hard case, where fit leaves room and moral principle helps decide.
  • The strongest case. Hart is right that most cases, like (a), sit in the core of settled meaning. Singapore's LMS court likewise declined to judge a law's object without legal standards. But a policy of restraint is itself a theory of how judges should judge.
🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

theories of law are necessarily implicated in every case; always; common law and statutes; in a constitutional democracy.

109.9 Why judges converge

📘 Learn 9.9 in Lesson 9 →
🔑 Trigger words: shared backgrounds, converge, what apart from rules
▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS
  1. Judges agree with each other less because of shared backgrounds than because they share a practice of justification.
  2. Harris reports Llewellyn: a lawyer who soaked up the ways of an appellate court could predict outcomes eight times out of ten.
  3. So easy cases are easy because lawyers share a theory. The tenth case is where that theory is argued over, and not predicted.

Also on the sheet:

  • In support. The realists' underlying ethical pluralism (Week 1b, slide 16†). Kennedy says shared application of rules is not really objectivity, though he sometimes cannot budge a rule.
  • A point against. Dworkin says hard cases are perhaps just those where fit yields no unique reading.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The 90% Court

Ruritania's Court of Appeal is unanimous in 90% of its cases. A columnist says that all the judges went to the same two schools and the same law firms, and that shared backgrounds, and not law, explain it.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Offer a better explanation, then add the two qualifications.

  • A better explanation. The judges share a practice of justification. They agree on what counts as a good legal argument. That is why a lawyer steeped in the court's ways can predict about eight cases in ten.
  • The tenth case. In the remaining cases, the shared theory runs out and the judges argue about it. Those are the hard cases.
  • For the realists. Kennedy warns that shared application is not the same as objectivity. A similar bench can agree on something that only looks objective. Yet he also admits he sometimes cannot budge a rule, so the rules do have force.
  • For Dworkin. The hard cases may be exactly those where fit gives no unique answer.
🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

judges converge because of shared backgrounds; what, apart from rules, decides cases?.

119.10 Chain novelist, author and critic

📘 Learn 9.10 in Lesson 9 →
🔑 Trigger words: chain novel, author, critic, one coherent story
▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS
  1. The artist interprets while creating, and the critic creates while interpreting. Yet Dworkin says there is a difference between interpreting while creating and creating while interpreting.
  2. Each chain novelist after the first has the dual responsibilities of interpreting and creating. After the second, no single author has intentions that decide.
  3. So the judge, a partner in a complex chain enterprise, has a duty to interpret the legal history found. The judge must not invent a better history.

Also on the sheet:

  • A qualification. Fit has no algorithm, and value is political and not aesthetic (Dworkin's political hypothesis).
  • A point against. Kennedy's judge works the legal field towards how the judge wants the case to come out (13.1).
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Writing Class

A creative-writing class writes a novel in turn, one chapter each. Writer 1 introduces a detective. Writer 5 inherits four chapters that hint the detective is the murderer. Writer 5 would love to make it a romance instead. Meanwhile, Judge Lee inherits forty years of Ruritanian cases on employers' liability for their workers' wrongs.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Compare the writer and the judge.

  • Writer 5's double job. Writer 5 must interpret the story so far, asking what kind of novel this is, and create the next chapter. Writer 5 cannot ignore the clues and switch to romance. No single earlier author's intention decides. Writer 5 must read what the chapters together have become.
  • Judge Lee is in the same position. The judge must interpret the case law inherited and add the next chapter, making the law the best it can be. But it must be the best version of this law, and not a better history invented from scratch.
  • The qualifications. There is no formula for how well a reading must fit. And best here means best in political morality, such as justice and fairness. It does not mean most beautiful.
  • Kennedy's contrast. Kennedy's judge starts from how the case should come out and works the field towards it. On that model, Writer 5 would decide on romance first, and then hunt for clues to justify it.
🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

the judge as chain novelist; author or critic?; one coherent story.

129.11 Conclusion, applied

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

The conclusion. The statement is overstated. Rules leave some cases open, but not all, and the cost of a flimsy ruling keeps most judges close to them. Where cases are open, judges must justify by fit and political morality, starting from the text and not from the goal. It is neither prediction nor preference. Theory is always involved and morality is always presupposed, but morality decides only where fit runs out or injustice becomes intolerable.

✔ APPLICATION · Applied to the hyposDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Here is where each part of the conclusion was shown.

  • Some cases open, but not all: the speeding driver and the rider (9.0).
  • Flimsy rulings cost: the two-line ruling (9.1.2).
  • Fit and political morality: Judge Reyes (9.5).
  • Text-first: Judge A on Suri (9.7).
  • Morality decides only at the margins: Judge Ng's two cases (9.8).

HYPO LESSON 10 · ARCHETYPE 10 · ABOUT 31 MIN · 51 QUESTIONS

Hypos: Lawyering (Pepper, Thunder, Kennedy)

⚡ BIG IDEA

The statement fails. The lawyer's role is moral. Law sets a floor, and prudence, dialogue and rare objection decide the hard cases above it.

The theory behind these hypos is taught in Lesson 10. Do that lesson first if the rules below look unfamiliar.

How to work through a hypo
  1. 1Read the rule (teal box). It puts the sheet's point in plain words. The exact wording to use in the exam is in the Lessons and Sheet tabs.
  2. 2Read the hypothetical (amber box). Before reading on, decide what the rule says about these facts.
  3. 3Tap Application (green box) and compare it with your answer.
  4. 4The exam cue (violet box) lists question words that should send you to this block. Each block ends with a quick check.
Applications:
ℹ NOTE
About these hypos

Each block on this page has three parts: the rule in plain words, a made-up set of facts, and a worked answer. Your exact sheet wording, with its quotations, is still in the Lessons and Sheet tabs.

Some terms come up throughout. Pepper defends the amoral role, where the lawyer serves the client within the law and does not judge the client's aims. Thunder argues that a lawyer stays a moral person inside the role. Legal positivism says whether something is law depends on its source and not on its merit. Natural law theory says law is tied to what is morally good. The Radbruch formula says a statute stops being law once its injustice is intolerable.

A dagger (†) marks a point from the slides. S13 means Session 13. Q95, Q100 and Q103 are the practice-bank questions the sheet names. The coverage table is the last section.

110.0 The archetype in one line

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

The position. The statement fails. The lawyer's role is moral. Law sets a floor, and prudence, dialogue and rare objection decide the hard cases above it.

The opening. The statement assumes that the lawyer's role can be sealed off from morality. Thunder mocks that view as just focusing on the law. Yet even Pepper defends the role morally, by appealing to autonomy and equality. So reject or qualify the statement. The role is moral and is bounded by law. Its hard cases call for prudence, dialogue and, rarely, refusal.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
"Just Focus on the Law"

A senior partner tells a new associate that the associate's job is the law, and that morality is the client's business.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Start with Pepper, because the partner's view sounds like Pepper's.

  • Even Pepper rejects the reasoning, though not the conclusion. Pepper's case for the amoral role is itself moral. Lawyers should serve clients fully because clients have a right to autonomy and to equal access to the law.
  • So the role is moral from the start. The law sets the floor, because the associate must never help a client break it. Above the floor, hard cases need judgment: prudent advice, moral dialogue with the client and, in rare cases, refusing to act.
🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

a lawyer's role is amoral; just focus on the law.

210.1 The floor

📘 Learn 10.1 in Lesson 10 →
🔑 Trigger words: turn away a client, distaste, abuses his position, hidden bodies

10.1.1 Choice of client, and Pepper's dilemma

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS
  1. The claim that turning a client away abuses the lawyer's position overstates Pepper. For Pepper, choice of client is troubling only if it closes off a person's access to the law.
  2. Pepper's best case is a dilemma. Conduct that is bad enough should, it seems, be made expressly unlawful. If it has not been, why impose the accident of one lawyer's conscience on the client?
  3. So the claim that the client's conscience must govern is itself a moral claim. And to spot Pepper's extreme cases, the lawyer must weigh morality all the time, so the role is less amoral than it looks. (Liu, S13: this is like Radbruch's judge, except that a refused client can find another lawyer.)
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Payday Lender

Wen, a solo lawyer in a city with hundreds of firms, is asked by a payday lender to draft loan agreements at the highest interest rate the law allows, aimed at low-income borrowers. It is entirely lawful. Wen finds it distasteful and declines. The lender says Wen has abused her position and is denying it the law.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Work through the lender's complaint.

  • It is not an abuse. For Pepper, choice of client is troubling only if it shuts someone out of the law. The lender can easily hire another of the city's lawyers, so its access is not closed off.
  • Pepper's dilemma does have force. If high-interest lending is bad enough, Parliament should ban it. If Parliament has not, why should Wen's personal conscience decide which lawful business gets served?
  • But the lender's own argument is moral. Saying that the client's choices must govern is a claim about what the lawyer ought to do.
  • Liu's point. To know when a case is extreme enough to refuse, Wen must weigh morality all the time. So even Pepper's model is not truly amoral. It resembles Radbruch's judge, who must watch for intolerable injustice. The difference is that a refused client, unlike a litigant before a judge, can find another lawyer.

10.1.2 AGAINST: the statement's verbs are moral

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

Points against.

  • The statement's verbs, abuses and denies, are moral premises.
  • Thunder says Pepper's role leaves the lawyer morally powerless for the sake of a moral principle.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

The lender says Wen abused her position and denied it access. Both verbs assume a moral standard for lawyers. And Thunder's charge is that Pepper removes the lawyer's moral agency in the name of a moral principle, autonomy. That undermines itself.

10.1.3 QUALIFY: Pepper's four zones of autonomy

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

A qualification. Pepper gives four zones of autonomy for the lawyer, which together form a meaningful field:

  1. practising at all;
  2. choice of client;
  3. dialogue with the client;
  4. objection, which is always available.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Even on Pepper's own model, Wen has room for her conscience:

  1. she could choose not to practise;
  2. she can turn the lender away;
  3. if she takes the work, she can raise her concerns with the lender;
  4. in an extreme case, she can refuse a specific task.

10.1.4 Hidden bodies (Q95 only)

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

Hidden bodies (for Q95 only). Objection should be rarely used, but it may reveal the live victim.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

A criminal client tells his lawyer, in confidence, that he left a kidnapped child locked in a basement, still alive.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Pepper says conscientious objection should be rare. But this is the extreme case it exists for, because disclosure could save a live victim. In the real hidden-bodies case the victims were already dead. Pepper's footnote draws the line between not revealing a dead body and revealing a live victim. So even a lawyer on Pepper's model may break ranks here.

10.1.5 TRAP: Pepper ≠ LP

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

A trap: Pepper is not the same as legal positivism.

  • Legal positivism only identifies what the law is, and a moral decision remains (Hart against Radbruch). So a positivist may side with Pepper or with Thunder.
  • Pepper is hard to square with natural law theory, because for natural law, finding the law already involves morality (Liu, S13).
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Do not write that Pepper is a positivist and so on. Wen could be a positivist and still think, with Thunder, that she must weigh morality in choosing clients. Positivism tells her what the law is. It does not tell her how to practise. A natural lawyer, by contrast, would find Pepper's picture of law without morality hard to accept at all.

10.1.6 AGAINST: inequality, and the replies

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

A point against: inequality. The rich buy more law, so a moral filter by lawyers could level things out. The replies (Pepper; Liu, S13):

  • the better fix is access to justice;
  • how legal help is distributed is a separate issue from what lawyers may do;
  • filters may hurt the poor more.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

A critic says Wen should filter. The lender is rich and can buy endless legal help, so moral filtering by lawyers evens things up.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

There are three replies.

  • Access to justice. The better fix is legal aid and free legal help for borrowers.
  • Distribution is not content. Unequal access to lawyers is a problem about how legal services are shared out. It is not a problem about what lawyers may do for clients.
  • Filters can backfire. Rich clients can always find a less scrupulous lawyer. A poor client stuck with one affordable lawyer suffers most from that lawyer's moral filter.
🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

turning a client away; distaste; abuses his position; hidden bodies.

310.2 The effluent case

📘 Learn 10.2 in Lesson 10 →
🔑 Trigger words: enforcement risk, what officials will actually do, full access
▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS
  1. Advising on the risk of enforcement is accurate and useful to the client (Pepper). The trouble is what realism does to Pepper's limit, the law. (Realism here means treating law as what officials will actually do.)
  2. In Pepper's effluent case, the legal limit is .050 grams per litre, but anything up to .075 is ignored. A client without strong moral guidance then feels no pressure to obey the law as written.
  3. So if law is only what officials will actually do, the promise not to encourage lawbreaking holds only by emptying the word law of meaning.

Also on the sheet:

  • A point against, from Thunder. Autonomy may have to give way to the beauty of our shared environment and to other people's health.
  • A qualification from Liu (S13). The example is lopsided. The rule against lying by omission, and probably the standard of care, require telling the client both figures. Weighing morality to reach the decision to tell is Thunder's method, while Pepper tells without asking.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Noise Limit

A factory's licence caps night-time noise at 65 dB. Everyone in the industry knows inspectors only act above 75 dB, because of budget cuts. The factory owner asks his lawyer, Daniel, what the real limit is.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Work through the four views.

  • Pepper. Telling the owner about the 75 dB practice is accurate and useful. It is information the client is entitled to.
  • The problem with realism. If the law just means what inspectors actually do, then 75 dB is the law. Daniel's promise not to help the client break the law becomes empty, because nothing between 65 and 75 counts as breaking it. And a client with no strong moral compass will feel no pull towards 65.
  • Thunder. The owner's freedom to run the factory may have to give way to the neighbours' sleep and health. A good lawyer would raise that.
  • Liu: the example is lopsided. Honesty forbids misleading by omission, and the standard of care probably requires Daniel to give both numbers anyway. Most lawyers would decide to tell by weighing morality, which is Thunder's method. Pepper would tell without asking the moral question at all.
🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

advise on enforcement risk; the law is what officials will actually do; full access to the law.

410.3 Moral dialogue

📘 Learn 10.3 in Lesson 10 →
🔑 Trigger words: moral dialogue, cost, criminal defendant, corporate officer
▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS
  1. Moral dialogue is only a partial answer. It makes the lawyer a moral educator, without judging or policing the client (Pepper).
  2. Its limits are Pepper's own. It is expensive, and a criminal defendant will be less open to it than a corporate officer.
  3. So dialogue works where it matches Thunder's prudence and tact. For Thunder's lawyer, it is ordinary practice, and not a repair to an amoral role.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Two Clients, One Afternoon

Lawyer Priya has two meetings.

  • (a) A company's HR director wants to make 40 staff redundant the week before their annual bonuses vest. It is lawful.
  • (b) A man charged with assault wants Priya to cross-examine the complainant about her past relationships, to make her look unreliable. That is lawful, within limits.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Compare the two meetings.

  • (a) suits dialogue. The HR director has time, is used to discussing reputation and fairness, and may change course if Priya raises the costs to morale and fairness. Priya educates without dictating.
  • (b) is harder. A defendant facing prison is understandably less open to hearing about the complainant's dignity. And every hour of dialogue costs him money.
  • So dialogue is a partial fix. For Thunder, raising such points tactfully is not a special repair to an amoral role. It is just what a good, prudent lawyer does.
🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

moral dialogue; it costs too much; criminal defendant v corporate officer.

510.4 Compartments

📘 Learn 10.4 in Lesson 10 →
🔑 Trigger words: soldiers, separate compartments, chaos, no one can say objectively

10.4.1 Thunder rejects the dramatic bifurcation

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS
  1. The claim that lawyers are like soldiers is the sharp split between person and role that Thunder rejects. Simply pointing to the role gives up on explaining it.
  2. Pepper fears that the moralising lawyer will turn into a policeman, a judge or a deceiver. Thunder holds that the lawyer stays accountable as a human being.
  3. So the claim that no one can say what a virtuous lawyer would do overstates. Roles are not completely personal to each lawyer, and prudence applies the virtues (4.7).
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Soldier Analogy

A litigator, Marcus, says lawyers are like soldiers who follow orders inside their role. If each brought their own morality there would be chaos, and anyway no one can say objectively what a virtuous lawyer would do.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Take Marcus's claims in turn.

  • Saying it is my role explains nothing. It does not explain why the role is worth doing, or how to do it well.
  • Pepper's worry. A moralising lawyer might police, judge or deceive the client. That is a real risk.
  • Thunder's reply. Marcus is still a human being who answers for what his work serves.
  • It is not chaos. Lawyering has known purposes, such as justice and fair process, so its virtues are not arbitrary. Prudence applies them case by case. And the claim that no one can say objectively is the sceptic's move that 4.7 answers.

10.4.2 CONCEDE: the office lawyer tests Thunder

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

A concession. Pepper's model of the office lawyer tests Thunder. Thunder's account of the lawyer's function, ensuring the accused a fair trial, fits courts better than offices. Concede that. Justice and public order still reach advice given in an office.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

Marcus moves to a corporate firm, drafting supply contracts. There is no accused and no trial.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Thunder's account of the lawyer's purpose, ensuring the accused a fair trial, does not obviously apply here. Concede it. But office advice still serves justice and public order, through honest contracts and lawful structures. So Thunder's view still reaches Marcus's desk.

10.4.3 QUALIFY: roles matter, but no pocket universe

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

A qualification. Thunder accepts that roles carry their own morality. The police officer owes courtesy and compassion, and not cold mechanical precision. But a role is not a world of its own, as Liu puts it. Thunder's lawyer interprets the role constantly in the light of the good life, while Pepper's lawyer steps outside it only in extreme cases (S13).

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Thunder agrees that roles matter. A police officer has duties a civilian does not have. But the officer should carry them out with compassion, and not mechanically. In the same way, Marcus interprets his role every day in the light of what a good life is. On Pepper's model, by contrast, he only steps outside his role in rare extreme cases.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

lawyers are like soldiers; separate compartments; it would be chaos; no one can say objectively.

610.5 Rules only

📘 Learn 10.5 in Lesson 10 →
🔑 Trigger words: conduct rules, nothing more nothing less, as written, too vague
▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS
  1. The claim that a lawyer may do anything no rule forbids mistakes a floor for the whole. Conduct rules assume a purpose (16).
  2. Thunder calls professional codes legalistic: mostly general rules and not aspirations. The lawyer's function is not to obey the letter of the law slavishly.
  3. So the claim that serving justice is too vague overstates. Thunder admits there is substantial disagreement on particular cases. But norms that are exploited against justice are subverted.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Discovery Avalanche

Big Corp is sued by a small supplier for $80,000. Big Corp's lawyer serves 4,000 discovery requests, knowing the supplier cannot afford to answer them and will drop the case. No professional conduct rule expressly forbids this. The lawyer says nothing in the rules stops it, and that serving justice is too vague to apply.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Answer the lawyer in three steps.

  • The rules are a floor. They exist to make litigation fair and efficient. Using them to crush a smaller party defeats their own purpose.
  • Thunder on codes. Professional codes are legalistic. A lawyer's job is not to obey their letter slavishly while ignoring what they are for.
  • Vagueness is no excuse. Thunder admits lawyers will disagree about many cases. But using discovery rules to bury a claim with merit is not a hard case. It turns a rule of fairness against fairness, and that subverts it.
🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

conduct rules, nothing more, nothing less; as written; serving justice is too vague.

710.6 The guilty client

📘 Learn 10.6 in Lesson 10 →
🔑 Trigger words: acquittal, believed guilty, technicality, refuse any part
▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS
  1. The claim that winning an acquittal for a client believed guilty is wrong fails. Defending the accused is the role working as it should.
  2. Thunder's lawyer serves by ensuring the accused a fair trial. For Pepper, full access to the law is clearest and most dramatic in criminal cases.
  3. So the claim that a lawyer must refuse any part fits an unjust system, or relying on an intolerably unjust rule such as a racist statute. It does not fit the unjust outcome of a just rule† (10.11).
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Unlawful Search

Lawyer Hannah believes her client stole the jewellery. The police found it during a search without a warrant, so the court excludes it, and the client is acquitted. A journalist writes that Hannah helped a thief walk free on a technicality, and that she should have refused any part in it.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Work out when refusal would and would not fit.

  • The role was working. The exclusion rule protects everyone from unlawful searches, and Hannah's job is to make sure the accused gets a fair trial. On Thunder's view she acted as a good lawyer. On Pepper's, criminal defence is the clearest case for full access to the law.
  • When refusal fits. Refusal could be right if the trial were in a corrupt regime's court, which is an unjust system. It could also be right if the defence depended on an intolerably unjust rule, such as a statute excluding a witness's evidence because of her race.
  • Not here. The exclusion rule is just. An unjust outcome from a just rule is not a reason to refuse (10.11).
🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

winning an acquittal for a client believed guilty; a technicality; he must refuse any part.

810.7 Junior lawyers

📘 Learn 10.7 in Lesson 10 →
🔑 Trigger words: junior lawyers, lawful instructions, superiors, public officials
▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS
  1. The claim that juniors following lawful instructions bear no moral responsibility fails. Legality settles what may be done. It does not settle who answers for it.
  2. Thunder's lazy lawyer will tend to take for granted the standards and expectations of peers and superiors. Courage resists the pressure to conform.
  3. So the junior shares responsibility. Raise the matter in dialogue first, and refuse only where the instruction would seriously harm others.

Also on the sheet:

  • A point against, from Thunder. The amoral lawyer gives up the right, and indeed the duty, to take at least some responsibility for what the lawyer's work serves.
  • Mei (for Q100 and Q103 only). Pleading the time bar is lawful, yet the win may be unjust, so start with dialogue. The concealed defect endangers the public, so objection is right (10.1).
  • The judge. Kennedy's five courses are for a judge (12.4; 15.10), and not for a junior.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Aisha's Two Instructions

Aisha, a second-year associate, gets two instructions from her partner.

  • (a) Plead the limitation period against an elderly widow who filed her claim against the client three days late.
  • (b) Draft a settlement with a confidentiality clause that would stop the claimant revealing a known brake defect in the client's cars, which are still on the road.

Aisha thinks that both are lawful and that she is only following instructions, so it is not on her.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Take responsibility first, then each instruction.

  • Lawful does not mean no responsibility. Legality says what Aisha may do. It does not say whether she answers for it. Thunder warns against the lazy lawyer who simply absorbs the standards of superiors. Courage means resisting the pressure to conform.
  • (a): dialogue first. Pleading the time bar is lawful, and limitation periods serve real purposes. But the result may be unjust to the widow. So Aisha should raise it with the partner and ask whether the client could settle. She should not refuse outright.
  • (b): objection may be right. Silencing evidence of a defect that endangers the public risks serious harm to others. That is the kind of case where refusing, as conscientious objection (10.1), becomes right.
  • Thunder's point against. If Aisha adopts a purely amoral stance, she gives up both the right and the duty to take responsibility for what her work serves.
  • Not Kennedy's five courses. Those are options for a judge whose sense of the law conflicts with how the judge wants to decide (12.4). Aisha's position is different. She can raise concerns, or refuse.
🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

junior lawyers following lawful instructions; superiors; public officials.

910.8 Lawyers' training and outlook

📘 Learn 10.8 in Lesson 10 →
🔑 Trigger words: conscience at the door, law school, argue any side, theory isn't relevant
▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS
  1. The advice to leave your conscience at the door describes an outlook that lawyers are trained into. It does not justify that outlook.
  2. Pepper reports that the remark we are all realists now is often heard from law professors today.
  3. So the claim that theory is not relevant is itself an unexamined theory. The realist lawyer already advises treating breach of contract as a cost.

Also on the sheet: Kennedy says progressive-minded students, fearing they will be changed without choosing it, ask whether law school will warp their minds.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Moot Coach

A first-year law student is told by her moot coach to leave her conscience at the door, that a good advocate can argue any side, and to forget jurisprudence because theory is not relevant to practice. A year later, she advises a client that breaching a contract will cost $50,000 in damages but earn $200,000, so the client should breach.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Work through the three points.

  • Describing is not justifying. The coach describes how lawyers are trained. That does not show the training is right.
  • We are all realists now. The student's advice treats breach of contract as just a cost. That is the realist view of law which Pepper says many law professors hold. So she has a theory after all, just one she never examined.
  • Kennedy. Idealistic students fear exactly this: that law school will change their minds without their choosing it.
🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

leave your conscience at the door; law school trains you to argue any side; theory isn't relevant.

1010.9 Transactional work

📘 Learn 10.9 in Lesson 10 →
🔑 Trigger words: transactional work, no opposing counsel, no judge
▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS
  1. In criminal defence, the law may allow more. Implying that a truthful witness lied brings no liability. Similar half-truths used to sell a termite-ridden house may be misrepresentation.
  2. So the statement holds in part. Realism is more likely from a lawyer advising a large corporate enterprise, where no judge or opposing lawyer checks the client.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Two Half-Truths
  • (a) Defence counsel cross-examines a witness she believes honest, suggesting he may be mistaken or lying, to raise reasonable doubt. That is allowed.
  • (b) A conveyancing lawyer, drafting the sale of a termite-ridden house, writes the disclosure so that it hints the house is structurally sound without saying so.
  • (c) A lawyer advises a large company alone, on a restructuring that shifts risk onto suppliers. No one else is in the room.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Compare who is there to check each lawyer.

  • (a) is permitted by the adversarial system. A judge and a prosecutor are there to test the case.
  • (b) may be misrepresentation. The buyer has no judge, and may have no lawyer, to catch the half-truth.
  • (c) is where realism tempts most. When advising a big corporation alone, with no judge or opposing lawyer to check it, the lawyer is most likely to treat the law as whatever the client can get away with.

So the statement that lawyers in transactional work may act more freely is only partly right. They need more care, because no one else is checking.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

transactional work; no opposing counsel; no judge.

1110.10 Thunder's diagnosis, and the natural-teleological view

📘 Learn 10.10 in Lesson 10 →
🔑 Trigger words: why we hold such views, purpose of law, hired gun, just do your job

10.10.1 Realism plus neo-Kantianism

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS
  1. Thunder traces the appeal of the amoral view, in large part, to the unwitting partnership of legal realism and neo-Kantian morality. (Neo-Kantian morality treats ethics as universal duties that apply to everyone alike.)
  2. Neo-Kantianism tends to make reasons based on a role look morally suspect. It treats prudence, the daily bread of the legal profession, as amoral. And it separates right conduct from the good life.
  3. Realism gives the view a comfortable philosophical home. Against both, law is meant ultimately, though not always immediately, for ends that are naturally good for human beings.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Hired Gun

A senior partner tells juniors that they are hired guns and should just do the job. What the law is for is none of their business, and a lawyer's ethics are the conduct rules and nothing else.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Thunder's diagnosis explains why this sounds plausible.

  • Realism teaches that law is just what officials will do, so asking what law is for seems idle.
  • Neo-Kantian ethics treats morality as universal duties for everyone alike. That makes role-based reasons look suspect. It treats prudence, a lawyer's daily judgment calls, as morally neutral. And it separates right conduct from living a good life.
  • Thunder's alternative. Law is ultimately for ends naturally good for human beings: peace, justice and flourishing. A lawyer who serves those ends well is a good lawyer and a good person, and not a hired gun.

10.10.2 STEELMAN: Pepper's reply

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

The strongest case for the other side. Pepper says that providing access to law makes the lawyer a good person.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

The partner's best defence is Pepper's. By giving clients full access to the law, the partner serves their autonomy, which is itself a moral good. So the hired gun is doing good, and not just following orders.

10.10.3 CONCEDE: a diagnosis is not a refutation

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

A concession. A diagnosis is not a refutation, and Thunder is less concerned to counter Pepper's argument blow by blow. Liu doubts the neo-Kantian half, and adds a more likely source: the intuition that a lawyer should not substitute the lawyer's judgment for the client's, which Thunder shares (S13). Concede this, and use 10.1 to answer it.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Explaining why the partner holds the view does not show that it is wrong. Liu suspects the real source is simpler than neo-Kantianism: the sense that it is not a lawyer's place to override a client's choices. Thunder shares that intuition. So concede the point, and answer the partner with the arguments in 10.1: the amoral role rests on moral claims, and spotting extreme cases requires constant moral weighing.

10.10.4 QUALIFY: same act, different reasons

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

A qualification: same act, different reasons (Liu, S13). A lawyer following Thunder may disclose a live victim, either as part of the role or because duties as a human being override it. A lawyer following Pepper may too, but only as objection in an extreme case. The gap is one of mindset, and not necessarily of outcome. The positive law sets how wide it is.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

Back to the kidnapped child (10.1.4). Two lawyers both disclose.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Compare their reasons.

  • The lawyer following Thunder may say that a good lawyer serves the law's purposes, so disclosure is part of the role. Or that lawyer may say that the duty as a human being outweighs the duty as a lawyer.
  • The lawyer following Pepper says the role demands silence, but that this is the rare extreme where objection is right.

It is the same act, with different reasoning. How often the two lawyers' actions would differ depends on how much the professional rules already require.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

why do lawyers hold this view?; the purpose of law; hired gun; just do your job.

1210.11 Liu's three scenarios†

📘 Learn 10.11 in Lesson 10 →
🔑 Trigger words: racist statute, coerced evidence, hide behind the system, institutional wrong
▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS
  1. Ask these in order†:
    1. Is the system, by and large, just?
    2. If so, is this rule intolerably unjust?
    3. If not, is this outcome unjust?
  2. Calling an unjust result the institution's wrong, and not the lawyer's, only moves the question†. Is the institution justified by finding the truth, by dignity, or by the cost of replacing it?
  3. Only truth and dignity make the lawyer's part good, and not merely excused. Pepper names both as defences of the adversary system.

Also on the sheet: Pepper limits client autonomy by the law, and not by the lawyer's morality. If the Radbruch formula denies a racist statute the character of law, even Pepper's lawyer may refuse.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Three Files on Lawyer Teo's Desk
  • File 1: defend a client in Kessland's Junta courts, where verdicts are fixed in advance.
  • File 2: in a just Ruritania, a landlord wants to evict a tenant under an old, still unrepealed statute that lets landlords evict tenants of one particular race.
  • File 3: in a just Ruritania, Teo's client confessed under coercion. The confession is excluded, and a guilty man will probably walk free.
✔ APPLICATION · Asking the questions in orderDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Take the files in order.

  • File 1: the system is not just. Teo's participation helps legitimise a sham. The case for refusing, or for acting only to protect the client from the system, is strongest.
  • File 2: a just system, but an intolerably unjust rule. A racially targeted eviction statute fails the Radbruch formula (8.8). Even on Pepper's view, client autonomy is limited by the law. So if the statute is not law, Teo may refuse.
  • File 3: a just system, a just rule, an unjust outcome. Teo may say the acquittal is the institution's wrong and not his. But that only moves the question: is the institution justified?
    • If it is justified by finding the truth (excluding coerced confessions makes verdicts more reliable) or by dignity (no one should be forced to incriminate himself), Teo's part is good. Pepper cites both.
    • If it is justified only by replacement costs, meaning that changing the system would cost too much, his part is merely excused.
🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

a racist statute; coerced evidence; hiding behind the system; it's the institution's wrong.

1310.12 Conclusion, applied

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

The conclusion. The statement is overstated. Pepper and Thunder are closer than their labels suggest:

  • Pepper defends the role morally and keeps a right of objection, which needs a lawyer weighing morality throughout;
  • Thunder accepts that roles carry their own morality, and that no legal system is perfect.

They differ in mindset more than in outcome, and the stronger the conduct rules, the narrower the gap (Liu, S13). The live question is how often conscience may override the role. The answer is rarely and openly, after dialogue, where serving the client would subvert the point of the law.

✔ APPLICATION · Applied to the hyposDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Here is where each part of the conclusion was shown.

  • Pepper's moral defence: the payday lender (10.1).
  • Weighing throughout: Liu's point in 10.1.1.
  • Same act, different reasons: the kidnapped child (10.10.4).
  • Conduct rules narrow the gap: the noise limit (10.2), where the standard of care already requires telling.
  • Rarely, openly, after dialogue: Aisha (10.7), with dialogue on the time bar and objection on the brake defect.
