HYPO LESSON 11 · ARCHETYPE 11 · ABOUT 33 MIN · 64 QUESTIONS

Hypos: Constitution and judicial role

⚡ BIG IDEA

The statement is overstated. The Constitution moves the debate between natural law and legal positivism, and does not settle it. Courts should presume a law valid, except at intolerable injustice.

The theory behind these hypos is taught in Lesson 11. Do that lesson first if the rules below look unfamiliar.

How to work through a hypo
  1. 1Read the rule (teal box). It puts the sheet's point in plain words. The exact wording to use in the exam is in the Lessons and Sheet tabs.
  2. 2Read the hypothetical (amber box). Before reading on, decide what the rule says about these facts.
  3. 3Tap Application (green box) and compare it with your answer.
  4. 4The exam cue (violet box) lists question words that should send you to this block. Each block ends with a quick check.
Applications:
ℹ NOTE
About these hypos

Each block on this page has three parts: the rule in plain words, a made-up set of facts, and a worked answer. Your exact sheet wording, with its quotations, is still in the Lessons and Sheet tabs.

This topic is about Singapore's Constitution, so most facts imagine invented bills or cases under the real Articles (Articles 4, 5(2), 9(1), 12, 15 and 156). The bills are made up. The real cases and what they said come from the sheet.

Some terms come up throughout. Legal positivism says whether something is law depends on its source and not on its merit. Natural law theory ties law to what is morally good. The Radbruch formula says a statute stops being law once its injustice is intolerable. Broad historical consensus is Tan Seow Hon's test for showing that injustice is intolerable: widespread agreement over time. A master rule is the rule a system uses to decide what counts as law. Part 4 is the part of the Constitution that sets out fundamental liberties. TSH is Tan Seow Hon. S14 means Session 14. A dagger (†) marks a point from the slides. The coverage table is the last section.

111.0 The archetype in one line

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

The position. The statement is overstated. The Constitution moves the debate between natural law and legal positivism, and does not settle it. Courts should presume a law valid, except at intolerable injustice.

The opening. The statement assumes that a supreme, written Constitution settles what law is. It does not:

  • Article 4 is a master rule only because it is accepted;
  • the words law, life, liberty and equal in Part 4 are contested moral terms.

So qualify the statement. Courts should presume a law is valid, yet strike down intolerable injustice.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
"The Constitution Has Settled It"

A law student writes that Singapore has a written, supreme Constitution. Whatever complies with it is law, and whatever conflicts with it is void. So the student says the debate between natural law and legal positivism does not matter here.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

There are three steps in the answer.

  • Article 4 depends on acceptance. It is supreme only because judges and officials treat it as supreme. A document cannot make itself supreme.
  • Part 4 needs interpreting. Suppose you must decide whether a law takes away someone's life or liberty otherwise than in accordance with law, or treats people unequally. You have to decide what those words mean. That is where natural law and legal positivism part ways.
  • So the debate moves inside the Constitution. It has not gone away. The sensible position is to presume statutes are valid, and strike down only what is intolerably unjust.
🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

the Constitution settles what law is; the written Constitution makes the debate irrelevant.

211.1 Supremacy

📘 Learn 11.1 in Lesson 11 →
🔑 Trigger words: Art 4; supreme law; settled it; check the text

11.1.1 A master rule exists because it is accepted

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS
  1. Article 4 makes the written Constitution supreme. But a master rule exists only because it is accepted. Tan Seow Hon says we cannot infer it from the written text alone.
  2. So the claim that the Constitution sets the test for validity holds only as a matter of form. The moral terms in Part 4 force a choice between the schools of thought (11.2, 11.3).
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Ignored Constitution

Imagine a country, Valdoria, whose written constitution says it is supreme. For decades, its judges ignore the constitution and treat the President's decrees as the highest law.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

In Valdoria, the real master rule is that the President's decrees are supreme, because that is what officials actually accept. The text's claim to supremacy changes nothing. Singapore's Article 4 is the master rule because Singapore's officials accept it, and not because it says so. Even when accepted, it only tells you where to look. What the moral words in Part 4 require is still open.

11.1.2 AGAINST: LP and morally loaded concepts

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

A point against. Tan Seow Hon says legal positivism does not shed light on morally loaded ideas like these. She asks whether the state should define person, life and liberty when it is not the giver of life.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Suppose Parliament passes an Act defining person in Article 9 to exclude anyone in a permanent coma. Legal positivism can tell you the Act was validly passed. It cannot tell you whether Parliament has the moral standing to decide who counts as a person. Tan Seow Hon's point is that these words point beyond the text.

11.1.3 QUALIFY: basic features

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

A qualification. Teo Soh Lung (High Court) rejected the basic features doctrine, the idea that some parts of a constitution cannot be amended. Yong Vui Kong (2015) left the point open. Tan Seow Hon relies on equal moral worth, so that even an amendment allowing genocide falls to the Radbruch formula.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

Imagine Parliament, with a two-thirds majority, amends the Constitution to permit the killing of a named ethnic group.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

On the view in Teo Soh Lung, there are no basic features that cannot be amended, so the amendment is valid as a matter of form. Tan Seow Hon's answer does not need basic features. Constitutional supremacy rests on equal moral worth. So an amendment allowing genocide is intolerably unjust and falls to the Radbruch formula, however properly it was passed.

11.1.4 TRAP: the Constitution includes morality, so NLT wins

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

A trap. Never argue that the Constitution includes morality, so natural law wins. That makes you a legal positivist who is very happy that morality is now part of the positive law. (A student said this, and Liu endorsed it in S14.) Tan Seow Hon's own thesis is that constitutionalism affirms a higher law.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Suppose you write that equal protection in Article 12 is a moral idea, so the Constitution proves natural law right. A positivist simply agrees: the positive law has taken in a moral standard (2.1.4). To make a real natural law point, argue as Tan Seow Hon does. Constitutionalism itself affirms a higher law that would bind even without the text.

11.1.5 CONCEDE: the master-rule point doesn't do much

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

A concession from Liu. In practice, the point about the master rule does not necessarily lead to much. What matters is how theory shapes judges' duty to law (S14).

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Concede that showing Article 4 rests on acceptance does not, by itself, change any case. The real difference is in how a judge sees the judge's duty. A positivist applies whatever the master rule picks out. A natural lawyer reads the Constitution's moral terms in the light of a higher law.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

Art 4; the Constitution is the supreme law; the Constitution has settled it; just check the text.

311.2 Art 9(1) law

📘 Learn 11.2 in Lesson 11 →
🔑 Trigger words: validly passed; fair trial only; invent rights; caning; international norms

11.2.1 In accordance with law

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS
  1. Reading law as whatever is validly passed begs the question. What could breach Article 9, then, if everything in force counts as law? (Tan Seow Hon)
  2. Applying Tan Seow Hon's test, caning for third-time littering survives the other readings. It falls under the Radbruch formula only if broad historical consensus condemns it. Arguably none does.
  3. So stopping at fair-trial rules is a choice of theory. The text does not force it. The Radbruch formula adds only a floor against intolerable injustice.

The readings of law in Article 9(1):

ReadingAuthority
Validly passedA remark in Jabar. Yong Vui Kong (2010)†: not about constitutionality. Nguyen read it to include constitutional validity.
Natural justiceOng Ah Chuan left substantive fairness open. Yong Vui Kong (2015)†: procedural. Tan Eng Hong (High Court): Article 12 brings in none.
Not absurd or arbitraryYong Vui Kong (2010)† suggested it. Tan Seow Hon: the plea in Tan Eng Hong failed on evidence, and not on principle.
International lawNguyen: statute beats custom. Yong Vui Kong (2010)†: read consistently where possible. No bar on inhuman punishment was adopted.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Littering (Caning) Bill

Suppose Parliament validly passes an Act making caning mandatory for anyone convicted of littering a third time. A convicted man argues that this takes away his personal liberty otherwise than in accordance with law under Article 9(1).

✔ APPLICATION · Reading by readingDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Take each reading of the word law.

  • Validly passed. If law just means any validly passed Act, a statute can never breach Article 9. That is Tan Seow Hon's point: the reading begs the question. (Nguyen read law to include constitutional validity, which is circular here.)
  • Natural justice. He gets a fair trial, so the procedural reading is satisfied.
  • Not absurd or arbitrary. Caning for repeated littering is harsh, but it has a rational aim, deterrence. So it is probably not arbitrary.
  • International law. Singapore's courts read statutes consistently with international law where possible. But a clear statute beats custom, and they have adopted no bar on inhuman punishment.
  • The Radbruch formula. The law falls only if broad historical consensus condemns caning for littering as intolerably unjust. Arguably no such consensus exists.

So the Act survives. And stopping at the fair-trial reading is a choice about how to read law. The text does not force it.

11.2.2 FOR: no rights out of whole cloth

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

In support. Yong Vui Kong (2015) said courts cannot create a right missing from the Constitution out of whole cloth, as natural law, so there is no right against caning. (The court gave no ruling on natural law's view of caning. For George, see 12.1.)

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

The government's best case is that the Court of Appeal refused to invent an unwritten right against caning from natural law. On that view, the convicted man cannot use natural law to add a right the text does not contain.

11.2.3 AGAINST: TSH on what the court rejected

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

Points against.

  • Tan Seow Hon says the Court of Appeal was aiming at American substantive due process, which she calls the opposite of natural law theory.
  • Lim Meng Suang found no right to privacy. Article 9 covers unlawful taking of life, and detention. Yong Vui Kong (2015)† adds unlawful use of force.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Tan Seow Hon says the Yong Vui Kong court was really rejecting American-style creation of rights by judges. That is the opposite of natural law, and so the court was not rejecting natural law itself. And Article 9 already covers unlawful force, which includes caning. So whether caning is in accordance with law falls squarely within Article 9.

11.2.4 STEELMAN: each judge a law unto himself

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

The strongest case for the other side. Richer readings risk making each judge a law unto themselves. Tan Seow Hon replies that letting manifest injustice stand defeats the very purpose of certainty.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

The risk is real. If law means just law, each judge applies a personal idea of justice. Tan Seow Hon's reply is that certainty exists to serve justice. So leaving a manifestly unjust law in place defeats the point of certainty. That is why the Radbruch floor is narrow: it applies only to manifest injustice.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

'law' in Art 9 means whatever is validly passed; Art 9 only guarantees a fair trial; judges would be inventing rights; caning; international norms.

411.3 Art 12

📘 Learn 11.3 in Lesson 11 →
🔑 Trigger words: intelligible line; legitimate object; unelected legislators; left-handed drivers

11.3.1 The LMS test

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS
  1. For Lim Meng Suang (Court of Appeal), a line that makes sense and is rationally linked to the law's object is usually enough, because courts are not mini-legislatures.
  2. On a double fee for left-handed drivers, the Court of Appeal asks whether the line rationally serves its aim. The High Court would also strike down an aim that is inherently bad.
  3. So the claim that judges who look into the object become legislators overstates. The Radbruch formula strikes down only intolerable injustice, which is a narrower ground than Wednesbury unreasonableness. (Wednesbury unreasonableness means a decision so unreasonable that no reasonable authority could have made it.)
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Left-Handed Drivers' Fee

Suppose a regulation doubles the licence fee for left-handed drivers. The stated aim is road safety, based on one old study suggesting that left-handers react more slowly.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Go through the tests one at a time.

  • The Court of Appeal's test (Lim Meng Suang). Is there a line that makes sense (left-handedness), and is it rationally linked to the object (road safety)? If the study is junk, the rational link fails. The court will not second-guess whether road safety is a good aim, because it is not a mini-legislature.
  • The High Court's extra step. The High Court would also strike down an aim that is inherently bad. Suppose the real aim were to discourage left-handedness. That would fail.
  • This is not judges legislating. Looking into the object this far is not the court making law. The Radbruch formula goes further only at intolerable injustice, which is narrower than Wednesbury unreasonableness. Courts do not strike down laws merely for being unwise.

11.3.2 FOR: a threshold test

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

In support, Lim Meng Suang (Court of Appeal).

  • The test is a threshold test.
  • There is no free-standing review of legitimacy, only a limited element of illegitimacy.
  • Wednesbury is rejected.
  • Use Article 12(2).
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

The Court of Appeal's approach is deliberately modest. It asks whether the line makes sense, and not whether the law is fair. Article 12(2) lists specific forbidden grounds: religion, race, descent and place of birth. Left-handedness is not among them, so the general threshold test applies.

11.3.3 QUALIFY: not cleanly LP v NLT

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

A qualification. This is not a clean contest between legal positivism and natural law.

  • Extreme illogicality or incoherence fails one limb of the test, and a ban on women driving might fail limb two.
  • Tan Seow Hon calls the test a sign of natural law at work.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

A different regulation bans women from driving, citing family stability.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Even the modest Lim Meng Suang test would probably catch this. A link between women driving and family instability is so far-fetched that the line fails for extreme illogicality. So the supposedly positivist threshold test still makes judgments of reason and coherence. That is why Tan Seow Hon calls it natural law at work.

11.3.4 AGAINST: equality is empty without a higher law

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

A point against, from Tan Seow Hon. Equality is empty of content without a higher moral law. The question is which differences are morally significant, so moral arguments are not outside the law under Article 12(1). Without them, laws that treat everyone equally badly pass (Week 13, slide 18†).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

Parliament passes a law forbidding all drivers from driving after 8 pm, to save fuel.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

No one is singled out, so there is no unequal line to test. Article 12 is silent, even though the law treats everyone equally badly. And for the left-handed fee, deciding whether left-handedness is a morally significant difference is a moral question. Equality only has content once you have a view of which differences matter.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

an intelligible line rationally related to the object; a legitimate object; judges as unelected legislators; left-handed drivers.

511.4 Four walls

📘 Learn 11.4 in Lesson 11 →
🔑 Trigger words: within its own four walls; foreign values; universal morality

11.4.1 Four walls needn't exclude universal standards

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS
  1. Reading the Constitution mainly within its own four walls, as Colin Chan did (Tan Seow Hon; legal positivism, on Liu's slide†), need not exclude universal standards.
  2. Reading Haw Tua Tau generously, Tan Seow Hon finds that fairness was universal, though how it showed itself varied with local conditions.
  3. So universal morality need not mean foreign values, if it is kept to manifest injustice (11.5).
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Foreign Precedent

A litigant challenging a Singapore law cites a European court's ruling on the right to a fair hearing. The Attorney-General replies that the Constitution must be read within its own four walls, without importing foreign values.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

The two sides can be reconciled.

  • The four-walls approach (Colin Chan) is a sound starting point. Read Singapore's Constitution in the light of Singapore's text and history.
  • But it need not exclude universal standards. On Tan Seow Hon's reading of Haw Tua Tau, fairness is universal, though how it is applied depends on local conditions.
  • So the litigant's real argument is not to follow Europe. It is that the basic fairness every legal system owes its people requires this, applied in Singapore's way, and only at the level of manifest injustice.

11.4.2 CONCEDE: higher law cuts both ways

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

A concession. Higher law cuts both ways. A committed follower of Aquinas may end up with judges who hold quite a different view of dignity (Lawrence; Tan Seow Hon). Concede this: no wide review, only a narrow trigger.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

A conservative natural lawyer who invites judges to apply universal morality may get judges whose view of dignity points the other way, as the United States Supreme Court's decision in Lawrence did for some. Concede that risk, and keep the trigger to manifest injustice.

11.4.3 QUALIFY: Liu on TSH's narrow LP

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

A qualification from Liu (S14). Tan Seow Hon's version of legal positivism is too narrow. Positivism requires little but allows more.

  • Where the text points to a moral idea, a positivist judge may follow it outward, just as commercial reasonableness brings in trade practice.
  • A positivist judge who reads for purpose may read the Constitution as protecting individuals.

Tan Seow Hon replies that reference to natural law is then mandatory. And she asks whether that judge can stop at popular morality.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

A positivist judge reading equal in Article 12 can follow that word out into moral reasoning, just as a commercial judge reads reasonable by looking at trade practice. So positivism does not confine judges to the four walls. Tan Seow Hon's reply is that if the judge must look outside the text, natural law cannot be avoided. And if the judge stops at popular morality, what stops majorities defining equal however they like?

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

within its own four walls; foreign values; universal morality.

611.5 Who decides (courts)

📘 Learn 11.5 in Lesson 11 →
🔑 Trigger words: for Parliament, not the courts; ballot box; unelected judges; activism
▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS
  1. Contested rights are for Parliament, but only until the threshold of injustice in the Radbruch formula is met (Tan Seow Hon).
  2. So the claim that judges must never strike down a law for injustice goes too far. Rubber-stamping is a vice too (12.2), and intolerable injustice must fall.

Also on the sheet:

  • The strongest case for the other side. Rajeevan (High Court, 1998), as Tan Seow Hon reports it: the legislature rightly determines the rights of the individual when there are no specific guarantees.
  • The threshold (broad historical consensus: 15.13). It is met for genocide and slavery. It is not met for Roe, Obergefell or section 12 of the Women's Charter. For the catch, see 11.7.
  • A qualification. Lim Meng Suang left Hart against Devlin to the Legislature (16). Tan Seow Hon says that is right only if no constitutional right was at stake.
  • The legislator. Where objective morality is not clear, a deliberative democracy can take a stand through its legislature (12.3).
  • To close, Liu's last slide† asks who decides, and says we are back where we started, but wiser.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Three Petitions

The High Court receives three challenges:

  • (a) to a law allowing debt bondage (working off debts as unpaid servants);
  • (b) to the definition of marriage in section 12 of the Women's Charter;
  • (c) to a law raising the drinking age to 21.

The government argues that these are for Parliament and the ballot box, and not for unelected judges.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Test each challenge against the threshold.

  • (a): the threshold is met. Debt bondage is slavery in substance, and broad historical consensus condemns it. A court that rubber-stamped it would be giving up its role.
  • (b): the threshold is not met. There is no broad historical consensus that the current definition of marriage is intolerably unjust, so it is for Parliament.
  • (c): ordinary policy. It is plainly for Parliament.
  • The strongest case. Rajeevan holds that, without specific guarantees, Parliament rightly decides individuals' rights. That supports deference on (b) and (c).
  • Lim Meng Suang and Hart against Devlin. The Court of Appeal left that question to Parliament. Tan Seow Hon's qualification is that this is right only if no constitutional right is at stake.
  • Where morality is unclear, as on (b), a deliberative democracy takes its stand through its legislature (12.3).
  • The catch (11.7). Consensus can shift or go wrong. As Liu's last slide says, we end up asking who decides, but wiser.
🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

it's for Parliament, not the courts; the ballot box; unelected judges; judicial activism.

711.6 Art 156

📘 Learn 11.6 in Lesson 11 →
🔑 Trigger words: repeal; marriage; leave it to Parliament; courts are binary
▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS
  1. In 2022, change came through Parliament. Section 377A was repealed. Article 156, which Tan Seow Hon says was meant as a pre-emptive strike against judicial activism, shielded laws on marriage between a man and a woman from Part 4.
  2. So leaving it to Parliament moved the question and did not remove it. A two-thirds majority (Article 5(2)) put those laws beyond Part 4 (11.7).

Also on the sheet:

  • In support. Shanmugam said courts can only make binary decisions (Hansard, 29 November 2022).
  • A qualification from Tan Seow Hon. Repeal was because of risk, and not because the section was unconstitutional. So laws that treat people differently are not incoherent in principle. After UKM, section 377A failed to do the work, which might explain the change of tactic.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Columnist's Claim

A columnist writes that by repealing section 377A in Parliament and adding Article 156, Singapore took the question away from the courts and settled it democratically. The columnist says that is what leaving it to Parliament means.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

The columnist is partly right.

  • Partly right. The change did come through Parliament. Shanmugam's point was that courts can only strike down or uphold, while Parliament can craft a package.
  • But the question moved. It did not vanish. Article 156 was itself a constitutional decision, made by a two-thirds majority under Article 5(2), which places marriage laws beyond the rights in Part 4. So the question became who holds two-thirds, and not what the rights require.
  • Tan Seow Hon's reading. The government repealed section 377A because of the risk of a court striking it down, and not because it was unconstitutional. So keeping other laws that treat people differently is not inconsistent in principle. And after UKM, section 377A was no longer doing the work of protecting the marriage framework, which may explain the switch to Article 156.
🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

repeal; marriage; leave it to Parliament; courts can only make binary decisions.

811.7 The Constitution makes philosophy unnecessary?

📘 Learn 11.7 in Lesson 11 →
🔑 Trigger words: neither philosophy nor personal morality; always sufficient; I just apply the law; my morals are private; without exception

11.7.1 The statement is itself a legal philosophy

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS
  1. The statement is itself a legal philosophy. It is too moralised for the positivist and too amoral for the natural lawyer.
  2. Hart, positivism's ablest defender, rejects its conclusion. He says law is not morality, and that we should not let it take morality's place.
  3. So the claim that complying with the law always gives enough moral guidance fails. Law is a floor and not a ceiling, and its open terms need theory.

Also on the sheet:

  • A dilemma. Hart's judge, in the unclear edge of a rule, may have to reach beyond the law. Dworkin's judge finds the answer in community morality that is also law. Either way, theory is needed.
  • The lawyer. Law is a floor. Devlin says it is concerned with the minimum and not the maximum. Pepper's own premise implies the same (10.1).
  • Article 5(2). A special two-thirds majority amends most provisions (Tan Seow Hon). There is no express core like article 79(3) of the German Basic Law. (For implied limits, see 11.1.) So treating compliance as moral guidance hands judgment to whoever holds two-thirds.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Judge's Speech

A newly appointed judge says that in Singapore, the Constitution gives us everything we need. The judge says there is no need for philosophy or personal morality, that following the Constitution will always be right, and that the judge's morals are private.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Work through the judge's claim.

  • It is a philosophy. Saying the Constitution is always enough moral guidance is a theory of law and morality. A positivist would reject it as too moralised, because positivists say legal and moral duty can come apart. A natural lawyer would reject it as too amoral, because it ignores any higher law.
  • Hart agrees. Even positivism's champion says that law is not morality, so do not let it replace morality.
  • The open terms. When the judge must decide what equal means, Hart's model has the judge using discretion at the unclear edge. Dworkin's has the judge finding community morality in the law. Either way, the judge uses theory.
  • The floor. As Devlin says, law sets the minimum and not the maximum. A lawyer who does only what the law demands has not done everything that is right.
  • Two-thirds. Most of the Constitution can be amended by two-thirds of Parliament, with no protected core. If compliance were always morally enough, morality would be whatever two-thirds of MPs decide.

11.7.2 STEELMAN: most cases are routine

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

The strongest case for the other side. Personal morality is subjective, so keep it out. Most cases are routine. Hart says that to be occupied with the unclear edge of rules is one thing, and to be preoccupied with it is another.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

The judge's best point is that most cases, such as contracts and sentencing within set ranges, never require moral theory. Hart's line warns against obsessing over the hard edge. Concede that, and then insist that the hard edge still exists.

11.7.3 AGAINST: refusal as fidelity

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

Points against.

  • A natural-law judge who refuses manifest injustice is showing fidelity to law, and is not merely acting on conscience (Tan Seow Hon).
  • Subjectivism defeats itself (4.7).
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

The judge assumes that any moral reasoning would be a private conscience at work. Tan Seow Hon's reply is that refusing manifest injustice is fidelity to law properly understood, and not personal preference. And the claim that morality is subjective, so keep it out, is itself a moral claim (4.7).

11.7.4 Without exception: Art 15

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

Without exception. Try a challenge under Article 15 to the law as applied in this case. But Article 15(4), read literally, does not have the necessity test found in article 18(3) of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (Tan Seow Hon). See 12.6.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

A law bans alcohol without exception, catching communion wine.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

A church could bring a challenge under Article 15, freedom of religion, to the law as applied to it. But on Tan Seow Hon's reading, Article 15(4) does not require restrictions on religion to be necessary, unlike the international Covenant. So the challenge is weak on the text, even if it is strong morally (12.6).

11.7.5 CONCEDE: TSH's catch

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

A concession: Tan Seow Hon's catch (8.5). Consensus is a gauge, and not a ground.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

If you argue that the judge should refuse intolerable injustice judged by broad consensus, concede that consensus only indicates injustice. It can be wrong (8.5.3).

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

the Constitution makes philosophy unnecessary; neither philosophy nor personal morality; compliance is always sufficient; I just apply the law; my morals are private; without exception.

911.8 Legitimacy, basic features, separation of powers

📘 Learn 11.8 in Lesson 11 →
🔑 Trigger words: what makes it legitimate; consent; unamendable; basic features; separation of powers; gatekeeper

11.8.1 Acceptance can't found legitimacy

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS
  1. The people's acceptance cannot be the foundation of legitimacy. The framers' will leaves open why it should still bind us, and treating the absence of revolt as agreement is artificial (Tan Seow Hon).
  2. Tan Seow Hon says our consent is meaningful only if we understand our equal dignity under natural law. Natural law answers this from within, while legal positivism must borrow another moral or political theory (Liu, S14).
  3. So the claim that natural law defeats the separation of powers fails. On the weak thesis, morality overrides only at the Radbruch threshold. And Tan Seow Hon agrees that a representative legislature's mandate should generally prevail over judges' opinions on contested moral norms.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Student's Two Claims

A student makes two arguments:

  • (i) The Constitution is legitimate because the people accepted it in 1965, and no one has revolted since.
  • (ii) Natural law would let judges overrule Parliament on any moral issue, so it destroys the separation of powers.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Both arguments fail.

  • (i) fails. Why should the framers' choice in 1965 bind citizens born decades later? And treating no revolt as consent is artificial, because people stay quiet for many reasons. Consent means something only if we are equals in dignity, which is a natural-law premise. A positivist must borrow some other moral or political theory to explain legitimacy.
  • (ii) fails. Weak natural law lets morality override law only at intolerable injustice. On contested moral questions, Tan Seow Hon agrees that Parliament's mandate should generally prevail over judges' opinions.

11.8.2 QUALIFY: Liu's two further answers

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

A qualification: Liu's two further answers (S14).

  1. Reason converges, so, properly applied, all three branches of government reach one result.
  2. The debate between natural law and legal positivism asks what law is. The separation of powers asks how power is organised. So a democrat or a dictator could hold either view.
✔ APPLICATION · To (ii)Decide your answer first, then tap to compare.

If moral reasoning done well converges, a natural-law Parliament and a natural-law court should not clash. And the two questions are separate. A positivist can be a dictator's lawyer, and a natural lawyer can be a committed democrat.

11.8.3 AGAINST: the gatekeeper problem

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

A point against: the gatekeeper problem.

  • A positivist judge defers, leaving the legislature as moral gatekeeper.
  • A natural-law judge tests law against a higher law, so the conflict is real (Radbruch).
  • German courts applied the formula to a fallen regime's laws (Liu, Week 11).
  • Whether Singapore's judges hold this view is debatable, and they prefer a constitutional basis.
  • Against a sitting legislature, it is untested (S14).
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Concede that there is a real difference. Under natural law, the court is a backstop gatekeeper. But the German use of the formula was against a regime that had already fallen. Using it against a sitting Parliament has never been tested in Singapore. And Singapore's judges would look for a constitutional peg, such as Articles 9 and 12, instead of relying on natural law directly.

11.8.4 Basic features

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

Basic features:

  • Kesavananda (India) held that some features of the constitution cannot be amended. Those suggested include the separation of powers and its secular character (Tan Seow Hon).
  • The doctrine was rejected in Singapore (11.1).
  • Liu says it is easier for natural law, because a good constitution has a purpose that some amendments would destroy.
  • Tan Seow Hon says to argue from natural law, and not by second-guessing what the framers of the constitution intended.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

A two-thirds majority amends the Constitution to abolish the courts' independence.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

India's Kesavananda doctrine would strike down the amendment as destroying a basic feature. Singapore has rejected that doctrine. A natural lawyer has a better argument than guessing what the framers intended. The Constitution exists for an end, protecting citizens' equal dignity under law, and an amendment that destroys judicial independence defeats that end. As Liu says, natural law finds this argument easier to make.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

what makes the Constitution legitimate?; consent; unamendable; basic features; separation of powers; who is the gatekeeper?.

1011.9 Conclusion, applied

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

The conclusion. The statement is overstated. Article 4 and Part 4 move the debate between natural law and legal positivism, and do not settle it. So judges choose a theory whenever they read law or equal. The Constitution narrows the practical gap between natural-law and positivist judges, and makes the Radbruch formula rarely needed. But it leaves open the extreme case, our attitude to law, and who decides by what standard (Liu, S14). Judges should presume a law is valid, but strike down intolerable injustice. No clause relieves anyone of conscience.

✔ APPLICATION · Applied to the hyposDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Here is where each part of the conclusion was shown.

  • A theory is chosen: the Littering (Caning) Bill (11.2) and the Left-Handed Drivers' Fee (11.3).
  • The gap narrows: most of the examples come out the same for natural-law and positivist judges.
  • The extreme case: the genocide amendment (11.1.3) and debt bondage (11.5).
  • Who decides: Article 156 (11.6).
  • Conscience: the judge's speech (11.7).

HYPO LESSON 12 · ARCHETYPE 12 · ABOUT 21 MIN · 33 QUESTIONS

Hypos: Roles, who decides

⚡ BIG IDEA

The statement is right as a presumption. Roles have limits, but where they lie is contested, and refusing your own work is a vice too.

The theory behind these hypos is taught in Lesson 12. Do that lesson first if the rules below look unfamiliar.

How to work through a hypo
  1. 1Read the rule (teal box). It puts the sheet's point in plain words. The exact wording to use in the exam is in the Lessons and Sheet tabs.
  2. 2Read the hypothetical (amber box). Before reading on, decide what the rule says about these facts.
  3. 3Tap Application (green box) and compare it with your answer.
  4. 4The exam cue (violet box) lists question words that should send you to this block. Each block ends with a quick check.
Applications:
ℹ NOTE
About these hypos

Each block on this page has three parts: the rule in plain words, a made-up set of facts, and a worked answer. Your exact sheet wording, with its quotations, is still in the Lessons and Sheet tabs.

Some terms come up throughout. Usurpation means doing someone else's job. Abdication means refusing to do your own. The Radbruch formula says a statute stops being law once its injustice is intolerable. Broad historical consensus is Tan Seow Hon's test for showing that injustice is intolerable: widespread agreement over time. Legal positivism says whether something is law depends on its source and not on its merit. Natural law theory ties law to what is morally good. TSH is Tan Seow Hon. A dagger (†) marks a point from the slides. The coverage table is the last section.

112.0 The archetype in one line

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

The position. The statement is right as a presumption. Roles have limits, but where they lie is contested, and abdication is a vice too.

The opening. The statement treats the limits of each role as settled. Roles do have limits, because a constitutional democracy divides power. But:

  • where a role ends is contested, and drawing that line is a moral judgment;
  • refusing your own work is as much a vice as taking someone else's;
  • refusing extreme injustice is fidelity to law, and it is not taking over someone else's job.

The frame for questions on roles. The statement is almost word for word George, as Tan Seow Hon reports him. At least in a basically just regime, natural law requires judges and other officials to respect the limits of their own authority. The statement drops that condition and adds lawyers.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Statement on the Paper

An exam question says: Judges, officials and lawyers must respect the limits of their own roles, and leave to others what is rightfully theirs. Discuss.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Answer it in three moves.

  • Spot the source. This is George's claim, with two changes. It drops the words about a basically just regime, and it adds lawyers.
  • Agree as a presumption. In a just democracy, judges should not legislate, officials should not make policy, and lawyers should not police their clients' morals.
  • Then push back in three ways:
    1. who decides where a role ends is itself contested;
    2. a judge who rubber-stamps everything fails the role as surely as one who legislates;
    3. a judge who refuses to apply a law ordering genocide is not overstepping the role. That judge is being faithful to law.
🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

respect the limits of their roles; leave to others what is rightfully theirs; who decides?.

212.1 Source and frame

📘 Learn 12.1 in Lesson 12 →
🔑 Trigger words: limits of their own authority; rightfully others'; who decides?; for Parliament, not the courts

12.1.1 A role's limits come from a theory of the role

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS
  1. The statement assumes we know where roles end. For George, sharing out authority is a determinatio: a prudent choice among options that are all morally acceptable.
  2. Tan Seow Hon's reply is the question George leaves open: who rightfully decides whether the choice was prudently made?
  3. So the phrase what is rightfully others' assumes its own answer. The limits of a role come from a theory of the role.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Euthanasia Case

A terminally ill man asks Ruritania's top court to declare that the ban on assisted suicide breaches his right to life and liberty. The government says that whether to allow assisted dying is rightfully for Parliament and not the courts.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Work through the three points.

  • George. How a society divides authority between courts and Parliament is a determinatio. There are several morally acceptable ways to do it, and the choice is one of prudence. Natural law does not dictate it.
  • Tan Seow Hon's question. But who decides whether that division was prudently made? When the government says it is rightfully for Parliament, it assumes the answer.
  • So the court needs a theory of its role. Is the court there to protect individuals against majorities on fundamental rights, or to defer on contested moral questions? Only then can it say what is rightfully for Parliament.

12.1.2 STEELMAN: Rajeevan and YVK

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

The strongest case for the other side.

  • Rajeevan (11.5): the legislature rightly determines individual rights, when there are no specific guarantees.
  • Yong Vui Kong (2015), citing George: some have argued that natural law requires judges to respect the boundaries of authority.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

The government's best case is that Singapore's courts themselves have adopted this deference. Rajeevan gives Parliament the lead on rights the Constitution does not specifically guarantee. Yong Vui Kong even notes the natural-law argument for judges keeping within their bounds. So deference is not against natural law.

12.1.3 CONCEDE: TSH's impasse

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

A concession. Tan Seow Hon's impasse binds my side too. Natural law condemns giving authority to a random group of bandits, but it cannot say who decides. Still, she says the condition, despite the impasse, must be right in principle.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

If you argue that the court may override Parliament at extreme injustice, concede that natural law cannot tell you exactly who should decide hard cases. It only rules out the absurd, such as handing power to bandits. But George's condition, to respect role limits only in a basically just regime, is right in principle. In an unjust regime, deference loses its basis.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

respect the limits of their own authority; leave to others what is rightfully theirs; who decides?; for Parliament, not the courts.

312.2 Twin vices: usurpation and abdication

📘 Learn 12.2 in Lesson 12 →
🔑 Trigger words: usurp; leave it to Parliament; non-enforcement; just focus on the law

12.2.1 Every role can fail twice

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS
  1. Every role can fail in two ways: by doing others' work (usurpation) or by refusing its own (abdication). The statement names only the first.
  2. Tan Seow Hon names both for judges. Acting in bad faith, they would either legislate from the bench, or rubber-stamp whatever law Parliament passes.
  3. So respecting the limits of your role is half the duty. The other half is doing the role's own moral work.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Two Judges
  • Judge Ang strikes down a tax law because she thinks a flat tax is fairer.
  • Judge Bala upholds every law that comes before him, including one letting police detain anyone indefinitely without charge. He says it is not his place.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Compare the two judges.

  • Ang usurps. She does Parliament's work by deciding tax policy.
  • Bala abdicates. He refuses the court's own work, which is to check laws against the Constitution and against intolerable injustice.
  • The lesson. The statement warns only against Ang's error. Tan Seow Hon names both failings: legislating from the bench, and rubber-stamping. Respecting your limits is only half of doing your job well.

12.2.2 The twin vices by role

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS
RoleThe sheet's exampleMade-up twistWhat it shows
The officialSection 377A (2007) was kept but not actively enforced. Arguably Parliament abdicated and the executive made law in all but name (7.7).Ruritania's Parliament keeps a law it will not defend, and the Attorney-General announces that it will not be prosecuted.Parliament avoided deciding (abdication), and the executive in effect changed the law by announcement (usurpation).
The judgeBridge's unwarranted abdication (McLoughlin, page 441; 9.2).A judge refuses a new kind of claim only because no earlier case has allowed it.Refusing to develop the law when principle requires it is abdication.
The lawyerScreening clients usurps (Pepper). Just focusing on the law abdicates (Thunder).One lawyer refuses all clients whose politics she dislikes. Another drafts anything lawful without a thought.The first takes over the job of courts and Parliament in deciding who gets the law's help (usurpation, on Pepper's view). The second gives up his own moral agency (abdication, on Thunder's view).
🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

usurp; leave it to Parliament; non-enforcement; just focus on the law.

412.3 The legislator's hat

📘 Learn 12.3 in Lesson 12 →
🔑 Trigger words: majoritarian will; sole concern; as accurately as possible; poll; referendum; whip

12.3.1 Trustee, not stenographer

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS
  1. Majority will settles who may make law in a democracy. It does not settle what the law is or what it should say.
  2. Devlin, the statement's natural ally, tells law-makers that majority opinion is surely not enough. His standard does not depend on counting heads.
  3. So the legislator does what the words sole concern forbid. A legislator judges, as a trustee, and does not simply take dictation.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The MP's Pledge

A new MP pledges that the MP's sole concern is to reflect the voters' will as accurately as possible, and to vote however the latest constituency poll says, on every bill.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Work through the MP's pledge.

  • Majority will has a role. It explains why this MP is the one who gets to vote. It does not say how to vote on a bill to, say, cut legal aid.
  • Even Devlin. The MP might cite Devlin. But Devlin says counting heads is not enough. Legislators must judge what is truly beyond the limits of tolerance.
  • So the MP is a trustee. The MP must use judgment on the voters' behalf, and not simply copy down a poll.

12.3.2 STEELMAN, LEGISLATOR and QUALIFY

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS
  • The strongest case for the other side. Equal respect when people disagree, and a fear of rule by judges (Tan Seow Hon). Poa (2022) sought a referendum, because marriage is a matter of social norm.
  • The legislator. Masagos told Poa in 2022 that MPs must come to a decision, even and perhaps especially on difficult and polarising social issues.
  • A qualification. Tan Seow Hon says legislators who do not follow natural law may not regard themselves as bound by higher standards. Liu says that need not does not mean will not. A legislator who wants good laws, and not merely valid ones, weighs morality (the minimum content in 14.4; Hart against Devlin). Legal positivism uses morality in one dimension (good law). Natural law uses it in two (good law, and law at all).
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

The MP, facing a divisive bill on the definition of marriage, says this is a social norm, and proposes a referendum. A minister replies that MPs must decide hard questions themselves. A third MP, a positivist, says that because law need not be moral, that MP is not bound by any higher standard.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Take each speaker in turn.

  • The referendum idea has a real basis: treating citizens as equals when they disagree, and preferring the people to judges. That is Poa's argument.
  • The minister's reply is Masagos's. MPs are elected precisely to decide hard and polarising issues, and not to hand them back.
  • The positivist MP is right that a positivist need not treat any higher standard as binding on what counts as law. But that does not mean a positivist will not weigh morality. A legislator who wants good laws, and not merely valid ones, must weigh it, just as Hart did in arguing against Devlin. The difference is that positivists use morality in one dimension: is it a good law? Natural lawyers use it in two: is it a good law, and is it law at all?
🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

majoritarian will; the legislator's sole concern; as accurately as possible; a poll; a referendum; the whip.

512.4 The judge's hat

📘 Learn 12.4 in Lesson 12 →
🔑 Trigger words: if passed, would you enforce it?; strike down; refuse; validly passed; applying the law

12.4.1 The judge's ladder

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS
  1. The judge asks what the law is and what fidelity to it requires. The judge does not ask whether the law is wise.
  2. Climb a ladder:
    1. validity;
    2. then interpretation by principle and purpose;
    3. then discretion within the statute;
    4. refusal only at the Radbruch threshold.
  3. So saying I would enforce it is a moral conclusion, reached through a theory of the judicial role. It is not an escape from morality.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Curfew for Under-16s

Ruritania passes a law saying no person under 16 may be in a public place after 10 pm. Breach is punishable by a fine of up to $1,000, payable by the child. Judge Lee thinks the law is unwise. A 15-year-old is charged for walking home from a late hospital visit to her mother.

✔ APPLICATION · Up the ladderDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Climb one rung at a time.

  1. Validity. It was properly passed, and it is constitutional on its face.
  2. Interpretation. Read by principle and purpose, which is to keep children safe and not to punish necessity, does in a public place cover a child walking straight home from a hospital? A reading based on purpose may exclude it.
  3. Discretion. If it does apply, the statute says up to $1,000, so the judge can impose a very small fine.
  4. Refusal? The law is unwise, but nowhere near intolerable injustice. So refusal is off the table.

So Judge Lee enforces the law, gently. And that decision rests on a moral theory of the judicial role: fidelity to valid law, read by its purpose.

12.4.2 Kennedy's five courses

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

Kennedy's five courses (15.10):

  • He does not endorse or exclude any of them in advance.
  • The public's devil's compact is that the judge will defend the decision as plausibly legal, change it, or withdraw. This assumes a certainty in the law that insiders know is false.
  • He finds it unconvincing that the rule of law means obeying it.

Candour, my own standard, rules out his last two, which are covert. The refusal line is genocide and slavery. It does not include Roe.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

Judge Lee, a crit like Kennedy, wants the girl acquitted, but the legal field will not budge: the words plainly cover her. The options are:

  1. apply the law, and write an opinion denouncing it;
  2. withdraw from the case;
  3. acquit, saying openly that the law is wrong;
  4. acquit using an argument the judge thinks implausible;
  5. find, falsely, that the girl was not in a public place.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Go through the options.

  • Kennedy refuses to rule any of these in or out in advance. He thinks the public's picture, that the judge must show the law supports the decision, change it, or step aside, assumes the law is more certain than insiders know it is.
  • A standard of candour rules out options 4 and 5, because both are covert: a bad-faith argument, and a false finding.
  • The refusal line. Option 3 is open only at the Radbruch threshold, such as genocide and slavery. A curfew, or issues of the Roe kind, do not reach it.
  • So Judge Lee should take option 1, or perhaps option 2.

12.4.3 CONCEDE: TSH's catch

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

A concession: Tan Seow Hon's own catch. Concede the risk. For her reply, see 8.5.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

If consensus decides where the refusal line falls, consensus could one day move it somewhere mistaken. Concede that. Then use Tan Seow Hon's reply (8.5.3): any other decision-maker is no more reliable.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

if passed, would you enforce it?; strike it down; refuse; it was validly passed; I'm only applying the law.

612.5 The official's and the junior's hat

📘 Learn 12.5 in Lesson 12 →
🔑 Trigger words: officials tasked with enforcing; lawful instructions; superiors; junior; deference
▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS
  1. Officials owe fidelity to law, and not deference to rank. Fuller warns against confusing mere respect for those in authority with fidelity to law.
  2. In a rogue state, Alexy's risk effect reaches a judge or other office-holder who is neither a saint nor a hero. If non-positivism prevails, that person risks later prosecution.
  3. So obeying lawful instructions is not blameless. As Thunder says, simply pointing to the role gives up on explaining it.

Also on the sheet:

  • A concession. Thunder accepts that virtue does not settle every case (10.5). So start with dialogue, and refuse only at the extreme.
  • Thunder's librarian, who mistreats customers under official library policies, cannot plead the role.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Clerk Jurić, Again

Under the Junta, clerk Jurić (8.4) is ordered by his superior to stamp seizure orders confiscating the Kel minority's property. He is no hero. He just wants to keep his job.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Work through what Jurić owes.

  • Fidelity is not deference. Jurić owes fidelity to law, and not obedience to whoever outranks him. Respecting authority is a different thing.
  • The risk effect. Alexy's point is aimed at ordinary office-holders like Jurić, who is neither a saint nor a hero. If non-positivism becomes the accepted view, then after the Junta falls, the seizure orders may be held never to have been law, and Jurić may face prosecution. That prospect gives him a reason to refuse now.
  • Saying I was just doing my job explains nothing. As Thunder says, pointing to your role does not explain why the role justifies what you did.
  • The concession. Thunder admits that being virtuous does not settle every case. So for a less extreme instruction, Jurić should raise concerns first, and refuse only at the extreme.
  • Thunder's librarian. A librarian who is rude to customers because official library policies say so cannot hide behind the role either. Roles shape how you act, but they do not excuse acting badly.
🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

officials tasked with enforcing; lawful instructions; superiors; a junior; deference.

712.6 The two-hats problem frame

📘 Learn 12.6 in Lesson 12 →
🔑 Trigger words: a bill proposes; would you vote for it?; if passed, would you enforce it?; Ruritania
▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS
  1. As an MP, I would vote against the bill and propose narrower measures. As a judge, I would apply it if validly enacted, refusing only at the Radbruch threshold.
  2. The scope of the bill does the damage. It reaches consumption as well as sale and, because it is without exception, it catches communion and temple wine.
  3. The answers differ because the roles ask different moral questions: what the law should be, and what fidelity to it requires.

The grounds, put at their strongest and then tested:

GroundAt its strongestTest, then verdict
FaithAddiction undermines practical reasonablenessDenying worship normally breaks reciprocity. Faith gets a voice but is not a ground.
HarmHart accepts paternalismIt protects buyers. So license, and do not jail.
Poll85% at least somewhat support itThat is not Devlin's real feeling of disapproval (page 17). It is evidence and not a mandate.

Also on the sheet:

  • Yaacob Ibrahim said in 2005 that drinking and other activities Muslims consider vices are not banned. The critics' teetotallers show that which offence counts is chosen morally.
  • The judge. Read literally, Article 15(4) has no necessity test (Tan Seow Hon), so a challenge to the law as applied is weak. The law is harsh but not intolerable, because no broad historical consensus condemns prohibition. So apply it.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Ruritanian Prohibition Bill

A bill in Ruritania proposes that the sale and consumption of alcohol be prohibited, without exception. Breach is punishable by up to two years in prison. Its supporters cite:

  • a faith that teaches drinking is sinful;
  • the harm alcohol causes;
  • a poll showing 85% at least somewhat support it.

The question is this: as an MP, would you vote for it? As a judge, if it passed, would you enforce it?

✔ APPLICATION · As MP: vote against, and propose narrower measuresDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Take each ground in turn, and then the fix.

  • Faith. At its strongest, addiction does undermine practical reasonableness, a basic good. But a faith's teaching cannot by itself justify coercing citizens who do not share it. And the bill would stop other faiths' worship, such as communion wine and temple offerings, which normally breaks reciprocity. The faith gets a voice in the debate, but it is not a ground for the law.
  • Harm. At its strongest, Hart accepts paternalism. But Hart's paternalism protects buyers whose consent may be impaired. That supports licensing and controlling sale, and it does not support jailing drinkers.
  • Poll. At its strongest, 85% is a lot. But somewhat supporting a bill is not Devlin's real feeling of disapproval, and a poll is evidence and not a mandate (7.11).
  • A Singapore comparison. In 2005, Singapore's minister Yaacob Ibrahim noted that drinking and other activities Muslims consider vices are not banned. And the offence teetotallers take at drinking is one the law chooses to ignore. That shows that which offences count is a moral choice (7.2.3).
  • The fix. Use licensing hours, taxes, drink-driving laws, and an exemption for religious use.
✔ APPLICATION · As judge: apply it, if validly enactedDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

The judge asks a different question.

  • Article 15. A church could bring a challenge to the law as applied to it. But read literally, Article 15(4) has no necessity test, so the claim is weak.
  • The Radbruch formula. Prohibition is harsh, but no broad historical consensus condemns it as intolerable. So refusal is not justified.
  • The result. The judge applies it, reading it as narrowly as its words allow.

Why the answers differ. The MP asks what the law should be. The judge asks what fidelity to a valid law requires. Different roles ask different moral questions.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

a bill proposes…; would you vote for it?; if passed, would you enforce it?; Ruritania.

812.7 Conclusion, applied

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

The conclusion. No role ends moral duty. The statement is right that roles have limits. But drawing those limits is itself a moral judgment, and the vice is not only taking others' work but also refusing your own.

✔ APPLICATION · Applied to the hyposDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Here is where each part of the conclusion was shown.

  • Roles have limits: Judge Ang (12.2.1).
  • Drawing them is moral: the Euthanasia Case (12.1.1).
  • Refusing your own work is a vice: Judge Bala (12.2.1) and the MP who only copies down polls (12.3.1).
  • No role ends moral duty: Clerk Jurić (12.5), and the MP and the judge on the Prohibition Bill (12.6).
