⚡ BIG IDEA

The same few distinctions come back in every topic. The Core cards (Core version) turn them into four ready-made answers.

How to work through a hypo
  1. 1Read the rule (teal box). It puts the sheet's point in plain words. The exact wording to use in the exam is in the Lessons and Sheet tabs.
  2. 2Read the hypothetical (amber box). Before reading on, decide what the rule says about these facts.
  3. 3Tap Application (green box) and compare it with your answer.
  4. 4The exam cue (violet box) lists question words that should send you to this block. Each block ends with a quick check.
Applications:
ℹ NOTE
About these hypos

Each block on this page has three parts: the rule in plain words, a made-up set of facts, and a worked answer. Your exact sheet wording, with its quotations, is still in the Lessons and Sheet tabs.

  • 13.1 and 13.2 (comparisons and current controversies) are in both versions.
  • 13.3 to 13.6 (Core cards A to D) are in the Core version only.

For the comparison rows, one scenario shows what the two theorists share and where they split. For the Core-card statements (P1 to P6, Q1 to Q6, L1 to L6), each example is an exam-style statement with a concrete issue. The worked answer gives the card's verdict, how each theorist lines up, and where to look.

Some terms come up throughout. Legal positivism says whether something is law depends on its source and not on its merit. Natural law theory ties law to what is morally good. The Radbruch formula says a statute stops being law once its injustice is intolerable. TSH is Tan Seow Hon. A dagger (†) marks a point from the slides. The coverage table is the last section.

113.1 Comparisons

13.1.1 LP v Rawls: pluralism

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS
  • What they share. Both set contested morals to one side. Legal positivism finds law in its sources. Rawls finds legitimacy in shared political values.
  • Where they split. Neither is neutral. Acceptance is the test for legal positivism, and the word reasonable is Rawls's filter. Finnis adds that some basic rights have one right answer.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL

A religious minority objects to a new Ruritanian law requiring all schools to teach evolution.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Compare the two approaches.

  • Legal positivism says the law was validly enacted, so it is law, and whether it is wise is another question. That sets morality to one side.
  • Rawls says it is legitimate if justified by public reasons, such as scientific literacy for citizens. That sets full doctrines to one side.
  • Neither is neutral. The positivist's verdict rests on choosing official acceptance as the test (2.1.2). Rawls's rests on whom he counts as reasonable (6.11).
  • Finnis would add that on some basic rights there is one right answer, and setting it aside is not fair.

13.1.2 Autonomy: Mill, Hart, Finnis, Pepper

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS
  • What they share. All four value autonomy, and all four limit it. Mill limits it by harm to others. Pepper's idea of first-class citizenship serves it.
  • Where they split. Hart allows some paternalism. Finnis limits autonomy by practical reasonableness. Pepper limits it by law alone, and not by the lawyer's morality, except in extreme cases.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL

An adult wants to sell his kidney, and asks his lawyer to draft the contract.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Take each writer in turn.

  • Mill. It is his body and his choice, unless others are harmed.
  • Hart. Desperate sellers may have defective consent, so restricting the sale is justified paternalism.
  • Finnis. Autonomy is used well only within practical reasonableness. Selling a kidney for cash may treat a basic good, life and bodily integrity, as a mere means.
  • Pepper. If it is lawful, the lawyer drafts it. Only the law limits the client, and not the lawyer's morals, except in extreme cases.

13.1.3 Kennedy v the chain novel

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS
  • What they share. Both put the judge inside inherited materials. Fit and value constrain Dworkin's judge. Work and the risk to credibility constrain Kennedy's.
  • Where they split. Kennedy starts from how he wants the case to come out, and Dworkin starts from the text (Liu, Week 11). Kennedy answers the claim that there is always a right answer with his felt sense of openness and of free ethical or political choice, and he does not claim a verdict.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL

A judge hears a case on whether striking workers may block a factory gate.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Compare the two judges.

  • Both must work with forty years of picketing cases.
  • Dworkin's judge reads them to find the principle that best fits and justifies them.
  • Kennedy's judge decides first that the workers should win, and then works the cases towards that result, paying in effort and credibility.
  • Where they part. Kennedy reports moments when the law felt truly open and he chose freely. He will not claim that his account is the right one.

13.1.4 Fuller v the RF

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS
  • What they share. Both deny that enactment alone settles whether something is law. Fuller tests form. The Radbruch formula tests content.
  • Where they split. Fuller grades by degree, so an unclear statute is less a law. The Radbruch formula strikes down only intolerable injustice.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL

Valdoria's Junta passes (a) a vaguely worded ban on disloyal attitudes, and (b) a clear decree confiscating a minority's homes.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Each test catches a different law.

  • Fuller says (a) is less a law, because no one can follow it. He has less to say about (b), because its form is fine.
  • The Radbruch formula passes over the vagueness of (a), but strikes down (b) if its injustice is intolerable.
  • Both reject the view that it was enacted, so it is law, and that is the end of it.

13.1.5 Religious freedom: Finnis v Rawls

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS
  • What they share. Both protect religious freedom, and neither does so neutrally. Finnis protects it as a basic good. Rawls protects it as equal liberty of conscience.
  • Where they split. Rawls takes the truths of religion off the political agenda. Finnis values the search for answers, whatever the answer.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL

A sect asks for an exemption from compulsory schooling, so that it can teach children at home in its scriptures.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Both start out sympathetic.

  • Rawls protects the sect's liberty of conscience without asking whether its beliefs are true. Religion's truth is off the agenda. But children's education as future citizens is a political value that may limit the exemption.
  • Finnis protects the sect because seeking answers about ultimate questions is a basic good, even if the answers are agnostic or negative. But he would also weigh the children's own good of knowledge.

13.1.6 Whose morality (obscenity, immoral contracts)?

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS
  • What they share. It must be more than the judge's personal preference:
    • Devlin's right-minded person;
    • Hart's critical morality (Devlin too invokes a critical principle);
    • the objective morality of natural law.
  • Where they split.
    • Devlin looks to honest belief, right or wrong.
    • Tan Seow Hon's second option, not favoured in Rajeevan, lets judges filter out incoherent opinions.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL

A court must decide whether a contract to pay for a companion is void as contrary to public morals.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

None of the theorists lets the judge use personal taste.

  • Devlin's judge asks what the right-minded person honestly believes, right or wrong.
  • Hart asks whether a critical principle justifies making it void.
  • Natural law asks what objective morality requires.
  • Tan Seow Hon's alternative lets the judge set aside popular opinions that are incoherent. Singapore's Rajeevan did not favour that option.

13.1.7 Finnis v liberalism

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS
  • What they share. The common good is a set of conditions, and the state's role is only to keep peace and justice.
  • Where they split. Finnis is not neutral. He says reason requires us to favour the basic forms of good. He is liberal in means, and not in ends.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL

Port Meridian considers funding public libraries and taxing casinos heavily.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Look at what they agree on, and why they differ.

  • A liberal and Finnis agree that the state should create conditions, such as libraries and order, in which citizens pursue their own lives, without making them good.
  • But Finnis openly favours knowledge (libraries) and discourages what damages the goods (heavy casino taxes) because they are good or bad. A neutral liberal would need another reason. That is the sense in which Finnis is liberal in means and not in ends.

13.1.8 Finnis v Fuller

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS
  • What they share. They complement each other. Fuller covers procedure, and Finnis covers substance (Liu, Week 5).
  • Where they split. For Finnis, law treats people as partners in public reason through promulgation, clarity, generality and stability. And Finnis can condemn punitive retroactivity by its effects.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL

Ruritania retroactively raises penalties for a tax offence.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

They reach the same place by different routes.

  • Fuller condemns it as a breach of the inner morality of law.
  • Finnis agrees that law must treat citizens as partners in public reason, which is essentially Fuller's list. He can also condemn the law by its effects on the goods of those punished. Procedure and substance work together.

13.1.9 Fuller v Hart on validity

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS
  • What they share. They are compatible.
  • Where they split. Fuller tests form. Hart takes what officials accept, so Ordinance 11 may pass (Liu, Week 10).
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL

The Junta's published, clear Citizenship Ordinance (8.3).

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Here the two come out alike.

  • Hart. Officials accepted it, so it was law, though too evil to obey.
  • Fuller. A clear, published, general ordinance passes his tests of form, so he cannot easily deny that it was law.
  • So the two are compatible here. Both may call it law. It is the Radbruch formula that would deny it.

13.1.10 Hart v Devlin

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS
  • What they share. Both usually spare private acts (7.3).
  • Where they split. They are not fully reconciled. Devlin can punish what meets none of Hart's grounds. An example is cruelty to animals, a law that Hart explains by the animals' suffering (Liu, Week 9).
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL

A man privately tortures his own pet, and no one sees.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Compare their reasons.

  • Devlin. It is beyond the limits of tolerance, even in private, so it may be punished.
  • Hart. It is not harm to other people, not paternalism and not public offence. But he explains the cruelty law by the animal's suffering, so he agrees with the result for a different reason.
  • Where they would split. On private conduct that disgusts but harms no one, not even an animal, Devlin could punish and Hart could not.

13.1.11 Devlin v Rawls and Finnis

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS
  • What they share. Shared ground, and reasonable judgment.
  • Where they split. Rawls needs only enough overlap, while Devlin needs deep agreement. Devlin's reasonable person feels. Finnis's reasons (Liu, Week 7).
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL

A society of many faiths debates banning gambling.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Compare what each one needs.

  • Rawls needs only enough common ground for a political idea of justice.
  • Devlin needs a deep shared morality, and a society of many faiths may not have one.
  • Devlin's reasonable person reacts with feeling, such as disgust. Finnis's reasonable person reasons from the basic goods. They might reach the same verdict on gambling by very different routes.

213.2 Current controversies

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS
  • The repeal of section 377A and Article 156 (2022)†. Section 377A was repealed, and Article 156 shielded laws on marriage between a man and a woman from Part 4 of the Constitution, both from 3 January 2023. In theory terms, this is the coercion gradient. Punishment was withdrawn, and marriage was promoted (15.7, 7.9, 11.6).
  • A qualification. Hart's lines survive. Non-consensual acts, acts with young persons and public indecency stay crimes. Only private consensual conduct between adults is freed (Shanmugam, 2022). For Liu's exercises, see 16.5.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Columnist's Two Claims

A columnist writes that the 2022 package means the law no longer cares about sexual morality at all.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

The columnist is wrong in two ways.

  • Wrong that the law no longer cares. On the coercion gradient (7.9), the state stopped punishing private consensual conduct, but moved to promoting a view of marriage (Article 156). That is a change in the kind of enforcement, and not an end to it.
  • Wrong to say at all. Hart's lines remain in the criminal law. Non-consensual acts, acts with minors, and public indecency are still crimes. Only private consensual conduct between adults was freed.
  • For the theorist exercises, see 16.5.
ℹ NOTE
Core cards

The next four sections are in the Core version only.

313.3 Core A: law-making and morality

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

For questions about legislators.

The spine. No law on a moral question is neutral. Permitting, punishing and promoting all take a stand. So pluralism cannot mean neutrality. It means discipline in three things:

  • reasons: open to every citizen, and sound on the merits;
  • coercion: matched to the strength of those reasons;
  • forum: the legislature decides, as a trustee, and does not just take dictation.

13.3.0 Flaws F1–F4: how to attack a statement

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS
FlawSignal wordsWhat to do
F1: a gap in the reasoningtherefore, however, only then, lestFix on the linking word, and draw the distinction that shows the step does not follow.
F2: an absoluteonly, all, simply, mustFix on the word, and restate it as a condition.
F3: it refutes itselfnoneApply the statement to itself once, and number the steps.
F4: one word, two meaningsnoneConcede one meaning, and go conditional on the other.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
A Statement with All Four Flaws

All moral opinions are equally valid; therefore the state must remain neutral, and only harm to others can ever justify coercion. Legislators must simply follow what society thinks.

✔ APPLICATION · Flaw by flawDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Take the flaws one at a time.

  • F1, a gap: fix on therefore. Even if opinions were equally valid, it does not follow that the state can be neutral. Tell apart the two ideas: equal validity of opinions, and equal respect for persons.
  • F2, an absolute: fix on only, must and simply. Turn each into a condition. Harm to others is a strong presumption, but it is not the only ground. Society's view is evidence legislators should weigh, and it is not an instruction.
  • F3, it refutes itself: apply the statement to itself, once, and number the steps. (1) If all moral opinions are equally valid, then so is the opinion that the state should not be neutral. (2) So the statement's own demand for neutrality has no special claim.
  • F4, one word with two meanings: what society thinks. Concede one meaning, that legislators should listen to public opinion. Then go conditional on the other: if it means the majority's view must decide, that confuses who decides with what is right.

13.3.1 P1 The state should be neutral

🔑 Trigger words: not endorse moral values; take no side; fixed conception; moral truth
▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

The verdict. Neutrality of outcome is impossible, and even Rawls's neutrality of justification rests on moral values. The part that can be defended is narrower. The state should not make one full doctrine official, or use force on reasons that only its followers can accept.

How each one lines up:

  • Hart: partly;
  • Devlin: rejects;
  • Rawls: partly; the natural ally, but in the weak form only;
  • Finnis: rejects the strong form, accepts a limit.

See 6.2, 7.5 and 6.10.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL

The state should never endorse moral values. On surrogacy, it should take no side.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Work through the statement.

  • Neutrality of outcome is impossible. Allowing or banning surrogacy takes a side either way (6.0).
  • Even Rawls's neutrality of justification rests on values such as fairness and equality.
  • What survives. Ruritania must not make one faith's view of the family the official doctrine, or ban surrogacy on reasons that only that faith accepts.
  • The theorists. Rawls is the closest ally, in the weak form. Devlin would reject the idea. Hart would agree only partly, because he still defends critical moral principles. Finnis rejects strong neutrality, but accepts that the state should not impose a full plan of life.

13.3.2 P2 Moral opinions are equally valid

🔑 Trigger words: equally valid; denial of moral truth; suspension of judgment; skeptical
▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

The verdict. Equal validity defeats itself and cannot deliver the tolerance it promises. What survives is fallibility, the fact that we may be wrong. That calls for deliberation, provisional judgment and caution in using force. It does not call for silence.

How each one lines up:

  • Hart: rejects;
  • Devlin: partly; a dangerous ally;
  • Rawls: partly (on Liu's reading);
  • Finnis: rejects, but not in favour of a single right answer on everything.

See 4.2 and 4.7.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL

On euthanasia, all moral opinions are equally valid, so Parliament should suspend judgment.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Work through the statement.

  • It defeats itself. If all opinions are equally valid, then the view that Parliament should suspend judgment is no more valid than the view that Parliament should ban it (4.2).
  • What survives is fallibility. Parliament should deliberate, decide provisionally, and be cautious about using the criminal law. It should not be silent.
  • The theorists.
    • Devlin is a dangerous ally. His cultural relativism treats each society's morality as valid for it, which supports enforcing the majority's view and not tolerance.
    • Rawls partly fits. On Liu's reading, he treats reasonable doctrines as equally entitled in politics.
    • Hart and Finnis reject it, though Finnis allows a range of reasonable answers.

13.3.3 P3 Only harm to others justifies coercion

🔑 Trigger words: only; protect others; wrongdoer; objectively necessary
▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

The verdict. Harm to others is the right presumption for punishment. But it is not the only ground, and it is not a neutral fact. What counts as harm, and who counts as another person, are moral questions.

How each one lines up:

  • Hart: partly;
  • Devlin: rejects;
  • Rawls: it is the wrong test;
  • Finnis: partly; a ground, but not the only one, and no ban on everything that fails to pursue a good.

See 7.1, 7.2 and 6.10.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL

Only harm to others justifies coercing a wrongdoer. So the state cannot restrict the sale of veridine (7.0).

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Work through the statement.

  • The right presumption, but not the only ground. Hart himself adds paternalism, which justifies restricting sale to protect buyers whose consent is defective (7.2).
  • It is not neutral. Is a user's family another person for this purpose? Is a public hospital?
  • The theorists.
    • Rawls would say the test is wrong in kind. The question is whether the reasons are public, and not whether there is harm.
    • Finnis accepts harm as one ground but not the only one, and he would not ban everything that fails to pursue a good.
    • Devlin rejects the test of harm alone entirely.

13.3.4 P4 A right to decide intimate matters

🔑 Trigger words: fundamental decisions; own destinies; intimate relationships; child rearing; private behaviour
▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

The verdict. The right is real, but it is itself a moral claim with moral limits. It rules out punishing private consensual conduct for its immorality alone. It does not rule out regulation or promotion. And it cannot settle cases where a third party, the child or the unborn, is at stake.

How each one lines up:

  • Hart: largely agrees;
  • Devlin: rejects in principle, often agrees in practice;
  • Rawls: partly;
  • Finnis: partly.

See 4.5 and 7.9.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL

Everyone has a right to decide intimate matters, including how to raise their children, so the state may not require vaccination or schooling.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Work through the statement.

  • The right is real where only the adults are concerned. The state should not jail them for private consensual choices.
  • But it is a moral claim (4.5), and it stops where a third party is at stake. The child's health and education are the child's own goods.
  • Regulation and promotion remain open. The state can require schooling, which is regulation, and run vaccination campaigns, which is promotion.
  • The theorists.
    • Hart largely agrees with the core.
    • Devlin rejects it in principle, but would usually leave private adult conduct alone in practice.
    • Rawls and Finnis each accept part.

13.3.5 P5 Majority or societal morality

🔑 Trigger words: majority; majoritarian will; certain groups; minority rights; poll
▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

The verdict. The majority settles who decides, and not what is right. Majority feeling is evidence to weigh, and never the reason that settles the law. And protecting minorities is itself a moral judgment, and not an escape from one.

How each one lines up:

  • Hart: rejects it as a reason;
  • Devlin, the natural ally, refuses to count heads;
  • Rawls: rejects;
  • Finnis: rejects, from the other side.

See 7.3, 7.11 and 12.3.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL

A poll shows 70% oppose a minority group's festival in a public park, so the law should ban it.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Work through the statement.

  • The majority decides who makes law, through elections. It does not decide whether a ban is right.
  • The poll is evidence, and not a mandate (7.11).
  • Protecting the minority is a moral judgment about equal respect, so it is not neutral either.
  • The theorists.
    • Devlin, the supposed ally, refuses to count heads (7.3).
    • Hart and Rawls reject majority feeling as a reason.
    • Finnis rejects it, because the question is what is truly good and not what most people think.

13.3.6 P6 Enforcing morality is (il)legitimate

🔑 Trigger words: legislating morals; unjust; illegitimate; intractable moral conflicts
▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

The verdict. Enforcing morality is not illegitimate as such, because every law enforces some morality. What can make it unjust is the reasons used, the coercion chosen, and who bears it. So the limits are moral and prudential, and they do not come from scepticism.

How each one lines up:

  • Hart: partly;
  • Devlin: agrees;
  • Rawls: partly;
  • Finnis: agrees.

See 7.5 and 7.9.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL

Legislating morality is illegitimate, because moral conflicts cannot be resolved. So Ruritania should not make cruelty to animals a crime.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Work through the statement.

  • Every law enforces some morality. An animal cruelty law enforces the view that animals' suffering matters. So the claim that legislating morality is illegitimate proves too much.
  • The real question. Are the reasons open to all and sound? On animals' suffering, yes. Is the coercion proportionate? Who bears it?
  • Conflicts that cannot be resolved call for restraint. They do not call for doing nothing.
  • The theorists. Devlin and Finnis agree that enforcing morality is legitimate in principle. Hart and Rawls accept parts of the claim.

13.3.7 Pivots and repaired statements (Core A)

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

Pivots.

  • Neutrality is impossible (6.5, 7.5).
  • The coercion gradient (7.9).
  • Majority is not legitimacy (7.11, 12.3).
  • Scepticism answered (4.7).
  • Fixed is a matter of degree. No theorist imposes one complete plan of life, and every theorist fixes some limits.

Repaired statements (use one per script):

ThemeRepaired statement
NeutralityLegislators should treat all citizens, not all opinions, as equal, and coerce only on reasons every citizen can examine.
HarmLegislators should presume against punishing conduct that harms no one else, and need stronger reasons the more coercive the law.
AutonomyChoices about one's intimate life deserve strong protection from punishment, but not immunity from all regulation, or from the state's promotion of other goods.
MajorityThe majority decides, but must decide on reasons it can defend to the minority.
EnforcementEnforcing morality is legitimate when its reasons are accessible and sound and its coercion proportionate. Scepticism is no objection, but fallibility is a reason for restraint.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL

The statement is: The state must not impose a fixed conception of the good life.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Use a pivot and then a repaired statement.

  • Pivot on the word fixed. No theorist imposes a complete plan of life, as even Finnis's state is a framework. And every theorist fixes some limits, as even Mill bans harm to others. So fixed is a matter of degree.
  • Close with the repaired neutrality line from the table above.

413.4 Core B: judges, lawyers and morality

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

For questions about judges and lawyers.

The spine. No judge or lawyer works without theory or morality:

  • identifying the law is already an evaluation;
  • hard cases turn on rival theories of the grounds of law;
  • every role is justified by what it is for.

But that does not make legal work mere preference or private conscience. Morality is:

  • always presupposed;
  • operative at the margins, meaning in hard cases and at intolerable injustice;
  • disciplined by role: fit and candour for judges, and the law as a floor for lawyers.

13.4.1 Q1 Judges only apply the law

🔑 Trigger words: no substantive moral judgments; only what the law is; I just apply the law
▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

The verdict. Morality is always presupposed in judging, and sometimes operative. It is presupposed in legality, and in every claim that a ruling is correct. It is operative in hard cases and at intolerable injustice. A judge concerned only with what the law is already holds a theory of what law is.

How each one lines up:

  • Hart: partly agrees;
  • Dworkin: rejects;
  • the realists: reject, for a different reason;
  • Tan Seow Hon: rejects for constitutional cases.

See 9.8, 11.2 and 11.3.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL

The statement is that judges make no substantive moral judgments and decide only what the law is. Test it on Judge Ng's two cases (9.8): a parking fine, and the insurance claim by a son who assaulted his mother.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Test it on each case.

  • The parking fine. Morality is presupposed, in deferring to clear rules, but it does not decide the case.
  • The insurance claim. This is a hard case, where moral principle helps decide.
  • The theorists.
    • Hart partly agrees, because most cases are core cases.
    • Dworkin rejects it, because law is interpretive all the way down.
    • The realists reject it, because they think judges decide on preference anyway.
    • Tan Seow Hon rejects it for constitutional cases, where law, equal and liberty carry moral content (11.2, 11.3).

13.4.2 Q2 Adjudication is politics

🔑 Trigger words: politics; pretence; rules don't decide; essentially
▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

The verdict. Judging is political in Dworkin's sense. Where fit runs out, judges choose between principles of political morality. It is not politics in the party sense that the word pretence needs. Rules leave some cases open, but not all, and judges must justify and cannot simply predict.

How each one lines up:

  • the realists: partly;
  • Unger and the crits: agree in part;
  • Kennedy: partly; the most honest witness;
  • Dworkin: rejects the party-political reading.

See 9.1, 9.3 and 9.7.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL

The statement is that judging is essentially politics, and that legal reasoning is a pretence. Test it on Suri's case (9.3, 9.7).

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Test it on Suri's case.

  • Political in Dworkin's sense. Choosing between freedom of contract and fairness is a choice of political principle.
  • Not party politics. Judge A justified the choice publicly by fit and value, and did not pretend.
  • And many cases are not open at all, such as the speeding driver (9.0).
  • The theorists.
    • Kennedy is the most honest witness. He admits his politics, but shows how much work and risk the law imposes.
    • The crits agree in part.
    • The realists agree partly.
    • Dworkin rejects the party-political reading.

13.4.3 Q3 Theory is irrelevant to practice

🔑 Trigger words: theory isn't relevant; just do your job; no practical need
▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

The verdict. True in a weak sense: lawyers rarely cite theory, and most cases are easy. False in the strong sense: every lawyer acts on a theory of what law is and what the role permits. The only choice is between examined and unexamined theory.

How each one lines up:

  • Fish: partly;
  • Dworkin: rejects;
  • Thunder: rejects, and names the source;
  • legal positivism: rejects, even on its own terms.

See 2.6, 10.8 and 10.10.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL

The statement is that a practising lawyer has no practical need for legal theory, and should just do the job. Test it on the associate who quoted Rawls (2.6.1), and the student who advised treating breach of contract as a cost (10.8).

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Separate the weak and strong senses.

  • Weakly true. Quoting Rawls in a steel case was window dressing, and Fish partly agrees.
  • Strongly false. Treating breach as a cost is realist theory in action. Thunder names the source: realism plus neo-Kantianism (10.10). Dworkin rejects the statement. And even legal positivism is a theory of law the lawyer is relying on.

13.4.4 Q4 Lawyers serve clients within the law

🔑 Trigger words: client; lawful; adversarial system; hired gun
▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

The verdict. The lawyer's role is itself moral, and law sets its floor and not its ceiling. Above the floor, prudence, dialogue and rare objection decide hard cases. Pepper and Thunder differ more in mindset than in outcome.

How each one lines up:

  • Pepper: agrees, on moral grounds;
  • Pepper's own limits undercut Pepper;
  • Thunder: rejects;
  • Liu's three scenarios: a test, and not a side.

See 10.1, 10.2 and 10.11.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL

The statement is that a lawyer's only duty is to serve the client within the law, as a hired gun in an adversarial system. Test it on Aisha's two instructions (10.7) and Teo's three files (10.11).

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Test it on Aisha and Teo.

  • Pepper agrees, but for moral reasons: autonomy and equal access. Pepper's own outlets, objection and choice of client, concede that the role has moral limits.
  • Thunder rejects it.
  • Liu's three questions sort Teo's files. Is the system just? Is the rule intolerably unjust? Is the outcome unjust? They do not take a side between Pepper and Thunder.
  • Above the floor, use dialogue for Aisha's time bar and objection for the brake defect.

13.4.5 Q5 Stay within your role

🔑 Trigger words: limits of their own authority; usurp; officials; for Parliament, not the courts
▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

The verdict. Right as a presumption. A constitutional democracy divides power, so roles have limits. But where a role ends is contested, abdication is as much a vice as usurpation, and refusing extreme injustice is fidelity to law and is not usurpation.

How each one lines up:

  • George and Tan Seow Hon: agree, then ask who decides;
  • Tan Seow Hon's twin vices add the missing half;
  • Fuller: fidelity is not deference;
  • Alexy and Kennedy: the outer limit.

See 12.1, 12.2 and 12.5.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL

The statement is that judges and officials must respect the limits of their authority, leaving contested issues to Parliament. Test it on Judges Ang and Bala (12.2) and Clerk Jurić (12.5).

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Test it on each person.

  • The presumption holds against Ang, who usurps.
  • But Bala's rubber-stamping is the twin vice.
  • Jurić owes fidelity to law, and not deference to rank (Fuller).
  • At the outer limit, Alexy's risk effect and Kennedy's options show that refusing extreme injustice is part of the role, and not a breach of it.

13.4.6 Q6 Law and justice

🔑 Trigger words: rule of law; essence; certainty, procedure; necessarily connected
▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

The verdict. Justice is the point of the rule of law and its outer limit. Certainty and procedure are its everyday content. Validity never settles obedience, and only intolerable injustice defeats legal character.

How each one lines up:

  • Fuller: partly;
  • Hart: separates them, for the sake of candour;
  • Radbruch and Alexy: a narrow link;
  • Tan Seow Hon: disciplines the link for courts.

See 3.3, 8.2 and 8.5.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL

The statement is that the essence of the rule of law is certainty and procedure, and that justice has nothing to do with it. Test it on Vos's party ban (3.3) and the Residence Act (8.8).

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Test it on each law.

  • Certainty and procedure are the everyday content. Vos's ban is clear and public, which matters. Fuller partly agrees.
  • But justice is the point and the outer limit. The Residence Act is intolerably unjust, so Radbruch and Alexy deny it the character of law.
  • Hart keeps law and justice apart, for the sake of candour.
  • Tan Seow Hon disciplines the link. Courts may use it only on broad historical consensus (8.5).

13.4.7 Pivots and repaired statements (Core B)

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

Pivots.

  • Presupposed, but not always operative (9.8).
  • Easy cases rest on a shared theory (9.9).
  • A floor and not a ceiling (11.7).
  • Twin vices (12.2).
  • The judge's hat (12.4).
  • Practical need: concede that extremes are rare. The law still leaves several lawful paths, above all for lawyers, and it cannot choose between them (11.1, 10.7).

Repaired statements (use one per script):

ThemeRepaired statement
JudgesJudges should not decide by personal conviction. They bring political morality to bear through fit and candour, and override the law only at intolerable injustice.
PoliticsAdjudication is political in the sense of political morality, not partisanship. Where the rules leave a case open, judges must justify, not pretend.
TheoryLawyers need not cite theory, but they cannot practise without one. The choice is between examined and unexamined theory.
LawyersA lawyer serves the client within the law, but the law is a floor: dialogue above it, and refusal only at the extremes.
RolesLegal actors should respect the limits of their roles and do their roles' own moral work, refusing only intolerable injustice.
Rule of lawJustice is the rule of law's point and its outer limit. Certainty and procedure are its everyday content.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL

There is no practical need for lawyers to engage with morality, because extreme cases almost never arise.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Concede, pivot, and close.

  • Concede that extremes are rare.
  • Then pivot. Even in ordinary work, the law leaves a lawyer several lawful paths. Aisha could plead the time bar or suggest settlement (10.7), and the law cannot choose between them. Morality does that work.
  • Close with the repaired lawyers line from the table above.

513.5 Core C: what law is, and what we owe it

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

For questions about the nature of law, and about citizens.

The spine. People make law, so its sources can be found by looking. But deciding that sources are all that count is an evaluation. And finding the law never settles what it should be or what anyone should do. Keep three questions apart:

  1. what counts as law: sources, plus, for non-positivists, a narrow moral limit;
  2. what the law should be: reasons, and not facts about opinion;
  3. what I owe it: a moral question on every theory, with a strong default of obedience.

13.5.1 L1 Law is a social fact

🔑 Trigger words: made by human beings; social fact; what people accept; whatever is enacted
▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

The verdict. The sources of law are facts, and usually a lawyer needs no more. But deciding that sources are all that count is an evaluation. Law is a social fact only on a theory of what law is.

How each one lines up:

  • Hart: agrees, more narrowly;
  • natural law: accepts the premise, denies the conclusion;
  • Dworkin: rejects;
  • Tan Seow Hon and Liu: naming law is an evaluation.

See 2.1 and 2.5.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL

The statement is that law is made by human beings, so it is simply a social fact: whatever people accept as law. Test it on Professor Lim and the Land Decree (2.1.2).

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Work through the statement.

  • The sources are facts. For a normal client question, looking them up is enough.
  • But choosing official acceptance as the test made the Decree's injustice irrelevant, and that is an evaluation (Tan Seow Hon, Liu).
  • The theorists.
    • Hart agrees, in a narrower form: only officials' acceptance counts, and not everyone's.
    • Natural law accepts that humans make law, but denies that this makes it a mere fact.
    • Dworkin rejects the whole idea.

13.5.2 L2 No necessary link between law and morality

🔑 Trigger words: absurd; necessarily connected; law is law
▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

The verdict. The word absurd fails, because a narrow necessary link is a serious position. But the link that survives is weak. Only extreme injustice defeats legal character, and ordinary unjust laws stay law.

How each one lines up:

  • Hart: agrees, with care;
  • Fuller: rejects, thinly;
  • Radbruch and Alexy: reject, narrowly;
  • Finnis and weak natural law: reject absurd, and keep the distinction.

See 2.3, 8.2 and 8.3.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL

The statement is that it is absurd to say law and morality are necessarily connected, because law is law. Test it on Judge Tan's three files (2.3.2).

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Work through the statement.

  • Absurd overstates. It is a serious position that file (c), the Redheads Act, is not law.
  • But the surviving link is weak. Files (a) and (b), unjust but not extreme, remain law.
  • The theorists.
    • Hart agrees with the statement, carefully.
    • Fuller rejects it in a thin, procedural way.
    • Radbruch and Alexy reject it, narrowly.
    • Finnis rejects the word absurd, but keeps the distinction between unjust law and no law.

13.5.3 L3 Facts about opinion settle the debate

🔑 Trigger words: positions and views; solely concerned; as a matter of fact; naturally follows
▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

The verdict. Facts about what people think are evidence to weigh, and they show what is at stake. They cannot settle what the law should be, because no ought follows from an is alone.

How each one lines up:

  • Hart: rejects;
  • Devlin: the nearest ally, but stops short;
  • Rawls: starts from a fact, and ends with a norm;
  • Finnis: rejects outright.

See 4.4, 6.3 and 7.1.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL

As a matter of fact, most citizens hold traditional views on marriage. It naturally follows that the law should reflect them.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Work through the statement.

  • The facts matter. They show what is at stake, and how a law would be received.
  • But the words naturally follows jump from what is to what ought to be (4.4).
  • The theorists.
    • Devlin comes closest, but even he requires a deliberate judgment that the practice harms society.
    • Rawls starts from the fact of reasonable pluralism, but ends with a norm of public reason (6.3).
    • Hart and Finnis reject the inference.

13.5.4 L4 Law is simply will or power

🔑 Trigger words: simply an expression; majoritarian will; command; whatever Parliament enacts
▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

The verdict. Will makes law only through rules that officials accept, and those rules also bind the will. Law is more than what the strongest or the most want, and that is why we can criticise them by it.

How each one lines up:

  • Austin: agrees, crudely;
  • Hart: rejects;
  • Fuller: rejects;
  • Tan Seow Hon: rejects for Singapore.

See 3.7, 12.3 and 14.3.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL

Law is simply an expression of whatever Parliament wills.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Work through the statement.

  • Will acts through rules. Parliament's will becomes law only through rules of recognition that officials accept. And those rules also bind Parliament, through manner and form and the Constitution.
  • And we can criticise Parliament by law's own standards. Fuller's reciprocity (3.7) shows how. When Parliament breaks the rules it announced, we can say so.
  • The theorists.
    • Austin fits the statement, crudely, with law as command.
    • Hart rejects it, because law needs the internal point of view.
    • Tan Seow Hon rejects it for Singapore. Article 4 makes the Constitution supreme, and not Parliament's will (14.3).

13.5.5 L5 Valid law must be obeyed

🔑 Trigger words: validly-enacted; obligation to obey; recipe for disaster; chaos
▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

The verdict. There is a strong default of obedience, but it is a moral default. Validity only tells us that the rule is law. The default can be defeated, but only by grave injustice, and not by disagreement.

How each one lines up:

  • Hart: separates validity from obedience;
  • Fuller: grounds the duty in reciprocity;
  • Radbruch and Alexy: a default, then a threshold;
  • Aquinas and Finnis: conscience, with a brake.

See 8.7 and 3.7.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL

The statement is that validly enacted laws must be obeyed, and that anything else is a recipe for chaos. Test it on Mrs Goh and the cat by-law (8.7.4), and Petra and the Radio Decree (8.7.1).

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Test it on each person.

  • Mrs Goh should obey. There is a strong moral default, from fair play and reciprocity, and her disagreement does not defeat it.
  • Petra may be right to disobey. Grave injustice can defeat the default.
  • It is not chaos. Every theory confines disobedience to grave cases.
  • The theorists.
    • Hart separates the legal and moral questions.
    • Fuller grounds the duty in reciprocity.
    • Radbruch and Alexy set a default, and then a threshold.
    • Aquinas and Finnis give conscience a role, with a brake: obey to avoid scandal, or so that a just system is not weakened.

13.5.6 L6 A moral link licenses private disobedience

🔑 Trigger words: own moral reasoning; justifiably disobey; conscience; who decides
▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

The verdict. The licence, if it is one, is not special to those who link law and morality. Every theory leaves room for moral refusal, and every serious one confines it. The real problem is who decides.

How each one lines up:

  • Hart: the same licence, stated honestly;
  • Alexy: rejects the target;
  • Tan Seow Hon: accepts the question of who decides;
  • Fuller: the risk runs both ways.

See 8.2, 8.7 and 12.1.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL

If law is linked to morality, every citizen can disobey whenever their own moral reasoning says a law is unjust.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Work through the statement.

  • Hart gives the same licence. He says some valid laws are too evil to obey (8.2). He just states it honestly, as a moral choice.
  • Alexy rejects the target. His link applies only at extreme injustice, and not whenever a citizen disagrees.
  • Tan Seow Hon accepts that the real question is who decides (12.1).
  • Fuller. The risk runs both ways. Blind obedience to wicked law is as dangerous as too much private judgment.

13.5.7 Pivots and repaired statements (Core C)

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

Pivots.

  • What people made is not what they should make (4.4).
  • A social fact is not public opinion: sources are different from a society's accepted morality (12.3).
  • Three questions about obedience (8.7).
  • A threshold and not a licence (8.2, 8.5).

Repaired statements (use one per script):

ThemeRepaired statement
Social factLaw's sources are matters of social fact, but what law should be is not, and facts about opinion are evidence to weigh, never the answer.
Necessary linkLaw and morality may be separable in identifying most law, but validity never settles obedience. Extreme injustice is the narrow case where the two questions meet.
DisobedienceCitizens owe a strong moral duty to obey, which grave injustice can defeat and mere disagreement cannot.
WillMajority will settles who may make law, within rules that bind it. It does not settle what the law should say.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL

The statement is that law is a social fact, so public opinion is the law. Use the pivot that a social fact is not public opinion.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

The social facts that identify law are the practices officials use to recognise sources, such as statutes and cases. They are not the public's moral views, which are a society's accepted morality (12.3). Then close with the repaired social-fact line from the table above.

613.6 Core D: testing a theory on a new issue

🔑 Trigger words: soundness; "[X]'s theory"; bear on this debate; the best way
▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

The spine. A theory is not refuted because it needs moral judgment, or because it fails to dictate an answer. Each of these four supplies a question and not a verdict:

  • Rawls asks which reasons;
  • Finnis asks what the act does to a basic good;
  • Hart asks what justifies this coercion;
  • Devlin asks what society can tolerate.

So test a theory three ways:

  1. Does it hold together?
  2. Does it give a defensible answer on the hard case?
  3. Does it beat its rivals?

Tasks.

  • Assess a theory: cards 14.8, 14.10, 14.13 and 14.15.
  • Apply it: say what it rules out, what it requires and what it leaves open (16.5).
  • Compare: the word best needs a rival, a job and a cost.

Pivots.

  • Needing moral judgment is fatal only if the theory promised to avoid it (14.13).
  • A framework needs inputs, so the word demands is usually wrong.
  • Sound means that it holds together, answers the hard case and beats its rivals.
  • Hart limits punishment most tightly, but says little on promotion (7.9).

Repaired statements (use one per script):

ThemeRepaired statement
AutonomyAutonomy deserves great weight in the common good, but it demands no particular law. Parliament must decide on reasons those who disagree can examine, and protect those whose consent is least free.
HartHart's theory needs moral judgement, which is no objection to it, and it is the tightest limit on punishment we have. It is not a complete account of what law may do.
Named theory[Theory] sets a sound discipline on [reasons / coercion], but its contested premise means it cannot settle [the issue] alone.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Assisted Dying Question

The statement is: Hart's theory demands that Ruritania legalise assisted dying. Assess the soundness of Hart's theory, and whether it is the best way to approach this debate.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Work through it step by step.

  • Apply each theory's question.
    • Hart. What justifies coercing a doctor who helps a competent, consenting patient die? Harm to others? Paternalism, if the patient's consent may be impaired by depression or pressure? Public offence does not arise.
    • Rawls. Are the reasons for and against public?
    • Finnis. Does it choose directly against life? Yes, so it is barred.
    • Devlin. Can society tolerate it?
  • The word demands is wrong. Hart's framework needs inputs, such as how free the consent of terminally ill patients really is. So it does not demand legalisation. It supplies a question.
  • Soundness, three ways.
    1. Hart's view holds together.
    2. It gives a defensible answer on the hard case: perhaps legalise, with strong safeguards against defective consent.
    3. It beats Devlin on ground where people disagree. Against Finnis, the cost is that it treats life as a good a person may waive.
  • Needing moral judgment is no objection, because Hart never promised to avoid it (14.13).
  • Gaps. Hart says little about promotion, such as whether the state should fund palliative care over assisted dying (7.9).
  • Best needs a rival, a job and a cost. Hart is best for the job of limiting punishment. The cost is his silence on promotion.
  • Close with the repaired Hart line from the table above.
