HYPO LESSON 14 · SECTION 14 · ABOUT 68 MIN · 56 QUESTIONS

Hypos: Theorist bank

⚡ BIG IDEA

Every theorist card runs purpose, claim, strength, critique and verdict. Each example makes you use every line of one card on one set of facts.

How to work through a hypo
  1. 1Read the rule (teal box). It puts the sheet's point in plain words. The exact wording to use in the exam is in the Lessons and Sheet tabs.
  2. 2Read the hypothetical (amber box). Before reading on, decide what the rule says about these facts.
  3. 3Tap Application (green box) and compare it with your answer.
  4. 4The exam cue (violet box) lists question words that should send you to this block. Each block ends with a quick check.
Applications:
ℹ NOTE
About these hypos

Each block on this page gives one theorist's card in plain words, one made-up set of facts, and a worked answer that uses every line of the card. Your exact sheet wording, with its quotations, is still in the Lessons and Sheet tabs.

  • Most cards are identical in the two versions.
  • 14.8, 14.10, 14.13 and 14.15 differ. Both versions are given here, marked [Theorist] and [Core].
  • 14.9, 14.14, 14.17, 14.20, 14.21 and 14.28 are in the Theorist version only.
  • The only other differences are cross-references. In 14.5, the Theorist version adds a reference to 15.9. In 14.19, Core refers to 8.3 and Theorist to 15.8.

Each card uses these labels: PURPOSE is the question the theorist answers. CLAIM is the answer. TEST is how to apply it. STRENGTH is why it is persuasive. CRITIQUE is the best objection, with the reply. CONCEDE is what you should admit. SAY is a phrase worth using, and its exact words are on your sheet. TRAP is a common mistake. SG is the Singapore link. VERDICT is your overall judgment.

Many examples reuse the facts from earlier lessons, so you meet the same facts from the theorist's side.

Some terms come up throughout. Legal positivism says whether something is law depends on its source and not on its merit. Natural law theory ties law to what is morally good. The Radbruch formula says a statute stops being law once its injustice is intolerable. Broad historical consensus is Tan Seow Hon's test for showing that injustice is intolerable. TSH is Tan Seow Hon. A dagger (†) marks a point from the slides. The coverage table is the last section.

114.1 Fish

🔑 Use: 2.6, 10.5, 10.8
▤ IN PLAIN WORDS
The card
  • PURPOSE: Is theory useless to a lawyer, beyond doctrine and tactics?
  • CLAIM: Practice uses doctrine inside an enterprise with a purpose. That enterprise is shaped by a view of how the state may and may not use its monopoly of legal force.
  • STRENGTH: Searle's football example: describing only the physical facts misses the game. An expert's field is already shaped by understanding what is at stake.
  • CRITIQUE: The complaint Segal reports is that law school, jurisprudence included, never taught the tricks of the trade. Reply: the tricks would not amount to much without knowing what the trade is.
  • SAY: Law is surely a practice, but it is also a subject.
  • VERDICT: Fish is right that practice assumes a view of the state's force, but he never says which view is true.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Training Head's Memo

A firm's head of training writes that trainees should learn the tricks, such as how to draft a winding-up petition and how to time an injunction, and that jurisprudence is a waste of their time. That week, a trainee drafts a petition that will let a bank seize a small family's home.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Use each line of the card.

  • Claim. Every step of the trainee's petition uses the state's power to force a family out. Knowing when that use of force is justified, meaning proportionate and procedurally fair, is a view about legal force. It shapes how the petition should be argued.
  • Strength (Searle). Described only in physical terms, the trainee is just filling in a form. Only someone who understands what is at stake, the debt, the home and the state's force, sees what the form is doing.
  • Critique and reply. The memo repeats Segal's complaint that law school should teach the tricks. Fish's reply is that tricks without knowing what the trade is would not amount to much.
  • Say. Law is surely a practice, but it is also a subject.
  • Verdict. Fish shows that the trainee needs a view of the state's force, but not which view is right. For that, use Finnis, Rawls or Hart.

214.2 NLT and Aquinas

🔑 Use: 2.1, 2.3, 2.8, 8.7, 11.2
▤ IN PLAIN WORDS
The card
  • PURPOSE: Must law meet a higher standard, known by reason, in order to bind?
  • CLAIM: Human law binds to the extent that it comes from natural law, by deduction or by determination. Law contrary to natural law is defective as law.
  • TEST:
    • Aquinas: an unjust law is a corruption of law, though obedience is owed, perhaps in certain special cases, to avoid scandal or danger.
    • Finnis: it only lacks its power, at first sight, to bind in conscience (page 18).
    • Tan Seow Hon: a manifestly unjust law is not law.
  • CRITIQUE: Tan Seow Hon asks who may pronounce on the content of higher law. Reply: discernment, unlike mere command, must hold together and stay open to revision.
  • VERDICT: Natural law explains why some enactments fail as law, but it must first settle who decides.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Three Ruritanian Laws
  • (a) Murder is a crime.
  • (b) The speed limit on highways is 90 km/h.
  • (c) Every citizen must report any relative who practises a minority religion.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Use each line of the card.

  • Claim.
    • (a) comes from natural law by deduction: do not kill the innocent.
    • (b) is a determination. Natural law says to protect life on the roads, but the exact number is a reasonable choice, like an architect picking one design for a house.
    • (c) contradicts natural law, so it is defective as law.
  • The three readings of (c).
    • Aquinas: a corruption of law, though a citizen might obey it in special cases to avoid scandal or danger.
    • Finnis: it lacks the power to bind in conscience, but it is not simply void.
    • Tan Seow Hon: a manifestly unjust law is not law.
  • Critique and reply. Who says (c) is unjust? Tan Seow Hon presses that question. The reply is that a judgment that (c) is unjust must fit with everything else we know, and stay open to revision. It is not mere say-so.
  • Verdict. Natural law explains why (c) fails as law, but it still has to settle who gets to declare that (12.1).

314.3 Austin

🔑 Use: 2.2, 8.7, 11.1, 12.3
▤ IN PLAIN WORDS
The card
  • PURPOSE: What is law, as a fact, without moral premises?
  • CLAIM: Law is the command of a sovereign who is habitually obeyed and who obeys no one, backed by a sanction.
  • STRENGTH: Candour. Austin says the existence of law is one thing, and its merit or demerit is another.
  • CRITIQUE: Hart says habits miss the internal sense of ought, and that rules which give powers enable people and do not require anything. Reply: Dworkin accepts that Austin's main idea, restated by Hart, has never lost its grip on jurisprudence.
  • SG: Against the idea that the sovereign is simply Parliament: Article 4 makes statutes void to the extent they are inconsistent with the Constitution (Tan Seow Hon; 11.1).
  • VERDICT: Austin is honest that wicked law gets enforced, but habit or fear cannot explain why officials treat law as binding.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Warlord and the Will
  • (a) A warlord controls a valley. Villagers habitually obey his orders, backed by beatings, and he obeys no one.
  • (b) In Singapore, a woman makes a will signed before two witnesses.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Use each line of the card.

  • Claim. On Austin's test, (a) is law: the commands of a habitually obeyed sovereign, backed by sanctions.
  • Strength. Austin can say candidly that it is law, and that whether it is good law is another question.
  • Critique. But the villagers obey out of fear and habit. Nobody treats the warlord's orders as standards they ought to follow, so Hart's internal sense of ought is missing. And (b) does not fit at all. The rule on witnesses commands no one. It enables her to make a valid will.
  • Reply. Dworkin admits that Austin's core idea, refined by Hart, still has a grip on jurisprudence.
  • Singapore. If someone says Singapore's sovereign is simply Parliament, Article 4 answers that statutes inconsistent with the Constitution are void. Parliament is not an unlimited sovereign of the kind Austin describes.
  • Verdict. Austin is honest that bad law gets enforced, but fear and habit cannot explain why judges treat law as binding.

414.4 Hart: The Concept of Law

🔑 Use: 2.1, 2.2, 11.1, 11.7, 12.3
▤ IN PLAIN WORDS
The card
  • PURPOSE: Why do lawyers say ought, if law is neither command nor morality?
  • CLAIM: Law is the union of primary rules (which set duties) and secondary rules of recognition, change and adjudication, which officials accept from an internal point of view.
  • TEST: A system exists when primary rules are generally obeyed and officials accept the secondary rules. The secondary rules cure uncertainty, rigidity and scattered social pressure. Soft positivism lets the rule of recognition adopt moral tests if it happens to.
  • CRITIQUE 1: Dworkin says many Nazi officials obeyed Hitler only out of fear. If that is acceptance, Hart comes close to Austin. If not, there was no law in Nazi Germany. Reply: acceptance even from fear, self-interest or habit still treats rules as standards.
  • CRITIQUE 2: Tan Seow Hon says that because only officials need accept, Hart may not be very different from the view that law is power, and legal positivism is not necessarily democratic. Reply: describing law is not praising it.
  • SAY: Officials have a critical reflective attitude. And Hart warns that the sheep may end up in the slaughter-house.
  • TRAP: Hart's minimum content of natural law is no test of legality. People are not members of suicide clubs, so every society needs rules against violence, theft and deceit. That is a practical necessity, unlike Radbruch's override (Liu, Week 10). Harris calls it a sociological idea, consistent with institutional slavery or racial oppression.
  • VERDICT: Hart maps a working legal system most accurately, yet deciding what the map shows is already an evaluation.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Island Settlement

Two hundred shipwrecked people settle an island.

  • Year 1: they live by customs, such as not stealing and sharing water. Disputes arise: is there a custom about fishing rights? Nobody can change a bad custom, and enforcement is by angry crowds.
  • Year 3: they agree that rules written in the Council Book are binding, that the Council may change them, and that three elders settle disputes.
  • Year 10: a faction takes over the Council. Its officials accept the Book as binding, and most settlers obey only out of fear.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Use each line of the card.

  • Claim and test.
    • Year 1 has only primary rules, with three defects: uncertainty (is there a fishing rule?), rigidity (no way to change customs) and scattered pressure (mob enforcement).
    • Year 3 adds secondary rules: recognition (the Book), change (the Council) and adjudication (the elders). Now there is a legal system, because the rules are generally obeyed and officials accept the secondary rules.
  • Soft positivism. If the Book said that no rule is valid if grossly unfair, the rule of recognition would contain a moral test.
  • Critique 1 (Dworkin). In Year 10, do officials obeying only out of fear count as accepting? The reply is that if they use the Book as a standard to judge conduct, criticising and correcting, that is acceptance, whatever their motive.
  • Critique 2 (Tan Seow Hon). Only officials need to accept. The settlers may be sheep led to the slaughter-house, so Hart's system is not necessarily democratic. The reply is that Hart describes and does not praise.
  • Say. Officials have a critical reflective attitude.
  • Trap. That the island needs rules against violence, theft and deceit (Hart's minimum content) is a practical necessity for survival, and not a test of legality. Harris notes that such a natural law is consistent even with slavery.
  • Verdict. Hart's map fits the island best. But calling the Year 10 regime law is already an evaluation.

514.5 Dworkin

🔑 Use: 2.4, 2.5, 9.2, 9.5, 9.10
▤ IN PLAIN WORDS
The card
  • PURPOSE: Why do judges disagree about the law, and what constrains them in hard cases?
  • CLAIM: Law is interpretive. Judges read the legal record by fit and political value, so law is political, but it is never personal or partisan.
  • TEST: A reading must both fit the practice and show its point or value. Where several readings fit, political morality decides. (The Theorist version adds a reference to 15.9.)
  • STRENGTH: It explains theoretical disagreement, which the plain-fact view cannot, though Liu thinks this is unfair to legal positivism (2.5).
  • CRITIQUE: The realists and crits say fit leaves readings open, so value is the judge's politics. Reply: Dworkin accepts that fit will often fail to produce one unique interpretation. He does not accept that law is personal or partisan.
  • CONCEDE: A judge's best reading rests on beliefs other judges need not share, and integrity gives no way out of a wicked legal history (2.4). Concede both. Radbruch guards the outer limit (14.19).
  • SG: Lim Meng Suang (Court of Appeal) relied on a central theme of Dworkin's theory to set aside extra-legal considerations that are for the Legislature alone. That this means principle against policy is Tan Seow Hon's guess.
  • SAY: Law is deeply and thoroughly political.
  • VERDICT: Dworkin best explains how principle constrains hard cases, granted that fit often cannot settle them alone.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The "Reasonable Rent" Clause

Ruritania's Tenancy Act lets tribunals reduce rent that is unreasonable. Two tribunal members disagree over a 40% rent rise in a gentrifying area. One says market rates make it reasonable. The other says tenants' security makes it unreasonable.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Use each line of the card.

  • Claim and test. Each member offers a reading that fits the Act and the past decisions, and shows the Act's point: market efficiency, or tenants' security. Where both fit, political morality decides which reading is best.
  • Strength. This explains their disagreement as a dispute about the grounds of law, and not a gap. Liu would add that soft positivism can explain it too.
  • Critique and reply. A realist says each member is just voting their politics. Dworkin accepts that fit often will not produce one answer. But he holds that the choice must rest on principles about what tenancy law is for, and not on party loyalty.
  • Concede. The winning reading rests on beliefs the other member need not share. And if Ruritania's tenancy law had a wicked history, such as excluding a minority, integrity alone gives no way out. The Radbruch formula is the outer limit.
  • Singapore. In Lim Meng Suang, the Court of Appeal relied on a central idea of Dworkin's to leave extra-legal considerations to the Legislature. Tan Seow Hon guesses that the court meant the distinction between principle and policy.
  • Say. Law is deeply and thoroughly political, in the sense of political morality.
  • Verdict. Principle constrains the tribunal, but fit alone cannot settle it.

614.6 Fuller

🔑 Use: 3, 8.4, 2.4, 13.1
▤ IN PLAIN WORDS
The card
  • PURPOSE: What separates law from naked power, and why do failures of form wrong citizens?
  • CLAIM: Law is the enterprise of subjecting human conduct to the governance of rules, with an inner morality of eight requirements.
  • TEST: See 15.1. Total failure in one requirement yields something that is not properly called a legal system at all. Otherwise, whether a legal system exists is always a matter of degree.
  • STRENGTH: It binds lawmakers first. Being at the top of the chain of command intensifies their duty of legality.
  • CRITIQUE: Liu's slides† ask whether this is about morality at all, and suggest the label may be wrong. Perhaps it is about efficacy (Week 2, slide 17). Reply: legality respects responsible people (Week 2, slide 17†), and it grounds the duty to obey through reciprocity (3.3).
  • CONCEDE: Legality is thin. A clear, public, forward-looking law can still be wicked. Concede it, and let the Radbruch formula test content (13.1).
  • SAY: There is no greater legal monstrosity than a secret statute. Balancing the requirements is no less a task than being a lawgiver.
  • TRAP: The point that not all cases are hard concerns legality, and not how judges decide. Fuller did not adopt the Radbruch formula. He asks how much of a legal system survived.
  • VERDICT: Fuller shows that legality is a real but modest morality binding rulers. He does not show that it makes their laws just.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Parliament's Secret Annex

Ruritania's Parliament passes a Public Safety Act whose Schedule of offences is kept secret for security reasons. Separately, it passes a clear, published law excluding a minority from public jobs.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Use each line of the card.

  • Claim and test. The secret Schedule fails the requirement of publication. If all criminal law were secret, there would be no legal system at all. Here it is one Act, so the system survives, but degraded. Legality is a matter of degree.
  • Strength. Parliament, at the top of the chain of command, has an intensified duty of legality. It has no better excuse than judges or police would.
  • Critique and reply. Is this just about efficacy, about whether the law works? No. A secret offence denies citizens the chance to choose as responsible people, and it breaks the reciprocity that grounds their duty to obey.
  • Concede. The published job-exclusion law passes Fuller's tests and is still wicked. Concede that legality is thin, and let the Radbruch formula test its content.
  • Say. There is no greater legal monstrosity than a secret statute. Balancing the eight requirements is no less a task than being a lawgiver.
  • Trap. If you write about which cases are easy or hard, that concerns legality, meaning whether citizens can follow the rules. It does not concern how judges decide. And Fuller did not adopt the Radbruch formula. Facing the Junta's laws, he would ask how much of a legal system survived.
  • Verdict. Real, but modest.

714.7 TSH: moral subjectivism

🔑 Use: 4.1, 4.2, 4.3, 4.5, 4.7
▤ IN PLAIN WORDS
The card
  • PURPOSE: Is morality a matter of personal or cultural opinion, and can subjectivists argue with anyone?
  • CLAIM: Subjectivists cannot hold others to any standard independent of their belief without ceasing to be subjectivists. So their moral dialogue is gravely limited.
  • TEST: Does a sceptic's premise bind someone who rejects it? A relativist who binds outsiders relies on a standard above any one culture. If it honours equal moral worth, that person is a moral realist.
  • STRENGTH: The genocide example. Moral dialogue breaks down. If all may do as they please, everyone becomes equally worthless. Admit any limits, and the subjectivist is just another moral realist.
  • CRITIQUE: Epistemic sceptics, Tan Seow Hon's second kind, ask who can know the moral facts. Reply: this is a legitimate variant, but a dead end for law-making. Finnis's goods offer a way forward (Liu, Week 3; 14.8). Realism involves a commitment to deliberation, with judgments held more provisionally.
  • CONCEDE: She shows that subjectivists' moral dialogue is gravely limited, but not which realist content is right. The rest is a squabble within the family of moral realists.
  • VERDICT: Tan Seow Hon shows that a subjectivist who argues or demands must turn realist, and that the case for subjectivism is inconclusive. She does not show that moral facts exist. How we know what is right is left to deliberation.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Two Islands Dispute

The people of Aster Island believe it is right to enslave anyone born on neighbouring Brin Island. Brin's government, whose official philosophy is cultural relativism, protests that Aster must respect its people's right to govern themselves.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Use each line of the card.

  • Test. Brin's protest is meant to bind Aster, which rejects it. That relies on a standard above any one culture: cultural self-determination. If Brin grounds it in equal moral worth, Brin is a moral realist.
  • Strength. If Brin stays a true relativist, it can only say that its norms do not bind Aster, and Aster can say the same back. Dialogue breaks down, leaving force. And if everyone may do as they please, everyone is equally worthless.
  • Critique and reply. A Brin philosopher says that moral facts may exist, but asks who can know them. That is a legitimate position, but it leaves Brin with nothing to argue. Finnis's basic goods offer a way to make progress, and realism, properly held, means deliberating with provisional judgments.
  • Concede. Tan Seow Hon shows that Brin must argue as a realist. She does not show which realist view is right. That is a squabble within the realist family.
  • Verdict. It is an argument that persuades, and not a proof that moral facts exist.

814.8 Finnis

🔑 Use: 5, 6.2, 6.5, 2.3, 4.4
▤ IN PLAIN WORDS
[Theorist] card
  • PURPOSE: What makes choices and laws reasonable, without deriving ought from nature?
  • CLAIM: Seven self-evident basic goods and nine requirements of practical reasonableness yield moral norms, and a common good that rules out many laws.
  • TEST: See 15.3 and 15.4. A requirement plus the circumstances tells you that this act ought or ought not to be done (Week 4, slide 11†).
  • STRENGTH 1: The goods are grasped and not inferred. There is no inference from fact to value.
  • STRENGTH 2: The state's role is not to make people wholly good, but only to keep peace and justice, on principles open to all people whatever their religious beliefs.
  • CRITIQUE: Liu's slides† doubt self-evidence and the seventh requirement (Week 4, slide 13). Harris says facts about human nature creep back in (pages 15 to 16). Reply: we are not dealing with logical necessities, yet it is still reasoning.
  • CONCEDE: Being open to all is not being accepted by all. Reasonable people dispute the list and how to use it. Concede that this limits the coercion he can justify (5.7).
  • VERDICT: Finnis gives lawmakers usable limits and a helping state. But his self-evidence rests on contested intuitions, and Liu finds the seventh requirement artificial.
▤ IN PLAIN WORDS
[Core] card

This replaces the card above in the Core version.

  • PURPOSE: The same.
  • TEST: See 15.3 and 15.4.
  • STRENGTH: Finnis gives legislators real limits without a state plan for life. The common good is a set of conditions, and there is no inference from fact to value. He can say why some things are wrong even if most people approve.
  • CRITIQUE:
    • Self-evidence rests on intuitions shaped by upbringing (Liu).
    • Being open to all is not being accepted by all.
    • The line between means and side-effect is, as Liu puts it, pretty artificial. And since consent cures nothing, it is a heavy limit on autonomy (Liu). Reply: there is no magic in the number seven, we are not dealing with logical necessities, and dissent may be an innocent mistake without being fully reasonable.
  • VERDICT: Reasonable disagreement limits what the state may coerce, even where Finnis is right about the good.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Assisted Dying Bill (5.0), Finnis's Way

Ruritania's Assisted Dying Bill would let doctors give lethal injections on request. 70% of citizens approve.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Use each line of the card.

  • Claim and test. Life is a basic good. The seventh requirement bars choosing directly against it. In these circumstances, a lethal injection is chosen as the means to end suffering, so it ought not to be done. Authorising it is not something the state may do.
  • Strengths.
    • Finnis does not infer that life is good from biology. It is grasped directly.
    • He can explain why the Bill is wrong even though 70% approve.
    • And he does not need a state plan for life. The state's role is peace and justice, the common good as a set of conditions, on reasons open to everyone regardless of religion.
  • Critiques.
    • Is life's goodness really self-evident, or is that intuition shaped by a Catholic upbringing?
    • Harris says facts about human nature creep into the reasoning.
    • The line between means and side-effect is artificial. A doctor may give a large dose of painkiller foreseeing death, as a side effect, but may not intend it.
    • And the dying man's own consent counts for nothing.
  • Replies. The list is not sacred. It is not logical deduction, but it is still reasoning. Those who disagree may be mistaken without being to blame.
  • Concede. Being open to all is not being accepted by all. Many reasonable citizens reject Finnis's view of life.
  • Verdict. Even if Finnis is right, the depth of reasonable disagreement limits how far the state should coerce. So a legislator following Finnis might vote against the Bill, while being cautious about jailing desperate relatives who help a loved one die.

914.9 Seligman and Tierney [Theorist only]

🔑 Use: 5.6, 5.1
▤ IN PLAIN WORDS
The card
  • PURPOSE: Does human nature push us by urges, or pull us towards ends (Topic 4, on following nature)?
  • CLAIM: Minds are built for looking ahead. Memory and emotion serve planning, so we are pulled by ends and not pushed by the past.
  • STRENGTH: It fits Finnis's first requirement. Living merely from moment to moment, following immediate cravings, is unreasonable.
  • CRITIQUE: Hume and Finnis say psychology cannot ground norms (14.8). Reply: the essay shows how goods appear in experience. It does not show that they are goods.
  • TRAP: Only a summary is in the folder, so paraphrase and never quote.
  • VERDICT: Seligman and Tierney make Finnis's planner look true to life. That is an illustration and never a proof.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Student's Proof

A student writes that Seligman and Tierney prove Finnis right, because science shows humans are built to plan, so we ought to live by a plan of life.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Use each line of the card.

  • Claim and strength. The research does fit Finnis. We spend more time imagining futures than recalling the past, which makes the plan of life natural to us, and living moment to moment goes against the grain.
  • Critique and reply. But saying we are built to plan states a fact. That we ought to plan does not follow from it (Hume), and Finnis himself denies any inference from fact to value. The research shows how goods appear in experience. It does not show that they are goods.
  • Trap. Only a summary of the essay is in the folder, so paraphrase it. Do not put words in quotation marks.
  • Verdict. Use it as an illustration, and never as a proof.

1014.10 Rawls

🔑 Use: 6.1, 6.2, 6.3, 6.11, 13.1
▤ IN PLAIN WORDS
[Theorist] card
  • PURPOSE: When is coercion legitimate among citizens who reasonably disagree about the good?
  • CLAIM: Power is fully proper only under a constitution whose essentials all citizens, as free and equal, may reasonably be expected to endorse.
  • TEST: See 15.5.
    • Scope: constitutional essentials, basic justice and questions bordering on them, as far as possible, in the public political forum.
    • Reciprocity: offer reasons others might also reasonably accept, and not merely understand, as Servetus understood Calvin.
  • STRENGTH: It is not secularism. Public reason is not secular reason, and the proviso admits religious argument if public reasons follow in due course.
  • CRITIQUE 1: Finnis calls the principle illegitimate, unreasonable and uncivil, leaving the gravest questions to sheer power of numbers or influence. Reply: Finnis accepts that the ideal of reciprocity seems broadly reasonable. The dispute is about who is reasonable.
  • CRITIQUE 2: Tan Seow Hon says that unless Rawls counts heads, reasonable needs a standard outside the citizens. Reply: his standard is moral though political, and it is not a head-count.
  • VERDICT: Rawls sets the right discipline for public argument, though deciding who counts as reasonable already takes a moral side.
▤ IN PLAIN WORDS
[Core] card
  • PURPOSE: The same.
  • TEST: See 15.5. Reciprocity: offer reasons others might also reasonably accept.
  • STRENGTH: Rawls explains how a law can bind people who reject its premises. He favours no doctrine in advance, and public reason is not secular reason. Secular full doctrines are limited in the same way.
  • CRITIQUE:
    • Finnis's dilemma: read as a prediction, the test gives a gross form of veto. Read as a norm, it judges merits.
    • Finnis calls the principle illegitimate, unreasonable and uncivil, leaving the gravest questions to sheer power of numbers or influence.
    • Reasonable needs a standard outside the citizens (Tan Seow Hon).
    • On abortion, Rawls moved from saying denial was to that extent unreasonable to saying Catholics need not exercise the right. Reply: his standard is moral though political, and it is not a head-count. Finnis accepts that the ideal of reciprocity seems broadly reasonable. The dispute is about who is reasonable.
  • VERDICT: Rawls sets the right discipline for public argument. But deciding who counts as reasonable already takes a moral side, and public reason may still end in a vote.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Servetus Test

In a debate on surrogacy (6.0), MP Lim says the MP will explain the MP's faith's view so clearly that every citizen will understand the opposition to it.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Use each line of the card.

  • Claim and test. Surrogacy touches basic justice, through exploitation and children's welfare, so public reason applies as far as possible. Being understood is not enough. Calvin's reasons for burning Servetus were understood by Servetus. Lim must give reasons others might reasonably accept, such as the risk of exploiting poor women.
  • Strength. Lim may still mention faith, if public reasons follow in due course. A secular MP arguing from a full philosophy of autonomy faces the same limit, so it is not secularism.
  • Core strength. If the law passes on public reasons, it binds even citizens who reject its premises.
  • Critiques.
    • Might reasonably accept: predicted, or deserved? The first gives a veto, and the second judges merits.
    • Finnis says it leaves the gravest questions to numbers.
    • Tan Seow Hon says reasonable needs an outside standard.
    • Core adds that on abortion, Rawls himself shifted, from unreasonable to need not exercise.
  • Replies. The standard is moral and not a head-count, and Finnis accepts the ideal of reciprocity itself.
  • Verdict. It is the right discipline for Lim's argument. But labelling opponents as unreasonable takes a moral side, and (in Core) the debate may still end in a vote.

1114.11 TSH: religion and public reason

🔑 Use: 6.4, 6.5, 6.7
▤ IN PLAIN WORDS
The card
  • PURPOSE: In a multi-religious democracy, may law-makers rely on religious arguments?
  • CLAIM: Judge arguments by whether they are open to all and by their merit, and not by their religious motive. Setting a metaphysical question aside already answers it.
  • CRITIQUE: Rawls says using state power against reasonable dissenters is unreasonable or worse. Reply: she asks only for reasons open to all, and she says marking off a political sphere is artificial.
  • CONCEDE: Her close: agreement on human worth does not at present extend to who counts as human. She suggests a pragmatic strategy of arguing from consequences. Concede that principle alone may not move Parliament.
  • SAY: The debate shatters the illusion of an accommodating solution.
  • VERDICT: Tan Seow Hon exposes the unfairness of sorting arguments by motive. She does not show how a divided Parliament should settle contested questions.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Abortion Review Campaign

A coalition, partly religious, campaigns for Ruritania to lower its abortion limit from 24 to 20 weeks. A minister dismisses them as religious people with religious motives.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Use each line of the card.

  • Claim. The minister is sorting by motive. Tan Seow Hon says to judge the arguments themselves. Are they open to all, such as foetal pain research and viability, and are they sound? And keeping the question of when life begins out of the debate already answers it, by permitting abortion at 24 weeks.
  • Critique and reply. A follower of Rawls says the coalition wants to use state power against reasonable dissenters. Tan Seow Hon replies that she asks only for reasons open to all, and that the line between political and metaphysical is artificial.
  • Concede. Society has not agreed on who counts as human, so arguing from principle may not move Parliament. Her pragmatic strategy is to argue from consequences everyone accepts, such as data on women's health.
  • Say. The debate shatters the illusion of an accommodating solution.
  • Verdict. She shows the minister's dismissal is unfair, but not how a split Parliament should finally decide.

1214.12 Mill and Wolfenden

🔑 Use: 7.1, 7.2, 7.5
▤ IN PLAIN WORDS
The card
  • PURPOSE: What may the criminal law prohibit: only harm to others, or private immorality too?
  • CLAIM: Coercion is justified only to prevent harm to others. Private immorality that neither harms nor offends in public is not the concern of the criminal law.
  • TEST: Wolfenden: preserve public order and decency, protect people from what is offensive or injurious, and safeguard the vulnerable against exploitation or corruption.
  • STRENGTH: In Hart's words, free choice may be a value in itself, or valuable because it lets people experiment in living.
  • CRITIQUE 1: Devlin says consent is no defence to murder or assault, so the law already enforces moral principle. Reply: Hart says such rules can be paternalist and not moralist.
  • CRITIQUE 2: Tan Seow Hon says harm and self-regarding are unclear ideas, and if only legal interests count, the test appears to be circular. Reply: the harm line needs moral argument, openly made.
  • SG: Shanmugam said in 2022 that Singapore's position is broadly similar to Wolfenden's (7.5).
  • SAY: Not the law's business (Wolfenden).
  • VERDICT: Mill and Wolfenden rightly make liberty the default, but they cannot draw the harm line without moral argument.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Sex-Work Review

Ruritania reviews its laws on sex work. A committee proposes to:

  • (a) decriminalise private, consensual adult sex work;
  • (b) keep street solicitation an offence;
  • (c) keep severe penalties for trafficking and for exploiting minors.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Use each line of the card.

  • Claim and test. (a) follows Mill: private, consensual adult conduct is not the law's business. (b) protects public order and decency. (c) safeguards the vulnerable against exploitation. Together, they are Wolfenden's model.
  • Strength. Adults' free choice has value in itself, and lets people live as they judge best.
  • Critique 1. Devlin says the law already denies that consent excuses assault, so it enforces morality. Hart's reply is that this rule protects people, which is paternalism, and does not enforce morality as such.
  • Critique 2. Tan Seow Hon asks whether a sex worker's long-term psychological harm is self-regarding, and whether a client's family is harmed. If harm means only harm to legal interests, the test is circular. The reply is that the line can be drawn, but only by moral argument, made openly.
  • Singapore. Shanmugam said Singapore's position is broadly similar to Wolfenden's.
  • Verdict. Liberty is the right default, but drawing the harm line takes moral argument.

1314.13 Hart: Law, Liberty, and Morality

🔑 Use: 7.1, 7.2, 7.4, 7.9
▤ IN PLAIN WORDS
[Theorist] card
  • PURPOSE: May the criminal law enforce morality as such, beyond preventing harm to others?
  • CLAIM: Coercion is objectionable at first sight, and it needs a good that outweighs that. Paternalism and public decency can supply one, but bare moral condemnation cannot.
  • TEST: See 15.7.
    1. It is a question of critical morality about enforcing a society's accepted morality.
    2. There are two costs: punishing offenders, and coercing those who never offend.
    3. Paternalism, where consent is defective.
    4. Decency: punish the public act.
  • STRENGTH: Bigamy, if punished to protect religious feelings from a public act, is punished as a nuisance, and neither as irreligious nor as immoral. Whether to punish turns on contestable estimates of offence against freedom lost.
  • CRITIQUE: Tan Seow Hon says it can be argued that paternalism is, in the end, based on morals. Reply: Hart accepts that applying his grounds takes moral judgment. He denies only punishing immorality as such (Liu, Week 9).
  • VERDICT: Hart wins the case against punishing private immorality as such, though moral judgment still decides where his paternalism and decency apply.
▤ IN PLAIN WORDS
[Core] card
  • PURPOSE: The same.
  • TEST: See 15.7.
  • STRENGTH: Hart asks the right question: is the bare fact that a society's accepted morality condemns conduct any reason to punish it? He finds no evidence for disintegration, which he says deserves no more respect than the Emperor Justinian's statement about earthquakes. Bigamy is punished as a nuisance, and neither as irreligious nor as immoral.
  • CRITIQUE: Tan Seow Hon says:
    • paternalism is, in the end, based on morals, because morals pick its targets (apotemnophilia against dangerous sports);
    • harm is an unclear idea, and if only legal interests count, the test appears to be circular;
    • decency has the same problem, because teetotallers can be offended too. Reply: Hart accepts that applying his grounds takes moral judgment. He denies only that immorality as such is a reason to punish (Liu).
  • VERDICT: Hart wins against punishing private immorality as such, but moral judgment still decides where his paternalism and decency apply.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Mock Wedding

Ruritania makes bigamy a crime. Raj, already married, lives with a second partner and holds a full church-style wedding ceremony with her, with guests and a cake. A second couple in the same position simply live together, with no ceremony, and commit no crime.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Use each line of the card.

  • Claim and test.
    1. The question is one of critical morality: is the community's condemnation of bigamy a reason to punish Raj?
    2. Punishment costs Raj his liberty, and it threatens everyone else.
    3. No defective consent is involved, so paternalism does not apply.
    4. Decency: the law punishes the public ceremony, which offends those for whom marriage is sacred.
  • Strength. That explains why only Raj, and not the cohabiting couple, is punished. He is punished as a nuisance, and neither as irreligious nor as immoral. Core adds that Hart asks the right question, whether bare condemnation is any reason, and that there is no evidence that tolerating private arrangements disintegrates society.
  • Critique. Tan Seow Hon asks why we protect these religious feelings but not teetotallers' offence at public drinking (Core). And why ban surgery for apotemnophilia but allow dangerous sports? Morality picks the targets.
  • Reply. Hart accepts that applying his grounds needs moral judgment. He rejects only punishing immorality as such.
  • Verdict. Hart wins on Raj's private cohabitation. But where the line of public offence falls is a moral call.

1414.14 Stephen [Theorist only]

🔑 Use: 7.8
▤ IN PLAIN WORDS
The card
  • PURPOSE: May criminal law punish vice as such? This is Stephen's reply to Mill.
  • CLAIM: Stephen holds what Hart calls the extreme thesis: enforcing morality is valuable in itself. Devlin, for most of his essay, holds the moderate one: a shared morality as the cement of society.
  • CRITIQUE: Hart says it does not follow. What to punish and how severely are separate and independent questions. Reply: Hart still lets wickedness be a partial factor in severity.
  • SAY: Criminal law is a persecution of the grosser forms of vice (Stephen).
  • VERDICT: Stephen is a useful contrast. Beside his extreme thesis, Devlin's moderate one and Finnis's limit of peace and justice look narrow.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Two Burglars

Two burglars steal the same amount. Ana stole to feed her children. Bo stole to fund gambling, and mocked the elderly victim. Bo gets a longer sentence. A commentator says this shows the criminal law punishes vice, so Stephen was right.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Use each line of the card.

  • Claim. Stephen would say yes. Criminal law is a persecution of the grosser forms of vice, and enforcing morality is good in itself. Devlin, more moderately, defends shared morality as what holds society together.
  • Critique. Hart says it does not follow. That we grade sentences by wickedness does not show we punish because of wickedness. Whether to punish burglary, which is about harm, and how severely, which is partly about wickedness, are separate questions.
  • Reply. Hart still allows wickedness to be a partial factor in severity, which is why Bo gets longer.
  • Verdict. Next to Stephen, Devlin (protect society) and Finnis (only peace and justice) look narrow.

1514.15 Devlin

🔑 Use: 7.3, 7.4, 15.6
▤ IN PLAIN WORDS
[Theorist] card
  • PURPOSE: May society enforce its shared morality by law, and how is that morality found?
  • CLAIM: Society may use law to protect the shared morality that holds it together, against conduct beyond the limits of tolerance.
  • TEST: See 15.6. It is the reasonable, and not the rational, person in the jury box: what any twelve people chosen at random could be expected to agree on unanimously after discussion. It is not majority opinion, and it is not every citizen's agreement. It does not depend on counting heads (page 15).
  • STRENGTH: Consent is no defence to murder, because the offence is against society (pages 6 to 7).
  • CRITIQUE 1: Hart says there is no evidence, and it deserves no more respect than the Emperor Justinian's statement about earthquakes. Reply: deviation and subversion are only capable by their nature of threatening society, and if morality changes, the law can change. But if only capable, why harsh sanctions now (Liu, Week 9)?
  • CRITIQUE 2: Tan Seow Hon, for moral realists, says treating secular moral judgment as simply a feeling (page 17) comes close to non-cognitivism, the view that moral claims only express feelings. Reply: her generous reading, that reasonable is objective, she herself finds too generous, given Devlin's relativism.
  • SAY: Society is held together by the invisible bonds of common thought (page 10).
  • TRAP: Devlin argues as a cultural relativist (Liu, Week 7). Monogamy binds because it is built into the house in which we live (page 9). Honest belief, right or wrong, makes immorality a question of fact. Privacy is only something to be taken into account.
  • VERDICT: Devlin rightly denies that law is morally neutral, but wrongly lets common feeling, and not reason, fix what it enforces.
▤ IN PLAIN WORDS
[Core] card
  • PURPOSE: The same.
  • TEST: See 15.6.
  • STRENGTH: Devlin rightly denies that law is morally neutral. Consent is no defence to murder because the offence is against society, and no society can do without intolerance, indignation and disgust.
  • CRITIQUE:
    • Hart says there is no evidence that private deviation threatens society.
    • Devlin argues as a cultural relativist (Liu). Monogamy binds because it is built into the house in which we live, so a persecuting society has the same claim.
    • Plural Singapore may lack the consensus he assumes. Reply: he says only that immorality is capable by its nature of threatening society, and that if morality changes, the law can change. But if only capable, why harsh sanctions now (Liu)?
  • SAY: Society is held together by the invisible bonds of common thought.
  • TRAP: Honest belief, right or wrong, makes immorality a question of fact. Privacy is only something to be taken into account.
  • VERDICT: Devlin leaves much to individual morality in practice, but he lets common feeling, and not reason, fix what the law enforces.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Suspension Parties (7.3), Devlin's Way

Back to the private hook-suspension parties.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Use each line of the card.

  • Claim and test. Would twelve random Ruritanians, after discussion, be unanimous that these parties are beyond the limits of tolerance? It is not a 65% poll, and it is not universal agreement. If unanimity is unlikely, Devlin's test is not met.
  • Strength. Devlin is right that law is not morally neutral. Consent would not excuse a murder, because murder offends society. Core adds that no society can do without indignation and disgust.
  • Critiques.
    • Hart says there is no evidence that tolerating private parties threatens society, and that the claim is as unsupported as Justinian's earthquakes.
    • Tan Seow Hon says calling moral judgment simply a feeling is close to non-cognitivism.
    • Core adds that a plural society may lack the deep consensus Devlin needs, and that his relativism gives a persecuting society the same claim.
  • Reply. Devlin says only that immorality is capable of threatening society, and that the law can change when morality does. But then why jail anyone now?
  • Trap. For Devlin, what the right-minded person honestly believes, right or wrong, is the morality the law may enforce. Immorality becomes a question of fact. Privacy is only a factor. He is a relativist and not a realist.
  • Say. Society is held together by the invisible bonds of common thought.
  • Verdict. In practice, Devlin would probably leave the parties alone (Core). In principle, he lets feeling, and not reason, decide.

1614.16 TSH: Pragmatism

🔑 Use: 7.6, 7.7
▤ IN PLAIN WORDS
The card
  • PURPOSE: What is criminal law for, and what did the 2007 compromise settle?
  • CLAIM: Tan Seow Hon argues that we simply cannot avoid the moral question. By 2007, the two camps really clashed over what is right.
  • TEST: Six functions of criminal law:
    1. harm;
    2. paternalism;
    3. public decency;
    4. averting disintegration;
    5. morals as good in themselves;
    6. moral ecology, meaning the moral climate of society.
  • CONCEDE: The map ranks no function, and her slope based on principle may read as advocacy. Concede both, and rank the functions using Hart or Finnis.
  • TRAP: The phrase tangible harm is Tan Seow Hon's summary of the case for keeping the law. It is not the words of those who wanted to keep it.
  • VERDICT: Tan Seow Hon's map is the best diagnostic. It shows the moral question is unavoidable, without answering it.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Cohabitation Law (7.4), Mapped

Run Ruritania's cohabitation law through Tan Seow Hon's six functions.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Take the six functions, then the rest of the card.

  1. Harm: does cohabitation harm anyone? Opponents point to children's stability.
  2. Paternalism: does it protect cohabitants from themselves? That is weak.
  3. Public decency: private homes involve no public act.
  4. Disintegration: see the four readings in 7.4.
  5. Morals as good in themselves: a view of Stephen's type.
  6. Moral ecology: does the law shape the culture of family life?
  • Claim. Each function forces a view on whether cohabitation is wrong. The moral question cannot be avoided.
  • Concede. The map does not say which function matters most, so use Hart (harm first) or Finnis (the common good) to rank them. And her argument about a slope based on principle can sound like advocacy.
  • Trap. If you write that those who wanted to keep the law claimed tangible harm, attribute the phrase to Tan Seow Hon and not to them.
  • Verdict. It is the best diagnostic, and not an answer.

1714.17 TSH: Marriage [Theorist only]

🔑 Use: 7.9, 11.6
▤ IN PLAIN WORDS
The card
  • PURPOSE: What did Article 156 add to the 2022 repeal of section 377A?
  • CLAIM: Tan Seow Hon argues that repeal answered legal risk, and was not a finding of unconstitutionality, which would imply equal treatment. So marriage laws between a man and a woman stay coherent.
  • STRENGTH: Article 156 shields only the definition of marriage as between a man and a woman and the laws based on it, reaching marriage's moral, social and cultural setting.
  • CONCEDE: Shanmugam also called repeal the right thing to do (Hansard, 29 November 2022), so risk was only part of the reason. Concede that, and keep her point that Article 156 rejects equal treatment.
  • SAY: A pre-emptive strike against judicial activism.
  • VERDICT: The 2022 package was a deliberate split: the criminal law withdrawn, and marriage promoted.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Housing Challenge

In 2027, a same-sex couple challenges a housing scheme open only to married couples. They argue that if section 377A was repealed because it was discriminatory, the housing rules must fall too.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Use each line of the card.

  • Claim. On Tan Seow Hon's reading, repeal was about the risk of a court striking down section 377A. It was not a finding that treating couples differently is unconstitutional. So the housing rules are consistent with the repeal.
  • Strength. Article 156 protects laws based on the definition of marriage as between a man and a woman, and it reaches marriage's wider setting. The housing scheme is probably shielded from challenges under Part 4.
  • Concede. Shanmugam also said repeal was the right thing to do, so it was not only about risk. Concede that, but Article 156 still rejects equal treatment.
  • Say. Article 156 was a pre-emptive strike against judicial activism.
  • Verdict. It was a deliberate split: the criminal law was withdrawn, and marriage was promoted.

1814.18 Hart: separation (1958)

🔑 Use: 8.1, 8.2, 8.7
▤ IN PLAIN WORDS
The card
  • PURPOSE: Should a wicked rule be denied the name of law, or called law and condemned?
  • CLAIM: Hart separates law as it is from law as it ought to be. Validity never settles whether to obey.
  • TEST: If punishment needs retroactivity, choose openly between two evils, by statute.
  • STRENGTH: Plain speech. Saying something is law but too evil to be obeyed is among the most powerful moral criticisms, because it is the simplest.
  • CRITIQUE 1: Fuller says legal positivism never gives any coherent meaning to fidelity to law, and the question then seems to be who should do the dirty work. Reply: only a statute gives up a principle openly, and the bridge to obedience is moral (8.7).
  • CRITIQUE 2: Alexy says that where the injustice was evident at the time, the court is finding the law then in force, so there is no hidden retroactivity. Reply: even Alexy calls candour the strongest argument against non-positivism, though not its downfall.
  • SAY: Candour is more than one minor virtue among many.
  • TRAP: The Bamberg court did not declare any 1934 statute void, as Hart supposed. Hart later accepted the error (Alexy).
  • VERDICT: Hart wins on labels for observers and historians. A judge deciding today needs more than candour.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Kovač the Informer (8.1), Hart's Way

Same facts as the hypo in 8.1; reread them first.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Use each line of the card.

  • Claim and test. The Insult Decree was law, but too evil to obey. To punish Kovač, Valdoria must choose openly between two evils: letting him go, or a retroactive statute. Parliament, and not the courts, should make that choice.
  • Strength. Calling it law but too evil to be obeyed is a condemnation everyone can understand.
  • Critique 1 (Fuller). If the Decree was law, what does fidelity to law mean? And Hart's statute treats the Decree as void anyway, so the real question is who does the dirty work. The reply is that only Parliament openly owns up to giving up a principle, and obedience is a moral question.
  • Critique 2 (Alexy). If the injustice was evident in 2012, a court in 2020 finding the Decree void is just stating what the law was then, so nothing is secretly retroactive. The reply is that even Alexy admits candour is the strongest objection.
  • Say. Candour is more than one minor virtue among many.
  • Trap. In the real informer case, the Bamberg court did not declare the Nazi statute void. Hart got that wrong, and later admitted it.
  • Verdict. For a historian describing 2012, Hart's labels win. For a judge in 2020 deciding Kovač's case, candour alone is not enough.

1914.19 Radbruch and Alexy

🔑 Use: 8.3, 8.4 (Theorist adds 15.8)
▤ IN PLAIN WORDS
The card
  • PURPOSE: Does extreme injustice take away a norm's character as law, and for whom?
  • CLAIM: Positive law prevails even when unjust, unless its injustice reaches an intolerable degree (Alexy). Then, for the participant, it is not law.
  • TEST: See 8.3 (Core) or 15.8 (Theorist). Participants include the court, the lawyer and the person the law is addressed to (Topic 7 seminar). Alexy's example is the judge.
  • STRENGTH 1: Every judicial decision necessarily claims to be correct, and extreme injustice fails that claim.
  • STRENGTH 2: Liu says neither side argues truth, only desirability, and the practical case is more or less a draw. So on what basis should we decide (Week 11)? Alexy says the objections were answered at least well enough to tie the score. There are three tie-breakers:
    • the risk effect;
    • necessity after a regime collapses;
    • fit with nulla poena, the rule against punishment without a prior law.
  • CRITIQUE: Hart says Radbruch only half digested the spiritual message of liberalism. Reply: Fuller credits him with seeing the dilemma as one of order against good order.
  • CONCEDE: Answering relativism needs a rational justification for at least some minimum moral requirements. Concede that the formula is only as sound as that core. Tan Seow Hon's broad historical consensus (14.26) disciplines judges, but it is evidence and not proof.
  • SAY: Positivism left both jurist and the people defenceless (Alexy).
  • TRAP:
    • Radbruch did not oppose denying legal quality. He warned of its frightful dangers, and for the informers he too preferred a retroactive statute.
    • Calling tier 2 (8.8) not law is Alexy's reading.
    • Broad historical consensus is Tan Seow Hon's test, and not Alexy's.
  • VERDICT: The formula earns its place as a narrow backstop, if its minimum core can be defended without counting votes.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Kel Exiles' Claim (8.3), Alexy's Way

Same facts as the hypo in 8.3; reread them first.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Use each line of the card.

  • Claim and test. The Citizenship Ordinance's injustice is intolerable. So it is not law for the participants: Judge Petrov, the exiles' lawyer, and the officials it was addressed to.
  • Strength 1. Petrov's ruling claims to be correct, and an extremely unjust norm cannot be correctly applied.
  • Strength 2. On the practical arguments, it is roughly a tie, which is Liu's point. Alexy breaks it with three tie-breakers:
    • the risk effect: Junta officials faced later liability;
    • necessity: after the Junta fell, courts had to deal with its laws;
    • nulla poena: evident injustice means no unfair surprise.
  • Critique and reply. Hart says Radbruch misunderstood liberalism. Fuller says Radbruch saw the real dilemma, between order and good order.
  • Concede. The formula needs a defensible minimum moral core. Broad consensus, Tan Seow Hon's test, is evidence of that core and not proof.
  • Say. Without the formula, positivism left both jurist and the people defenceless.
  • Trap. Radbruch himself warned of the dangers, and preferred a retroactive statute for informers. Calling tier 2 not law is Alexy's reading. Broad historical consensus is Tan Seow Hon's test, and not Alexy's.
  • Verdict. A narrow backstop, if the minimum core holds.

2014.20 ALR [Theorist only]

🔑 Use: 9.1, 10.2
▤ IN PLAIN WORDS
The card
  • PURPOSE: Do rules decide cases, or do officials and the facts they find?
  • CLAIM: Realists treat law as a prediction of what officials do. Rules leave leeways, and fact-finding steers outcomes.
  • STRENGTH: Harris reports Llewellyn: a lawyer steeped in a court's ways could predict most outcomes (9.9).
  • CRITIQUE: Thunder says judges are not predicting their own behaviour. Reply: realism is a method and nothing more.
  • SG: Cheng San GRC†: does within a radius of 200 metres reach a candidate inside the station? The Attorney-General said no (9.1).
  • VERDICT: Realism is right about leeways and wrong about rules. Predictability itself comes from a shared craft.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Candidate Tan (9.1), the Realist's Way

Same facts as the hypo in 9.1; reread them first.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Use each line of the card.

  • Claim. A realist lawyer predicts whether Tan will be convicted, by asking how this court reads election statutes and which facts the magistrate will find. Was Tan waiting, or working?
  • Strength. A lawyer soaked in the court's habits would predict it right about eight times in ten.
  • Critique and reply. The magistrate cannot predict the magistrate's own ruling, and must decide and justify it (Thunder). The realist answers that realism is a method for lawyers, and not a guide for judges.
  • Singapore. In the real Cheng San episode, the Attorney-General advised that being inside was not caught by the provisions on outside and within 200 metres.
  • Verdict. Realism is right that the statute leaves leeway. But predictability exists because lawyers share a craft of reading statutes, which shows that the rules matter.

2114.21 CLS and Unger [Theorist only]

🔑 Use: 9.3, 9.7
▤ IN PLAIN WORDS
The card
  • PURPOSE: Is doctrine coherent principle, or a truce between contradictory ideals?
  • CLAIM: The crits say doctrine can be argued either way, and that it makes hierarchy look legitimate. Unger finds counterprinciples that may reorganise a whole field.
  • TEST: Two pairs:
    • freedom to contract against community;
    • freedom of contract against fairness (duress, undue influence, frustration†). Unger's deviationist doctrine aims to turn the deviant into the dominant.
  • CRITIQUE: Harris says there could be no such thing as a crit judge in today's courts. Reply: so much the worse, a crit might say, for our existing institutions.
  • VERDICT: The crits expose real contradictions, but exposure alone cannot tell a judge which side justice favours.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Suri the Rider (9.3), the Crit's Way

Same facts as the hypo in 9.3; reread them first.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Use each line of the card.

  • Claim and test. Suri's case sets freedom of contract, the platform's terms, against fairness, unconscionability. A crit argues that the counterprinciple, fairness, should become the starting point of platform contracts, turning the deviant into the dominant.
  • The community pair. Freedom to contract against community: the platform's freedom to choose and drop riders, against the riders' reliance on a working relationship.
  • Critique and reply. Harris says no court would appoint a judge who openly aims to overturn contract law, so there can be no crit judge. The crit replies that this is so much the worse for our institutions.
  • Verdict. The crit shows the contradiction. But to say fairness should win, you need a standard of justice, and exposure alone does not supply one.

2214.22 Kennedy

🔑 Use: 12.4, 15.10, 13.1
▤ IN PLAIN WORDS
The card
  • PURPOSE: What is judging like when the law and the judge's sense of justice conflict?
  • CLAIM: Kennedy's judge is neither simply bound nor free. Law is a medium that constrains, but what it rules out depends on what the judge is trying to do.
  • TEST: The strikers' lie-in. At first the rule just applies itself. The judge then works it towards how the judge wants the case to come out, paying in time and in cost to legitimacy.
  • STRENGTH: Legality requires building the best case for the other side. What would betray it is the wrong attitude at the end. Sometimes the rule feels objective, and he cannot budge it.
  • CRITIQUE: Hart, against those sceptical about rules, says rules have a core of central meaning. Reply: how much of a field is open, taken in itself, simply cannot be answered.
  • SAY: The judge is free to deploy work in any direction. And the field is me, resisting myself.
  • TRAP: There are five courses, and never three (15.10, 12.4). Against the claim that there is always a right answer, he sets the experience of free ethical or political choice, and not a thesis.
  • VERDICT: Kennedy describes judging more honestly than he justifies it. He shows the choice is moral, and then leaves it for another time.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Eviction Order

Judge Okafor, who sympathises with tenants, hears a landlord's claim to evict a family that is two months behind on rent after the father lost his job. The tenancy statute seems clearly to allow eviction.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Use each line of the card.

  • Claim and test. At first, the statute just applies itself: eviction. Okafor wants the family to stay. So the judge works the materials. Perhaps the landlord's notice was defective, or a hardship provision can be stretched. That costs time, and risks credibility.
  • Strength. To be faithful to legality, the judge must build the landlord's best case and test the first impression against it. Only the wrong attitude at the end, deciding against what the judge concludes the law requires, betrays legality. And the judge may find that the rule simply cannot be budged.
  • Critique and reply. Hart says that pay rent or be evicted has a core of settled meaning. Kennedy says how much of the field is open cannot be answered in the abstract. It depends on the work.
  • Say. The judge is free to deploy work in any direction, yet the field is me, resisting myself.
  • Trap. If the law will not budge, Kennedy lists five courses, and not three (12.4.2). And he does not claim there is never a right answer. He reports his experience of free choice.
  • Verdict. Honest about the choice, and silent on how to make it.

2314.23 Pepper

🔑 Use: 10.1, 10.3, 15.11
▤ IN PLAIN WORDS
The card
  • PURPOSE: May a lawyer help a client do lawful things the lawyer thinks immoral?
  • CLAIM: Pepper argues that lawful help is morally justified, because access to law serves autonomy and equality. The client, and not the lawyer, is accountable.
  • TEST: See 15.11. Law is a public good available to all. Autonomy is a moral good. Access needs lawyers, so screening means rule by an oligarchy of lawyers.
  • STRENGTH: Equality. Screening would add inequality on top of inequality. If conduct is bad enough, it seems it ought to be made expressly unlawful.
  • CRITIQUE 1: Pepper's own problem is that realism plus the amoral role leaves no moral input or constraint. Reply: dialogue, choice of client, and conscientious objection, rarely used.
  • CRITIQUE 2: Liu† (Week 12, slide 5) asks why an institutional wrong is more acceptable than a personal one, and whether the institution is justified. Reply: first-class citizenship justifies it.
  • SAY: Morality comes through the door as part of the client. And the role is not comfortable, but it is good.
  • VERDICT: Pepper justifies access to law, and not every service. Pepper's own exceptions leave the lawyer a conscience the role cannot silence.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Tax Scheme

A wealthy client asks lawyer Farah to structure a lawful but aggressive scheme that shifts profits offshore to pay almost no tax. Farah thinks it is immoral.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Use each line of the card.

  • Claim and test. The tax law is a public good available to everyone. The client's autonomy in arranging his affairs is a moral good, and he needs a lawyer to use the law. If Farah refused because of her personal morals, lawyers would become an oligarchy deciding who gets the law.
  • Strength. If such schemes are bad enough, Parliament should ban them. Screening by lawyers would add a second inequality, a lawyer's approval, on top of the first, who can pay.
  • Critique 1. If the client thinks of law as just costs (realism), and Farah applies no morality, nothing restrains him. Pepper's replies are that Farah can raise her concerns, refuse the client at the outset or, in an extreme case, object.
  • Critique 2. Why is an unjust result acceptable as the system's wrong and not Farah's? Pepper answers that the system gives everyone first-class citizenship.
  • Say. Morality comes through the door as part of the client. Pepper's model is not comfortable, but it is good.
  • Verdict. Pepper justifies the client's access to law, and not every service Farah might be asked to provide. Her conscience survives.

2414.24 Thunder

🔑 Use: 10.4, 10.10, 12.5
▤ IN PLAIN WORDS
The card
  • PURPOSE: Can a good person be a lawyer without splitting professional from personal ethics?
  • CLAIM: Thunder holds that a lawyer's role is justified only by what it adds to justice and flourishing, so the good lawyer stays a good person.
  • TEST: The natural-teleological view. Law is meant ultimately, though not always immediately, for natural goods such as justice. The lawyer's function is to further justice, public order and the rule of law.
  • STRENGTH: Diagnosis. The amoral view draws its appeal from unlikely and unwitting partners: neo-Kantian rule-morality and legal realism.
  • CRITIQUE: Pepper says screening means rule by an oligarchy of lawyers. Reply: access to law is not access unchecked by others' judgment, and projects are properly hampered.
  • CONCEDE: Thunder admits there is substantial disagreement on particular cases, and that integrity is rarely, if ever, fully achieved. Concede that Thunder guides character more than cases. Settle hard cases by dialogue, with refusal only at the extremes (10).
  • SAY: Without this, lawyers are the slaves of their clients' consciences, however warped.
  • TRAP: Thunder's phrase just focus on the law voices the amoral view Thunder rejects, as does the practice question's phrase about just focusing on doing your job.
  • VERDICT: Thunder says better than Pepper what lawyers are for, but virtue names the goal without deciding the hard case.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Farah's Tax Scheme, Thunder's Way

Same facts as the hypo in 14.23; reread them first.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Use each line of the card.

  • Claim and test. Tax law ultimately serves justice and public order, by funding the common good. Farah's role is to further justice and the rule of law, and not just to serve the client. So she cannot treat the scheme as morally irrelevant.
  • Strength. Thunder explains why just doing the job feels natural: realism, where law is only costs, plus a rule-based ethics that sees reasons from a role as suspect.
  • Critique and reply. Pepper says that if Farah screens, she becomes part of an oligarchy of lawyers. Thunder says that having access to the law does not mean having it unchecked. A client's projects are properly hampered by other people's judgment, including his lawyer's.
  • Concede. Lawyers will disagree about whether this scheme crosses the line, and full integrity is rare. So Farah should start with dialogue, and refuse only if the scheme is extreme.
  • Say. Without that, lawyers become the slaves of their clients' consciences, however warped.
  • Trap. If a question says just focus on the law or just focus on doing your job, that is the view Thunder attacks, and it is not Thunder's own.
  • Verdict. Thunder names the goal. Dialogue and prudence must decide the hard case.

2514.25 TSH: Constitutional Jurisprudence

🔑 Use: 11.1, 11.7, 12.1
▤ IN PLAIN WORDS
The card
  • PURPOSE: Does a written, supreme Constitution make Singapore positivist?
  • CLAIM: Tan Seow Hon argues that the debate between natural law and positivism can never be settled by any declaration of supremacy. Contested terms force a choice of school, and constitutionalism affirms a higher law.
  • TEST: Two levels:
    1. what a contested term means, such as law, life and personal liberty in Article 9(1);
    2. what the supremacy clause in Article 4 brings with it.
  • CONCEDE: Who rightfully decides? George says that in a basically just regime, judges respect their limits. Tan Seow Hon admits there is no available formula. Concede the impasse: consensus may be the best gauge of morality, but it is not its ground.
  • VERDICT: Tan Seow Hon shows that the Constitution moves the debate between natural law and positivism and does not end it, leaving the question of authority open.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Detention Challenge

A man detained for 30 days without charge under a new Public Order Act argues that this takes away his personal liberty otherwise than in accordance with law (Article 9(1)). The government replies that the Act was validly passed, and that Article 4 says the Constitution is supreme, and not natural law.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Use each line of the card.

  • Level 1. What does law in Article 9(1) mean: any valid Act, or law that meets basic standards of justice? To choose is to choose a school of jurisprudence.
  • Level 2. Article 4 makes the Constitution supreme, but that does not make Singapore positivist. Supremacy rests on officials' acceptance, and constitutionalism itself affirms a higher law that limits power.
  • Concede. Who should decide whether 30 days is unjust: the court or Parliament? Tan Seow Hon admits there is no formula. Consensus is the best gauge available, but it is not the ground of what is right.
  • Verdict. The debate moves into the Constitution. It does not end there.

2614.26 TSH: Judicial Oligarchy

🔑 Use: 11.3, 11.5, 15.13
▤ IN PLAIN WORDS
The card
  • PURPOSE: How far may courts strike down laws on moral grounds?
  • CLAIM: Tan Seow Hon argues that courts should presume legislation constitutional, unless Radbruch's threshold of injustice is met, as shown by broad historical consensus.
  • TEST: See 15.13. Judges show the higher law by reference to broad historical consensus: racial genocide and slavery. Peremptory norms, the most basic rules of international law, count as evidence only.
  • STRENGTH: The alternatives are worse. A lower threshold invites judges to be reckless, and positivism leaves a brute majority unchecked.
  • CRITIQUE: Tan Seow Hon's own objection is that the Radbruch formula is not in the Constitution the nation accepted. Reply: constitutionalism rests on equal moral worth, so a majority vote must not approve its violation, even by amendment.
  • CONCEDE: Her catch: a lasting worldwide trend could, decades on, override a legislature trying to do right. Concede the risk. For her reply, see 8.5.
  • SG: Lim Meng Suang (Court of Appeal) rightly avoided rule by judges, but it was too optimistic about future Parliaments.
  • TRAP: Presumed constitutional does not mean presumed just.
  • VERDICT: Tan Seow Hon's threshold is the most defensible test for Singapore judges, once her own catch is conceded.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Judge Lim's Four Challenges (8.5), TSH's Way

Same facts as the hypo in 8.5; reread them first.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Use each line of the card.

  • Claim and test. Judge Lim presumes all four laws constitutional. Only the debt-bondage law, which is slavery in substance, meets the threshold, as shown by broad historical consensus. International peremptory norms against slavery support that, but only as evidence.
  • Strength. A lower threshold would let judges strike down the voting-age law recklessly. Pure positivism would let a brute majority enslave debtors.
  • Critique and reply. The Radbruch formula is not written into the Constitution. Tan Seow Hon replies that constitutionalism rests on equal moral worth, so even an amendment cannot authorise slavery.
  • Concede. Decades on, a worldwide trend could push judges to strike down a law that a local legislature is rightly keeping. Concede that, with her reply (8.5.3).
  • Singapore. Lim Meng Suang was right to avoid rule by judges, but too trusting about future Parliaments.
  • Trap. Being presumed constitutional does not mean the laws are just. The voting-age law may still be unwise.
  • Verdict. The most defensible test, once the catch is conceded.

2714.27 Same-question grid

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

Fuller 14.6Yes: legality's inner moralityAsk how much of a legal system survived
Finnis 14.8An unjust law lacks moral force at first sightPeace and justice; may ban acts intending harm to a goodReason, and not the sheer power of numbersMay owe obedience so that a just system is not weakened
Dworkin 14.5Yes: law in its best lightJudges, by fit and value
Rawls 14.10Not on full doctrines aloneCitizens as ideal legislators

Radbruch, Alexy 14.19Weakly: extreme injustice is not lawJudges, at extreme injustice onlyDeny it the character of law

Thunder 14.24It aims at justice and the common goodEach lawyer, by prudenceThe role is no excuse for a racist law
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Gambling Ban

Ruritania bans all private gambling, with jail terms. A court upholds the ban, a lawyer is asked to defend a poker player, and citizens must decide whether to obey.

✔ APPLICATION · Reading the grid acrossDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Read across the grid for each theorist.

  • Aquinas. If the ban is unjust, it is a corruption of law. Rulers decide, for the common good. Obey only to avoid scandal.
  • Hart. The ban is law. May it be justified? Only by harm, paternalism or decency, and private poker fails all three, except perhaps paternalism for addicts. Obedience is a moral question.
  • Fuller. Is the ban public, clear and followed by officials? If it is enforced only against some players, ask how much legality survives.
  • Finnis. The state keeps peace and justice, and may ban acts that intend harm to a good. Is casual poker such an act? Probably not. Disobedience may be limited, so that a just system is not weakened.
  • Dworkin. The judge must read the ban in its best light, by fit and value.
  • Rawls. The ban needs public reasons, and not one faith's condemnation of gambling. Citizens should vote as ideal legislators.
  • Devlin. Is private poker beyond the limits of tolerance, judged by the jury box? That is unlikely.
  • Radbruch and Alexy. The ban is not intolerably unjust, so it is law.
  • Kennedy. A judge who hates the ban works the field. If it will not budge, the judge picks among five courses.
  • Tan Seow Hon. The moral question cannot be avoided. The legislature decides, and the court strikes down only at the threshold of broad historical consensus, which is not met here.
  • Pepper. Parliament decided, and the lawyer serves the client within the law.
  • Thunder. The lawyer, by prudence, serves justice. The role is no excuse for a racist law, but this is not one.

2814.28 Cross-examination lines [Theorist only]

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

The six lines:

  1. Hart to Devlin. Why preserve a persecuting society whose disintegration might be morally better than its continuing to exist?
  2. Fuller to Hart. If positivism gives fidelity no coherent meaning, what does a judge owe a secret or retroactive Nazi statute?
  3. Tan Seow Hon to Alexy. If consensus nearly refutes relativism, what may a judge do once it goes badly wrong while a legislature tries to do right locally?
  4. Finnis to Rawls. If public reason sets moral truth aside, are the gravest questions not left to the status quo established by sheer power of numbers?
  5. Kennedy to Dworkin. When fit runs out and value is contested, is the chain novelist's best reading more than free ethical or political choice?
  6. Pepper to Thunder. If each lawyer screens by the lawyer's own virtue, what prevents rule by an oligarchy of lawyers?
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL

You are writing an answer and need one sharp objection for each paragraph. Where does each line fit?

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Match each line to an example.

  1. Hart to Devlin fits the Cohabitation Law (7.4). If Ruritania's old moral code persecuted cohabiting couples, why is losing it bad?
  2. Fuller to Hart fits the secret Schedule (14.6). What fidelity does a judge owe a secret statute?
  3. Tan Seow Hon to Alexy fits the twist set forty years on (8.5.3).
  4. Finnis to Rawls fits the Late-Limit Bill (6.5). Does setting aside the status of the unborn not leave it to numbers?
  5. Kennedy to Dworkin fits the Reasonable Rent clause (14.5). When both readings fit, is the choice more than politics?
  6. Pepper to Thunder fits Farah's tax scheme (14.24). If Farah screens by her own virtue, who checks her?

Use each line once, as the critique in that paragraph, and then give the reply from the relevant card.
