HYPO LESSON 15 · SECTION 15 · ABOUT 24 MIN · 29 QUESTIONS

Hypos: Frameworks

⚡ BIG IDEA

A framework is a test you run in order. Each example runs one framework, step by step, on made-up facts.

How to work through a hypo
  1. 1Read the rule (teal box). It puts the sheet's point in plain words. The exact wording to use in the exam is in the Lessons and Sheet tabs.
  2. 2Read the hypothetical (amber box). Before reading on, decide what the rule says about these facts.
  3. 3Tap Application (green box) and compare it with your answer.
  4. 4The exam cue (violet box) lists question words that should send you to this block. Each block ends with a quick check.
Applications:
ℹ NOTE
About these hypos

Each block on this page gives one framework in plain words, one made-up set of facts, and a worked answer that runs the steps in order and then applies the verdict rule. Your exact sheet wording, with its quotations, is still in the Lessons and Sheet tabs.

The Core version is the Theorist version without 15.2, 15.8, 15.9, 15.12 and 15.14, which are marked [Theorist only] below.

Some terms come up throughout. The Radbruch formula says a statute stops being law once its injustice is intolerable. Broad historical consensus is Tan Seow Hon's test for showing that injustice is intolerable: widespread agreement over time. TSH is Tan Seow Hon. A dagger (†) marks a point from the slides. The coverage table is the last section.

115.1 Fuller: legality checklist

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

The key question: can people follow this rule as it is made and applied? Use it for 3.1.

▤ IN PLAIN WORDS
The framework
  • The requirements. Is the rule (1) general? (2) published? (3) forward-looking? (4) clear? (5) consistent? (6) possible to obey? (7) stable over time? (8) matched by what officials actually do?
  • The verdict rule. Total failure of one requirement yields something that is not properly called a legal system at all. Short of that, legality is a matter of degree. It is not substantive justice (15.13).
  • Rex, who failed in all eight ways and so made no law at all:
    1. case-by-case rulings;
    2. a secret code;
    3. rulings with hindsight;
    4. an obscure code;
    5. contradictions;
    6. impossible demands;
    7. constant amendment;
    8. rulings unrelated to the code.
  • Traps.
    • Requirement (1) means having rules at all, and it is not about how broad they are. Palm-tree justice (deciding each case on a whim), laws aimed at named people, and unlimited discretion all fail it.
    • Requirement (2) needs access, and not that everyone actually knows.
    • Requirement (3) bars only abuse (Liu, Week 2).
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Port Meridian Protest Law

Port Meridian's new Protest Act:

  • lets the Commissioner approve or refuse each protest as the Commissioner sees fit;
  • is published online, though few read it;
  • applies only to future protests;
  • bans protests likely to cause unease;
  • contains a clause requiring 30 days' notice, and another allowing protests on 7 days' notice;
  • requires organisers to guarantee that no participant feels distressed;
  • has been amended six times in two months;
  • is enforced only against opposition groups.
✔ APPLICATION · Step by stepDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Run the eight requirements in order.

  1. General? It largely fails. Approving protests as the Commissioner sees fit is unlimited discretion, which is closer to case-by-case rulings than to rules. Generality means having rules at all, and not broad ones.
  2. Published? Yes. It is accessible, even if few read it. Everyone knowing about it is not required.
  3. Forward-looking? Yes. Only abuse of retroactivity is barred.
  4. Clear? No. Likely to cause unease tells no one what is banned.
  5. Consistent? No. It requires both 30 days' notice and 7 days' notice.
  6. Possible? No. No organiser can guarantee that no one feels distressed.
  7. Stable? No. There were six amendments in two months.
  8. Matched by official action? No. It is enforced only against the opposition.

The verdict. No requirement fails totally across the whole system, so Port Meridian still has a legal system. But this Act is badly degraded as law, or as Fuller puts it, less a law. And a fully compliant Act could still be unjust. That is a question for the Radbruch formula and 15.13, and not for Fuller.

215.2 Is–ought repair [Theorist only]

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

The key question: which unstated premise about what ought to be done yields this conclusion? Use it for 4.4.

▤ IN PLAIN WORDS
The framework
  1. Liu's method (Week 3). List the premises a neutral listener must accept. Mark the moral ones, including the hidden ones. Defend each. The dispute shrinks to one bedrock premise.
  2. Split the facts (what is) from the conclusion (what ought to be). No ought follows from an is alone (Hume).
  3. Supply the missing major premise. Once the parties agree on it, they can go on to deduce conclusions about what ought to be done (page 13).
  4. Test that premise. Is it self-evident on reflection (Finnis), or mere preference?

The verdict rule. Argue about the premise, and not about the inference.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Screen-Time Study

A study shows that teenagers who use social media more than 3 hours a day report more anxiety. A minister concludes that the law should therefore ban social media for under-16s.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Run the steps in order.

  1. The premises a neutral listener must accept:
    • (a) the study is accurate (factual);
    • (b) social media causes the anxiety (factual);
    • (c) the state should protect children's mental health (moral);
    • (d) protection justifies a ban and not lesser measures (moral, and hidden);
    • (e) the costs to teenagers' freedom and friendships are outweighed (moral, and hidden). The dispute shrinks to (d) and (e).
  2. Split is from ought. The fact that teenagers who use it more are more anxious is an is. Banning it is an ought. The first alone cannot give the second.
  3. Supply the missing premise. The state ought to prevent serious, avoidable harm to children's health by the least restrictive effective means. If both sides accept that, the facts can then decide whether a ban, or something lesser, follows.
  4. Test the premise. Is protecting children's health self-evidently good? On Finnis's view, life, including psychological health, is a basic good. But doing so by a ban is not self-evident.

The verdict. Argue about premises (d) and (e), and not about whether the study proves the ban.

315.3 Finnis: is this act permissible?

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

The key question: does it choose directly against a basic good? Use it for 5.3.

▤ IN PLAIN WORDS
The framework
  1. Which basic good is being pursued?
  2. Is a basic good damaged as an end or as a means? Then it is wrong. Do not choose directly against a basic value.
  3. Side effects must pass the golden rule. Would I have thought the act reasonable if I had been the person harmed?

The verdict rule. Intended damage is never allowed. Side effects are allowed only if fair.

Liu's rulings (Week 5).

  • Barred: the hostage (even a volunteer); the footbridge push; self-injury for insurance; the death penalty, even for Hitler; euthanasia; suicide.
  • Permitted or arguable: the trolley switch; triage; a mining job that damages the lungs; shooting to disarm, with death foreseen.

Requirement (6) weighs, and requirement (7) vetoes.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Four Hospital Decisions
  • (a) A surgeon could save five patients by taking the organs of one healthy visitor who has not consented.
  • (b) In a mass-casualty event, doctors leave the most hopeless patients untreated to save the most lives.
  • (c) A doctor gives a dying patient high-dose morphine to relieve pain, foreseeing it may hasten death.
  • (d) A doctor gives a lethal injection at a patient's request.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Run the test on each decision.

  • (a) Life is damaged as a means, through the organs. It is barred, whatever the numbers. Requirement (7) vetoes the efficient answer that requirement (6) would weigh.
  • (b) The good pursued is life. Not treating is not killing, and death is a side effect. Is it fair? Would I accept it if I were the hopeless patient, knowing others could be saved? Arguably yes. It is permitted, like triage.
  • (c) The good pursued is freedom from pain, which is part of life in Finnis's broad sense. Death is a foreseen side effect and not the aim. If it is proportionate and fair, it is arguable, like shooting to disarm.
  • (d) Death is the means of ending suffering. It is barred, as euthanasia.

415.4 Finnis: may the state legislate this?

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

The key question: does it serve the common good, intending no harm? Use it for 5.5.

▤ IN PLAIN WORDS
The framework
  1. Two uses (Liu, Week 5; Week 4, slide 11†):
    • judge laws directly: authorising an act against a good is wrong (for Finnis, the death penalty and abortion);
    • judge facilitation: coordination counts, such as driving on one side of the road, and requirement (3) bars arbitrary distinctions between citizens.
  2. Aim: peace and justice, and not making people wholly good.
  3. Means: never intend damage to a good. The state may prohibit acts that intend it (Week 4, slide 12†).
  4. Reasons must be open to all people, whatever their religious beliefs.
  5. Prudence: not enforcing a law can be reasonable, to avoid a war that one cannot win.

The verdict rule. Prohibit intended harm, on reasons open to all, where it is prudent.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Online Falsehoods Bill (POFMA-style)

Port Meridian proposes a law letting a minister order corrections to deliberately false statements of fact online.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Run the steps in order.

  1. Two uses. Directly, the law does not itself authorise any act against a good. As facilitation, it protects the conditions for public knowledge, and it coordinates a shared factual basis for public debate. It must not draw arbitrary lines, such as applying only to opposition parties.
  2. Aim. Peace and justice, meaning an information environment that serves citizens' own pursuit of knowledge. It is not aimed at making citizens think correctly.
  3. Means. The state must not itself lie or suppress truth. It may prohibit deliberate falsehoods, because those intend to damage knowledge.
  4. Reasons. Protecting public knowledge is a reason anyone can accept, religious or not.
  5. Prudence. A broad ministerial power risks chilling honest speech. Narrow scope and court review may be wiser, and in some settings, not enforcing it may be prudent.

The verdict. It is permissible in principle, if it is confined to deliberate falsehoods, justified by reasons open to all, and prudently limited.

515.5 Rawls: is this law legitimate?

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

The key question: could every reasonable citizen endorse the reasons? Use it for 6.1.

▤ IN PLAIN WORDS
The framework
  1. Is it a constitutional essential, or a matter of basic justice?
  2. Is the speaker acting in the public forum, including citizens voting as if they were legislators?
  3. Are the reasons political values, or full-doctrine reasons backed by public ones in due course (the proviso)?
  4. Reciprocity. Are the reasons acceptable to others as free and equal citizens, and not as people dominated or manipulated? Denying basic liberties normally fails.

The verdict rule. It is legitimate if (3) and (4) hold.

Completeness. No argument may jump too quickly from a doctrine to a policy. These are not political values: moral autonomy, moral desert, and monogamy as such.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Casino Licence Debate

Port Meridian's Parliament debates licensing a second casino.

  • MP A argues that gambling is a sin.
  • MP B argues that it will raise problem-gambling rates and harm families, and that studies show this.
  • MP C argues that adults' moral autonomy requires allowing it.
  • MP D argues that those who gamble deserve to lose their money.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Run the steps in order.

  1. Essential or basic justice? Partly. It touches economic justice and family welfare, so public reason applies as far as possible.
  2. Public-forum actors? All four are MPs, so yes.
  3. Political values?
    • A's reason comes from a religious doctrine, with no public reason following. It fails, unless A later adds public reasons.
    • B's reasons are political values: family welfare and public health. They pass.
    • C's reason, moral autonomy (Mill's individuality), is not a political value. It fails as stated, but it could be reframed as political liberty.
    • D's reason, moral desert, is not a political value. It fails.
  4. Reciprocity. B's reasons could be accepted by gamblers and non-gamblers as free and equal citizens. A's could not be accepted by non-believers.
  • Completeness. No MP may jump straight from a doctrine to licensing or banning. Each must work through political values.

The verdict. A decision based on reasons like B's is legitimate, whichever way it goes.

615.6 Devlin: the interrogatories

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

The key question: is it beyond the limits of tolerance? Use it for 7.3.

▤ IN PLAIN WORDS
The framework
  1. May society judge morals?
  2. May the law enforce that judgment?
  3. Always, or on what principles (Devlin)?
  4. Do not count heads. Ask what twelve people chosen at random could be expected to agree on unanimously after discussion (page 15).
  5. Elastic principles: the maximum individual freedom consistent with the integrity of society, and a real feeling of disapproval (pages 16 to 17).
  6. A vice so abominable that its mere presence is an offence may be eradicated. One that is tolerable if confined calls for a balance (page 17). The law sets the minimum and not the maximum.

The verdict rule. A majority's dislike is far from enough (page 17).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Private Cockfighting

A group in Ruritania holds private cockfights for betting, on a remote farm. A poll shows 60% dislike it.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Run the steps in order.

  1. Judge morals? Yes. Cruelty to animals is a moral matter society may judge.
  2. Enforce by law? In principle yes, because Devlin sets no theoretical limit.
  3. On what principles? See steps 4 to 6.
  4. The jury box. Would twelve random Ruritanians, after discussion, be unanimous that cockfighting is intolerable? Very likely, given the animals' suffering, unlike many contested questions of sexual morality.
  5. Elastic principles. Maximum freedom consistent with society's integrity. Is there a real feeling of disapproval, deeply felt and not manufactured? Probably yes.
  6. Eradicate or balance? Devlin treats cruelty to animals as beyond tolerance even in private, so it may be eradicated.

The verdict. The 60% poll is not enough. But the jury-box test, properly applied, supports a ban. Hart reaches the same result by a different route: the animals' suffering.

715.7 Hart: may the criminal law prohibit it? (and the coercion gradient)

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

The key question: what justifies this coercion, besides immorality as such? Use it for 7.9.

▤ IN PLAIN WORDS
The framework

Coercion is objectionable at first sight.

  1. Harm to others? Distress at the bare knowledge of others' conduct does not count.
  2. Paternalism, if consent is defective: for example, punishing drug supply except on prescription.
  3. Public decency: the offence must be serious and likely, weighed against the freedom lost.
  4. Moralism alone: never.

The verdict rule (the sheet's own, on Liu's map; all law rests on force, criminal law most directly, Week 9). The more coercive the measure (punish, regulate, promote), the stronger the reason needed. Hart's own question is about punishment only.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Recreational Veridine (7.0), Three Measures

Ruritania considers (a) jailing veridine users, (b) prescription-only sale, and (c) public-health campaigns.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Run the steps in order.

  1. Harm to others. Private use harms mainly the user. Neighbours' distress at merely knowing it happens does not count.
  2. Paternalism. Consent may be impaired, through addiction or passing desires. That supports (b), restricting supply, as Hart did for drugs.
  3. Public decency. Public intoxication could be an offence. Private use is not.
  4. Moralism alone. The claim that using veridine is degrading cannot justify (a).

The gradient. Punishment in (a) needs the strongest reason, and that is lacking. Regulation in (b) has a paternalist reason. Promotion in (c) needs the least. And Hart's own question concerns only (a).

815.8 Alexy: should a judge deny it legal character? [Theorist only]

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

The key question: is the injustice extreme, to a participant? Use it for 8.3.

▤ IN PLAIN WORDS
The framework
  1. Take the participant's view, such as a judge's, and not the observer's.
  2. The weak thesis: legal character is lost only at an intolerable degree of injustice (Alexy).

Concede. Definitions cannot, as such, change reality. And candour is the strongest argument against non-positivism, though not its downfall.

The verdict rule. Deny legal character only where the injustice was evident when it was done, so that there is no hidden retroactivity.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Junta's Property Decree

A Valdorian judge in 2021 must decide whether a 2010 Junta decree seizing the homes of the Kel minority was law, in a claim by the dispossessed owners against the current occupants.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Run the steps in order.

  1. Participant. The judge must decide what the law was, as a participant claiming correctness, and not as a historian describing Junta practice.
  2. Intolerable? Seizing the homes of one ethnic group, without compensation, is extreme injustice. Legal character is lost.
  • Concede. Calling it not law does not change what happened to the owners in 2010. Candour remains the strongest objection.
  • The verdict rule. Was the injustice evident in 2010? Racial dispossession was obviously unjust at the time, so the occupants had notice. Denying the decree legal character is not hidden retroactivity. The owners succeed.

915.9 Dworkin: fit, then value [Theorist only]

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

The key question: which principle best fits and justifies the legal history? Use it for 9.2.

▤ IN PLAIN WORDS
The framework
  1. List the rival principles.
  2. Fit: interpret the legal history you find, and do not invent a better one.
  3. Value: choose the one that states a sounder principle of justice.

The verdict rule. Concede that fit will often fail to produce one unique interpretation, and state the political morality openly.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Rescue Volunteer (9.2)

Same facts as the hypo in 9.2; reread them first.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Run the steps in order.

  1. Rival principles.
    • (A) Liability for psychiatric harm extends to those foreseeably drawn into the danger, including rescuers.
    • (B) Liability extends only to close relatives at the scene.
  2. Fit. Both fit some cases. (A) fits cases where rescuers recovered for physical injury. (B) fits the nervous-shock cases. Neither is invented.
  3. Value. (A) states a sounder principle of justice. People who answer the call to rescue should not bear the cost of the defendant's negligence.
  • The verdict rule. Concede that fit did not settle it. State openly that the choice rests on fairness to rescuers.

1015.10 Kennedy: the five courses

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

The key question: the law and the outcome the judge wants conflict, so what may the judge do? Use it for 12.4 and 8.7.

▤ IN PLAIN WORDS
The framework
  1. Go along, and denounce the law.
  2. Withdraw, leaving the dirty work to another judge.
  3. Decide openly on what the law should be.
  4. Use an implausible legal argument.
  5. Find facts known to be false, which is obviously an extreme measure.

The verdict rule.

  • Kennedy does not endorse or exclude any of them in advance.
  • The sheet's own rule: in a basically just system, choose (1) or (2). Choose (3) only at the Radbruch threshold. (4) and (5) fail candour (12.4).
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Deportation Order

In just Ruritania, a judge must order the deportation of a long-term resident whose visa lapsed through a clerical error. The statute leaves no discretion. The judge thinks deportation cruel.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Run through the five courses.

  1. Go along. Order it, and write an opinion criticising the statute. That fits a basically just system.
  2. Withdraw. Step aside so another judge decides. This is available, but it passes the dirty work on.
  3. Decide by what the law should be. Refuse to order it. That is only for the Radbruch threshold, and a deportation is harsh but not intolerable injustice. So no.
  4. An implausible argument. For example, that the visa did not truly lapse. This fails candour.
  5. A false finding. For example, that the resident proved residency rights. This fails candour, and it is extreme.

The verdict. Choose (1), perhaps with a call for ministerial discretion.

1115.11 Pepper: the limit and the remedies

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

The key question: it is lawful but wrong, so what may the lawyer do? Use it for 10.1.

▤ IN PLAIN WORDS
The framework
  1. Law is the limit. Conduct that is bad enough, it seems, ought to be made expressly unlawful (Pepper).
  2. Responses to legal realism:
    • for society: more enforcement, which is a daunting task, or rebuilding moral authority beyond law;
    • for lawyers: not to be policeman, judge or deceiver, but to have moral dialogue, which is costly and needs a receptive client.
  3. Conscientious objection, rarely used.

The verdict rule. Advise on the law, add moral dialogue, and object only in extreme cases.

Liu (S13, meaning Session 13).

  • Leaving practice is a pretty weak kind of answer.
  • Choice of client is more respectable, but it assumes someone else will act. That fails if a view is widespread, or if only the least scrupulous lawyers remain.
  • Pepper accepts that this can mean second-class citizenship.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Landlord's Lawful Eviction

A landlord asks lawyer Kai to evict an elderly tenant on the earliest lawful date, two weeks before the tenant's hip surgery. It is fully lawful.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Run the steps in order.

  1. The limit is the law. If this were bad enough, Parliament should ban it. It has not.
  2. Kai should not act as policeman, judge or deceiver. He must not refuse to tell the landlord the landlord's rights, or mislead the landlord. He can raise moral dialogue, by asking whether a month's delay would cost much. That costs time, and needs a receptive client.
  3. Objection is for extreme cases. This is probably not one.
  • The verdict rule. Advise, discuss, and act.
  • Liu. If Kai simply quit practice, that would be a weak answer. If Kai declined the client, that is more respectable. But if every scrupulous lawyer declined, only the least scrupulous would remain, and the landlord would get served anyway. And Pepper admits that a client refused by every lawyer gets second-class citizenship.

1215.12 Liu's three lawyering scenarios† [Theorist only]

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

The key question: where is the injustice: in the system, the rule, or the outcome? Use it for 10.11.

▤ IN PLAIN WORDS
The framework
  1. Is the system, by and large, just?
  2. If so, is this rule intolerably unjust?
  3. If the rule is just, is only this outcome unjust, as when a coerced confession is excluded (Week 12, slide 9)?

Thunder (Week 12, slide 8†: the good life over the role; question roles; courage and moderation; personal and professional excellence depend on each other):

  • Does the work serve justice, public order and the rule of law?
  • Does it need courage against pressure to conform, or moderation short of avoidable injustice?

The verdict rule (the sheet's own):

  • in (3), defend fully;
  • in (2), refuse, or argue the formula;
  • in (1), the role gives no shelter.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Teo's Three Files (10.11)

Same facts as the hypo in 10.11; reread them first.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Take each file.

  • File 3 (coerced confession excluded). The system and the rule are just, and only the outcome is unjust. Defend fully. The work serves justice and the rule of law. It may take courage against pressure from colleagues who think the client should be convicted.
  • File 2 (racist eviction statute). The system is just, but the rule is intolerably unjust. Refuse, or argue in court that the formula denies the statute legal character. Moderation means not going further than avoiding the injustice.
  • File 1 (the Junta's sham courts). The system is not just. The role gives Teo no shelter. Saying he was only a lawyer will not excuse lending legitimacy to the sham.

1315.13 TSH: should a court strike it down? (RF plus BHC)

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

The key question: is it manifestly unjust by broad historical consensus? Use it for 11.5 and 12.4.

▤ IN PLAIN WORDS
The framework
  1. Presume a law is constitutional, unless the threshold of injustice in the Radbruch formula is met (Tan Seow Hon).
  2. Proof: a long-lasting consensus across many jurisdictions, for the same reason.
  3. Met (genocide, slavery): strike it down, even if it is an amendment. Not met (Roe): legislatures decide.

Her catch. A world trend might carry the formula decades on, and consensus can go badly wrong.

The verdict rule. This test is for courts only. Legislators need no such consensus.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Child Labour Act

Ruritania amends its Constitution, by two-thirds, to permit children aged 10 and up to work 12-hour shifts in mines. Separately, a statute limits Sunday trading hours.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Run the steps in order.

  1. Presume both are constitutional.
  2. Proof. Is there a long-lasting consensus across many jurisdictions, for the same reason, that forcing 10-year-olds into 12-hour mine shifts is intolerably unjust? Plausibly yes. It is a form of child servitude, condemned across the world for generations. For Sunday trading limits, there is no such consensus.
  3. Strike down the child-labour amendment, even though it is an amendment. Leave the Sunday trading law to Parliament.
  • The catch. Concede that consensus could someday go wrong.
  • The verdict rule. A legislator deciding whether to repeal the Sunday trading law needs no consensus, just good reasons.

1415.14 Who decides? [Theorist only]

▤ THE RULE · IN PLAIN WORDS

The key question: who rightfully decides, and is anyone usurping or abdicating? Use it for 12.1.

▤ IN PLAIN WORDS
The framework
  1. Positive law shares out authority (a determinatio). In a basically just regime, judges taking over power are acting unjustly, even in what they take to be good causes (George).
  2. But who rightfully decides whether the sharing out was prudent? This is an impasse.
  3. A whipped Parliament may not reflect consensus (6.8), and courts may be urged to uphold higher law and not play politics.

The verdict rule. Honour the allocation, and depart from it only at the Radbruch threshold (15.13).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Euthanasia Case (12.1)

Same facts as the hypo in 12.1; reread them first.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Run the steps in order.

  1. The allocation. Ruritania's Constitution gives Parliament the power to make criminal law. In a basically just regime, if the court invented a right to assisted death, that would be usurpation, even for a good cause (George).
  2. The impasse. But who decides whether giving Parliament that power was prudent? There is no clear answer.
  3. Caveats. If Parliament was whipped on euthanasia, its vote may not reflect consensus (6.8). And courts should uphold higher law, and not play politics.
  • The verdict rule. Honour the allocation. Euthanasia law is not at the Radbruch threshold, so it is for Parliament.

HYPO LESSON 16 · SECTION 16 · ABOUT 17 MIN · 25 QUESTIONS

Hypos: Singapore bank

⚡ BIG IDEA

Singapore material is evidence, and not a trump card. Each example tests a claim about Singapore against what actually happened.

How to work through a hypo
  1. 1Read the rule (teal box). It puts the sheet's point in plain words. The exact wording to use in the exam is in the Lessons and Sheet tabs.
  2. 2Read the hypothetical (amber box). Before reading on, decide what the rule says about these facts.
  3. 3Tap Application (green box) and compare it with your answer.
  4. 4The exam cue (violet box) lists question words that should send you to this block. Each block ends with a quick check.
Applications:
ℹ NOTE
About these hypos

Each block on this page gives the item in plain words, a made-up set of facts where you would reach for it, and a worked answer. Your exact sheet wording, with its quotations, is still in the Lessons and Sheet tabs.

The bills and fact patterns are invented. The Articles, cases and Hansard speakers are real and come from the sheet.

Some terms come up throughout. Legal positivism says whether something is law depends on its source and not on its merit. Natural law theory ties law to what is morally good. The Radbruch formula says a statute stops being law once its injustice is intolerable. Part 4 is the part of the Constitution that sets out fundamental liberties. TSH is Tan Seow Hon. A dagger (†) marks a point from the slides. The coverage table is the last section.

116.1 Articles

16.1.1 Arts 4 and 162: supremacy

▤ IN PLAIN WORDS
The item

The Constitution is the supreme law. A later inconsistent law is void. An earlier law is read to conform (Week 13, slide 8†). Use: this does not mean legal positivism has been chosen (11.1).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL

A colonial-era ordinance from 1955 lets officials bar people of bad character from public parks. A 2020 Act lets the police detain protesters without any hearing. Both are challenged as inconsistent with Part 4.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Treat the two laws differently.

  • The 1955 ordinance is pre-existing law. So under Article 162 it is read to conform with the Constitution. For example, bad character is read narrowly, to fit Article 12.
  • The 2020 Act is a later law. To the extent it is inconsistent with the Constitution, Article 4 makes it void.
  • Neither result makes Singapore positivist. Article 4 is supreme because officials accept it. And reading a law as consistent with Part 4 still requires deciding what liberty and equal mean (11.1).

16.1.2 Art 5(2): amendment

▤ IN PLAIN WORDS
The item

Two-thirds of elected MPs can amend most provisions. Use: the basic features doctrine, the idea that some parts cannot be amended, was rejected in Teo Soh Lung, and left open in Yong Vui Kong (2015).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL

Parliament, by two-thirds, amends Article 9 to allow detention without trial for economic saboteurs.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Work through the checks that remain.

  • As a matter of form, Article 5(2) allows it.
  • There is no basic-features shield. Singapore's High Court in Teo Soh Lung rejected the Indian doctrine of basic features that cannot be amended, and the Court of Appeal in Yong Vui Kong (2015) left it open.
  • So the only legal check left is the narrow one Tan Seow Hon defends. An amendment that is intolerably unjust, such as genocide or slavery, falls to the Radbruch formula (11.1.3). Economic detention probably does not reach that threshold, which shows how much power two-thirds holds (11.7).

16.1.3 Art 9(1): in accordance with law

▤ IN PLAIN WORDS
The item

No person may be deprived of life or personal liberty except in accordance with law. Use: the four readings of law† (Week 13, slides 16 to 17).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL

The Littering (Caning) Bill (11.2).

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Run the four readings:

  1. validly passed;
  2. natural justice;
  3. not absurd or arbitrary;
  4. consistent with international law.

The Bill survives each one, and falls to the Radbruch formula only if broad historical consensus condemns it. Choosing among the readings is a choice of theory (11.2).

16.1.4 Art 12: equality

▤ IN PLAIN WORDS
The item

All persons are equal before the law and entitled to its equal protection. Use: reasonable classification (11.3).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL

The Left-Handed Drivers' Fee (11.3).

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

The court asks whether left-handed is a line that makes sense and is rationally linked to the regulation's object, road safety. If the link rests on junk science, the classification fails. And Tan Seow Hon adds that deciding which differences are morally significant needs a moral view of equality.

16.1.5 Art 156: marriage

▤ IN PLAIN WORDS
The item
  • (1) The law may define, regulate, protect, support and promote marriage.
  • (3) to (4) Part 4 cannot make void any law or executive act based on the definition of marriage as between a man and a woman, which stays in statute (Interpretation Act, section 2(1); Women's Charter, section 12(1)).

Use: Tan Seow Hon calls this a pre-emptive strike against judicial activism. Liu notes it is unentrenched, so a simple majority may change it (Week 9).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL

A couple challenges a Housing Board rule giving priority to married couples of a man and a woman, relying on Article 12.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Article 156 answers the challenge, for now.

  • Article 156 shields it. The rule is an executive act based on the definition of marriage as between a man and a woman (Women's Charter, section 12(1)). So Part 4, including Article 12, cannot make it void.
  • Tan Seow Hon's view. This is exactly what Article 156 was for: stopping a court from redefining marriage through equality rights.
  • Liu's point. Article 156 itself is not entrenched, so a future Parliament with a simple majority could change it. The shield is political and not permanent.

216.2 Cases

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Eleven Problems, Eleven Cases

For each fact pattern, identify the authority and the angle.

#Fact patternCaseWhat it heldThe angle to argue
1An accused says the word law in Article 9 requires a fair procedure, and not just any statute.Ong Ah Chuan (Privy Council)Law in Article 9 includes the fundamental rules of natural justice.Substantive fairness was left open, and has since been narrowed (Yong Vui Kong, 2015†).
2The State argues that any validly passed law binds, fair or not.Jabar (Court of Appeal, 1995)A remark that a validly passed law binds, whether or not it is fair, just and reasonable.A legal positivist line, but limited by Yong Vui Kong (2010)†: it is not about whether a statute is constitutional.
3The Attorney-General urges the court to ignore foreign rights cases.Colin Chan (High Court, 1994)The Constitution is read within its own four walls, and unity is the paramount aim.The positivist approach, on Liu's slide† (Week 13, slide 6). Answer with universal fairness in Haw Tua Tau (11.4).
4A prisoner argues that a life sentence meant 20 years when he was sentenced.Abdul Nasir (Court of Appeal, 1997)†Life imprisonment means natural life, but for the future only.A problem of constancy (8.6), and not of being branded as criminals.
5A challenger says a moral law breaches Article 12, and that Article 9 protects privacy.Lim Meng Suang (Court of Appeal, 2014)Section 377A passes Article 12. Article 9 covers unlawful taking of life and detention, and not privacy.Hart against Devlin is very much for Parliament.
6A statute is so arbitrary that no framer could have meant it as law.Yong Vui Kong (Court of Appeal, 2010)†Article 9 may exclude laws so absurd or arbitrary that the framers could not have meant them as law (Week 13, slide 17).A natural-law hook, short of the Radbruch formula.
7A convict argues that natural law forbids caning.Yong Vui Kong (Court of Appeal, 2015)No right may be made out of whole cloth as natural law, so there is no right against caning.There was no ruling on what natural law says of caning. And natural justice is procedural† (Week 13, slide 17).
8Activists seek a declaration that section 377A was unconstitutional.Tan Seng Kee (Court of Appeal, 2022)No standing. In passing: Articles 9 and 14 probably not breached, and Article 12 less certain.The Syed Suhail test might fail section 377A. The law was unenforceable until the Attorney-General gave notice†.
9A gay father seeks to adopt his son, born through surrogacy.UKM (High Court, 2018)He was allowed to adopt, despite section 377A.The moral signpost failed (11.6).
10A citizen convicted for corruption committed abroad claims Article 12 discrimination.Taw Cheng Kong (Court of Appeal, 1998)Section 37(1) of the Prevention of Corruption Act reaches citizens' acts abroad, even without effects here. There is no Article 12 breach, as all are caught as a class.The presumption of constitutionality.
11A litigant in 2021 asks what the last ruling on section 377A held.Ong Ming Johnson (High Court, 2020)Section 377A upheld against Articles 9 and 12.The last ruling before the doubt about Article 12 in Tan Seng Kee.

How to use the table. In an essay, one case per point is enough. For example, in 11.2 use Ong Ah Chuan with Yong Vui Kong (2015) for the natural-justice reading. In 3.2, use Tan Seng Kee for non-enforcement. In 7.6, use UKM for why the moral signpost failed to do its work.

316.3 Hansard: who said what

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Ruritania's Cohabitation Debate

Ruritania's Parliament debates repealing its cohabitation law (7.4). You want a real Singapore speaker for each argument. The lines below are paraphrased, and the exact words are on your sheet.

The argument you are makingSpeaker and what they saidHow to use it
Public feeling is strong and divided, and the law is not actively enforcedHo Peng Kee, 22 October 2007: feedback was emotional and divided, with most calling for the law to stay. Police were not actively enforcing it.Shows Devlin-style slowness, and the non-enforcement compromise (7.6, 7.7).
Repeal will spill over into public lifede Souza, 22 October 2007: what is private will not stay private.The principled slope (7.4).
The law breaches equality, and harm must be concreteSiew Kum Hong, 22 October 2007: section 377A breaches Article 12(1). Citing Hor, harm must be recognisable and tangible.The harm principle, made demanding (7.1, 7.8).
Follow the majority, unless a minority needs protectionIndranee Rajah, 22 October 2007: in most cases we would go with the majority view, unless there is a reason to protect the minority.The strongest case for majority rule (7.11).
Harm can be intangibleThio Li-ann, 22 October 2007: harm can be both physical and intangible.Widens the idea of harm (7.6).
Unenforced laws damage credibilityHri Kumar Nair, 22 October 2007: toothless laws hurt our credibility.Against non-enforcement (7.7). He also noted that the 70% who frowned on the conduct were never asked about making it a crime (7.11).
Keep the status quo, and lag behind moral changePM Lee, 23 October 2007: keep the status quo, and stay a step behind on moral change.Devlin's slowness, and pragmatism (2.7, 7.6).
A crime needs a public-order reasonShanmugam, 28 November 2022: a crime generally needs a public order or public interest issue, broadly similar to Wolfenden.The case for repeal (7.5, 14.12).
Relying on non-enforcement is dangerousPerera, 28 November 2022: an unenforced law that rests on the word of the government of the day is unsatisfactory and dangerous.The strongest case against non-enforcement (3.2.2).
Sin is not crimePritam Singh, 28 November 2022: in any secular society, sin and crime are separate categories.Against faith-based bans (7.10).
MPs must decide hard questionsMasagos, 29 November 2022: Article 156 is meant to prevent a change in social norms following the repeal, and MPs have a duty to come to a decision.The line for legislators (12.3).
Let the people decide by referendumPoa, 29 November 2022: a referendum, because marriage is a matter of social norm.The strongest case for a referendum (12.3).
Even an unenforced law stigmatisesHe Ting Ru, 29 November 2022: a law that is plainly discriminatory sends a signal that an identity should be seen as criminal, even if only on paper.Against keeping symbolic laws (3.2, 7.7).
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

In the Ruritanian debate, pair each argument with its Singapore speaker. For example, you might say that as Pritam Singh put it, in any secular society sin and crime are separate categories, so the faith-based case for keeping the law fails. Or you might say that, as Perera warned, a law resting only on a promise not to enforce it is unsatisfactory and dangerous. Use one or two speakers per essay, and not all thirteen.

416.4 Statutes and PCR

16.4.1 Penal Code s 377A

▤ IN PLAIN WORDS
The item

It made acts of gross indecency between males a crime, in public or in private. The repeal (2022) came into force on 3 January 2023.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL

A student writes in 2026 that section 377A is still in force but not enforced.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

That is wrong. It was repealed, with effect from 3 January 2023. Use section 377A as history: the 2007 compromise (7.6), Tan Seng Kee (3.2.3), and the 2022 package (13.2).

16.4.2 Penal Code s 121A (before 2019)†

▤ IN PLAIN WORDS
The item

Imagining the President's death, hurt or restraint was punishable by death or life imprisonment. It is Liu's example of congruence and discretion (Week 2, slide 11; 3.2, 3.4).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL

A question asks how a law can fail Fuller's requirement of congruence, meaning that officials act on the rules as stated.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Old section 121A is the ideal example. Imagining cannot be observed, so it could only be enforced arbitrarily. That guarantees a gap between the rule and official action, which is the congruence problem. And enforcement is left to prosecutors' discretion (3.4).

16.4.3 Termination of Pregnancy Act (as TSH described it, 2010–11)

▤ IN PLAIN WORDS
The item
  • Abortion up to 24 weeks for any reason. From 16 weeks, only by a qualified practitioner.
  • Later than that, only to save life or prevent grave permanent injury.
  • Counselling, then a 48-hour wait.
  • The 1969 Act passed 32 to 10 on a free vote.
  • The 1974 Act left the choice to the woman, and was among the most liberal in the world.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL

An essay on whether Parliament can stay neutral on abortion (6.5).

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Use the Act in three ways.

  • The 1974 Act, by leaving the choice to the woman, is the supposedly neutral permissive model. Tan Seow Hon says it actually settles the metaphysical question.
  • The 1969 free vote is the precedent for lifting the whip on matters of conscience (6.8).
  • A caveat. Tan Seow Hon described the law as it stood in 2010 to 2011, so say that this is how she described it.

16.4.4 Professional conduct (Liu, S13)

▤ IN PLAIN WORDS
The item

Pepper's limit includes the enforced conduct rules: fairness to unrepresented persons, not misleading the court, and disclosing adverse authority. So the stronger those rules are, the less the choice between Pepper and Thunder changes what a lawyer does.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL

A lawyer following Pepper and a lawyer following Thunder both face an unrepresented opponent and an adverse precedent the opponent has missed.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Both must disclose the adverse authority, and both must treat the unrepresented person fairly, because the conduct rules require it. So here, the two lawyers act alike. The gap between them is mindset and not outcome (10.10.4).

516.5 Applying the theorists: the 2022 package, and Liu's prompts

16.5.1 Liu's exercise on the 2022 package (W6, W9)

▤ IN PLAIN WORDS
The item
  • Mill: not enough. A safeguard (Article 156) was kept because the majority was not ready.
  • Finnis: probably approves, because of the common good, life including procreation, and Article 156's promotion of marriage. Whether it is arbitrary depends on your premises.
  • Rawls, on balance, approves:
    • consultation was the background culture;
    • the consensus reached was not criminal, and it was not full equality;
    • Article 156 stops courts from going beyond that consensus;
    • sending a divisive question to Parliament, and not unelected judges, is a public reason.
  • Against Rawls's approval: Rawls's model of public reason is the Supreme Court (Liu, Week 9).
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL

The statement is that the 2022 package was a principled compromise. Assess it from the perspectives of Mill, Finnis and Rawls.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Take each theorist.

  • Mill. Repeal is right, because private consensual conduct harms no one. But Article 156 goes further than Mill needs, preserving inequality because the majority was not ready.
  • Finnis. Probably approves. The state promotes marriage, which serves the goods of life and sociability, without making private conduct a crime. Whether treating same-sex couples differently is arbitrary depends on whether you accept his premises about marriage.
  • Rawls, on balance, approves. The consultations were the background culture. The overlap reached was that it should not be a crime, and not full equality. Article 156 stops judges from going beyond that consensus. And letting Parliament, and not unelected judges, decide divisive questions is itself a public reason.
  • The counterpoint. For Rawls, the model of public reason is a supreme court. So keeping the question from the courts sits awkwardly with his own model.

16.5.2 Week 5b prompts†

▤ IN PLAIN WORDS
The item

Apply Rawls and Finnis to surrogacy, casino gambling, the online falsehoods law (POFMA) and euthanasia (Week 5b, slide 9). The pointers:

  • POFMA: 15.4 and 5.5;
  • casinos: 15.5, 6.4 and 5.7;
  • surrogacy: UKM (16.2);
  • euthanasia: Hart's point about clouded consent; and for Finnis, intending death chooses against life.

Four Bills in One Session

Port Meridian's Parliament considers four bills, on these four issues.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
IssueFinnisRawlsAlso use
